chapters.title: What the bank should buy first

segments.text:
\chapter*{What the bank should buy first}
\addcontentsline{toc}{chapter}{What the bank should buy first}

A bank considering a better deposit rate must pay for money it already holds
as well as money the offer attracts. A collections team must account for how
today's contact changes tomorrow's information. A discovery algorithm may
return several explanations of the same observations, with opposite implications
for a pricing decision. An apparently clean customer table may still conceal
misrecorded treatment or incorrectly linked accounts. These are four different
reasons why a persuasive numerical answer can fail to improve a decision.

An increase in one account's recorded balance can be a transfer from another
account at the same bank. The funding outcome must aggregate the intended
household and distinguish new external money from internal movement. Competitor
repricing can also change balances during the same period. A lender's threshold
comparison concerns the applicants affected at that margin, while a treasury
shock analysis must separate the external shock from the bank's own response.
These economic distinctions determine which comparison is useful before a
statistical model is chosen.

The proposal is to make a small class of defensible studies easier to conduct
and compare. The first investment should be a comparative integration using
established methods, a precise study description and a report that preserves
uncertainty. A capable economist using existing tools is the reference
alternative. The proposed service earns a place only if the completed study
is better or cheaper at equivalent quality. Broad replacement of the bank's
statistical estate is not justified by the evidence presented here.

That conclusion follows from the examples, rather than from an assumed
advantage of a common interface. In the constructed offer study, a population
balance effect is carried through sampling uncertainty into annual contribution.
The servicing calculation shows why a correctly fitted regression can still
answer the wrong policy question. The graph example gives identical observed
laws with different intervention values. The observation example shows how
additional measurement knowledge can reverse a financial conclusion. Each
case tells us what a service must preserve and what it must decline to infer.

The evidence has different roles. Established causal results justify inference
under stated assumptions. The project's exact derivations and generated studies
expose target errors, weak support and unresolved models. Public data reveal
realistic timing and measurement difficulties. Local interface executions
establish that particular requests retain their meaning through particular
clients. None of these substitutes for an independently reviewed study on
authentic bank information. Their combined value is to identify a useful and
bounded next experiment before undertaking that more expensive work.

chapters.title: How to read the argument

segments.text:
\chapter*{How to read the argument}
\addcontentsline{toc}{chapter}{How to read the argument}

The opening develops an annual deposit decision and four worked journeys.
Their cross-references distinguish exact supplied-law calculations, fitted
public and generated evidence, and unresolved identification. The longitudinal
and panel foundations are followed by the servicing and funding studies;
the observation foundations lead directly into the linkage bounds. The graph
journey points to the restricted temporal confidence construction and its
additional-information argument. The discovery foundations also develop the
completed search-repair comparison in Section~\ref{repair29:discovery}: a
computational stopping rule must not be mistaken for a scientifically
established relationship.

The evidence and method-choice part compares statistical targets before
selecting software. Chapter~\ref{scisyn:software} is the authoritative
software treatment: developed comparisons, the seventeen-area selection,
commercial alternatives and a target-weight illustration sit together.
Chapter~\ref{rewrite:assistance-tasks} brings formulation, measurement,
benchmark evidence and task selection into one assistance treatment.
The subsequent detailed parts supply source-specific derivations and
comparisons for readers examining a particular method or operating route.

The final investment part distinguishes the value of information from the
value of a common analytical product. Chapter~\ref{rewrite:investment-decision}
brings the annual benefit account, multi-year cost examples, institutional
variation and value-of-information calculation into one conditional decision.
Its recommendation is tested against expert composition and existing
commercial capability. PDF bookmarks expose the detailed sections; chapter
and section references carry the reader between the opening question and
the supporting result.

Throughout the opening case, assignment of an offer, delivery of that offer,
acceptance and the resulting price are separate quantities. Balances and
contribution have different symbols and a stated one-year horizon. Other
journeys introduce their own units and decision dates explicitly. A number
from a constructed example is not a bank forecast. A method documented in an
inspected source is not thereby an executed integration. These distinctions
are essential to interpreting the proposal.

Research coverage retains the cutoff of 7 October 2026. Editions, acquisition
dates, inspected anchors and omissions remain in the source records. The
comparative recommendation does not claim that every literature or language
cell is complete. The unanswered questions that could change the first
investment are stated where that choice is made.

chapters.title: What would make the bank better off?
From an offer effect to annual contribution

segments.text:
\chapter{From an offer effect to annual contribution}
\label{rewrite:deposit}

\section{Fix the intervention before estimating its value}
The preceding accounting calculation defines the question for the first
complete study. Let $Z_i$ denote assignment of the offer to eligible household
$i$, $R_i$ its delivery, $D_i$ acceptance, and $r_i$ the paid annual rate.
These variables describe successive events, not synonyms. Let $B_i(z)$ be
the household's average eligible deposit balance over the following year under
assignment $z$, and let $C_i(z)$ be contribution over that same year. For a
population fixed before assignment, the policy targets are
\[
 \tau_B=\E[B_i(1)-B_i(0)],\qquad
 \tau_C=\E[C_i(1)-C_i(0)].
\]
A statement about the effect among acceptors generally answers neither target.
Acceptance can depend on intentions that also determine balances. Dividing an
assignment effect by an acceptance rate additionally requires an instrumental
variable argument and changes the population to the relevant compliers; the
derivation and restrictions are in Chapter~\ref{r3:instruments}.

Here the constructed design makes a narrower intervention explicit. Every
assigned offer is delivered, and assignment automatically reprices the eligible
balance for one year. Thus $R=Z$ and the price rule is $r=r_0+Z\Delta r$;
acceptance does not gate the payment. A voluntary activation campaign would
need a different expense equation. Assume no interference across households,
no lost outcomes, and unchanged funding margin and direct cost. If the
expected no-offer balance is $B_0$, the incremental expected contribution is
\begin{equation}
 \tau_C=(m-\Delta r)\tau_B-\Delta r B_0-c.
 \label{rewrite:value-map}
\end{equation}
To obtain this expression, subtract $mB_i(0)$ from
$(m-\Delta r)B_i(1)-c$, then take expectations. It charges the rate
increase on the balance that would have remained without the intervention.
The familiar accounting shortcut is justified by this particular price rule.
It would overcharge a campaign that paid only newly acquired funds and would
misdescribe a campaign whose delivery itself failed.

\section{A deliberately transparent assignment design}
The example has two equally weighted customer strata, $X=0,1$. Assignment is
independent of potential balances within each stratum, with probabilities
$e_0=0.5$ and $e_1=0.1$. Both strata have mean no-offer balance
\pounds10,000. The stipulated balance effects are $b_0=0$ and $b_1=2,400$,
with independent normal household noise of standard deviation \pounds400.
These are generated customers. In particular, the independence and normal
law are supplied by construction and have not been inferred from bank data.

Consistency, assignment exchangeability within $X$, and positive assignment
probabilities give
\[
 \tau_B=\sum_{x=0}^1 w_x
   \{\E[B\mid Z=1,X=x]-\E[B\mid Z=0,X=x]\},
 \qquad w_0=w_1=\tfrac12.
\]
The two weights describe the target population, not the observed distribution
of offered customers. The population contrast is therefore \pounds1,200.
A saturated cell-mean estimator uses the same weights. It is a useful first
implementation because every contribution to the answer can be inspected;
with two strata there is no need to learn a complex outcome surface.

A constant residual projection gives a different average when effects vary.
Its weights are proportional to $w_xe_x(1-e_x)$, giving weight
$0.09/(0.25+0.09)$ to the high-benefit stratum and a population coefficient
of about \pounds635.29. That is a valid projection target. Calling it the
equal-stratum population effect would change the financial answer from
positive \pounds3 to about negative \pounds12.53. Chapter~\ref{scisyn:evidence}
retains the separately executed repeated experiments on this target error
and on sparse support. The current single sample demonstrates the full report;
it does not add another calibration experiment.

\section{Carry uncertainty through the expense equation}
Write $n_{xa}$, $\bar B_{xa}$ and $s_{xa}$ for the count, mean and sample
standard deviation of each observed cell. For a total error allowance
$\alpha=0.05$, construct four mean intervals
\[
 I_{xa}=\bar B_{xa}\ \pm\
 t_{n_{xa}-1,1-\alpha/8}\frac{s_{xa}}{\sqrt{n_{xa}}}.
\]
Each interval has conditional noncoverage $\alpha/4$ under its normal
independent sampling law. The union bound implies simultaneous coverage
at least $1-\alpha$, without assuming independence among the four interval
events. Conditioning on the observed assignment counts is legitimate here
because assignment is independent of the outcome errors within strata.
A cell with fewer than two observations returns unsupported rather than a
zero standard error.

If $h_{xa}$ denotes a cell half-width, interval arithmetic yields
\[
 \widehat\tau_B=\tfrac12(\bar B_{01}-\bar B_{00})+
                     \tfrac12(\bar B_{11}-\bar B_{10}),\qquad
 I_B=\widehat\tau_B\ \pm\ \tfrac12\sum_{x,a}h_{xa}.
\]
This construction permits different cell variances. It is conservative and
can become too wide to guide action. The earlier generated study shows why
a narrower pooled interval needs an additional common-variance assumption.
A shared service should expose that tradeoff, not silently choose the
narrower result. The present argument does not justify the Student intervals
under heavy tails, common calendar shocks or dependent households.

With $m=0.03$, $\Delta r=0.0025$, $B_0=10,000$ and $c=5$, equation
\eqref{rewrite:value-map} is increasing in $\tau_B$. Its endpoints
therefore transform directly: $I_C=0.0275 I_B-30$. Uncertainty in these
accounting inputs would need an additional joint set or sensitivity analysis.
Here they are fixed illustrative quantities. The deterministic seed and
8,000 generated observations give the following actual calculation.
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{lrr}
\toprule Quantity & Estimate & Interval\\\midrule
Annual average balance effect (\pounds) & \DepositEstimate & [\DepositLow, \DepositHigh]\\
Annual contribution per household (\pounds) & \DepositNet & [\DepositNetLow, \DepositNetHigh]\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
The four cells contain 2,039 unoffered and 1,961 offered households in the
first stratum, and 3,624 unoffered and 376 offered households in the second.
The positive contribution interval supports the action under this declared
model and expense rule. Its margin is small: an additional certain expense
above the lower endpoint removes that interval-based assurance. The result
is unsuitable as a bank forecast; its value is to make the target, support,
uncertainty and accounting inseparable in the completed report.

\section{What the implemented example actually returns}
The local callable estimator takes the three-column generated data, target
weights, four accounting inputs and $\alpha$. It returns cell counts and
uncertainty, the balance target, its interval, contribution and its interval,
and a conditional decision. The same calculation is available at the command
line from the repository root:
\begin{lstlisting}
python3 tools/run_rewrite_examples_20261029.py --report-only
\end{lstlisting}
The callable result and a separate command-line process agree exactly in
the retained execution. The generated data, code, seed and numerical results
are supplied with the study. This is a specific estimator implemented for
the example; it is not evidence that an external causal package was qualified.

The earlier MCP walkthrough establishes graph syntax, conditional
adjustment, information-date checks and refusal of a dependent sampling law.
The public study in Chapter~\ref{gap29:public} additionally sends actual
fitted estimates and covariance summaries through library, CLI and MCP.
It preserves the resulting interval and conditional or contradicted
assignment status. Neither path exposes the deposit raw-data estimator
as an MCP operation.
Chapter~\ref{scisyn:investment} gives the observed requests and the initial
timeout as well as the successful retry. These separate operations do not establish a raw-data-to-financial-report
MCP endpoint.
A future adapter must carry the complete report, including assumptions and
unsupported outcomes, before that claim becomes available.

\section{From the household offer to broader funding evidence}
Two extensions show what this transparent report leaves to be learned.
Chapter~\ref{gap29:public} estimates an assignment contrast from the retained
public experiment, compares adjusted and unadjusted estimators, examines
influence, and subtracts an explicit cost. Its earnings units and population
are different from the deposit account: the exercise tests an inferential
and reporting route, not transport of an earnings effect into bank balances.
Chapter~\ref{gap29:funding} follows institutions rather than households and
asks whether fixed effects can repair a misassigned outcome. They cannot
recover the institution's identity merely by absorbing a persistent level.
The structural funding and calendar arguments explain the additional shock
and dependence assumptions needed for that journey.

For the offer study, the next source of information is assignment support and
correct household aggregation; for the institutional panel it is a coherent
exposure and outcome history. A bank cannot substitute a successful estimate
in one of these populations for the missing design evidence in the other.
The shared report can preserve both questions without pretending they have
the same estimator or sampling law.

chapters.title: Servicing decisions change the next decision's information

segments.text:
\chapter{Servicing decisions change the next decision's information}
\label{rewrite:servicing}

A servicing policy chooses whether to contact a borrower at two dates. Let
$A_0,A_1$ be contact decisions, $L_0$ baseline borrower state and $L_1$ the
state observed between contacts. For this constructed example, $Y$ is
gross contribution in pounds over the two-period horizon, excluding contact
cost. The policy comparison is sustained contact versus no contact, not
the regression coefficient of one contact conditional on every later event.

The exact law developed in Chapter~\ref{r3:longitudinal} is
\begin{align*}
 P(L_0=1)&=0.5,\\
 P(A_0=1\mid L_0)&=0.2+0.6L_0,\\
 P(L_1=1\mid L_0,A_0)&=0.1+0.5L_0+0.2A_0,\\
 P(A_1=1\mid H_1)&=0.15+0.5L_1+0.1A_0,\\
 Y&=20+3A_0+4A_1+10L_1+6L_0.
\end{align*}
Here $H_1=(L_0,A_0,L_1)$ is the history available for the second action.
Independent innovations implement these kernels. The actions have support
for every possible history, and the example has no hidden confounding.
Consequently, replacing both action kernels with a specified policy and
retaining the state-transition law identifies its mean. This is the
g-formula developed from sequential exchangeability in the retained chapter
and its primary treatment. \citep[Chapter 21]{hernan2020}

\section{Average the state produced by each policy}
For a constant policy $a$, the mean intermediate state is
$\E[L_1(a)]=0.1+0.5(0.5)+0.2a=0.35+0.2a$. Hence
\[
 \psi(a)=20+7a+10(0.35+0.2a)+6(0.5)=26.5+9a.
\]
The gross means are \pounds26.50 and \pounds35.50. At a stipulated
\pounds2 per contact, the net contrast is $9-2(2)=\pounds5$.
The reported exact enumeration independently averages the finite state law
and reweights the observed action paths; both recover the same two means.
There is no finite-sample confidence claim in this calculation.

A regression of $Y$ on all four variables correctly recovers action
coefficients 3 and 4. Their sum misses the extra $10(0.2)=2$ contributed
through the change in $L_1$. Removing $L_1$ from the second-stage regression
does not repair the analysis: the historical second action depends on it.
The calculation therefore distinguishes a fitted conditional equation from
the policy mean obtained by averaging that equation over policy-specific
histories. The distinction changes net value from an erroneous \pounds3
to \pounds5 even in this noise-free conditional outcome model.

\section{What changes when the law must be learned}
In an observed study, the kernels and outcome regressions are estimated.
G-computation substitutes fitted transition and outcome laws and averages
under the target policy. Reweighting instead uses ratios of target to
historical action probabilities. Doubly robust constructions combine these
ideas; their longitudinal scores, nuisance restrictions and remainders are
derived in Chapter~\ref{r3:longitudinal}, rather than assumed from their
name. None removes the requirement that the historical records include
the information responsible for action selection.

For sustained contact, a useful diagnostic is the count and weight
distribution of complete histories supporting that policy. Many borrower
rows do not guarantee enough such histories. A policy learned by maximizing
the same estimated value must be evaluated with the additional selection
uncertainty or an honest evaluation sample. An outcome law conditional on
a hidden state introduces another identification problem; a well-fitting
state-space model does not establish that its intervention meaning is correct.

The product implication is to begin with a fixed, short-horizon policy and
observable histories, retaining a direct g-computation and a weighting
comparison. If support is inadequate or an important action determinant is
unrecorded, changing the collection or trial design is more informative than
adding a flexible learner. The positive \pounds5 example explains the
accounting; it does not establish a real contact policy's benefit.

\section{Estimated policies, missing rewards and decision uncertainty}
Chapters~\ref{gap29:servicing} and \ref{gap29:policy-uncertainty} carry the
policy question into fitted data. They use a separate three-decision economy,
with continuous states and rewards already net of the stipulated action cost.
Those reward units are not the pounds in this two-contact example. Whole
customers, rather than isolated rows, supply the sampling units. A separate
training sample chooses the policy; evaluation and resampling hold that
selected policy fixed.

The fitted comparison is informative precisely because it can fail.
Under its maintained state and observation model, improvement coverage is
94\% with an average interval width of 0.711 reward units. Future-dependent
dropout reduces coverage to 6\%; omitting a state predictor reduces it to
61\%. These observed fractions have Monte Carlo uncertainty, reported in
the study. They demonstrate that resampling an estimated model does not
repair an invalid observation assumption.

The financial interpretation follows the reward definition. Where costs are
already subtracted, subtracting contact cost again would double-count it.
Where a bank's reward law and initial distribution must also be estimated,
the supplied-law components of the generated comparison cannot be treated
as known. Outcome follow-up, action support and measured decision history
therefore determine whether its narrower uncertainty can be useful.

chapters.title: A learned graph can leave the pricing decision unresolved

segments.text:
\chapter{A learned graph can leave the pricing decision unresolved}
\label{rewrite:discovery}

Suppose $X$ measures a proposed rate change in percentage points, $M$ an
intermediate market quantity and $Y$ gross funding contribution in thousands
of pounds. The units and coefficients in this section are authored for the
example. Consider the centered Gaussian observational covariance
\[
 \Sigma=\begin{pmatrix}
 1&0.6&0.48\\0.6&1.36&1.088\\0.48&1.088&1.8704
 \end{pmatrix}.
\]
The law satisfies $X\perp Y\mid M$. A chain $X\to M\to Y$, a
fork $X\leftarrow M\to Y$, and a reverse chain $X\leftarrow M\leftarrow Y$
can all reproduce it using independent Gaussian errors.

For the first chain, take $M=0.6X+\varepsilon_M$ and
$Y=0.8M+\varepsilon_Y$, with variances $\Var(X)=1$,
$\Var(\varepsilon_M)=1$ and $\Var(\varepsilon_Y)=1$. The intervention
slope of $Y$ on $X$ is $0.6(0.8)=0.48$. For the fork, take
$\Var(M)=1.36$, $X=(0.6/1.36)M+\eta_X$, and $Y=0.8M+\eta_Y$,
with residual variances $1-0.6^2/1.36$ and $1$. The resulting covariance
is the same, but intervening on $X$ has zero effect on $Y$. The reverse
chain uses the corresponding conditional regression coefficients and also
has zero effect. The numerical check reconstructs all three covariance
matrices and verifies positive residual variances.

\section{Keep the causal ambiguity in the financial report}
Within this specified three-model family, the slope set is $\{0,0.48\}$.
At a quarter-point intervention and a stipulated \pounds60 action cost,
net value is
\[
 1000(0.25)\{0,0.48\}-60=\{-60,60\}
 \quad\hbox{pounds}.
\]
There is no sign-robust recommendation across the retained explanations.
Returning the slope from the forward chain alone would hide the unresolved
orientation that determines the action. A probability for each graph would
require additional justified modelling; equal probabilities are not supplied
by observational equivalence. Nor should the discrete set be called a
confidence interval. It represents identification ambiguity even if the
covariance is known exactly.

The example's finite graph family and linear Gaussian law are restrictions.
They do not describe every model compatible with arbitrary banking records.
When the covariance and graph class are estimated, uncertainty must cover
both the observed law and the retained models before mapping them to effects.
An edge bootstrap conditional on one chosen graph does not supply that
combined guarantee. The foundations and detailed temporal-discovery
comparisons retain the arguments for unresolved orientations, latent causes
and class-to-effect propagation.

For a bank, useful additional information could be a defensible ordering
that excludes two orientations, a valid instrument, or an intervention on
$X$. The cost of obtaining that information should be compared with the
consequence of a mistaken action. More precise estimation of this same
covariance cannot distinguish these three laws. The proposed service should
therefore preserve a class or explicit refusal and ask what would narrow it,
instead of completing arrows solely to make a diagram look decisive.

\section{From a known covariance to estimated effect sets}
Chapter~\ref{exec13:temporal-region} supplies the next inferential step under
a restricted stationary Gaussian time-series model. It constructs a region
jointly over the observed covariance, a continuous unknown common lag and a
declared family of causal models, then maps that region to effects. The
coverage argument keeps the true model and observed-law uncertainty together;
it does not condition on an orientation chosen for convenience. The chapter
also shows what a direct intervention can add.

This is a developed restricted construction, not an executed general
bank-discovery pipeline. The maintained graph family, scalar lag and
innovation law must be defensible before applying it. An unrestricted latent
model may leave the whole line admissible. In the opening pricing example,
the narrower set already contains opposite net values, so a more elaborate
estimator is useful only if its information or restrictions can resolve a
consequential ambiguity. A labelled whole-line result can be the correct
answer to a well-defined question. A separate computational issue arises
when a search has not tested the conditioning sets needed to remove a link.
Section~\ref{repair29:discovery} compares a repair on exact-oracle cases and
shows why an unfinished search needs an explicit status. Search completeness,
statistical uncertainty and identification ambiguity are different limitations.

chapters.title: Correcting records can change the action

segments.text:
\chapter{Correcting records can change the action}
\label{rewrite:observation}

A treatment record is a measurement of an event. Let $A$ be true randomized
receipt, $W$ recorded receipt and $Y$ gross contribution in pounds at a
fixed horizon. In this separate finite example, $P(A=0)=P(A=1)=1/2$
and $\E[Y\mid A=0]=100$, $\E[Y\mid A=1]=140$. Receipt is
randomized by construction; correcting its record would not establish
randomization in an observational campaign.

Suppose misclassification is nondifferential with a known matrix
\[
 K=\begin{pmatrix}0.9&0.2\\0.1&0.8\end{pmatrix},
 \qquad K_{wa}=P(W=w\mid A=a,Y).
\]
Writing $p_a=P(A=a)$ and $q_a=\E[Y\mathbf1(A=a)]$, the recorded
shares and outcome moments obey
\[
 p_W=Kp_A=(0.55,0.45)' ,\qquad q_W=Kq_A=(59,61)' .
\]
Thus the recorded contrast is $61/0.45-59/0.55=28.2828\ldots$.
The matrix has determinant $0.7$, so its inverse recovers
$p_A=(0.5,0.5)'$ and $q_A=(50,70)'$, giving the true contrast
$70/0.5-50/0.5=40$. This is the moment version of the joint-law
argument in Chapter~\ref{r3:observation}. It is checked by direct
multiplication and solution, with no estimated audit law.

\section{The value of knowing the observation law}
At a stipulated action cost of \pounds35, the recorded comparison gives
net value about $-\pounds6.72$, whereas the corrected contrast gives
\pounds5. That reversal is conditional on the known error law. If an
identity matrix and the displayed matrix both remain admissible, the same
recorded shares and moments are compatible with different latent effects
and opposite recommendations. Reporting only the corrected number would
replace measurement uncertainty with a convenient assumption.

In a real validation sample, estimating $K$ would add uncertainty. The audit
must identify true receipt and represent the relevant customers and periods;
a classifier's own label is not an external truth measurement. Near-singular
matrices amplify error, and a singular matrix destroys recoverable information.
The retained chapter gives the symmetric-error example where receipt becomes
uninformative. More rows with the same deficient measurement law do not
restore its rank.

Entity linkage poses a related but distinct problem. A household may hold
several accounts, and a mistaken join can change both its treatment and its
outcome. Correctness counts alone may fail to identify the needed contrast;
the detailed linkage studies and their adverse results remain in this book.
The next useful observation is a correctly sampled, truthful linked history
when that is what the estimand requires, not merely a higher aggregate match
score. Likewise, event time, availability time and revision time must remain
separate when constructing a prospective decision view.

The four journeys now imply a common requirement for the proposed service.
It must keep the economic target and the information that identifies it
attached to the numerical result. Their statistical procedures remain
different: stratified assignment contrasts, sequential policy averaging,
model-set propagation and observation-law inversion. The next chapters
develop those differences before the software and investment synthesis chooses
which ones are ready for a bounded comparison.

\section{A fitted linkage analysis needs an external information budget}
Chapter~\ref{gap29:observation} studies a different observation problem:
matching randomized participants to outcomes when identifiers are corrupted.
It compares exact and fuzzy rules, keeps unmatched customers in the target,
and derives a contribution bound when at most a supplied number of candidate
lists omit the true match. Sampling uncertainty is then added under explicit
support and assignment assumptions. This is not an estimate of the receipt
matrix used above; the two studies concern different measurement mechanisms.

At 30\% outcome-dependent corruption, the robust population interval averages
119.1 outcome units in width, compared with about 4.1 for the fuzzy analysis.
The extra width prices justified ignorance. The corruption budget and outcome
support are external premises, not quantities learned from matching confidence.
A monetary decision first maps those outcome units and bounds into its own
expense equation. When the admissible set straddles that decision threshold,
an independently resolved audit sample can be more valuable than a forced
match. The detailed history and audit studies retain the further complications
of dependent records and uncertain audit truth.

chapters.title: Constructing a causal model and identifying its questions

segments.text:
\chapter{Constructing a causal model and identifying its questions}
\label{r3:graphs}
\section{Begin with the intervention, unit and observation process}
The annual repricing example distinguished assignment from receipt. This
chapter uses a separate ninety-day activation example to show what changes
when customers choose whether to take up an invitation. Its outcome and
action symbols are local to that example.

Consider a household eligible for a preferential deposit product. Let $Z$
denote the bank's invitation, $A$ actual activation, $M$ a subsequent change
in balances and $Y$ the ninety-day funding contribution. An intervention on
$Z$ is operationally different from forcing $A=1$. An increase in the
database field recording $A$ is different again. The bank can randomize an
invitation; it cannot generally compel activation or create liquidity merely
by changing a recorded balance. A causal question must identify the mechanism
that the proposed decision actually changes.

The unit is a household rather than an account when money can move between
accounts owned by the same people. The outcome includes an agreed transfer
price, interest paid and servicing cost, with movements within the household
consolidated. This is part of defining $Y$, rather than a correction performed
after estimating an account-level effect. For a fixed population and horizon,
write $Y(a)$ for the outcome under a specified activation intervention, and
$Y^{Z=z}$ for the outcome under invitation assignment $z$. Two initial targets
are
\begin{equation}
 \theta_A=\E\{Y(1)-Y(0)\},\qquad
 \theta_Z=\E\{Y^{Z=1}-Y^{Z=0}\}.
 \label{r3:targets}
\end{equation}
They differ even in an ideal randomized invitation experiment. An invitation
may have costs or affect trust without activation. Such effects belong to
$\theta_Z$ and threaten an exclusion restriction used to infer $\theta_A$.

Consistency means that a household exposed to the specified action has its
corresponding potential outcome. It requires clarity about price, duration,
channel, eligibility, execution and outcome measurement. It is not ensured
by giving all those interventions the same binary code. Interference would
require $Y_i(\mathbf a)$, or a justified exposure mapping, instead of $Y_i(a_i)$.
The present single-period derivations assume a population of noninterfering
units and a fixed version of each action. Cluster or network designs must
change those assumptions explicitly \citep[Chapters 1--3]{hernan2020}.

For clarity most graph calculations below use discrete variables and sums.
Continuous versions use conditional densities or probability kernels, with
absolute continuity and integrability stated at the estimation stage. This
distinction matters: an intervention at one exact continuous treatment value
can be identifiable as a conditional-law functional without admitting the
same regular root-$n$ estimator as a binary-treatment average effect.

\section{Structural equations define what an intervention changes}
\begin{definition}[Acyclic structural model]
An acyclic structural causal model $\mathcal M$ consists of endogenous
variables $V=(V_1,\ldots,V_d)$, exogenous variables $U$, a joint law $P_U$,
and assignments
\[
 V_j:=f_j(V_{\pa(j)},U_j),\qquad j=1,\ldots,d,
\]
whose endogenous parent graph is a DAG. A hard intervention $\doop(A=a)$
replaces the assignment for $A$ by the constant $a$ and retains the remaining
assignments and exogenous law.
\end{definition}
The colon distinguishes an assignment from an algebraic identity that may
be inverted freely. A regression residual is constructed to be orthogonal
to fitted regressors; a structural disturbance represents omitted causes
and need not be orthogonal to the action. Autonomous mechanisms are what
make intervention replacement meaningful \citep[Sections 3.1--3.2]{pearl2009}.

If all $U_j$ are mutually independent, the model is Markovian relative to
its displayed endogenous DAG. Hidden common causes can instead be displayed
as latent parents, producing a larger DAG, or left as dependence in $P_U$.
One must not draw an observed DAG and silently assume independent disturbances
after omitting a common cause. Both the functions and the disturbance law
are components of the causal model.

Potential outcomes can be generated by recursively evaluating the modified
assignments at the same exogenous realization: $Y(a)=f_Y(\ldots;a,U)$.
This constructs consistency and expresses $P\{Y(a)\}$ as the distribution
of $Y$ in the intervened model. Conversely, a potential-outcome analysis
need not posit mutually independent disturbances for every structural
equation. In particular, assumptions sufficient to identify each
single-world intervention distribution need not determine joint quantities
involving incompatible interventions.

The SWIG construction makes this distinction explicit. Split an action node
into its random part $A$, retaining incoming arrows, and a fixed part $a$,
retaining outgoing arrows. Relabel its descendants as counterfactual
variables. For $X\to A$, $X\to Y$, $A\to Y$ this yields a graph for
$(X,A,Y(a))$ in which $A\perp Y(a)\mid X$ can be read by separation.
It does not simultaneously supply a graph for the unobserved pair
$(Y(0),Y(1))$. The SWIG framework covers the less restrictive FFRCISTG
model as well as the independent-error structural submodel
\citep[Section 2, node splitting and modularity]{swig2013}. Consequently,
identifying a mean effect does not identify individual gains or their
variance: $\Var\{Y(1)-Y(0)\}$ additionally involves the unobserved
$\Cov\{Y(1),Y(0)\}$.

\section{A diagram is constructed from mechanisms}
\label{r3:graph-construction}
Before drawing an arrow, define the decision clock. Here $X$ is measured
before invitation, $Z$ is assigned next, $A$ records subsequent activation,
$M$ is later behavior, and $Y$ closes the horizon. Let $U$ be unrecorded
liquidity need and $V$ a servicing difficulty that also affects outcomes.
Let $C$ indicate whether the episode has a complete outcome record. A
candidate mechanism graph is shown in Figure~\ref{r3:bank-graph}. It is
an assumption to be challenged with process owners and data provenance.

Each omitted arrow makes a substantive claim. Absence of $Z\to Y$ and
$Z\to M$ says that the invitation affects the economic outcome only through
activation. Absence of causes shared by $Z$ and $(U,X,V)$ represents genuine
random assignment in this example. Absence of $U\to M$ says that liquidity
need affects later balances only through activation or through mechanisms
already represented by $X$; this might be implausible and should be revised.
A discovered small regression coefficient cannot establish any of these
omissions. Arrows allow a mechanism; their presence does not prescribe its
sign, magnitude, linearity or monotonicity.

A useful construction procedure has five concrete steps.
\begin{enumerate}
 \item Define the actor, feasible action, unit, economic endpoint and clock.
       Separate assigned, received, recorded and measured quantities.
 \item List causes of the action and of the endpoint, including private
       decisions, calendar conditions, common counterparties and selection.
 \item Order mechanisms at the finest relevant time resolution. Replace
       apparent contemporaneous feedback by a justified within-period order
       or an explicitly cyclic/dynamic model.
 \item Mark what is observed and when it becomes available; draw observation
       and inclusion mechanisms instead of treating missingness as a blank cell.
 \item Examine every exclusion needed by the intended identification route.
       Record its business justification, plausible violations and what an
       experiment or additional measurement could resolve.
\end{enumerate}
This procedure separates a causal diagram from data lineage. A lineage edge
from transactions to an aggregated balance describes a calculation. It does
not mean that intervening on the stored aggregate changes the underlying
transactions. Deterministic accounting identities also create conditional
dependencies that require care in discovery algorithms relying on generic
faithfulness assumptions.

\section{Paths, colliders, latent variables and learned graphs}
\label{r3:separation}
A path ignores the direction of its successive edges. An internal node is
a collider when both adjacent edges have arrowheads into it. A DAG path is
active conditional on $S$ when every noncollider is outside $S$ and every
collider has itself or a descendant in $S$. Two sets are d-separated when
no such path connects them. In a distribution Markov to the DAG,
d-separation implies conditional independence
\citep[Definition 1]{pearl2009}. Faithfulness is the additional converse
assumption used by many discovery procedures; it is not needed to deduce
independences from a stipulated causal graph.

In the bank graph, conditioning on $X$ blocks $A\leftarrow X\to Y$ but
leaves $A\leftarrow U\to Y$ open. Adding $M$ can block a causal path and
therefore change the target. Conditioning on $A$ opens the collider
$Z\to A\leftarrow U\to Y$: invitation and latent need need not remain
independent among activators. This is why analyzing compliance strata defined
by observed receipt is not the same as randomizing receipt. Conditioning on
$C=1$ can also open $A\to C\leftarrow V\to Y$.

For a numerical collider example, let $A,V$ be independent fair binary
variables, $Y=V$, and let $C=1$ exactly when $A=V$. Action has zero causal
effect on $Y$. Among records with $C=1$, however, $Y=A$, so the observed
contrast is one. Positive marginal action probabilities and perfect outcome
prediction within the selected sample do not repair selection bias.

Marginalizing latent nodes can yield an acyclic directed mixed graph (ADMG).
In the simple common-cause motif, $A\leftarrow U\to Y$ becomes
$A\leftrightarrow Y$; a directed latent path can induce a directed observed
edge. Directed and bidirected edges can coexist. The corresponding separation
rule, m-separation, uses arrowheads to define colliders in the same way.
A bidirected edge records a permitted hidden common-cause route; it is not
an instruction to regress in two directions. With selection and more general
latent structures, maximal ancestral graphs and PAGs require their own
semantics; an ADMG is not interchangeable with those objects. The
latent-time-series setting of \citet[Section 2]{gerhardus2020}, for example,
explicitly excludes selection
and targets a time-window-dependent ancestral equivalence object.

A DAG supplied by an analyst, a CPDAG representing a DAG Markov-equivalence
class, and a PAG representing latent/selection-compatible ancestral graphs
are different inputs. For DAGs the same skeleton and unshielded colliders
give the same implied conditional independences
\citep[Definition 6.24 and Lemma 6.25]{peters2017}. Two variables alone do
not observationally distinguish $A\to Y$ from $Y\to A$. Known timing may
exclude the latter but still leave hidden confounding. A discovery score
cannot turn the remaining graph ambiguity into a unique causal effect by
choosing whichever orientation permits an estimator to run.

\section{Identification is a property of a model class}
\label{r3:identification}
Let $\mathfrak M$ be the class of causal models permitted by the assumptions,
$P_{\mathcal M}$ their observed-data law, and $\theta(\mathcal M)$ the
requested effect. Identification means
\begin{equation}
 P_{\mathcal M_1}=P_{\mathcal M_2}
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
 \theta(\mathcal M_1)=\theta(\mathcal M_2)
 \quad\text{for every }\mathcal M_1,\mathcal M_2\in\mathfrak M.
 \label{r3:id-definition}
\end{equation}
It permits writing $\theta=\Theta(P)$ for a statistical functional
\citep[Definition 2]{pearl2009}. Identification does not assert that the
functional is well conditioned, estimable at root-$n$ rate, or supported
with useful precision by the observed sample. Conversely, failure to find
an adjustment set does not prove nonidentification: another transformation
may identify the target.

\begin{proposition}[Truncated factorization for a fully observed Markovian DAG]
Assume independent structural disturbances, acyclicity and autonomous
assignments. For a hard intervention on a node set $I$, the density of the
remaining variables is
\begin{equation}
 p^a(v_{-I})=\prod_{j\notin I}p(v_j\mid v_{\pa(j)})\big|_{v_I=a}.
 \label{r3:truncated}
\end{equation}
Observed conditional kernels identify the right-hand side wherever the
required parent configurations have support.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Order nodes topologically. Independent disturbances imply that each
assignment generates a kernel conditional on its parents, giving the
observational product $\prod_j p(v_j\mid v_{\pa(j)})$. Replacing an
assignment by a constant removes its kernel and substitutes its value in
the arguments of each child kernel. The other kernels remain invariant
by autonomy. Iterating in the same order gives Equation~\eqref{r3:truncated}.
Without support, a conditional kernel is not determined by observational
data at the parent configurations that the intervention creates.
\end{proof}
This is the causal Markov and truncated-factorization argument in
\citet[Theorem 1 and Corollary 1]{pearl2009}. For a graph with hidden $U$,
the full product may still be written and integrated over $U$, but its
factors involving $U$ are not automatically observable. Replacing them by
conditionals of observed variables alone is an additional identification
claim, not a consequence of the chain rule.

\subsection{Adjustment and its potential-outcome proof}
Suppose a pretreatment set $X$ blocks all paths entering $A$ through an
incoming arrow and contains no descendants of $A$. The back-door criterion
is a sufficient graphical route to exchangeability in the stated model;
it is not the most general adjustment criterion
\citep[Definition 3]{pearl2009}. In potential-outcome notation the needed
conditions for each action $a$ are consistency, $Y(a)\perp A\mid X$, and
$P(A=a\mid X=x)>0$ for almost every target $x$. Then
\begin{align}
 \E\{Y(a)\}
 &=\sum_x\E\{Y(a)\mid X=x\}p(x)\nonumber\\
 &=\sum_x\E\{Y(a)\mid A=a,X=x\}p(x)\nonumber\\
 &=\sum_x\E[Y\mid A=a,X=x]p(x).
 \label{r3:adjustment}
\end{align}
The first step averages over the target population; the second uses
exchangeability; the third uses consistency, with positivity making the
conditional mean observable. The graph is one justification for those
equalities, not an alternative to them. For the bank graph containing
$A\leftarrow U\to Y$, $X$ alone does not justify the second step.

If instead all common causes are measured in $X$ and the mediator has the
law $p(m\mid a,x)$, the total-effect mean is
\[
 \sum_{x,m}\E[Y\mid a,m,x]p(m\mid a,x)p(x).
\]
The mediator distribution must change with $a$. Regressing on $M$ and
reading off an action coefficient while holding $M$ fixed generally
answers a different question. The difference is visible before choosing
a regression family.

\subsection{Front-door identification when adjustment fails}
Consider the distinct graph $A\to M\to Y$ with a hidden common cause of
$A$ and $Y$, no direct $A\to Y$, no confounding of $A\to M$, and all
back-door paths from $M$ to $Y$ blocked by $A$. Assume the required
$p(a,m)$ support. Under these restrictions,
\begin{equation}
 p(y\mid\doop(a))
 =\sum_m p(m\mid a)\sum_{a'}p(y\mid m,a')p(a').
 \label{r3:frontdoor}
\end{equation}
To see the steps, $A\to M$ is unconfounded, so its interventional law is
$p(m\mid a)$. Setting $M=m$ cuts the incoming $A\to M$ edge; adjustment
by $A$ identifies $p(y\mid\doop(m))$ as the inner sum. In this graph
intervening on $A$ changes $Y$ only by changing $M$; the response kernel
under an intervention on $M$ is invariant to that $A$ intervention.
Composing these two intervention kernels gives the displayed expression.
It is not ordinary adjustment for a post-treatment covariate
\citep[Section 6.7, Example 6.46]{peters2017}.

For deposits, measured balance change is rarely a defensible front-door
mediator: liquidity need may directly affect it and funding contribution
may have activation-related cost channels outside balances. The formula
is useful because it states which measurements and exclusions would be
needed. It must not motivate deleting inconvenient arrows from
Figure~\ref{r3:bank-graph}.

Do-calculus generalizes these transformations by conditions for deleting
observations, exchanging actions and observations, and deleting actions
in modified graphs. For example,
\[
 p(y\mid\doop(a),z,x)=p(y\mid\doop(a),x)
 \quad\text{if }Y\perp_G Z\mid A,X\text{ in }G_{\bar A},
\]
where $G_{\bar A}$ removes edges entering $A$ and the separation statement
is evaluated in that modified graph. The action/observation exchange rule
requires a different modification, removing outgoing edges of the variable
being exchanged. A compiler must retain the actual rule and separation
witness for each step. The next subsection explains how an identification
algorithm organizes such operations and distinguishes a failed search
from a proof of nonidentification.

\subsection{District decomposition and an obstruction certificate}
\label{r3:id-algorithm}
In a semi-Markovian ADMG a district is a maximal set joined by bidirected
paths. A singleton without a bidirected neighbor is also a district.
For $S\subseteq V$, define the interventional kernel
$Q[S]=p(s\mid\doop(v\setminus s))$. It is a function of $s$ and the
fixed outside values; in general it is not the ordinary conditional
$p(s\mid v\setminus s)$. Shared hidden disturbances couple variables
within a district. Integrating over distinct independent latent groups
factorizes an intervention kernel over districts in its remaining graph.

The ID algorithm exploits this decomposition recursively. With no
intervention it marginalizes the supplied law. It first restricts to
ancestors of the requested outcome, summing irrelevant variables. It
can then add interventions on remaining nonancestors in the graph with
the original intervention nodes removed, because they cannot change the
target in that graph. When the remaining graph has several districts,
it identifies their kernels separately, multiplies them, and marginalizes
nonoutcome variables. When one district remains, it either extracts
topologically ordered conditional factors for a district already
available in the current kernel, recurses inside a larger containing
district, or returns a failure witness. These steps are made precise in
\citet[Section 4, Figure 2]{id2006}; they apply to its specified
semi-Markovian model class.

The obstruction is a \emph{hedge}. An $R$-rooted C-forest is a
bidirected-connected subgraph whose observed nodes have at most one
directed child, with childless root set $R$. Two such forests
$F'\subset F$ form a hedge for the query when $F$ meets the intervention
set, $F'$ does not, and their common roots are ancestors of the outcome
in the intervened graph. The source proves that such a pair witnesses
nonidentification and establishes completeness of ID for the specified
queries. These are inherited theorems; the following small case makes
their practical meaning concrete.

For the bow graph $A\to Y$, $A\leftrightarrow Y$, take
$F=\{A,Y\}$ and $F'=\{Y\}$, with common root $Y$. The larger
forest contains $A$ and the smaller does not. Thus failure to identify
$p(y\mid\doop(a))$ is certified, rather than merely caused by a
search routine finding no adjustment set. Section~\ref{r3:nonidentification}
constructs two positive observed-law examples witnessing that same
failure. The front-door graph avoids this obstruction for the total
effect through an identifiable composition of district kernels.

Conditional interventional queries require another distinction. Dividing
an identified $p(y,z\mid\doop(a))$ by its $z$ margin works when that
joint law is identified and the denominator is positive, but failure
to identify the joint law need not settle the conditional query.
The IDC algorithm first exchanges eligible conditioning variables for
interventions using do-calculus, then invokes ID and normalizes the
remaining joint kernel \citep[Section 5, Figure 3]{id2006}.
Its input is a conditional interventional distribution, not a generic
cross-world mediation or personalized counterfactual request.

\subsection{A recursive call trace, including a conditional rescue}
\label{r3:id-trace}
The front-door functional can now be reconstructed as an execution of
ID, rather than supplied as a memorized template. Use the topological
order $(A,M,Y)$ in the three-node front-door graph above. The original
districts are $\{A,Y\}$ and $\{M\}$. Write $\mathrm{ID}(B,I;K,G)$
for a call identifying the law of $B$ after setting $I$, from the supplied
kernel $K$ and graph $G$. The line numbers below refer to
\citet[Figure 2]{id2006}.
\begin{enumerate}
 \item In $\mathrm{ID}(Y,A;p,G)$, all nodes are ancestors of $Y$.
 Removing $A$ leaves districts $\{M\}$ and $\{Y\}$. Line 4 returns
 $\sum_m\mathrm{ID}(M,\{A,Y\};p,G)
             \mathrm{ID}(Y,\{A,M\};p,G)$.
 \item For the first factor, ancestor reduction (line 2) restricts the
 graph to $\{A,M\}$ and the input to $p(a,m)$. The intervention set
 becomes $\{A\}$. In this graph $\{M\}$ is an original district;
 line 6 extracts $p(m\mid a)$.
 \item For the second factor, the remaining singleton $\{Y\}$ is
 contained in the larger original district $\{A,Y\}$. Line 7 recurses
 inside that district with intervention $A$ and kernel
 \[
    q(a,y\mid m)=p(a)p(y\mid a,m).
 \]
 This is a normalized kernel with $m$ fixed. It is generally different
 from $p(a,y\mid m)$ because $p(a\mid m)\ne p(a)$.
 \item The induced graph on $\{A,Y\}$ has a bidirected edge and no
 directed edge. Its ancestors of $Y$ are just $\{Y\}$. Line 2
 therefore marginalizes $a$, leaving
 $q_Y(y\mid m)=\sum_{a'}p(a')p(y\mid a',m)$ and an empty
 intervention set. Line 1 returns that kernel.
 \item Multiplication and the final sum over $m$ recover
 Equation~\eqref{r3:frontdoor}. The dummy $a'$ in the second kernel
 is distinct from the intervention value $a$ in the first.
\end{enumerate}
For a fully specified finite check, let $U$ be fair binary and use
independent innovations with probabilities
\[
 P(A=1\mid U)=.2+.6U,\quad P(M=1\mid A)=.1+.7A,\quad
 P(Y=1\mid M,U)=.1+.5M+.2U.
\]
All observed cells are positive. Direct intervention gives
$\E[Y(a)]=.25+.35a$, while the observed regression gives
$\E[Y\mid A=a]=.19+.47a$. Enumerating the latent law and evaluating
the ID expression agree on the effect $.35$; direct adjustment for no
covariates produces $.47$. The numerical check validates this supplied
example and its algebra, not an implementation of general ID.

A second graph shows why IDC has a separate role. Let
$A\to M\to Y$ and $A\leftrightarrow M$, with no other edges.
The joint $p(m,y\mid\doop(a))$ is not identifiable: marginalizing
an identified joint would identify $p(m\mid\doop(a))$, contradicted
by the bow-graph hedge on $\{A,M\}$. Yet the conditional is identified.
In $G_{\bar A,\underline M}$, where incoming edges to $A$ and outgoing
edges from $M$ are removed, $Y$ is separated from $M$ given $A$.
IDC line 1 exchanges the observation of $M$ for an action:
\[
 p(y\mid\doop(a),m)=p(y\mid\doop(a),\doop(m)).
\]
ID then extracts the original singleton district $\{Y\}$, giving
$p(y\mid a,m)=p(y\mid m)$. Positivity is still required at the
conditioning value. Normalizing a failed joint-identification result
would have missed this valid conditional query. Conversely, the result
does not identify the distribution of $M$ under the action or the
unconditional action effect. This trace exemplifies the distinction in
\citet[Figure 3 and Theorems 7--8]{id2006}.

An identification compiler should therefore carry typed kernels and
intervention sets through each transformation. Multiplying a district
kernel as if it were an ordinary regression conditional is a semantic
error even if the expression is numerically evaluable. A graph outside
the supported class should produce an unsupported-method result;
an actual hedge or paired-model witness supports nonidentification.

\section{Two observationally identical worlds}
\label{r3:nonidentification}
Here is a strictly positive counterexample adapted as a project derivation
to the identification definition. In model I, $U$ is a fair binary variable,
$P(A=1\mid U)=0.2+0.6U$, and, independently of the action noise,
$P(Y=1\mid U,A)=0.2+0.6U$. Action has no effect. In model II, $A$ is
independent and fair, with $P(Y=1\mid A)=0.32+0.36A$. Both yield
\[
 \begin{array}{c|cc}
  &Y=0&Y=1\\\hline
 A=0&0.34&0.16\\
 A=1&0.16&0.34
 \end{array}
\]
because, for instance, model I gives
$P(A=1,Y=1)=\tfrac12(0.2^2+0.8^2)=0.34$. Their ATEs are zero and
$0.36$, respectively. A class allowing hidden $A/Y$ confounding and an
action effect contains both models. Its observed law therefore fails
Equation~\eqref{r3:id-definition}. More data can estimate the common
table accurately but cannot choose between the intervention distributions.

One can still describe an identified set. For binary $Y$, under consistency
alone, let $q_a=P(Y=1,A=a)$ and $p_a=P(A=a)$. The unobserved part of
$\E[Y(a)]$ lies between zero and $1-p_a$, so
\begin{equation}
 \theta_A\in[q_1-q_0-p_1,\ q_1+p_0-q_0].
 \label{r3:consistency-bounds}
\end{equation}
These elementary bounds follow by assigning the missing binary potential
outcomes to their extremes; simultaneous assignments attain the endpoints
under the unrestricted consistency model. For the table above they are
$[-0.32,0.68]$. They do not encode an IV, monotonicity or substantive
confounding sensitivity restriction. Adding one of those assumptions means
optimizing over a smaller, explicitly stated model class.

\section{Selection, mediation and the population being answered}
Suppose $C=1$ marks observed outcomes. If $Y\perp C\mid A,X$ and
$\pi(a,x)=P(C=1\mid A=a,X=x)>0$, and $X$ and $A$ are observed for the
full target cohort, then
\[
 \E[Y\mid a,x]=\E\!\left[\frac{CY}{\pi(a,x)}\,\middle|\,a,x\right].
\]
The identity follows by conditioning on $Y,A,X$ and canceling $\pi$.
It can be combined with Equation~\eqref{r3:adjustment} only if the causal
adjustment assumptions also hold. If servicing difficulty $V$ in
Figure~\ref{r3:bank-graph} affects both completeness and outcome, this
conditional observation assumption may fail. Conditioning on retention
or survival does not automatically define an effect for the original
eligible population. When an endpoint is undefined after an event, an
imputation rule alone cannot make the causal target well defined.

Mediation adds another distinction. A controlled direct effect compares
$\E[Y(1,m)-Y(0,m)]$ at a feasible fixed mediator intervention. A natural
direct effect compares $\E[Y(1,M(0))-Y(0,M(0))]$. The latter combines
counterfactuals from incompatible worlds and requires restrictions beyond
those for the total effect. Under consistency, suitable support, and
assumptions implying $Y(a,m)\perp M(a')\mid X$ together with the
required action and mediator exchangeabilities, one obtains
\[
 \E[Y(a,M(a'))]
 =\sum_{x,m}\E[Y\mid a,m,x]p(m\mid a',x)p(x).
\]
The cross-world independence is an additional assumption, not something
proved by fitting the two observed regressions. Treatment-induced
mediator--outcome confounding invalidates this simple construction. A
single-world analysis and the stronger independent-error model must
therefore remain distinguishable \citep{swig2013}.

\subsection{Edge assignments and a single-world alternative}
\label{r3:mediation-interventions}
For the simple independent-error system
$M=f_M(A,X,U_M)$ and $Y=f_Y(A,M,X,U_Y)$, with conditional
independence of the relevant disturbances given $X$, an edge
intervention can send $a'$ along $A\to M$ and $a$ along $A\to Y$.
The resulting response is
$f_Y(a,f_M(a',X,U_M),X,U_Y)$. Integrating the independent
disturbances yields exactly the mediation functional above. This
derivation makes its stronger model explicit: splitting a node into
different edge values is not the same intervention as setting the
single node once. A manipulation of a composite product that changes
only a pricing channel also requires the claimed separation of those
mechanisms to have operational meaning.

Now introduce a post-action covariate $L$ that affects both $M$ and
$Y$. The natural response $Y(a,M(a'))$ involves $L(a)$ in the outcome
path and $L(a')$ inside the mediator path. The observed conditional
kernels do not generally determine the joint law of these two
counterfactual values. The same node would have to transmit different
versions of its history along its outgoing paths; ordinary
single-world g-computation does not supply that joint law.

A feasible alternative can be defined by a new randomized mediator
draw $G_{a'}$ from $p(m\mid A=a',X)$, conditionally independent of
the customer's other innovations given $X$. Under action
exchangeability, mediator--outcome exchangeability given $(A,L,X)$,
consistency and the requisite cross-regime support, direct mechanism
replacement identifies the project-defined target
\begin{equation}
 \E[Y(a,G_{a'})]=\sum_{x,l,m}
 \E[Y\mid a,l,m,x]p(l\mid a,x)p(m\mid a',x)p(x).
 \label{r3:random-mediator}
\end{equation}
The proof is the sequential g-formula: draw $X$, let $L$ develop
under $a$, independently draw the mediator from the stipulated
baseline-conditional distribution, then apply the invariant outcome
kernel. This intervention requires no joint $(L(a),L(a'))$ law.
It can be unrealistic if the drawn mediator is infeasible for the
resulting $L$, so support and operational feasibility remain essential.

Differences between $(a,a')$ pairs decompose effects of these new
interventions. They do not automatically decompose the original
total effect: even $Y(a,G_a)$ can differ from $Y(a)$ because the
fresh draw removes the natural association between $L$ and $M$.
For example, if $L$ is fair binary, $M=L$ and $Y=LM$, the natural
mean is $1/2$ while independently drawing $G$ from the same binary
margin gives $1/4$. This algebraic example explains the target
difference; it does not satisfy mediator support for estimating the
randomized intervention from that deterministic observational law.
Stochastic mediator policies conditional on the realized $L$ define
yet another target. A product must preserve the chosen mechanism
and conditioning information instead of returning all of these as
one ``indirect effect.''

\section{What the evidence allows us to conclude}
\label{r3:graph-contract}
The mathematical input is an intervention, target population, observed
information and model class. Its identification output is either a
functional with an assumption-dependent derivation, a set of possible
values, or a demonstrated failure of identification. A missing software
implementation is a fourth state: it says nothing about identification.

For the graph in Figure~\ref{r3:bank-graph}, a result cannot be labeled
``adjusted ATE'' after simply fitting $Y$ on $(A,X)$. A valid result might
instead report the randomized invitation effect, the consistency bounds,
or an IV analysis with extra assumptions. If multiple candidate graphs
remain, compute the effect for each supported graph or carry their union
of identified sets. Reporting the spread across two handpicked graphs is
only a sensitivity exercise for those graphs, not a confidence interval
covering all plausible causal structures.

The initial product can implement explicit DAG back-door checks and
registered functional templates with human-supplied assumptions. It should
record variable meanings, graph version, intervention transformation,
required kernels, support restrictions and target population weights.
Discovery and automated data preparation can propose inputs to this
process; they cannot certify the absence of unmeasured causes. The next
chapter shows why an instrumental-variable route changes the returned
object even when it uses the same customers, actions and outcomes.

chapters.title: From a causal diagram to instrumental-variable estimation

segments.text:
\chapter{From a causal diagram to instrumental-variable estimation}
\label{r3:instruments}
\section{Why an invitation is not an adjustment covariate}
Suppress $X,M,C$ temporarily and consider
$Z\to A\to Y$ with $A\leftarrow U\to Y$. In a randomized invitation
study, $Z$ changes receipt while $U$ confounds receipt and outcome. The
graph expresses that $Z$ is independent of the common causes and that
all directed paths from $Z$ to $Y$ pass through $A$. Neither condition
is equivalent to $Z\perp Y\mid A$: conditioning on receipt opens the
collider path through $U$. An empirical association between $Z$ and $Y$
among activators is therefore not by itself evidence against exclusion.

The graph alone does not generally identify $\E[Y(1)-Y(0)]$
\citep[Section 3.5]{pearl2009}. Linear homogeneous effects, monotone
binary compliance, and a nonparametric structural response each add
different restrictions. This chapter develops the first two and connects
them to the inverse problem that arises in the third. Calling all three
outputs an ``IV effect'' would lose the scientific distinction.

\section{Structural exclusion becomes an observable moment}
\label{r3:linear-iv}
First suppose
\begin{equation}
 Y=\beta A+h(X)+\varepsilon,
 \qquad \E[\varepsilon\mid Z,X]=0.
 \label{r3:iv-structural}
\end{equation}
The coefficient is a homogeneous structural effect: holding the
disturbance fixed, changing $A$ by $\Delta$ changes $Y$ by $\beta\Delta$.
The structural function has no direct $Z$ argument. This exclusion and
the conditional disturbance restriction are assumptions. A structural
common cause of $A$ and $Y$ allows $\E[\varepsilon\mid A,X]\ne0$.
The linear example in \citet[Section 2]{angrist1996} starts from precisely
this distinction between endogenous receipt and exogenous assignment.

Let $r(X)=\E[A\mid X]$, $\ell(X)=\E[Y\mid X]$ and
$m(X)=\E[Z\mid X]$. Iterating the conditional disturbance restriction
gives $\ell(X)=\beta r(X)+h(X)$. Thus
\begin{align}
 0&=\E[(Z-m(X))\{Y-\ell(X)-\beta(A-r(X))\}],\nonumber\\
 \beta&=\frac{\E[(Z-m(X))(Y-\ell(X))]}
                   {\E[(Z-m(X))(A-r(X))]},
 \label{r3:residual-iv}
\end{align}
provided the denominator $\kappa$ is nonzero. Exogeneity justifies the
zero moment; relevance makes it invertible. Conditional centering removes
$h(X)$ without asserting that it is linear. A regression that uses a
finite linear basis for $X$ instead imposes the corresponding approximation
or correct-specification condition; it does not automatically perform
this population residualization.

Without covariates and with binary $Z$, the ratio reduces to
\begin{equation}
 \beta=\frac{\E[Y\mid Z=1]-\E[Y\mid Z=0]}
                   {\E[A\mid Z=1]-\E[A\mid Z=0]}.
 \label{r3:wald}
\end{equation}
Indeed, $\Cov(Z,Y)=P(Z=1)P(Z=0)\{\E[Y\mid Z=1]-\E[Y\mid Z=0]\}$,
and the same factor cancels in the receipt covariance. Nothing in this
algebra proves a homogeneous-effect model; the next section gives a
different interpretation under heterogeneous potential outcomes.

\subsection{Two-stage least squares and GMM}
For linear controls let the design matrix $D$ contain the endogenous
regressors and included controls, and let $W$ contain the instruments and
those same controls. With $W'W$ nonsingular, define
$P_W=W(W'W)^{-1}W'$. Fitting $D$ on $W$ gives $\widehat D=P_WD$;
regressing $Y$ on $\widehat D$ gives
\begin{equation}
 \widehat\beta_{\rm 2SLS}=(D'P_WD)^{-1}D'P_WY.
 \label{r3:2sls}
\end{equation}
This follows because $P_W$ is symmetric and idempotent. The structural
error used for uncertainty is $\widehat\varepsilon=Y-D\widehat\beta$,
not the residual from regressing on $\widehat D$. Treating the predicted
regressors as ordinary fixed observations with the latter residual yields
the wrong variance calculation.

More generally, define $\bar g_n(\beta)=n^{-1}\sum_iW_i(Y_i-D_i'\beta)$
and minimize $\bar g_n'\Omega_n\bar g_n$ for positive-definite
$\Omega_n$. The population derivative is $-Q_{WD}=-\E[W_iD_i']$.
With $Q_{WD}$ of full column rank, suitable moments and an independent
sample CLT, the asymptotic covariance of $\sqrt n(\widehat\beta-\beta)$ is
\begin{equation}
 (Q_{DW}\Omega Q_{WD})^{-1}Q_{DW}\Omega S\Omega Q_{WD}
 (Q_{DW}\Omega Q_{WD})^{-1},
 \label{r3:gmm-variance}
\end{equation}
where $S=\Var(W_i\varepsilon_i)$. For 2SLS,
$\Omega=\E[W_iW_i']^{-1}$; efficient GMM within this moment class uses
$\Omega=S^{-1}$. The expression follows by linearizing the moment
equation and applying the CLT to $n^{-1/2}\sum W_i\varepsilon_i$.
For clusters or time series, $S$ must be the appropriate cluster or
long-run score covariance, with the normalization and asymptotic sampling
unit adjusted accordingly. Transaction count is not the sample size in
an experiment randomized across a few branches.

\section{The same ratio can identify a complier effect}
\label{r3:late}
Now let $Z,A\in\{0,1\}$, with receipt potentials $A(0),A(1)$ and
outcome potentials $Y(z,a)$. Assume well-defined interventions, no
interference, and randomized assignment:
\[
 Z\perp\{A(0),A(1),Y(z,a):z,a\in\{0,1\}\}.
\]
Assume both assignment arms have positive probability, exclusion
$Y(z,a)=Y(a)$, and consistency
$A=A(Z)$, $Y=Y(A(Z))$. Define $\tau=Y(1)-Y(0)$.
Binary receipt gives the exact individual identity
\begin{equation}
 Y(A(1))-Y(A(0))=\tau\{A(1)-A(0)\}.
 \label{r3:compliance-identity}
\end{equation}
Taking expectations and using random assignment identifies its left side
as the outcome intention-to-treat contrast. Similarly the receipt
intention-to-treat contrast is $\E[A(1)-A(0)]$.

Let $\mathcal C=\{A(1)=1,A(0)=0\}$ be compliers and
$\mathcal D=\{A(1)=0,A(0)=1\}$ defiers. Always-takers and never-takers
have zero receipt difference. Therefore the Wald functional is
\begin{equation}
 \frac{P(\mathcal C)\E[\tau\mid\mathcal C]
             -P(\mathcal D)\E[\tau\mid\mathcal D]}
       {P(\mathcal C)-P(\mathcal D)}.
 \label{r3:iv-with-defiers}
\end{equation}
Monotonicity $A(1)\ge A(0)$ removes defiers. Relevance then implies
$P(\mathcal C)>0$, yielding the local average treatment effect
\begin{equation}
 \theta_{\mathcal C}=\E[Y(1)-Y(0)\mid\mathcal C]
 =\frac{\Delta_Z Y}{\Delta_Z A}.
 \label{r3:late-result}
\end{equation}
This reconstructs \citet[Equation (9), Table 1 and Proposition 1]{angrist1996}.
Monotonicity is not an arrow property. An invitation can discourage some
customers, for example by attracting attention to a competing product.
Without monotonicity, Equation~\eqref{r3:iv-with-defiers} can lie outside
the range of subgroup average effects.

Compliance strata refer to joint receipt potentials, not observed groups.
An observed nonactivator under $Z=0$ may be a complier or never-taker.
The identified average effect therefore does not label individual
compliers. Changing the invitation, price or delivery channel can change
the complier population and its mean effect. LATE is not automatically
the gain from expanding the product to all eligible households.

\subsection{A constructive failure to identify the population ATE}
Take $40\%$ compliers, $30\%$ always-takers and $30\%$ never-takers,
with fair randomized $Z$. Among compliers set $(Y(0),Y(1))=(0,1)$.
Always-takers have observed $Y(1)=1$; never-takers have observed $Y(0)=0$.
Consider two completions of their missing potential outcomes:
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{lcc}
\toprule
Stratum & Completion I $(Y(0),Y(1))$ & Completion II $(Y(0),Y(1))$\\
\midrule
Complier & $(0,1)$ & $(0,1)$\\
Always-taker & $(1,1)$ & $(0,1)$\\
Never-taker & $(0,0)$ & $(0,1)$\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
Both satisfy exclusion and monotonicity and yield the same full observed
law of $(Z,A,Y)$: receipt rates are $0.3$ and $0.7$, with $Y=A$.
The first stage and reduced form are both $0.4$, so LATE is one. But
the ATE is $0.4$ in completion I and one in completion II. The observed
IV experiment cannot distinguish them. This is a project counterexample,
not an appeal to a generic statement that ``IV has limitations.'' It
identifies the exact missing outcomes that a population effect requires.

\subsection{Conditional instruments and the weights of the target}
If assignment is randomized only conditional on $X$, assume the IV
conditions within each $x$, and let $p(x)=P(Z=1\mid X=x)$,
$\Delta_A(x)=\E[A\mid Z=1,x]-\E[A\mid Z=0,x]$ and
$\tau_{\mathcal C}(x)$ be the conditional complier effect. Then
\[
 \frac{\E[(Z-p(X))Y]}{\E[(Z-p(X))A]}
 =\frac{\E[p(X)(1-p(X))\Delta_A(X)\tau_{\mathcal C}(X)]}
        {\E[p(X)(1-p(X))\Delta_A(X)]}.
\]
The identity follows by computing each conditional covariance. Even with
monotonicity, the residual-IV ratio weights strata by both assignment
variance and compliance. A policy that targets a different $X$ distribution
or uses different invitation probabilities generally changes the target.
The product must preserve these weights rather than translate the result
into an unqualified population ATE.

Transporting a complier effect needs more than target covariate weights.
Let $\kappa^*(x)=P^*\{A(1)>A(0)\mid X=x\}$ be the target-domain
compliance probability. Its overall complier effect is
\[
 \tau_{\mathcal C}^*
 =\frac{\E^*[\kappa^*(X)\tau_{\mathcal C}^*(X)]}
        {\E^*[\kappa^*(X)]}.
\]
Replacing the conditional complier effect by its source estimate
requires invariance of that complier response, a stronger restriction
than sharing an outcome name. Target compliance must also be identified,
for example from a valid target encouragement design, and have source
support. Different pricing or eligibility rules can change who complies.
An overall source Wald ratio and target demographics alone do not
identify this expression. This is a target-specific consequence of the
compliance decomposition, not a generic extrapolation guarantee.

\section{Weak and invalid instruments fail differently}
\label{r3:weak-iv}
In the scalar linear model write $N=\E[(Z-m)(Y-\ell)]$ and
$\kappa=\E[(Z-m)(A-r)]$, with $N=\beta\kappa$.
For fixed nonzero $\kappa$, a ratio expansion gives
\[
 \widehat\beta-\beta
 =\frac{(\widehat N-N)-\beta(\widehat\kappa-\kappa)}{\kappa}
  +o_p(n^{-1/2}).
\]
If $\kappa$ shrinks on the same scale as its sampling error, the
denominator is no longer stable and this expansion fails. Orthogonal
nuisance learning can reduce error in $\widehat N$ and
$\widehat\kappa$; it cannot create population relevance.

The local-to-zero experiment makes the failure precise. Suppress controls,
normalize $\E[Z^2]=1$, and let
$A=\pi_n Z+v$, $Y=\beta A+u$, $\pi_n=c/\sqrt n$.
Suppose the sample second moment converges to one and
$n^{-1/2}\sum_i(Z_i u_i,Z_i v_i)\Rightarrow(G_u,G_v)$, a
nondegenerate joint Gaussian vector. Then
\begin{equation}
 \widehat\beta-\beta
 =\frac{n^{-1/2}\sum_i Z_i u_i}
 {c\,n^{-1}\sum_iZ_i^2+n^{-1/2}\sum_iZ_i v_i}
 \ \Longrightarrow\ \frac{G_u}{c+G_v}.
 \label{r3:weak-limit}
\end{equation}
The error does not concentrate at zero, even as $n$ grows. This is the
scalar specialization of the local-to-zero construction in
\citet[Section 2A, equations (2.4)--(2.7)]{staiger1994}. The number of
customers alone therefore cannot certify that a weak encouragement
supports precise receipt-effect inference.

\subsection{Test the structural residual before dividing}
Let $X$ now denote a full-rank matrix of $k$ included controls, $Z$ a
matrix of $q$ excluded instruments, and $M_X=I-P_X$. Suppose
$[X,Z]$ has rank $k+q$. Set $\widetilde Z=M_XZ$,
$P_{\widetilde Z}=\widetilde Z(\widetilde Z'\widetilde Z)^{-1}
\widetilde Z'$ and $r_b=M_X(Y-bA)$. The Anderson--Rubin construction is
\begin{equation}
 F_{\rm AR}(b)=
 \frac{r_b'P_{\widetilde Z}r_b/q}
      {r_b'(M_X-P_{\widetilde Z})r_b/(n-k-q)}.
 \label{r3:ar-statistic}
\end{equation}
Under $b=\beta$, $r_b=M_Xu$. If conditional on $X,Z$ the structural
error is $N(0,\sigma^2I)$, the two quadratic forms divided by
$\sigma^2$ are independent chi-squared variables of ranks $q$ and
$n-k-q$: their projection spaces are orthogonal. Thus
$F_{\rm AR}(\beta)\sim F_{q,n-k-q}$ without a lower bound on the
first stage. Invert this test to form
$\{b:F_{\rm AR}(b)\le F_{q,n-k-q;1-\alpha}\}$.
The derivation reconstructs the exact Gaussian result reported in
\citet[Section 2D, equation (2.24) and Theorem 3]{staiger1994}; that
paper separately supplies an asymptotic result under its moment
conditions. Gaussian, homoskedastic fixed-design inference is not a
cluster-robust theorem.

With heteroskedastic or dependent observations, a candidate-specific
moment statistic can instead use
$n\bar m(b)'\widehat S(b)^{-1}\bar m(b)$, where
$m_i(b)=\widetilde Z_i(Y_i-bA_i-X_i'\widehat\gamma_b)$.
Its reference distribution requires a valid score CLT, a consistent
covariance and fixed-rank restrictions; estimated controls and learned
instruments need their own remainder analysis. Uniform validity across
weak first stages must be established for that construction, not inferred
from the Gaussian calculation. Independent training of a compressed
instrument can avoid using the same errors to select and test it;
the split-sample AR discussion in \citet[printed p.17]{staiger1994}
provides an early instance, with independence assumptions explicit.

\subsection{Why the answer can be disconnected}
For an elementary exact Gaussian illustration, suppose a reduced-form
statistic $(\widehat N,\widehat\kappa)$ has mean
$(\beta\kappa,\kappa)$ and known covariance $V$. Testing
$\widehat N-b\widehat\kappa$ gives the confidence-set inequality
\begin{equation}
 (\widehat\kappa^2-z^2V_{\kappa\kappa})b^2
 +(-2\widehat N\widehat\kappa+2z^2V_{N\kappa})b
 +(\widehat N^2-z^2V_{NN})\le0,
 \label{r3:ratio-set}
\end{equation}
where $z=z_{1-\alpha/2}$. This follows by squaring a normal test of a
linear combination; it is a project calculation in a specified Gaussian
experiment, not a claim that estimated sample covariances are exact.
When the leading coefficient is negative and the discriminant positive,
the accepted set consists of two exterior rays. It can also be all of
$\mathbb R$. Replacing that result by the smallest finite interval on
a plotting grid would discard the scientific content: the experiment
does not rule out very large effects. A bank may then prefer the
well-identified invitation ITT or a stronger encouragement design.
The same inverse structure reappears when uncertain entity linkage mixes two
portfolio responses. Section~\ref{s61:linkage-sets} diagonalizes that map and
constructs financial confidence sets from candidate responses and audit
counts, retaining rank failure and disconnected answers.

Invalidity is a different problem. For centered scalar variables,
suppose $A=\pi Z+v$ and $Y=\beta A+\delta Z+u$, with $Z$ orthogonal
to both $u,v$. Then
\begin{equation}
 \frac{\Cov(Z,Y)}{\Cov(Z,A)}=\beta+\frac{\delta}{\pi}.
 \label{r3:invalid-iv}
\end{equation}
The instrument may be strongly predictive and precisely estimated while
the exclusion is false. A direct invitation effect of $0.02$ outcome units
produces bias $0.05$ when $\pi=0.4$, but bias $1$ when $\pi=0.02$.
Weakness amplifies a small violation. An overidentification test can reject
a joint set of restrictions; failure to reject does not prove that all
instruments satisfy exclusion, especially when violations are shared.

For a declared sensitivity range $|\delta|\le d$ in this scalar model,
the admissible coefficient interval is centered at the covariance ratio
with radius $d/|\pi|$, before sampling uncertainty is added. That interval
comes from a substantive bound on a direct effect, not from a diagnostic
threshold chosen by software.

\section{Machine learning enters after the moment restriction}
\label{r3:iv-ml}
For Equation~\eqref{r3:iv-structural}, use the score
\begin{equation}
 \psi(O;\beta,\eta)=(Z-m(X))
       \{Y-\ell(X)-\beta(A-r(X))\},\quad \eta=(m,\ell,r).
 \label{r3:pliv-score}
\end{equation}
At the truth its derivatives in arbitrary square-integrable nuisance
directions vanish: an $\ell$ or $r$ perturbation multiplies a function
of $X$ by $Z-m(X)$, whose conditional mean is zero; an $m$ perturbation
multiplies a function of $X$ by $\varepsilon$, whose conditional mean
is zero. The derivative in $\beta$ is $-\kappa$, which must still be
bounded away from zero for conventional strong-identification inference.
This is the partially linear IV score of
\citet[Section 4.2, Equations (4.5)--(4.8)]{dml2018}.

Estimate $m,\ell,r$ on other folds, evaluate residual products on the
held-out units, and solve the sample moment. The nuisance contribution
to its population bias is
\[
 \E[(\widehat m-m)\{(\widehat\ell-\ell)
                         -\beta(\widehat r-r)\}],
\]
because the first-order terms have zero expectation. Cauchy--Schwarz
bounds this by a product of nuisance errors. The useful ML rates are
therefore rates for these moment errors and the score variance, not
merely predictive accuracy for $Y$. Dependence determines valid fold
construction and the CLT; arbitrarily splitting rows from the same
customer does not produce independent training and evaluation samples.

\section{Control functions use a triangular structural restriction}
\label{r3:control-function}
There is another IV route that must not be confused with adjusting
for an arbitrary first-stage residual. Suppose
\[
 A=h(Z,X,V),\qquad Y=f(A,X,U),\qquad
 Z\perp(U,V)\mid X,
\]
where $V$ is scalar, continuously distributed and $h(z,x,v)$ is
strictly increasing in $v$. Normalize $V\mid X$ to be uniform on
$(0,1)$. Then the observed conditional rank
\begin{equation}
 R=F_{A\mid Z,X}(A\mid Z,X)=V
 \label{r3:control-rank}
\end{equation}
almost surely. For fixed $z,x$, the event
