Its convergence result has explicit regularity, compactness, memory
and bandwidth conditions (Assumptions 1--8 and Theorems 1--2).
Performing one approximate Bellman update inside arbitrary MCMC does
not inherit that result.

For the normalized logit model, a value error at most $\epsilon_V$
changes each $v_d$ by at most $\beta\epsilon_V$. Since log-sum-exp
is one-Lipschitz in sup norm, each log choice probability changes by
at most $2\beta\epsilon_V$. Combined with the Bellman-residual bound,
this gives a transparent likelihood error budget. It is a deterministic
approximation bound, not a sampling theorem for the fitted preferences.

The bank's action $a$ should remain distinct from the customer's
response $d$. An offer can change a contractual cost in $u_d(x;a)$,
the transition law $P_d(\cdot\mid x;a)$, or the information available
to the customer. A structural intervention must state which mechanism
changes and what remains invariant. Competitor repricing, funding
conditions and capacity can then alter the environment again. A
single-customer policy response conditional on those quantities is
not automatically a banking-group equilibrium effect. The product
must return the corresponding target and require an explicit equilibrium
model for the latter question.

\section{A resolved information and inference design for servicing}
\label{s6:servicing}
The privately logged three-state model is useful precisely because it can
fail despite an identified population value. Resolving that failure requires
separating the statistical experiment from the optimizer and from the
proposed decision. Here the servicing decision is whether to offer temporary
assistance; the objective is discounted collected cash net of assistance and
operating cost. Signals arrive before the decision, while the cash rewards
used in this four-decision policy are settled after its decision horizon.
The policy may use signals and its own previous actions. It may not use the
later audited state or settled cash as contemporaneous information.

\subsection{What the retained failure actually shows}
For the original 600-trajectory experiment, all nine unavailable fits were
on a constrained transition-logit boundary. Reconstructing those exact seeds
reproduces the stored values, rather than diagnosing a different simulation.
With 90 emission labels, 76 of 80 fits were available: conditional coverage
was .8947, empirical value standard deviation 10.668 and mean model standard
error 9.657. With 600 labels, 75 were available: conditional coverage was
.9333, empirical standard deviation 9.141 and mean standard error 9.687.
Counting unavailable fits gives the previously reported .850 and .875.
The latter case therefore does not mainly show underestimated standard
errors among the usable fits. Availability, tail error and bias are different
questions. Eighty repetitions leave substantial Monte Carlo uncertainty.

The binding coordinates are transition logits, including near-zero
destinations under privately selected actions. Larger emission calibration
alone does not supply those scarce action/state transitions. The model's
positive population transition probabilities do not prevent an observed
likelihood maximum near the boundary. The observed fit reconstructions,
larger-trajectory follow-up and complete-state frequency experiment separate
this scarcity explanation from the earlier differencing/start checks. They
do not certify a global maximum or establish one universal cause of
undercoverage. At 3,000 observational trajectories and 600 independent
emission labels, all 120 follow-up fits are available; coverage is .9417,
bias $-.213$, empirical standard deviation 4.097 and mean reported standard
error 4.301. This supports a bounded larger-sample regime on this mechanism,
not a universal 3,000-customer rule. The failed 199-refit bootstrap remains
adverse evidence for the original design.

\subsection{A measurement acquisition alternative}
An independent representative audit now follows whole customer trajectories,
recording the state before each action, the same production signal, the
actual action and the eventually settled reward. The states must have an
operational definition: for example, a predecision classification of verified
repayment capacity and available liquidity into solvent, temporarily
constrained and persistent-shortfall categories. Definition and thresholds
are fixed before outcomes. Independent adjudication checks timestamped
income, obligations and accessible balances; disagreements and unavailable
documents remain measurement failures.

These categories are not automatically sufficient causal states. The model
asserts that, conditional on the state, the officer's private action
information adds no further outcome/transition cause; that the state is
Markov for this horizon; and that the audit and production emissions agree.
A coarse affordability label can violate all three. Audit selection must
represent the target population, or known inclusion probabilities and their
influence must enter the estimator. The implementation below assumes
representative independent trajectories. It does not silently replace a
convenience audit by a random sample.

Let $C_{i,sj}^E$ count signal $j$ in state $s$ along audited path $i$,
$C_{i,asj}^T$ count transitions from $s$ to $j$ under action $a$, and
$N_{i,as},R_{i,as}$ be state/action exposure and reward sums. The row-frequency
and reward estimators are
\[
 \hat E_{sj}=\frac{\sum_i C_{i,sj}^E}{\sum_{i,j'}C_{i,sj'}^E},\quad
 \hat T_{asj}=\frac{\sum_i C_{i,asj}^T}{\sum_{i,j'}C_{i,asj'}^T},\quad
 \hat r_{as}=\frac{\sum_iR_{i,as}}{\sum_iN_{i,as}}.
\]
Initial frequencies estimate $\mu$; action frequencies estimate the private
logger $q$. This is the complete-data likelihood estimate in the declared
finite model. It has no local mixture-likelihood optimization. It buys that
simplicity with a much more expensive observation design.

For any row with path counts $C_{ij}$, let $c_j=\E C_{ij}>0$ and use
logit coordinates $\ell_j=\log(c_j/c_K)$. Direct differentiation gives
\[
 \varphi_{ij}^{\ell}=C_{ij}/c_j-C_{iK}/c_K,\qquad
 \varphi_{i,as}^{r}=(R_{i,as}-r_{as}N_{i,as})/\E N_{i,as}.
\]
Stack these with the initial and emission coordinates. Their path-level
outer products preserve all within-trajectory covariance; treating visits
as independent would not. For the scaled reward coordinates divide the
reward influence by the known reward standard deviation. With fixed horizon,
positive row masses, finite second moments and accurate representative
labels, the multivariate iid central limit theorem and quotient delta method
give
\[
 \sqrt n(\hat\vartheta-\vartheta_0)
 =n^{-1/2}\sum_i\varphi_i+o_p(1),\qquad
 \widehat{\Var}(\hat V)=
 \nabla V(\hat\vartheta)'\left(n^{-2}\sum_i\hat\varphi_i\hat\varphi_i'\right)
 \nabla V(\hat\vartheta).
\]
An empty category makes these interior coordinates unavailable. Arbitrary
pseudocounts would define a different finite procedure; they are not added
to disguise support failure. This is a pointwise regular inference route,
not uniform coverage near vanishing state/action probabilities.

\subsection{A dynamic observable policy}
For a prior belief $b$ immediately before signal $o$, update
$b_o(s)=b(s)E_{so}/\sum_jb(j)E_{jo}$. If action $a$ is intervened on, the
next prior is $b_oT_a$. There is no private logger factor in that update:
the policy chose the action. For remaining horizon $h$,
\begin{equation}
 V_h(b)=\sum_oP(o\mid b)\max_a
       \{b_or_a+\gamma V_{h-1}(b_oT_a)\},\qquad V_0=0.
 \label{s6:belief-policy}
\end{equation}
The finite recursion is the belief-state planning construction
\citep{kaelbling1998}. Four signals, two actions and four decisions permit
exact tree enumeration here. The tree is optimized using an independent
2,000-trajectory audit pilot, then frozen in its entirety. Evaluation fits
kernels on separate audited trajectories and propagates their uncertainty
through this fixed tree. It differentiates neither the argmax nor the pilot
training procedure. The interval targets the value of the policy that was
actually trained, conditional on that pilot, not the unknown optimal value.

To evaluate the fixed tree without numerical posterior divisions, propagate
unnormalized state mass. At each signal branch multiply by $E_{\cdot o}$,
add the selected action's expected reward, and propagate through $T_a$.
Summing all leaves gives a polynomial in the kernels and initial law, linear
in the rewards. Its derivative is therefore well-defined for the fixed tree;
central differencing is checked against a smaller step and independent
likelihood/count perturbations. Exact enumeration avoids a filter
approximation error in this selected problem. Larger horizons require
pruning or approximate planning and an explicit value-loss bound.

On the common mechanism the frozen learned policy has true four-period
contrast 25.029 against never assisting. Some actions depend on earlier
signals even after holding the current signal and remaining horizon fixed;
this is a belief-history policy, rather than an immediate-reward rule.
At 1,200 audited evaluation trajectories, all 400 fits are available and
coverage is .950 for this contrast. The original eight-period fixed-signal
contrast has coverage .9425. At 300 audited paths, 54 of 400 fits have an
empty category; all-request coverage is .8275 for the learned policy even
though coverage conditional on availability is .9566. Measurement-supported
identification therefore still requires enough informative visits.

\subsection{Three information routes on the same servicing problem}
An observed-history g-formula substitutes the factual conditional law given
public signals and actions. Under private logging its state posterior after
action $a$ is proportional to $b_o(s)q_s(a)$, while the intervention posterior
is $b_o(s)$. Thus even an exactly estimated public-history conditional law
uses the wrong state mixture for the intervention. Adding a flexible learner
cannot remove this information gap. Recording the action-relevant private
information, or randomizing assistance with adequate support, changes that
conclusion. The common-mechanism comparison evaluates both recursions on the
same frozen policy. Its exact public-history g-formula contrast is $-35.647$,
against the intervention contrast $25.029$. The sign reversal occurs even
without nuisance estimation error.

Validated emissions can identify the kernels using the earlier marked
moment/hidden-likelihood route, with fewer labels but difficult finite
curvature and boundary behavior. Fully audited trajectories identify the
same kernels and policy target more directly, with the explicit acquisition
cost above. Their precision and availability are properties of different
sampling designs, not proof that hidden-state modeling is unnecessary.

Proximal evaluation instead seeks policy value without recovering named
states. For this servicing mechanism an action-side proxy might be a
separately recorded officer assessment, and an outcome-side proxy an
independent affordability measurement. Merely calling them proxies proves
nothing: after conditioning on the latent confounder and allowed context,
the action-side proxy and logged action must be independent of the
outcome-side proxy, proposed action and counterfactual continuation under
the source's hybrid laws. The proposed policy cannot reuse forbidden private
proxy information. \citet[Assumptions 1--2, Theorem 2 and Table 1]{bennettprox2023}
give these policy-dependent restrictions and the recursive action/outcome
bridges. In particular their outcome bridge targets
$\E[\mathbf1\{E_t=A_t\}Y_t\mid U_t,A_t=a]$, where $E_t$ denotes the
proposed action; dropping that indicator changes the theorem.

The source's recursive bridge score is a substantive challenger when the
bank can defend those exclusions and bridge existence/rank conditions but
cannot obtain accurate state labels. The production stream in this constructed servicing experiment has one
public signal stream and no independently validated second proxy. It cannot
invoke that theorem by relabelling the same signal twice. If an additional
proxy is collected, its conditional operator, range, regularization and
policy information set become new scientific inputs. This explains why the
audited trajectory route is selected for the bounded decision capability
and proximal evaluation remains a qualified alternative, rather than
claiming that one existing dataset satisfies all three information regimes.

\subsection{The initial product boundary}
The offering includes finite-state estimation and observable-history policy
evaluation under a qualified measurement design, plus the earlier exact
linear-Gaussian controlled likelihood. It does not include arbitrary nonlinear
private-state fitting with routinely calibrated policy intervals. Choosing
an extended Kalman or particle filter would require a declared likelihood,
initial/noise laws, derivative accuracy and policy-value comparison against
a numerical reference, following the approximation obligations already
derived. Section~\ref{c7:nonlinear} supplies a selected audited nonlinear
comparison with additional information and policy-class restrictions.
Those restrictions affect which bank requests can be accepted; they are
not postponed as a generic deployment check. A noisy or selected audit
also changes the statistical model, even when all matrices are well-conditioned.
In a separately registered 200-repetition sensitivity run, independently
misclassifying 10\% of predecision state labels at 1,200 audit trajectories
produces bias $-105.72$ for the original $59.56$ contrast and zero coverage.
This is a specific severe misspecification example, not a calibrated bound
for every 10\% audit-error process.

\section{An audited nonlinear servicing experiment}
\label{c7:nonlinear}
The exact Gaussian construction leaves a substantive question: what changes
when the state transition bends and a private binary decision reveals hidden
state information? A small servicing experiment gives a complete answer for
one identified model. It also exposes the difference between an accurate
likelihood and a reliable routine interval.

For each independent customer the order is state, signal, action, reward,
then next state. In units fixed by an accurate state audit, let
\begin{align}
 S_0&\sim N(\mu_0,v_0), & O_t&=S_t+e_t,\\
 S_{t+1}&=\rho S_t+\gamma\tanh(S_t)+\beta A_t+u_{t+1},\nonumber\\
 \Pr(A_t=1\mid S_t,O_t)&=\epsilon+(1-2\epsilon)
       \operatorname{expit}(\lambda_0+\lambda_sS_t+\lambda_oO_t),\nonumber\\
 R_t&=\eta_0+\eta_s S_t+\eta_a A_t+\eta_{sa}S_tA_t+v_t^R.
 \label{c7:nonlinear-law}
\end{align}
Independent Gaussian innovations have positive variances $q,r_o,r_R$.
Their log variances, both initial parameters, three transition coefficients,
three logger coefficients and four reward coefficients give 15 unknowns.
The fixed logger floor is $\epsilon=.05$; stability requires
$|\rho|+|\gamma|<1$. Rewards are in thousands of currency units. These are
synthetic scientific restrictions, not a fitted description of a real bank.

\subsection{Identification comes from the observation design}
Production observes $(O,A,R)$; an independent representative audit observes
complete labelled $(S,O,A,R)$ trajectories. The loading one in $O=S+e$ and
the labelled scale of $S$ fix state meaning. Under positive definite population
Gram matrices, regressing $S_{t+1}$ on $(S_t,\tanh S_t,A_t)$ identifies the
three transition coefficients and its residual identifies $q$. The signal
residual identifies $r_o$. Regressing reward on $(1,S_t,A_t,S_tA_t)$ identifies
its coefficients and variance; labelled initial states identify $(\mu_0,v_0)$.
The clipped logistic probability is strictly increasing in its index. Equality
of these probabilities on a full-rank support for $(1,S,O)$ therefore implies
equality of the logger coefficients. The positive action floor supports both
actions; full rank and representative labels remain substantive requirements.
This establishes identification before filtering. Filtering does not create
the audited states. Noisy or selected labels change this argument.

Write $f_p,g_p,a_p,h_p$ for transition, signal, logger and reward densities.
A production trajectory contributes
\begin{equation}
 L_i^O(p)=\int\nu_p(s_0)
  \prod_{t=0}^{H-1}g_p(o_t\mid s_t)a_p(a_t\mid s_t,o_t)h_p(r_t\mid s_t,a_t)
  \prod_{t=0}^{H-2}f_p(s_{t+1}\mid s_t,a_t)\,ds_{0:H-1}.
 \label{c7:nonlinear-likelihood}
\end{equation}
An audited trajectory contributes this integrand evaluated at the labelled
states. Joint inference sums log likelihoods over both independent samples.
The historical logger remains in the observed likelihood; the policy replaces
it in the interventional law. This combines the marginal likelihood recursion
of \citet[Theorem 12.1]{sarkka2013} with the mechanism-replacement principle
of \citet[Corollary 1]{pearl2009} for the specified controlled model.

\subsection{Likelihood, score and value need separate numerical checks}
Take grid points $s_j$, integration weights $w_j$, initial masses
$b_{0j}=\nu_p(s_j)w_j$, emissions
$e_{tj}=g_p(o_t\mid s_j)a_p(a_t\mid s_j,o_t)h_p(r_t\mid s_j,a_t)$,
and matrices $K_{a,jk}=f_p(s_k\mid s_j,a)w_k$. Then
\[
 z_t=\sum_j b_{tj}e_{tj},\quad
 \widetilde b_{tj}=b_{tj}e_{tj}/z_t,\quad
 b_{t+1,k}=\sum_j\widetilde b_{tj}K_{a_t,jk},\quad
 \ell_i^O=\sum_t\log z_t.
\]
Finite-domain transitions are not renormalized to conceal tail loss. Scaling
emissions to prevent underflow leaves the discretized log likelihood intact.
For a parameter direction, product and quotient rules give
\begin{align*}
 \dot z_t&=\sum_j(\dot b_{tj}e_{tj}+b_{tj}\dot e_{tj}),
 &\dot\ell_t&=\dot z_t/z_t,\\
 \dot{\widetilde b}_{tj}&=(\dot b_{tj}e_{tj}+b_{tj}\dot e_{tj})/z_t
                         -\widetilde b_{tj}\dot z_t/z_t,\\
 \dot b_{t+1,k}&=\sum_j(\dot{\widetilde b}_{tj}K_{a_t,jk}
                            +\widetilde b_{tj}\dot K_{a_t,jk}).
\end{align*}
Automatic differentiation evaluates these pure array derivatives in double
precision; installed source and version identities are preserved
\citep{jaxruntime2026}. It differentiates the discretized objective, not the
unapproximated integral. Central differences in all 15 directions check the
implemented score independently.

The reference compares 41, 61, 81 and 121 nodes and domains $[-7,7]$ and
$[-9,9]$. The registered 61-node likelihood, score and value checks pass.
Every final interior fit also compares with a finer, wider grid; an interval
is withheld if the observed log-likelihood discrepancy exceeds $10^{-4}$,
the maximum score discrepancy exceeds $10^{-3}$, or value changes by more
than 0.1 currency unit. These are observed refinements, not certified error
bounds for all parameters.

The assumed-density Gaussian challenger integrates the private action by
Gauss--Hermite nodes and replaces the posterior by its first two moments.
Agreement in likelihood alone does not qualify its score or policy value.
The exact Gaussian reduction requires both $\gamma=0$ and $\lambda_s=0$:
after observing the signal, a logger depending only on that signal adds no
hidden-state information. Retaining a state-dependent logistic logger would
invalidate the reduction. The bootstrap particle challenger instead keeps
the private logger in its weights. Eight independent seeds at 512 and 4,096
particles expose Monte Carlo variation. Coupled finite differences assess
stochastic likelihood perturbations; they are not a certified derivative
through a discontinuous resampling path. These are substantive alternatives
to Gaussian projection, as emphasized by \citet[Chapters 6--7]{sarkka2013}.

\subsection{Joint audit uncertainty and the policy target}
Let $s_i^O,s_j^A$ be production and audit trajectory scores and $J$ the
negative joint Hessian. The covariance estimate is
\[
 \widehat V_p=J^{-1}\left\{
  \sum_i\widetilde s_i^O\widetilde s_i^{O\prime}+
  \sum_j\widetilde s_j^A\widetilde s_j^{A\prime}\right\}J^{-1},
\]
with within-sample centering. Sample sizes enter as sums: an audit-identified
direction does not automatically inherit the production sample's information
rate. At an interior regular solution, value variance is
$\nabla V(p)'\widehat V_p\nabla V(p)$. Boundary solutions and singular
information do not receive this interval. Forty retained full refits resample
whole trajectories separately within the two samples on the first data set.
This is a bootstrap diagnostic, not precise tail calibration. Multiple starts
and their objective differences are recorded without claiming a global optimum.

The evaluated rule is $A_t=1\{O_t>c_t\}$. An independent 800-trajectory
pilot chooses from a 64-element three-date threshold library; evaluation freezes
the selected rule. This is a permitted observable-policy subclass, not the
unknown optimal belief-history policy. At state $s$ its action probability is
$\pi_t(1\mid s)=\Phi((s-c_t)/\sqrt{r_o})$. Interventional grid mass evolves
as $b_{t+1}=(b_t\odot(1-\pi_t))K_0+(b_t\odot\pi_t)K_1$, giving
\[
 V_p(c)=\sum_{t=0}^{H-1}.97^t\sum_j b_{tj}
   \{\eta_0+\eta_s s_j+(\eta_a+\eta_{sa}s_j)\pi_t(1\mid s_j)\}.
\]
Independent policy simulation checks the value. Full enumeration benchmarks
the Gaussian planner on the same finite library. Equality of selected policies
in the retained example is a result, not general planning optimality.

On a bounded numerical domain with reward bound $R_*$, telescoping transition
errors yields a value bound of the form
$\sum_t .97^t\{\varepsilon_r+2R_*\sum_{j\le t}\varepsilon_{K,j}\}$.
The original Gaussian law is unbounded; truncation adds
$\sum_t .97^t\E[|R_t|1\{\text{path exits domain}\}]$, which cannot be
silently set to zero. Locally, mean-score error $\varepsilon_s$ and Hessian
curvature at least $\kappa$ bound parameter displacement by
$\varepsilon_s/\kappa$ within that basin. A value-gradient bound $G$ adds
$G\varepsilon_s/\kappa$ to the monetary error budget. The executed grid and
seed comparisons measure errors; they do not establish those uniform bounds.

\subsection{Boundary failures and a fresh information comparison}
The first registered baseline uses 160 audits and 80 production trajectories,
with $|\rho|\le.55$, $|\gamma|\le.4$. Only 55 of 100 fits are interior;
45 hit a boundary. Of the 55 available intervals, 54 cover. Reporting only
$54/55$ would hide availability: coverage over requested calculations is
$54/100$. Misspecified transitions yield 25 unavailable fits out of 25.
Weak signals, scarce actions, biased audits and a six-date horizon are separate
retained arms; successful optimization does not validate their assumptions.

A fresh registered comparison keeps the original policy and tests
$|\rho|+|\gamma|\le.95$, each coefficient in $[-.9,.9]$, against the original
rectangle. Other bounds stay fixed. With 160 audits the stable domain gives
99 available intervals and 94 covering draws out of 100. With 640 audits all
100 are available and 95 cover, with Monte Carlo interval $[.8872,.9836]$.
Mean standard error falls from about 168.06 to 95.84 currency units. The
rectangular challenger is available in 59 and 79 draws on these same designs.
No result switches methods after observing its interval.

This supplies an identified and executed nonlinear reference, including a
useful larger-audit regime and explicit failures. It does not establish
routine validity for arbitrary private-state laws, erroneous audits, weak
information, unrestricted policies or unknown global optimizer behavior.
Those require renewed scientific arguments and evidence.

chapters.title: Repeated decisions and customers who disappear

segments.text:
\chapter{Repeated decisions and customers who disappear}
\label{gap29:servicing}

A servicing policy changes what happens next. A reminder, payment holiday or
collection action affects both the customer's state and the information the
bank subsequently observes. Estimating a policy from customers who remain in
the records can therefore answer a different question from the one the bank
faces. The relevant value averages over the initial eligible population,
including customers whose later outcomes are missing.

An explicitly generated study makes this distinction measurable. With a
correct observation model, weighting recovers the chosen policy's value on
average, but repeated actions and dropout leave little effective information.
When dropout depends on an unobserved future shock, the same calculation
becomes biased and its nominal 95\% interval covers the numerical reference
in only 80\% of replications. Analysing complete observed trajectories also
overstates value. These are findings under the stated constructed law,
not estimates of a bank's servicing policy.

\section{A policy changes a path, not just a row}
Each generated customer has a fixed characteristic $X\sim N(0,1)$ and initial
state $L_0=0.4X+\varepsilon_0$. There are three decisions, $t=0,1,2$.
The historical action is binary, with probability
\[
 p_t=\operatorname{clip}\{\operatorname{expit}(0.3X-0.5L_t+0.2A_{t-1}),0.2,0.8\},
 \qquad A_{-1}=0.
\]
Clipping is a feature of this generated assignment law, not a silent
alteration of weights estimated from observed bank data. The next state and
reward are
\[
 L_{t+1}=0.6L_t+0.25X-0.5A_t+\varepsilon_{t+1},\qquad
 R_t=10-2L_{t+1}^2-A_t+0.5A_tX,
\]
with independent standard-normal innovations. Actions have a direct cost
and change the future state. Rewards are illustrative units; the coefficients
have not been estimated from a bank.

Observation continues with probability
$g_t=0.65+0.30\operatorname{expit}(0.3L_t-0.2A_t)$ after the action but
before the next state and reward are observed. Dropout is absorbing in the
analyst's data. The baseline observation draw is independent of the next
innovation conditional on the known history and action. The adverse case
instead uses $\operatorname{expit}\{\operatorname{logit}(g_t)+1.5\varepsilon_{t+1}\}$.
The analyst cannot observe that innovation when specifying the observation
probability. This deliberately violates the assumption behind the weighting
and regression procedures.

The policy value is $V(\pi)=E_\pi[\sum_{t=0}^2R_t]$. The comparison includes
never acting and four threshold policies, which act when $L_t$ exceeds
$-0.5$, $0$, $0.5$ or $1$. A selected policy chooses among the thresholds
using 2,000 separate training trajectories; its evaluation uses 1,000 new
trajectories. Selection and evaluation therefore do not reuse outcomes.
The finite list is a meaningful alternative set, not the class of all
possible policies.

\section{The denominator must retain the initial customers}
For each observed reward, the prefix-weighted score is
\[
 S_i(\pi)=\sum_{t=0}^2 R_{it}
  \prod_{s=0}^t
  \frac{\mathbf1\{A_{is}=\pi(H_{is})\}\mathbf1\{C_{is}=1\}}
       {p_s(A_{is}\mid H_{is})g_s(H_{is},A_{is})}.
\]
The estimate averages $S_i$ over all initial customers. Successive conditional
expectations remove the observation and action probabilities when those
probabilities are correct, positive and based on sufficient observed history.
The reward-specific prefix is necessary: observing a reward at the last date
requires surviving every preceding observation decision.

The simple competing calculation averages total reward among customers whose
whole recorded action sequence matches the policy and whose records remain
complete. Its denominator selects customers. It has no reason to equal
$V(\pi)$. A fitted alternative estimates the state transition from observed
transitions and simulates policy paths using that regression. This
g-computation exercise receives the constructed reward rule and initial-state
law. Its smaller observed errors in the correctly specified examples do not
make it a ready-made bank estimator. Parameter uncertainty is not propagated
into an interval for this fitted alternative in the first comparison.
Chapter~\ref{gap29:policy-uncertainty} then examines that missing uncertainty
using whole-customer resampling and the same adverse mechanisms.

The study runs 200 independent replications in each of four cases: the
baseline; action probabilities allowed to range from 0.02 to 0.98; dropout
depending on the future innovation; and omission of $X$ from the fitted state
regression. Each policy also has a separate 100,000-trajectory numerical
reference, with its own Monte Carlo standard error. Reference trajectories
are unavailable to selection and estimation.

\section{A usable interval requires enough information}
For the fixed threshold 0.5 policy, the reference value is 20.250 with Monte
Carlo standard error 0.030. Never acting has value 19.493; their paired
reference difference is 0.756 with Monte Carlo standard error 0.014. In the
baseline, weighting has estimated bias -0.035 with Monte Carlo standard
error 0.142. The complete-case calculation overstates value by 1.915
(Monte Carlo standard error 0.083). This distortion comes from selection,
not from a language or interface difference.

\begin{table}[htbp]
\centering\small
\begin{tabular}{lrrrr}
\toprule
Case & Weighted bias & Complete-case bias & Fitted bias & Coverage \\
\midrule
Baseline & -0.035 & 1.915 & -0.006 & 0.950 \\
Wider assignment range & -0.053 & 1.987 & -0.025 & 0.950 \\
Future-dependent dropout & -1.874 & 3.036 & 1.773 & 0.800 \\
Omitted state predictor & 0.117 & 1.872 & -0.281 & 0.930 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Generated threshold 0.5 policy, 200 replications per case. Coverage
is for the normal prefix-weighted interval against the numerical reference;
fitted g-computation has no reported confidence interval. Bias is in
illustrative reward units, not currency.}
\end{table}

Baseline weighted coverage is 0.950, with a Monte Carlo standard error of
0.015 and a Wilson interval approximately [0.910, 0.973]. This is compatible
with the nominal rate, not a precise calibration certificate. Average
effective sample sizes fall from about 320 at the first reward to 97 and
29 at the later rewards. The average interval width is 8.047, far larger
than the policy improvement of 0.756. A positive lower bound for the paired
improvement appears in only 3.5\% of baseline replications. Correct weighting
therefore leaves an information problem even in this favourable construction.

With future-dependent dropout, the weighted bias is -1.874 (Monte Carlo
standard error 0.125), and coverage falls to 0.800. Its Monte Carlo Wilson
interval is approximately [0.739, 0.850]. Allowing for reference values within
their separate 95\% numerical band gives coverage bounds of [0.790, 0.820].
The failure is not explained by reference simulation noise. Fitted
g-computation is biased in the opposite direction, by about 1.773. The
observation problem affects both approaches.

When the state regression omits $X$, its estimated bias is -0.281 (Monte
Carlo standard error 0.033). Weighting still uses the correct observed-history
probabilities in that case. This is a useful distinction: a model can fail
because its transition equation is wrong, because its observation mechanism
is wrong, or because too few informative trajectories remain. These failures
call for different repairs.

The separately selected threshold has average regret about 0.248 relative
to the finite candidate list in the baseline. Selection is therefore not
equivalent to finding the best policy even when evaluation is kept separate.
The reference values nominate threshold 1 within this list; they establish
no universal policy optimum. This study does not rank viable estimators by
a few realised errors or declare that a single fitted model is generally
superior.

\section{What the next prototype must learn}
The bank needs to know why a customer's record ends, what was available at
each action, and whether all relevant actions had a reasonable chance of
being taken. More complete outcome follow-up or an audit sample can address
missing information. More representative action variation can improve
support. A better state model can help prediction, but it cannot by itself
recover outcomes selected by an unobserved future shock.

The software implication is concrete. Preserve the initial denominator,
reward-specific weights, information dates and policy-selection split; show
effective information and sensitivity alongside the effect. A commercial or
open-source implementation should be compared on these same meanings. A
successfully executed policy-value calculation does not settle the scientific
conditions that make it useful. Here the next experiment should test those
conditions before seeking a costly bank pilot.

chapters.title: A narrower policy interval can be more confidently wrong

segments.text:
\chapter{A narrower policy interval can be more confidently wrong}
\label{gap29:policy-uncertainty}
The servicing example leaves a natural question. If a fitted transition
model uses the observed histories more efficiently than weighting, can it
give an informative interval for the gain from intervention? The answer
depends on why outcomes are missing and whether the state equation is
adequate. Resampling quantifies variation in an estimated model; it does
not establish the model's economic assumptions.

\section{Follow the customer through the calculation}
The follow-up study uses the same three-decision economy as
Chapter~\ref{gap29:servicing}. It selects a threshold policy on 2,000
training customers and evaluates that fixed choice on 1,000 independent
customers. Each of 199 bootstrap draws resamples whole evaluation
customers, including their observation histories, and refits both
transition coefficients and innovation variance.

For a plug-in value estimate $\widehat V$ and bootstrap quantiles
$q^*_{.025},q^*_{.975}$, the basic interval is
$[2\widehat V-q^*_{.975},\,2\widehat V-q^*_{.025}]$.
The improvement over never acting is calculated within the same simulated
paths and resampled customers before forming its interval. Pairing retains
the covariance between policy values. No separate censoring model is fitted:
under the baseline's conditional independence, the observed transition
regression can estimate the common transition law. The adverse dropout case
violates precisely that premise.

The selected policy is held fixed during evaluation resampling. Its target
is the value of the policy selected on that separate training sample.
Repeating selection across independent experimental replications changes
the target accordingly, and each result is compared with the reference for
its selected policy. This is different from estimating the performance of
an entire future retraining procedure.

The study uses 100 independent replications in each of three cases, with a
separate million-trajectory reference. The initial-state distribution and
reward equation are supplied by the construction. Their estimation
uncertainty is consequently absent. Numerical integration uses 8,192
scrambled low-discrepancy normal paths shared across fits and bootstrap
draws. Eight separate scrambles at the true parameters check sensitivity
to numerical integration; parameter uncertainty remains a separate source
of variation. Across those eight scrambles, standard deviations are below
0.010 reward units for values and 0.009 for improvements. This observed
sensitivity is small relative to the statistical widths reported here; it
is not a uniform integration-error bound for every fitted parameter.

\section{Precision under a maintained assumption}
For the separately selected policy, the baseline interval for improvement
has empirical coverage 94\%, with Monte Carlo standard error 2.4 percentage
points. Its average width is 0.711 reward units. The matched weighting
interval has coverage 98\% and width 6.905. The difference in width is
descriptive evidence of what the parametric restrictions buy; the sample
of replications does not establish exact calibration or general superiority.
Three bootstrap coverage decisions lie near the separate reference's
numerical uncertainty band.

A positive lower bound for improvement occurs in 79\% of baseline fitted
analyses and 2\% of the weighted analyses. This is a decision frequency,
not by itself a measure of safety. The selected list includes an unprofitable
threshold in seven of the 100 training samples. Evaluation must preserve
the selected target and the possibility of a poor selection.

\section{Why the apparently useful interval can fail}
\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=.95\textwidth]{scientific-gap-closure/2026-10-29/policy-coverage.pdf}
\caption{Coverage of the separately selected policy's improvement, 100
independent replications per case. Bars are Wilson intervals for Monte Carlo
coverage uncertainty. Numerical-reference uncertainty is reported separately.
Narrow fitted intervals rely on correct observation and transition assumptions.}
\end{figure}
When dropout depends on the unseen next shock, the fitted value interval
covers its reference in none of the 100 replications. The fitted interval
for improvement covers in only 6\%, with Monte Carlo standard error
2.4 percentage points. Its bias is $+1.175$ (Monte Carlo standard error
$0.052$), and its average width is 1.140. Every fitted analysis has a
positive lower bound for improvement, including selections of an
unprofitable threshold. A compelling-looking decision can therefore be
an artefact of the observation process.

The weighted improvement interval covers in 96\% in that case, but has
bias about $+0.498$ and average width 6.348. Its value interval covers only
73\%. Cancellation and imprecision in a difference can mask biased value
estimates. The apparently satisfactory improvement coverage does not
validate the false observation model.

Omitting $X$ from the transition regression produces a different failure:
coverage for improvement falls to 61\%, with Monte Carlo standard error
4.9 percentage points. The estimated bias is $-0.253$ (Monte Carlo standard
error $0.019$), despite an average interval width of 0.689.
Resampling the fitted omission repeats it.

The calculation supports a conditional use of model-based precision and a
clear reason to test the observation and state assumptions before relying
on it. An outcome audit, better follow-up or a richer measured history can
change those assumptions' credibility. More bootstrap draws alone cannot.
These results remain a generated research comparison with known reward
and initial laws; a bank application needs its own economic specification,
sampling argument and measurement evidence.

chapters.title: Panel data: heterogeneity, timing and structural moments

segments.text:
\chapter{Panel data: heterogeneity, timing and structural moments}
\label{r3:panels}
\section{Repeated measurements do not specify the identification strategy}
A panel of branch deposits can support several different questions.
One can model a homogeneous response to price after removing stable
branch differences, identify an adoption-cohort effect from untreated
trends, fit an interactive-factor counterfactual, or estimate a dynamic
equation using lagged instruments. All use a rectangular data set;
their counterfactual assumptions are different.

Let $i=1,\ldots,N$ index branches and $t=1,\ldots,T$ calendar periods.
Write $Y_{it}(\bar a_t)$ for the outcome under an action history.
The shorter $Y_{it}(a_t)$ assumes away carryover. Let $G_i$ be the
first adoption date only when an absorbing intervention makes that
description meaningful. A price that rises and falls, a repeated
collections action and a permanent branch rollout do not share the
same treatment history merely because each is coded as a binary column.
\citet[Sections 2--4]{panelreview2024} emphasizes assignment pattern,
potential-outcome dynamics and the relative sizes of $N,T$ as distinct
organizing dimensions.

Banking measurements also change composition. Branch closure can remove
a low-performing unit, household transfers can move balances between
branches, and a merger can change the entity represented by an identifier.
An unbalanced panel is not automatically missing at random. The outcome
and unit definitions of Chapter~\ref{r3:graphs} remain part of the
panel estimand.

\section{Fixed effects remove a component, not all confounding}
\label{r3:panel-fe}
Consider the static linear structural specification
\begin{equation}
 Y_{it}=\alpha_i+\lambda_t+\beta A_{it}+X_{it}'\gamma+u_{it}.
 \label{r3:static-panel}
\end{equation}
The interpretation of $\beta$ as a common causal response requires
linearity, absence of omitted carryover and an invariant outcome
equation. A sufficient mean restriction for the within estimator is
strict exogeneity,
\[
 \E[u_{it}\mid \alpha_i,A_{i1:T},X_{i1:T}]=0
 \quad\text{for every }t,
\]
with common time components treated appropriately. This permits
$\alpha_i$ to correlate with the entire action/covariate history.
It rules out current shocks predicting future actions after conditioning
on the specified regressors. For example, an unexpected deposit outflow
that causes next month's retention offer threatens strict exogeneity,
even if the offer cannot affect past outcomes.

For a balanced panel, two-way demeaning gives
$\ddot A_{it}=A_{it}-\bar A_{i\cdot}-\bar A_{\cdot t}+\bar A$,
and analogously for $Y,X,u$. The stable branch effect and common time
effect vanish. Frisch--Waugh residualization by $\ddot X$ then gives
\[
 \widehat\beta-\beta
 =\frac{\sum_{it}\widetilde A_{it}\ddot u_{it}}
        {\sum_{it}\widetilde A_{it}^2}.
\]
Identification needs the numerator's mean restriction and nonzero
residual variation; the data transformation supplies neither.
For unbalanced panels, projecting on actual entity and time design
matrices replaces this simple double-demeaning formula. Treating
missing cells as zero changes that projection.

\subsection{Random and correlated effects change the restrictions}
Random-effects GLS uses between-unit as well as within-unit variation.
In the elementary model with $\alpha_i$ independent of regressors,
$\Var(\alpha_i)=\sigma_\alpha^2$ and independent homoskedastic
$u_{it}$, the within-unit covariance is
$\Omega_i=\sigma_u^2I_T+\sigma_\alpha^2\mathbf1\mathbf1'$.
Its eigenvalue in the constant direction is
$\sigma_u^2+T\sigma_\alpha^2$, and in the remaining directions
it is $\sigma_u^2$. Hence, up to a common scale, GLS quasi-demeans
each variable as $x_{it}-\vartheta\bar x_i$, with
\[
 \vartheta=1-\sqrt{\frac{\sigma_u^2}{\sigma_u^2+T\sigma_\alpha^2}}.
\]
This project covariance derivation explains its efficiency gain under
the stronger mean model and its exposure to confounding between units.

A correlated-effects specification instead posits, for example,
$\E[\alpha_i\mid A_{i1:T},X_{i1:T}]
=c+\delta\bar A_i+\bar X_i'\pi$ and adds those means to the
regression. It permits a particular dependence on histories while
restricting its functional form. It does not make arbitrary adaptive
assignment ignorable. Nonlinear models also introduce an incidental
parameter issue when one estimates many unit intercepts with small
$T$; removing linear means is not a general nonlinear solution
\citep[Sections 2 and 3]{panelreview2024}.

\section{Dynamics turn lagged outcomes into endogenous regressors}
\label{r3:dynamic-panel}
Consider
\begin{equation}
 Y_{it}=\rho Y_{i,t-1}+\beta A_{it}+\alpha_i+\lambda_t+u_{it}.
 \label{r3:dynamic-panel-model}
\end{equation}
Even if $u_{it}$ is a martingale difference relative to past outcomes,
the within transform of $Y_{i,t-1}$ contains earlier innovations
also present in the within transform of the error. Differencing gives
\[
 \Delta Y_{it}=\rho\Delta Y_{i,t-1}+\beta\Delta A_{it}
                        +\Delta\lambda_t+\Delta u_{it}.
\]
In the simplest case with no action, $\alpha_i=0$, $Y_{i0}=0$
and independent unit-variance $u_{i1},u_{i2}$, the two-period
regression uses $\Delta Y_{i1}=u_{i1}$ and
$\Delta Y_{i2}=(\rho-1)u_{i1}+u_{i2}$. Its population coefficient
is $\rho-1$, not $\rho$. More branches do not remove this short-panel
bias. This exact construction illustrates the problem without claiming
that its numerical bias formula applies at arbitrary $T$.

\subsection{The valid lag is determined by a moment restriction}
If innovations are serially uncorrelated and initial observations are
orthogonal to future innovations, then for appropriate $s\le t-2$
\begin{equation}
 \E[Y_{is}(u_{it}-u_{i,t-1})]=0.
 \label{r3:ab-moments}
\end{equation}
By contrast, $Y_{i,t-1}$ contains $u_{i,t-1}$ and is not a valid
instrument for the differenced equation. For action regressors, strictly
exogenous $A_{is}$ can supply all date moments. Predetermined actions
orthogonal to current/future innovations can supply $s\le t-1$;
actions correlated with current innovations require earlier valid
lags, typically $s\le t-2$ under the corresponding sequential
restriction. These are assumptions about the assignment/error clock,
not a software convention about lag length.

Stack valid instruments in $Z_i$ and differenced structural residuals
in $\Delta u_i(\theta)$, with $\theta=(\rho,\beta,\ldots)$.
The GMM criterion is
\[
 \widehat\theta=\arg\min_\theta
 \left\{N^{-1}\sum_i Z_i'\Delta u_i(\theta)\right\}'\widehat W
 \left\{N^{-1}\sum_i Z_i'\Delta u_i(\theta)\right\}.
\]
This is the moment-estimation framework of
\citet[Section 2, equations (2)--(6)]{arellano1991}. Its sampling
unit is an independent individual time series, with fixed $T$ in the
main argument. Differenced white-noise innovations have first-order
covariance $-\sigma_u^2$ and zero covariance at lag two; thus first-order
correlation in differenced residuals is expected, whereas a second-order
correlation diagnostic probes a key validity restriction. The paper's
Section 3 derives the test and its estimation corrections. Failure to
reject does not establish the exclusion of a bank's omitted policy
response or measurement process.

Persistent balances can make lagged levels weak instruments for
changes. A large menu of lags can also create many moments relative to
the number of independent branches. The weak-IV discussion then
matters inside the panel estimator. Extra level-equation moments, for
example $\E[\Delta Y_{i,t-1}(\alpha_i+u_{it})]=0$, require additional
initial-condition/mean-stationarity restrictions; they do not follow
from Equation~\eqref{r3:ab-moments}. A product option that adds such
moments must expose those extra restrictions explicitly. Section~\ref{s5:dynamic-panel} develops the additional initial-law
argument and GMM covariance, and distinguishes the implemented first-order
sandwich from an unimplemented finite-sample correction.

\section{Difference-in-differences identifies an untreated evolution}
\label{r3:did-identification}
In a two-period rollout let $D_i$ indicate treatment in the second
period and assume no one is treated in the first. For this subsection
write $\Delta Y=Y_1-Y_0$. Under no anticipation,
\[
 \operatorname{ATT}=\E[Y_1(1)-Y_1(0)\mid D=1].
\]
Conditional parallel trends imposes
\begin{equation}
 \E[Y_1(0)-Y_0(0)\mid D=1,X]
 =\E[Y_1(0)-Y_0(0)\mid D=0,X]=m_0(X).
 \label{r3:parallel-trends}
\end{equation}
It does not require equality of untreated levels. Subtract the
counterfactual untreated change within the treated population to get
\begin{equation}
 \operatorname{ATT}=\E[\Delta Y-m_0(X)\mid D=1].
 \label{r3:did-functional}
\end{equation}
This is a different identification route from
$Y(a)\perp A\mid X$ or sequential randomization. Neither implies
the other in general. Differencing can remove a stable latent level,
but not an unmeasured shock whose differential trend also drives
adoption. Adding a post-rollout balance to $X$ can additionally change
the causal conditioning set.

Let $p(X)=P(D=1\mid X)$ and $p_D=P(D=1)>0$. With overlap for
the control group on the treated covariate support,
\begin{equation}
 \operatorname{ATT}
 =\frac1{p_D}\E\!\left[
 \left\{D-(1-D)\frac{p(X)}{1-p(X)}\right\}
                       \{\Delta Y-m_0(X)\}\right].
 \label{r3:did-dr}
\end{equation}
Conditioning on $X$ proves the formula. If a candidate $m$ equals
$m_0$, its control residual has zero mean for any candidate propensity.
If a candidate propensity equals $p$, its weighting balances the
$X$ terms, cancelling an arbitrary candidate $m$. More precisely,
using candidates $\widetilde p,\widetilde m$ and the true normalizer,
the bias is
\[
 \frac1{p_D}\E\!\left[
 \frac{\widetilde p-p}{1-\widetilde p}
                         (\widetilde m-m_0)\right].
\]
This reconstructs the mechanism of the outcome, weighting and
DR representations in \citet[Section 2.4 and Theorem 1]{callaway2021}.
Estimated normalizers and aggregation weights also enter its sampling
influence function. A generic ATE standard-error routine does not
automatically supply ATT or event-study inference.

\section{Staggered adoption requires explicit comparison groups}
\label{r3:staggered}
For absorbing adoption date $G_i=g$, define
$\operatorname{ATT}(g,t)=\E[Y_{it}(g)-Y_{it}(\infty)\mid G_i=g]$.
With no anticipation and valid conditional untreated trends, use
baseline $g-1$ and a comparison group $C_{g,t}$ that is untreated
through $t$. A never-treated group and a not-yet-treated group impose
different trend restrictions and offer different support. If effects
can begin $\delta$ periods before recorded adoption, use baseline
$g-\delta-1$ and controls unexposed to anticipation through the
comparison horizon. These are the separate Assumptions 3--6 and
identification routes in \citet{callaway2021}.

Apply Equation~\eqref{r3:did-functional} to each eligible group/time
comparison, with its own covariate overlap, outcome difference and
control law. Then state the aggregation. An event-time curve
$\sum_g w_{g,k}\operatorname{ATT}(g,g+k)$ can change composition
with $k$ because later cohorts lack long follow-up. A balanced-cohort
curve uses common cohorts and different information. The product must
return the cohort weights and supported horizons, not just a line
labelled ``dynamic effect.''

\subsection{A negative coefficient with positive effects everywhere}
Two-way fixed-effects regression projects treatment on unit/time
indicators and uses residual $\widetilde D_{it}$. If untreated outcomes
have that additive form and treatment effects are $\tau_{it}$, its
population coefficient in a fixed design is
\begin{equation}
 \beta_{\rm TWFE}
 =\sum_{it:D_{it}=1}\omega_{it}\tau_{it},\qquad
 \omega_{it}=\frac{\widetilde D_{it}}
 {\sum_{js:D_{js}=1}\widetilde D_{js}}.
 \label{r3:twfe-weights}
\end{equation}
The weights sum to one, but need not be positive. The identity follows
from projection orthogonality and
$\sum\widetilde D D=\sum\widetilde D^2$; it is a direct
decomposition, not a causal justification for the weights.

Take three equally weighted branches and four periods, with treatment
histories $(0,1,1,1)$, $(0,0,0,1)$ and $(0,0,0,0)$. Set all
untreated outcomes to zero. The four treated-cell effects, ordered by
early periods 2, 3, 4 and late period 4, are $(1,1,20,1)$.
The corresponding TWFE weights are $(0.3,0.3,-0.1,0.5)$, giving
$\beta_{\rm TWFE}=-0.9$ although every effect is positive.
The equally weighted treated-cell ATT is $23/4=5.75$.
Group/time differences against the never-treated branch recover the
four effects exactly in this noiseless construction. The example
isolates target weighting; it is not a small-sample noise effect.
The heterogeneous-effects issue and alternative constructions are
developed in \citet{callaway2021,panelreview2024}.

If actions can reverse, first-adoption coding discards part of the
intervention path. One may instead compare a switching group's
realized path after its first change with maintaining its initial
treatment, using groups with the same initial treatment that have not
yet switched. No anticipation and parallel evolution of these
status-quo outcomes are new restrictions. The intertemporal estimators
of \citet[Assumptions 1--2 and Section 3]{dechaisemartin2024} develop
that route and make normalization across treatment increments explicit.
It does not identify arbitrary histories without support. For repeated
feedback-driven banking actions, the longitudinal g-method route may
be more suitable when sequential covariates are observed; the choice
is about assumptions and target histories.

\section{Synthetic controls replace common trends by a factor restriction}
\label{r3:synthetic-control}
Suppose untreated outcomes obey
$Y_{it}(0)=\delta_t+\lambda_t' f_i+\varepsilon_{it}$, with
time-varying factors $\lambda_t$ and unit loadings $f_i$. A
time-invariant fixed effect is a special case. For one treated unit,
choose donor weights $w_j\ge0$, $\sum_jw_j=1$, using pre-intervention
outcomes and covariates only. The untreated prediction error is
\begin{equation}
 Y_{1t}(0)-\sum_jw_jY_{jt}(0)
 =\lambda_t'\!\left(f_1-\sum_jw_jf_j\right)
                 +\varepsilon_{1t}-\sum_jw_j\varepsilon_{jt}.
 \label{r3:synth-error}
\end{equation}
Exact loading balance removes the factor component at every time.
In a noiseless model, exact pretreatment fit identifies that balance
only when the preperiod factor matrix spans all relevant loading
directions. A factor emerging only after rollout defeats that inference.
This algebra explains the factor-model motivation and convex-hull
conditions in \citet[Section 2.2 and Appendix B]{abadie2010}.

For example, donors with loadings $0$ and $1$ cannot convexly match a
treated loading $2$. An unconstrained extrapolation can match it with
weights $(-1,2)$, at a different variance and robustness cost. A
penalized augmentation can reduce imbalance under an additional
outcome model, while an interactive-factor estimator estimates factors
and loadings directly. Those choices exchange interpolation stability
for model dependence; good pretreatment fit alone does not choose
between them. Donor contamination from a common promotion or balance
transfers also violates the required untreated donor interpretation.

With one treated region, placebo reassignment describes an inference
procedure only under an appropriate assignment or exchangeability
argument. It is not automatically an exact randomized-experiment
$p$-value. A historical fit across a handful of branches is likewise
not an independent sample of policy rollouts. The inferential regime
must be stated with the counterfactual model.

\section{Uncertainty follows the independent information, not the row count}
\label{r3:panel-inference}
For a differentiable estimating equation let $s_{it}$ be a scalar
linearized score. The variance of the sample mean is
\[
 \Var\!\left(\frac1{NT}\sum_{it}s_{it}\right)
 =\frac1{N^2T^2}\sum_{it,js}\Cov(s_{it},s_{js}).
\]
Clustering by unit retains within-unit terms but misses covariance
between branches facing common calendar shocks. Clustering by time
does the reverse. If dependence is permitted whenever either index
matches and absent otherwise, an inclusion--exclusion estimator adds
outer products of unit score sums and time score sums and subtracts
outer products of intersection-cell sums. This is a covariance model,
not a guarantee valid for arbitrary network or serial cross-unit
dependence.

For the exact random-effects score model
$s_{it}=a_i+b_t+\epsilon_{it}$ with mutually independent components,
\begin{equation}
 \Var(\bar s)=\frac{\sigma_a^2}{N}
             +\frac{\sigma_b^2}{T}
             +\frac{\sigma_\epsilon^2}{NT}.
 \label{r3:panel-information}
\end{equation}
Millions of branches cannot eliminate the finite-calendar uncertainty
represented by $\sigma_b^2/T$. If $b_t$ is serially dependent, replace
that term by $T^{-2}\sum_{t,s}\Cov(b_t,b_s)$. The period
clusters are no longer independent and a corresponding time-series
argument is needed. Nor does subtracting a common time effect remove
every common score component in a heterogeneous or nonlinear model.

Cross-fitting must respect the same structure. Holding out rows from
a customer leaves information from that customer's other periods in
training. Under two-way clustered sampling, a held-out rectangle can
train on observations outside both its row and column groups. The
multiway DML results of \citet[Assumptions 1--3, Theorems 1--2]{cluster2021}
require separately exchangeable, dissociated arrays, growing cluster
dimensions, score regularity and nuisance rates. Ordered banking time
series need not be separately exchangeable across calendar dates.
Those theorems cannot be invoked for serial dependence merely because
the software accepts two cluster identifiers.

\section{Choosing the panel target and its evidence}
A panel request must identify whether it targets a structural coefficient,
a cohort/time ATT, a path contrast or a donor-based counterfactual. It
must include the action's reversibility and carryover, the independent
unit, the time asymptotic regime, the treatment/control support and
the allowed common shocks. Fixed effects, lag instruments, trend
restrictions and factor balance are alternative pieces of scientific
evidence, not defaults inferred from the table's shape.

An eligible output preserves aggregation weights, unsupported horizons,
instrument restrictions, donor contamination checks and the covariance
construction. The bank can then distinguish an effect that changes
sign because of economics from a regression coefficient that changes
sign because it averages positive effects with negative weights.
That distinction is a prerequisite for financially meaningful
cross-application reuse.

Two comparisons make that choice concrete. The first asks what additional
initial-condition information justifies system moments, and shows how those
moments fail when that information is wrong. The second follows cohort
normalization into uncertainty, then contrasts a randomized donor test
with a temporal inference route for observational assignments.

\section{System moments, initial conditions and the practical panel choice}
\label{s5:dynamic-panel}
The difference equation removes an individual effect; it does not create a
strong instrument. This distinction matters for persistent loan balances or
capital ratios. Consider first the scalar model
\[
 y_{it}=\alpha_i+\rho y_{i,t-1}+v_{it},\qquad |\rho|<1,
 \quad \E[v_{it}\mid\alpha_i,y_{i1},v_{i2},\ldots,v_{i,t-1}]=0.
\]
Independent entities and fixed $T$ define the sampling experiment. For
$s\le t-2$, both $\E[y_{is}v_{it}]$ and $\E[y_{is}v_{i,t-1}]$ vanish, giving
$\E[y_{is}\Delta v_{it}]=0$. These are the differenced moments already
derived above \citep{arellano1991}. Their validity does not require the
initial observation to have the stationary distribution.

Level equations permit a different restriction. Write
$y_{i1}=\alpha_i/(1-\rho)+e_{i1}$. Then
\[
 \Delta y_{i2}=(\rho-1)e_{i1}+v_{i2},\qquad
 \E[\Delta y_{i2}\alpha_i]=0
 \quad\text{if }\E[e_{i1}\alpha_i]=0.
\]
The recursion
$\Delta y_{it}=\rho^{t-2}\Delta y_{i2}+
\sum_{j=0}^{t-3}\rho^j\Delta v_{i,t-j}$ propagates this zero covariance.
Consequently $\E[\Delta y_{i,t-1}(\alpha_i+v_{it})]=0$.
Combining these level moments with differenced moments yields system GMM.
Mean stationarity is sufficient for this construction; equality of initial
and limiting variances is not required. Conversely a portfolio assembled at
loan origination or after a balance-sheet repair may systematically start
above or below its entity-specific long-run level. The additional moment can
then fail even when the differenced moments remain valid. This reconstructs
the initial-condition argument in \citet[Sections 3.1--3.3, pp.107--109]{blundellbond2023}.
The archived text is their 2023 account, not the original 1998 article.

Adding $\beta x_{it}$ requires a separate classification for $x$.
Contemporaneous endogeneity excludes $x_{it}$ as an instrument; lagged levels
must precede both innovations in $\Delta v_{it}$. Predetermination and strict
exogeneity allow different lag sets. A level moment using $\Delta x_{i,t-1}$
also needs $\E[\Delta x_{i,t-1}\alpha_i]=0$ and orthogonality to $v_{it}$.
No initial-condition theorem for $y$ automatically supplies this condition
for a bank's chosen action. With common macro shocks, cross-entity
independence itself fails and the fixed-$T$, large-$N$ argument must change.

\subsection{Weighting, covariance and what a correction can repair}
Let $b_i-G_i\theta$ collect the entity's moments after any prespecified lag
restriction and compression, where $\theta=(\rho,\beta)'$. For a positive
weight $W$, the quadratic criterion has minimizer
\[
 \hat\theta_W=(\bar G'W\bar G)^{-1}\bar G'W\bar b,
 \quad
 \sqrt N(\hat\theta_W-\theta_0)=
 (G'WG)^{-1}G'W\,N^{-1/2}\sum_i(b_i-G_i\theta_0)+o_p(1).
\]
The expansion needs $\bar G\to G$, a moment CLT, a nonsingular $G'WG$,
and consistent $W$. Thus the covariance estimator is
\[
 \widehat{\Var}(\hat\theta_W)=N^{-1}
 (\bar G'W\bar G)^{-1}\bar G'W\hat\Omega W\bar G
 (\bar G'W\bar G)^{-1},
\]
where $\hat\Omega$ is the covariance of the entire entity moment vector,
not of individual entity-date rows. Two-step GMM takes
$W=\hat\Omega(\hat\theta_1)^{-1}$ using an initial consistent estimator.
The first-order limit omits uncertainty in that estimated weight because
the population moment is zero. The finite-sample derivative is nevertheless
nonzero:
\[
 d\hat\theta_2=(\bar G'W\bar G)^{-1}\bar G'(dW)
 (\bar b-\bar G\hat\theta_2),\qquad
 dW=-W(d\hat\Omega)W.
\]
This displays the term whose variation a finite-sample correction must
address. The 2023 primary account explains the Windmeijer correction and its
motivation \citep[Section 2.3, p.105]{blundellbond2023}. The transparent local
reference implements the first-order sandwich, \emph{not} that correction;
the correction's original paper has not been substituted by a metadata record.
A production two-step adapter needs a source-qualified implementation of the
correction or a separately justified complete-refit alternative. Neither can
make invalid moments valid or rescue a rank-deficient Jacobian.

Compression also changes a statistical problem. An unrestricted triangular
lag matrix has $(T-2)(T-1)/2$ instruments in the scalar differenced model.
The reference collapses moments over dates and keeps lags two and three,
yielding four differenced moments for $(y,x)$, or six after adding level
moments. Scaling moments by observed root mean squares changes the one-step
weight; it leaves the population zero restrictions unchanged. The code
therefore reports this estimator as scaled identity-weight GMM, not the
canonical homoskedastic optimal one-step estimator. Small objective values
with many instruments can reflect overfitting. An overidentification test
is neither proof of exclusion nor evidence of adequate instrument strength.

\subsection{A paired comparison and a banking decision rule}
The synthetic short-panel experiment uses $N=800$, eight transitions after
an initial observation, and
$y_{it}=\alpha_i+\rho y_{i,t-1}+.6x_{it}+v_{it}$, with
$x_{it}=.5x_{i,t-1}+.4v_{it}+\eta_{it}$. A 400-period burn-in generates
the regular initial law. The initial-condition challenger then adds a
multiple of $\alpha_i$ to the initial balance; the serial-error challenger
changes the innovation law. The four methods use identical datasets.
Coverage below is joint for both coefficients, using two-coordinate
Bonferroni 95\% intervals across 400 repetitions.
\begin{center}\small
\begin{tabular}{lrrrr}\toprule
Regime & Difference 1 & Difference 2 & System 1 & System 2\\\midrule
Stationary & .955 & .950 & .958 & .948\\
Persistent & .985 & .983 & .968 & .933\\
Initial departure & .950 & .960 & .033 & .000\\
Serial-error violation & .000 & .000 & .000 & .000\\\bottomrule
\end{tabular}\end{center}
One and two denote weighting steps, not different causal targets. Near
95\% coverage, the Monte Carlo standard error is about .011. The very high
coverage of a weak differenced design is not a precision advantage; weak
moments can produce broad intervals and unreliable normal approximations.
The initial-departure failure is the decisive exclusion from an automatic
system-GMM default. For established comparable entities, system moments can
be a challenger after a substantive initial-law argument. For new portfolios,
the primary differenced route has the weaker initial-law requirement, but
must still report Jacobian strength, instrument count and residual serial
correlation. If those fail, the result is an unsupported inferential claim,
not a prompt to search until a small standard error appears.

Misspecification-robust moment inference is another distinct alternative.
\citet[Sections 2--3, Assumptions 1--2]{kleibergen2021} targets the minimizer
of a continuously updated population GMM criterion when no parameter makes
all moments zero. Its joint moment/Jacobian CLT and covariance conditions
support an identification- and misspecification-robust score construction.
That pseudo-true minimizer need not equal a causal response or a meaningful
risk premium. This use of ``double robust'' concerns weak identification and
moment misspecification; it is different from outcome/propensity robustness
in Chapter~\ref{r3:learning}. The inspected copy is the 2021 preprint of work
identified in 2025 journal metadata. It is a substantive inference challenger,
not a license to keep a causal label after the identifying restrictions fail.

\section{Normalized cohort effects, aggregation and a selected donor test}
\label{s6:panel-influence}
The normalized representation in the earlier panel section has uncertainty
from both its numerators and its denominators. For a fixed cohort/date pair,
write $G$ for membership of the cohort, $C$ for eligible controls,
$D=Y_t-Y_{g-1}$, $p(x)=P(G=1\mid G+C=1,X=x)$ and
$m(x)=\E[D\mid C=1,X=x]$. Require disjoint $G,C$, no anticipation,
conditional parallel trends, overlap in the eligible population, and the
same cohort/calendar target as in \citet{callaway2021}. Other cohorts may
have $G=C=0$. Put $b=Cp/(1-p)$, $p_G=\E G$, $p_b=\E b$ and
\[
 \mu_G=\frac{\E[G(D-m)]}{p_G},\qquad
 \mu_b=\frac{\E[b(D-m)]}{p_b},\qquad \tau=\mu_G-\mu_b.
\]
At the true nuisances, $p_b=p_G$, $\mu_b=0$ and $\mu_G=\tau$.
The sample estimator normalizes each weighted mean separately. Holding
nuisances fixed, quotient differentiation yields
\begin{equation}
 \varphi_{gt}=
 \frac{G}{p_G}(D-m-\mu_G)
 -\frac{b}{p_b}(D-m-\mu_b).
 \label{s6:att-if}
\end{equation}
In particular, the treated term contains $-G\tau/p_G$. Centering an
unnormalized score after the fact does not reproduce this random-cohort
contribution.

At the true nuisances, the derivative in $m$ is
$-\E[G\,dm]/p_G+\E[b\,dm]/p_G=0$. The propensity derivative
multiplies a control residual of conditional mean zero, including the
normalizer derivative. These equalities justify the orthogonal influence
under cross-fitting and the appropriate product-rate conditions. With just
one nuisance correct, point consistency can survive, but those two
derivatives need not both vanish at the fitted limits. A doubly robust point
estimate is not automatically a doubly robust standard error; either obtain
the stronger rates/correct limits or include the first-stage influence of
the misspecified-limit procedure. Cluster the full influence by the actual
independent sampling unit. Many customers observed under one branch rollout
do not create independent branch assignments.

For an event-time average over a fixed eligible cohort set $\mathcal G$,
let $P=\sum_{g\in\mathcal G}p_g$ and
$\delta=\sum_gp_g\tau_{g,g+e}/P$. Its influence is
\begin{equation}
 \varphi_\delta=
 \sum_g\frac{p_g}{P}\varphi_{g,g+e}
 +\frac1P\sum_g G_g(\tau_{g,g+e}-\delta).
 \label{s6:aggregate-att-if}
\end{equation}
The second term accounts for estimated cohort shares. It disappears only
when those shares are fixed externally or the component effects coincide.
The first term is one sum on the same observation: controls reused across
cohorts create covariance. Forming a diagonal matrix of separately reported
standard errors loses that covariance. If eligibility itself is selected
using estimated effects, this fixed-set derivation is no longer applicable.
Financial exposure weighting adds the analogous derivative of estimated
exposures; externally fixed accounting weights use the full covariance of
the component effects without that extra term.

\subsection{What an exact synthetic-control inference route actually needs}
Synthetic-control weights interpolate pre-intervention outcomes, usually
under nonnegative weights summing to one. Their value depends on pre-fit,
factor balance, donor contamination and whether the treated unit is inside
the donor support \citep{abadie2010,abadie2021,benmichael2021,synthdid2021}.
A fitted counterfactual curve is not a confidence procedure by itself.
Consider one precise banking design: one of $J$ eligible regions is selected
uniformly for a sustained pilot, after the eligibility set and fitting
algorithm are fixed. Under the sharp null of no effect in every post-period,
the complete untreated outcome matrix is invariant to this assignment.

For each candidate treated region $j$, refit its donor weights using its
own pre-period and the remaining $J-1$ regions. Apply the same fixed
regularization and fit exclusions to every candidate. Compute a discrepancy
$T_j$, such as post-period mean squared gap divided by a pre-period error
with a fixed positive floor. With observed assignment $a$,
\[
 p_a=J^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^J\mathbf1\{T_j\ge T_a\}
\]
is super-uniform under the randomization: conditional on the fixed outcome
matrix, $a$ is uniform over the $J$ positions in its rank list. Ties make
the displayed test conservative. Serial correlation, common shocks and
weight estimation do not invalidate this finite assignment argument because
the whole paths are held fixed and the fitting algorithm is applied
symmetrically. Few eligible regions impose coarse attainable significance.

For a sharp constant additive effect $\tau$ in every post-period, subtract
$\tau$ from the actual treated path to impute the untreated matrix. For
each possible assignment add the hypothesized effect to that region, then
recompute the discrepancy centered on $\tau$, including its donor fit.
Inverting the resulting tests gives a confidence set for this \emph{sharp
constant-effect model}. It is not automatically an interval for an arbitrary
average treatment effect under heterogeneous post-period effects.

An observationally selected distressed bank is not uniformly randomized
among healthy donors. Its donor placebo ranks are then descriptive unless
another exchangeability/design argument is supplied. A residual-permutation
or Bayesian structural time-series route substitutes its own temporal or
prior/model restrictions; neither inherits the assignment proof. This is
why the product selects the above test for randomized regional pilots and
returns an explicit additional-design requirement for observational donor
studies. The method choice concerns the source of uncertainty, not a claim
that one donor-fitting algorithm is universally preferable.


A stronger temporal challenger is the null-imposed conformal construction
of \citet{conformal2022}. It imputes the hypothesized untreated outcome,
refits the counterfactual prediction under that null, and ranks its residual
discrepancy over a declared permutation group. Exact validity follows under
the required exchangeability and permutation-equivariant fitting. For
dependent observations, their Theorem 1 instead assumes a fixed postperiod
length, stationary mixing shocks with a bounded discrepancy density and
small prediction errors both on average and at the tested dates. Theorem 2
uses estimator stability plus a stationary exponentially mixing data law.
These are substantive ways to trade assignment information for temporal
prediction restrictions. Neither is a license to permute arbitrary
nonstationary bank residuals, and neither automatically changes a sharp
path hypothesis into the mean effect in Equation~\eqref{s6:aggregate-att-if}.
For an observational regional rollout this challenger can be selected only
after its null prediction and temporal restrictions are defended. The
randomized pilot route was selected here because its source of repeated
assignment is specified directly.

chapters.title: When a bank in the data ceases to be the same bank

segments.text:
\chapter{When a bank in the data ceases to be the same bank}
\label{gap29:funding}
A funding study follows institutions through time. Its economic interpretation
requires the deposit outcome and the exposure to refer to the same institution.
A fixed effect removes a persistent level difference; it cannot repair an outcome
assigned to the wrong institution. This distinction matters before a bank spends
money on a more elaborate covariance estimator.

\section{A controlled comparison}
The generated study follows 60 institutions for 20 dates. Exposure follows
$x_{i,t}=0.5x_{i,t-1}+v_{i,t}$, starting from zero, and the outcome is
\[
 y_{i,t}=\alpha_i+0.2\sin(t/3)+0.4x_{i,t}+u_{i,t}.
\]
The institution effects, exposure innovations and outcome disturbances are
independent standard normal draws. The target slope is therefore $0.4$ in this
specified economy. It is an illustrative response, not an estimated bank elasticity.
One alternative adds a common innovation with an institution-specific loading.
Another circularly reassigns the outcomes of five institutions after the tenth
date while leaving their exposures unchanged. The latter is an artificial
record error, not an authentic merger history.

There are 300 independent panels in each of the three cases. We compare a
pooled regression with a regression that removes institution and date means.
For the latter, the uncertainty calculations use observation-level HC2,
institution-clustered covariance, or the sum of institution and date cluster
covariances less the observation intersection. Reported intervals use the
normal critical value $1.96$. These are finite experiments with 20 dates, not
a general justification for that reference distribution.

\section{What changed the conclusion}
In clean panels, the pooled HC2 interval covers the target in $82.7\%$ of
requests. Within-institution and date adjustment gives $94.7\%$ with HC2 and
$94.3\%$ with institution clustering. Monte Carlo standard errors for these
coverage fractions are about 1.3--2.2 percentage points. Removing a nuisance
level and repairing a sampling calculation are different operations.

With reassigned outcomes, the within estimate has bias $-0.0170$, with Monte
Carlo standard error $0.00169$. Coverage is $90.7\%$ for HC2, $93.7\%$ for
institution clustering and $91.3\%$ for two-way clustering. The evaluator's
correct mapping gives bias $0.00102$ and institution-cluster coverage $95.0\%$.
The point is the remaining bias: a wider interval can sometimes cover a target
without restoring the meaning of the observation.

Under heterogeneous common shocks, the three within-regression coverage
fractions are $96.3\%$, $96.0\%$ and $94.0\%$. This construction does not show
that two-way clustering is universally preferable. One two-way variance is
nonpositive and is reported unavailable; it is included as a noncoverage in
the denominator of 300 requests. It is never clipped to manufacture an interval.

\section{The information worth obtaining}
An institution-history audit has a different value from another standard-error
option. A supplied warning identifies all 300 deliberately corrupted panels
and prompts refusal; this says nothing about a system's ability to discover an
unknown break. The next useful evidence would join exposures, outcomes and
institution histories using externally checked identifiers, then test whether
the estimated response survives the corrected economic unit.

The calculation was checked against an explicit regression with institution
and date indicator variables. Coefficients and all three covariance formulas
agree to better than $10^{-10}$ on the independent small-panel check. This
supports the reported arithmetic. It does not validate an unobserved bank's
history, guarantee finite-panel coverage, or establish a preferred estimator
outside the specified cases.

chapters.title: Time series, structural shocks and observation frequency

segments.text:
\chapter{Time series, structural shocks and observation frequency}
\label{r3:time-series}
\section{A temporal prediction is not yet a shock intervention}
In treasury and deposit management, a bank may ask how a policy-rate
shock changes balances over the next year. In collections it may ask
how repeated assistance changes repayment along a customer trajectory.
Both have time indices, but the interventions differ. A structural
macroeconomic shock perturbs one innovation while the system's other
mechanisms continue to respond. A sustained policy replaces a sequence
of decision rules. A forecast conditions on observed historical values.
These are different operations on a dynamic model.

Let $X_t$ be a vector of observed series and let $\mathcal F_t$ be
their observed past. Granger noncausality of series $X^j$ for $X^i$
is a restriction saying that removing the past of $X^j$ from the
conditioning information does not change the conditional law, or in
its mean version the conditional mean, of $X^i_t$. It is a property
of a specified information set. It acquires an intervention
interpretation only under extra conditions on hidden causes, timing,
instantaneous effects and structural innovations
\citep[Chapter 10, Section 10.3]{peters2017}.

For a simple counterexample, let independent $U_t$ cause
$X_t=U_t+\eta_t$ and $Y_{t+1}=U_t+\nu_{t+1}$, with independent
noise. The past of $X$ helps predict $Y$ even though intervening on
the measurement $X_t$ leaves $U_t$ and $Y_{t+1}$ unchanged.
Conversely, an entirely instantaneous effect of $X_t$ on $Y_t$ with
independent observations over time need not generate any predictive
benefit from lagged $X$. Neither failure is repaired by a more
accurate nonlinear prediction model.

\section{Reduced and structural dynamics contain different information}
\label{r3:svar}
Consider a stable reduced-form VAR(1),
\[
 X_t=FX_{t-1}+u_t,\qquad \E[u_tu_t']=\Sigma_u.
\]
Suppose a structural model writes $u_t=B\varepsilon_t$ with
independent, unit-variance structural shocks. Under causal autonomy,
the response at horizon $h$ to a unit shock in coordinate $j$ is
\begin{equation}
 \operatorname{IRF}_j(h)=F^hBe_j.
 \label{r3:structural-irf}
\end{equation}
Iterate the recursion after changing only $\varepsilon_{j,t}$ to
prove this formula. It presumes that $F$ and the other mechanisms
remain invariant. Imposing a new interest-rate rule changes a mechanism
and can change $F$; that policy counterfactual is not generally a
single historical impulse response.

Gaussian likelihood identifies $F$ and $BB'$, but for any orthogonal
$Q$, $BQ(BQ)'=BB'$. Independent Gaussian shocks remain independent
after rotation. Hence identical observational dynamics permit
different shock responses unless restrictions attach an economic
meaning to a particular column. For example, with
$F=\operatorname{diag}(0.7,0.4)$ and $\Sigma_u=I$, both $B=I$
and
\[
 B=\frac1{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&-1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}
\]
fit the same Gaussian process. The first shock affects only the first
series in one representation and both in the other. Normalizing its
impact on the first series to one gives horizon-$h$ second-series
responses $0$ and $0.4^h$. Even knowing the entire observed
distribution cannot choose that financial interpretation.

Recursive zero restrictions, externally justified instruments,
heteroskedastic regimes, sign restrictions and non-Gaussian independent
innovations use different information to restrict $B$. Sign restrictions
can leave a set of admissible rotations, so the target can remain set
identified. A prior over those rotations gives a model-dependent
distribution over the set; it does not turn the restrictions into a
