The first assistant should propose a diagram and competing explanations
for review, then call a named discovery or identification method under
explicit assumptions. Numerical discovery contributes its own evidence;
textual plausibility cannot turn an unresolved equivalence class into
a validated graph. The three-model pricing example is a useful adverse
case because one unjustified orientation changes the financial sign.

\section{What causal reasoning benchmarks establish}
\label{gap29:frontier}
A banking analyst asks several different questions of an assistant. Can it
translate a request for higher deposits into an intervention and a measurable
target? Can it distinguish information known before an offer from information
created by the offer? Can it explain which arrows in a diagram are assumptions,
and recognise when several diagrams fit the same observations? A correct
answer to a narrative puzzle is useful evidence about some of these abilities,
but it does not establish all of them.

\subsection{Explanations deserve their own test}
Wang and Shen examine three constructed scenarios: coin operations, interrupted
file downloads and a hypothetical vaccination calculation. Four variants of
each scenario and three prompting approaches give 36 prompt conditions.
Their scoring distinguishes a correct result and explanation, a flawed
explanation, and an incorrect result. This is valuable because a correct
number can accompany a mistaken economic argument. The study reports mixed
changes from examples and guided reasoning, rather than a uniformly helpful
prompting intervention. \citep{gap29wangshen}

The terms used in a benchmark also need scrutiny. The paper calls reasoning
from an observed effect to a cause \emph{actual causality}. That task description
does not, by itself, specify a formal criterion for an individual's actual
cause. Its smallpox case asks which source produces more deaths in a stipulated
population. With the given numbers, vaccination reactions produce
$990{,}000(0.01)(0.01)=99$ deaths, while disease among unvaccinated people
produces $10{,}000(0.02)(0.20)=40$. Those population counts differ from the
per-person risks, $0.0001$ and $0.004$. Confusing a total with a risk is an
estimand error; the arithmetic alone does not establish a general
Simpson-reversal mechanism. These are deductions from the paper's stated
example, not new medical evidence.

The banking analogue is direct. A large customer group can contribute more
defaults while offering a smaller default risk per account. A deposit offer
can increase gross balances without increasing net contribution. An assistant
should state the denominator and economic target before presenting the
answer. The paper's prompts provide useful stress cases for that distinction.
The small scenario set and model configurations do not support a current
ranking of assistants for banking work. We have inspected the published
methods and results; we have not reproduced its model calls or inspected every
supplementary response.

\subsection{Scale does not remove uncertainty about the answer key}
MDC-Bench broadens the comparison to 8,422 questions across seven disciplines,
including business, economics and management. Its tasks distinguish reasoning,
intervention, decision and counterfactual questions. Questions are constructed
from causal narratives extracted from preprints, with model-generated
alternatives and a manual sampling check. The published protocol identifies
model versions, prompt templates, temperature and output limits.
\citep[Sections 2--3 and Appendix A]{gap29mdc}

Its harder condition requires two ranked answers instead of one. For example,
the reported Claude thinking configuration has average accuracy 84.56\% in
the basic condition and 59.25\% in the harder condition. These are different
response requirements on the same benchmark; their difference is not a
measured deterioration in one fixed banking task. The benchmark is useful
for comparing errors by causal structure and question type, provided its
answer-generation assumptions remain visible.

The detailed prompts reveal an important distinction. Reverse reasoning may
use necessity and sufficiency, or otherwise select an abductive explanation
judged probable from background knowledge. Intervention questions construct
an altered causal narrative; the answer alternatives are ranked by their
judged plausibility. These procedures do not supply a known structural
equation system, a randomised treatment effect or an identified posterior
over causal diagrams. Appendix A's sampling review helps detect poor
questions but does not turn model-generated causal statements into independent
economic truth. The authors also discuss weak long-chain relations and
distractors that may be too easy. \citep[Limitations; Tables 28--29 and
39--40]{gap29mdc}

\subsection{An agent architecture still needs an identified effect}
Chen combines language models, diffusion models and interacting agents in a
study of climate-policy sentiment. Section 6 describes 43,943 tweets and
comparisons with topic, language and diffusion baselines. It reports F1,
AUC, causal-chain precision, counterfactual error and simulated intervention
outcomes. Table 4 removes individual components to examine their contribution.
These are reported results of the paper; the model was not reproduced
locally. \citep[Sections 5.6 and 6; Tables 1--4]{gap29chen}

The causal interpretation needs more than those comparisons. Equation (16)
factorises a joint distribution according to a graph. Equation (17) defines
a conditional treatment contrast. Neither statement alone identifies that
contrast from the observed tweets. Equation (19) compares predicted and
reference counterfactual outcomes, but its accompanying text allows the
reference to come from annotations or simulated baselines. Section 6.1 does
not supply enough detail to reconstruct an independently identified
counterfactual for each tweet. F1 and AUC assess labelled prediction; they
do not repair that missing identification argument.

The useful proposal lesson is to separate an architecture from the evidence
for a decision. A bank may test whether a language model helps extract a
policy variable or whether a simulator represents a declared mechanism.
It still needs a defensible treatment assignment, observation model and
counterfactual comparison before attributing a financial gain to the policy.
The reported architecture is a research lead. Its stated improvements are
not evidence that the proposed banking service already delivers causal or
commercial benefits.

\subsection{A useful banking comparison}
The proposal should use such benchmarks to diagnose formulation and reasoning
failures, then add tasks whose consequences can be checked independently.
A compact questionnaire and an executable calculation are necessary
comparators. For a deposit question, all methods should receive the same
decision date, eligibility rule, alternative offer and contribution definition.
For servicing, all should see the same observed history and reasons for
dropout. For a diagram, an admissible set should remain admissible when the
observations cannot orient an edge.

The resulting assessment has distinct outcomes: whether the target is correct,
whether a proposed adjustment is justified, whether an unknown effect remains
unknown, whether the numerical calculation is correct, and how much analyst
time the assistance saves. Independent adjudication is needed for open-ended
economic formulations. Generated cases with known mechanisms can test
specific errors before an expensive bank exercise. The public experimental,
servicing and linkage studies in this volume provide numerical cases of that
kind, but no live assistant has yet been evaluated on them.

The inspected papers therefore sharpen the proposed experiment rather
than establishing a benefit from the proposed service. Repeated agreement
among prompts is especially weak evidence when their errors share a source,
as the repeated-measurement calculation shows. The useful next comparison
measures consequential mistakes and time on held-out tasks, with human
adjudication and a fixed cost allowance.

\section{A positive workflow result and its limits}
The retained ORCA study gives a more direct reason to test assistance in a
completed workflow. Twelve participants used a counterbalanced within-subjects
design; the baseline assistant already had tools, step gates and minimal
state. The paper's Figure 5 reports total task durations of 1,395 seconds
for the baseline and 1,107 seconds for ORCA, a reported reduction of about
21\%. Table 1 reports completion rates 0.75 and 0.83. This is positive
published evidence for a structured workflow on the study's relational,
generated causal tasks. It is not a measured benefit for this banking
proposal. \citep[pp.~3--5]{exec13_census_orca}

The interpretation changes when the outcome definitions and all attempted
analyses are retained. Completion means producing an ATE, regardless of
accuracy; discovery success requires the treatment and outcome nodes to be
present. The paper's confidence-interval metric is described as an estimated
ATE falling within a ground-truth interval, so its reported 0.083 and 0.50
must not be presented as conventional repeated-sample confidence coverage.
The full-data condition comparison for absolute ATE error has $p=0.321$;
after excluding configuration-error outliers, the reported OLS comparison
has $p=0.020$. Both belong in an assessment of completed work because
configuration errors are among the failures a service is supposed to avoid.
The abstract's claimed 42-percentage-point completion gain also differs
from the displayed 0.75-to-0.83 comparison; this synthesis uses the stated
table comparison rather than reconciling that discrepancy by invention.
\citep[pp.~1, 5, 17--18]{exec13_census_orca}

The proposal should therefore test whether shared intermediate results and
question clarification save full effort while preserving scientific quality.
It should retain all configuration failures and report separately the time
spent by the analyst, tool execution and correction. The external study
supports that experiment's plausibility. Its small participant sample,
specified tasks, outcome definitions and analysis exclusions prevent a
claim that the same benefit is established across bank studies.

\section{Identification, execution and reporting}
CLadder evaluates formal causal questions under constructed mechanisms;
its reported results concern historical models and that supplied task.
It does not measure elicitation of a new bank mechanism.
\citep{v12_la_2312_04350}
For identification, compare assistance with a defined formal procedure,
requiring the assistant to preserve both the answer and its conditions.
An appropriate refusal must explain the missing restriction, not simply
return an empty result. The benchmark literature and the retained
mechanism-clustering critiques give reasons to keep failed cases and
uncertainty denominators in the evaluation.

For execution, the existing local interface study shows equality for four
constructed requests, not model-driven analysis quality. A scripted
workflow is the credible baseline. Compare any assistant on request
construction, faithful tool use, errors detected and correction effort.
Do not give it credit for a calculation performed by the formal tool
while omitting the costs of choosing or correcting the request.

For reporting, a deterministic template is a strong comparator because
it can already state the estimand, assumptions, interval and scope.
The assistant's proposed value is explaining why the result changes a
decision or why it cannot yet support one. Check that explanation
against the actual result and the retained sources. A report that turns
a set crossing zero into a positive recommendation fails even if its
prose is persuasive. No local live-model evaluation establishes an
incremental benefit for this reporting task.

The preferred first assisted task is therefore question clarification
with evidence retrieval and explicit alternatives, evaluated against
the questionnaire. Identification and numerical results remain delegated
to defined procedures. Expansion to autonomous discovery, variable
construction or recommendations requires task-specific evidence. The
frontier evidence includes the three additional inspected originals discussed
in Section~\ref{gap29:frontier}. The current census is 85 inspected and
28 unread; these omissions still limit broad claims. A live comparison still
requires a fixed model version, held-out questions, matched information,
independent adjudication and a budget.

chapters.title: When a statistical difference changes a banking decision

segments.text:
\chapter{When a statistical difference changes a banking decision}
\label{scisyn:evidence}

The case for a shared analytical service is strongest when it prevents a
material mistake, exposes a valuable uncertainty or makes a defensible study
less costly. The following examples examine those propositions directly.
They are project-generated calculations, not measurements of bank returns or
claims of superiority over an installed commercial system. A fixed design
specifies the scenarios and comparisons before the simulation is run.

\section{A precise answer to the wrong offer question}
Consider an illustrative portfolio with equal proportions of two observed
customer strata, $S=0$ and $S=1$. An offer has no effect in the first stratum
and increases the outcome by 100 USD in the second. Potential outcomes are
\[
 Y(a)=50S+100Sa+\varepsilon,\qquad \varepsilon\sim N(0,50^2).
\]
Customers are independent. The offer is assigned using only $S$, with probability
$e(0)=1/2$ and $e(1)\in\{1/2,1/10,1/50\}$. The assignment is independent of
the potential-outcome noise conditional on $S$. The population average benefit
is 50 USD. The stipulated cost of a universal offer is 40 USD, leaving 10 USD
per eligible customer. These monetary values are illustrative assumptions.

The first estimator regresses residual outcomes on residual treatment using
the exact conditional means. This favourable assumption removes nuisance-model
error so that the comparison isolates the final constant-effect restriction.
The second estimates a treatment contrast separately within each stratum and
averages the two contrasts with the known population shares. Both use the same
observations. The residual estimate uses a heteroskedastic sandwich variance;
the stratified estimate uses independent-cell sample variances. Each interval
uses a normal critical value. A stratified estimate is unavailable if any of
its four cells has fewer than two observations.

The residual projection targets
\[
 \theta_*(e)=\frac{100e(1-e)}{1/4+e(1-e)}.
\]
It equals 50 under equal assignment probabilities, $450/17\simeq26.47$ when
$e=1/10$, and about 7.27 when $e=1/50$. The second estimator continues to target
50 whenever its contrasts are estimable. The projection formula follows from
the residual-regression objective inspected in the EconML comparison; the
experiment here is an independently written reference calculation, not an
EconML execution or a claim about every estimator in that package.
\citep{exec19_econml_source}

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\begin{tikzpicture}[x=17cm,y=.065cm,>=Stealth,font=\small]
\draw[->] (0,0)--(.54,0) node[right]{$e(1)$};
\draw[->] (0,0)--(0,62) node[above]{USD};
\draw[dashed,ink] (0,50)--(.5,50);
\draw[dotted,gray] (0,40)--(.5,40);
\draw[thick,teal,domain=.001:.5,samples=70] plot (\x,{100*\x*(1-\x)/(.25+\x*(1-\x))});
\foreach \x in {.1,.2,.3,.4,.5}{\draw (\x,0)--(\x,-1);\node[below] at (\x,-1){\x};}
\node[left] at (0,50){50};\node[left] at (0,40){40};
\node[above] at (.34,51){Population benefit};
\node[below] at (.36,39){Stipulated offer cost};
\node[above,align=center] at (.15,16){Constant residual\\projection};
\end{tikzpicture}
\caption{A restricted projection changes with the assignment probabilities
even though the population's causal benefit remains 50. Exact constructed
example with equally likely strata and effects 0 and 100.}
\label{scisyn:projection-figure}
\end{figure}

There are 500 replications for each of six scenarios, crossing sample sizes
500 and 2,000 with the three assignment probabilities. The fixed seed is
20261029. Table~\ref{scisyn:offer-results} reports the observed results.
The maximum Monte Carlo standard error of any displayed conditional proportion
is about 0.023; a proportion near 0.95 has a standard error of about 0.010 when
all 500 replications are available. A zero observed failure frequency does not
prove that the true probability is zero.

\begin{table}[htbp]
\centering\small
\begin{tabular}{rrlrrrr}
\toprule
$n$ & $e(1)$ & Method & Mean & ATE cover & Reject & Fail \\
\midrule
500 & 0.50 & Constant projection & 50.3 & 0.944 & 0.030 & 0 \\
500 & 0.50 & Stratum standardisation & 50.3 & 0.942 & 0.018 & 0 \\
500 & 0.10 & Constant projection & 26.3 & 0.044 & 0.988 & 0 \\
500 & 0.10 & Stratum standardisation & 49.8 & 0.940 & 0.070 & 0 \\
500 & 0.02 & Constant projection & 7.5 & 0.000 & 1.000 & 0 \\
500 & 0.02 & Stratum standardisation & 49.8 & 0.892 & 0.223 & 11 \\
2000 & 0.50 & Constant projection & 50.1 & 0.932 & 0.000 & 0 \\
2000 & 0.50 & Stratum standardisation & 50.0 & 0.954 & 0.000 & 0 \\
2000 & 0.10 & Constant projection & 26.4 & 0.000 & 1.000 & 0 \\
2000 & 0.10 & Stratum standardisation & 50.0 & 0.962 & 0.000 & 0 \\
2000 & 0.02 & Constant projection & 7.3 & 0.000 & 1.000 & 0 \\
2000 & 0.02 & Stratum standardisation & 50.0 & 0.948 & 0.056 & 0 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Project-generated offer study. True population benefit is 50 and
stipulated cost is 40 illustrative USD per customer. Coverage and rejection
frequencies condition on an available estimate; Fail counts unavailable
replications out of 500. These are independent reference calculations,
not outputs from an external causal package.}
\label{scisyn:offer-results}
\end{table}

At $n=2{,}000$ and $e(1)=0.1$, the mean projection is 26.447. Its interval covers
its own target in 97.2 percent of replications, but covers the population ATE in
none. A decision rule that wrongly treats it as the population benefit rejects
the profitable universal offer in all 500 replications. Stratum standardisation
averages 50.011, covers the ATE in 96.2 percent and makes no such point-rule
rejections in that scenario. Increasing precision around a different estimand
does not repair the economic interpretation.

The second estimator is not an unconditional winner. At $n=500$ and $e(1)=0.02$,
it is unavailable in 11 of 500 replications. Among the remaining 489, its normal
interval covers the ATE only 89.2 percent of the time, and its point estimate
falls below cost in 22.3 percent. Counting unavailable intervals as noncoverage
gives 87.2 percent. This is a useful adverse result: specifying the right target
does not guarantee accurate small-sample inference when treatment support is
weak. The proposal should report both the target and the information available
for estimating it, including failures.

The practical recommendation is narrow. Before comparing packages, require
the analysis to state whether it reports a population average, a conditional
effect or a projection. Compare the simplest estimator answering that question.
Where a subgroup is rarely treated, consider a narrower eligible population,
a better-designed pilot or an explicitly more conservative uncertainty method.
Those changes alter the proposed study and should be explained to its sponsor.

\section{A remedy can exchange precision for assumptions}
The adverse small-cell finding motivates a second, separately specified
experiment. It uses new random draws with $n=500$ and $e(1)=0.02$, 3,000
replications per scenario and seed 2026102902. In the first scenario all four
treatment-by-stratum cells have outcome standard deviation 50. In the second,
the rarely treated $S=1,A=1$ cell has standard deviation 150 while the other
three remain at 50. Assignment is still independent of potential-outcome noise
within stratum, and the ATE remains 50. The second scenario tests an assumption
used by one proposed remedy; it does not change the target.

Three intervals use the same stratum-standardised point estimate. The first is
the original normal Wald interval. The second pools the four within-cell
variances and uses a Student critical value with $n-4$ degrees of freedom.
Conditional on the counts, independent normal observations with a common
variance justify that pooled interval. The third constructs a two-sided Student
interval with error probability $0.05/4$ for each cell mean and combines the
four intervals with the contrast weights $(-1/2,1/2,-1/2,1/2)$. If $r_j$ is
the half-width for cell $j$, the half-width for the contrast is
$\sum_{j=1}^4 |w_j|r_j$. A union bound gives coverage of at least 95 percent
conditional on the counts under independent normal observations, allowing
different variances across cells. It is deliberately conservative.

\begin{table}[htbp]\centering\small
\begin{tabular}{llrrr}
\toprule
Noise scenario & Interval & Coverage & Mean width & Recommend offer \\
\midrule
Equal variance & Normal Wald & 0.876 & 44.7 & 0.195 \\
Equal variance & Pooled Student & 0.947 & 48.1 & 0.140 \\
Equal variance & Cellwise Student & 0.999 & 250.3 & 0.003 \\
Unequal variance & Normal Wald & 0.868 & 126.3 & 0.105 \\
Unequal variance & Pooled Student & 0.522 & 49.3 & 0.345 \\
Unequal variance & Cellwise Student & 0.995 & 629.6 & 0.005 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{New generated study of sparse-support remedies. All proportions
condition on four cells with at least two observations. There are 124
unavailable cases under equal variance and 116 under unequal variance, each
out of 3,000. Width is in illustrative USD. Recommend offer means that the
interval's lower endpoint exceeds the cost of 40.}
\label{scisyn:interval-remedies}
\end{table}

Pooling repairs much of the first scenario's undercoverage, but fails badly
when the rarely treated cell has greater variability: conditional coverage
falls to 52.2 percent. The cellwise construction retains coverage in both
scenarios at the expense of very wide intervals. Its median widths are 117.7
and 288.1 USD; a few extremely small cells drive still larger mean widths.
It almost never supports the offer through a lower bound above cost. That
hesitation is informative: the data contain little precision about the rare
treated subgroup. Unavailable replications remain unavailable under all three
methods; a conditional coverage guarantee cannot manufacture missing cells.

The comparison rules out a simple promise that an alternative critical value
will solve weak support. One remedy needs a substantively defensible common
variance; another accepts less decision-making precision under a broader
normal model. Non-normal monetary outcomes, dependent customers or estimated
population shares need additional analysis. A better-balanced experiment or a
larger sample may be the valuable next expenditure. The maximum Monte Carlo
standard error for the conditional proportions is approximately 0.0094, which
does not explain the large coverage losses in the adverse scenario.

\section{Graph ambiguity has an economic price}
The inherited pcalg example specifies a Gaussian covariance for a rate change
$X$, an intermediate response $M$ and a monetary outcome $Y$:
\[
\Sigma=\begin{pmatrix}
1&0.6&0.48\\0.6&1.36&1.088\\0.48&1.088&1.8704
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Three noncollider chains reproduce this covariance with positive independent
error variances. Their effects of $X$ on $Y$ are $0.48,0,0$. The new calculation
reconstructs all three structural systems and checks the equality of their
observational covariances. A program can therefore reproduce the observations
while leaving a consequential intervention ambiguity. The IDA source supplies
the effect-set interpretation; the displayed system is a project construction.
\citep{exec13_pcalg_reuse_primary}

If $X$ is in percentage points and $Y$ in thousands of currency units, a
25-basis-point action has gross benefit either 0 or 120 per modelled unit.
At an illustrative implementation cost of 60, the net values are $-60$ and
$60$. There is no sign-robust recommendation across those models. A diagram
assistant that selects the forward chain without evidence would make the
decision look settled while adding no identifying information. A justified
temporal restriction or experiment could resolve the choice. No expected value
of that information is calculated without probabilities over the competing
models and an account of the experiment's precision and cost.

\section{Panel weights express different investment questions}
In the inherited two-cohort panel, early adopters have effects 2 and 4, late
adopters have an observed effect of 10, and their population shares are $3/4$
and $1/4$. Recalculation confirms averages 4, $19/4$, 4 and $15/4$ under four
aggregation rules. They are not four estimates of an identical target. The
did source's distinct aggregation branches make this an implementation-relevant
comparison.
\citep{exec24_panelr_did}

A sponsor interested in benefits per exposed branch-period needs different
weights from one comparing the typical adoption cohort or the typical calendar
period. Costs must use the same units. A table of benefits in dollars does not
make mismatched denominators comparable. The next panel experiment should
freeze the target weights before it compares estimators, retain missing cells
and test sensitivity to deviations from the maintained trend restrictions.

\section{What better text measurement would have to accomplish}
Suppose an assistant extracts distress from customer notes. Let true distress
be $U$, measured distress $W=U+\varepsilon_W$, action $A=U+\varepsilon_A$ and
outcome $Y=\tau A+U+\varepsilon_Y$. All disturbances are mutually independent,
centred Gaussian variables, with unit variance except
$\operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon_W)=s$. The coefficient on $A$ in a population
regression adjusting for $W$ is
\[
 \beta_{A\mid W}=\tau+\frac{s}{1+2s}.
\]
The calculation was independently checked by solving the covariance normal
equations. For $\tau=-1/5$, the adjusted coefficient is zero at $s=1/3$ and
positive above that threshold. This is residual confounding from imperfect
measurement, even with an arbitrarily large sample. The retained review of
text-based adjustment motivates the measurement question; the equation is
a project derivation.
\citep{exec13_census_text_review_arxiv}

The useful contribution of a language model would be to improve measurement
enough to alter the effect or decision relative to a credible alternative.
It is insufficient to show that its summary is fluent. Compare human coding,
a dictionary, conventional supervised extraction and the language model on
the same permitted notes. Hold out customers and periods; retain errors and
abstentions; examine whether the text precedes treatment or is itself a
consequence of contact. A measurement-error variance below $1/3$ is a boundary
in this particular constructed system, not a transferable acceptance threshold
for real text.

\section{Public banking records: an impressive score can use unavailable information}
The UCI Bank Marketing archive provides an actual public-data test of the
information-date requirement. The selected full additional file contains
41,188 archived contact records. Its documentation states that the rows are
ordered by date, from May 2008 to November 2010, and explicitly warns that
call duration is unavailable before the call. The smaller overlapping sample
is excluded from this experiment.
\citep{pd15_uci_bank}

The new study freezes the data identity, features, preprocessing, splits and
models before fitting. Its primary split trains on the first 28,831 rows and
tests on the remaining 12,357. A separately specified random stratified split
of the same sizes provides a development comparison, using seed 20261029.
Neither establishes independent customers: the archive lacks a suitable
customer identifier, and ordered rows do not supply exact decision timestamps.
No independent-observation confidence interval is claimed.

The baseline predicts the training subscription rate. The candidate model is
an L2-regularised logistic regression using age, job, marital status, education,
credit default, housing loan, personal loan, days since previous contact,
previous contacts and previous campaign outcome. Their pre-call availability
remains a maintained assumption requiring confirmation in a deployment. The
sentinel 999 for days since previous contact is represented by a separate
indicator and a zero numerical value; unknown categories remain categories.
Scaling and one-hot encoding are fitted on training data only. The deliberately
infeasible comparison adds completed call duration. Campaign count, current
contact fields and macroeconomic aggregates are excluded because their
decision-time meaning requires further clarification.

Both regressions use the same prespecified settings: $C=1$, the L-BFGS solver
and a maximum of 2,000 iterations. There is no tuning on test outcomes.
All four fits converge without recorded warnings, and no test categorical
values are absent from their corresponding training set.

\begin{table}[htbp]\centering\small
\begin{tabular}{llrrr}
\toprule
Split & Model & AUC & Log loss & Brier score \\
\midrule
Later archive & Training-rate constant & 0.500 & 0.752 & 0.221 \\
Later archive & Candidate pre-call & 0.630 & 0.678 & 0.206 \\
Later archive & Plus unavailable duration & 0.793 & 0.665 & 0.193 \\
Random development & Training-rate constant & 0.500 & 0.352 & 0.100 \\
Random development & Candidate pre-call & 0.693 & 0.312 & 0.087 \\
Random development & Plus unavailable duration & 0.883 & 0.254 & 0.073 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Executed public-data prediction with a frozen specification. AUC
measures ranking; lower log loss and Brier score indicate better probability
predictions on the particular test set. Rows from different splits have
different outcome distributions and are not interchangeable performance tests.
The duration model is infeasible for the stated pre-call task.}
\label{scisyn:public-timing}
\end{table}

The apparent gain from duration is large: AUC rises from 0.630 to 0.793 on the
later archived records and from 0.693 to 0.883 on the random development split.
It cannot justify a pre-call ranking. Among the 1,236 highest-scored later
records, the candidate pre-call model identifies 620 recorded subscriptions,
while the duration model identifies 782. These are descriptive counts of
observed subscriptions among people already contacted, not estimates of extra
subscriptions caused by targeting them. The experiment supplies neither an
untreated comparison nor the assignment information needed for that causal
claim.

The ordered split also exposes a substantial composition change: the
subscription frequency is 5.57 percent in the early training rows and 24.55
percent in the later test rows. The random split has approximately 11.27 and
11.26 percent respectively. This contributes to the different prediction
problem; the experiment does not identify the cause of the change. AUC,
calibration and economic targeting value should not be collapsed into a single
claim that the model generalises.

The practical implication is observable without private bank data. A common
study interface should record which variables exist at the action date and
which records support the claimed evaluation. A simple rule excluding duration
already prevents one misleading improvement. Language assistance would need
to outperform that rule or uncover a harder omission to justify its extra
cost. The next experiment should compare completed analyst studies with these
requirements enforced, rather than rewarding the largest retrospective score.

chapters.title: What a public experiment can tell a bank

segments.text:
\chapter{What a public experiment can tell a bank}
\label{gap29:public}

A useful prototype should take an intervention question through to a decision
that an economist can defend. Public data permits that exercise before a bank
commits staff time, customer records and money to a pilot. Its value depends on
which question it answers. A public experiment can test whether an analysis
preserves the population, intervention and uncertainty. It cannot establish
that the same intervention works for a bank's customers.

The National Supported Work demonstration provides a concrete example. In the
retained experimental subset, the estimated increase in 1978 earnings is about
\$1,794, with an approximate 95\% interval from \$479 to \$3,109. These are
the archive's earnings units, without conversion to today's purchasing power.
The result supports a positive average contrast under the stated design
assumptions. It does not establish that the gain exceeds an illustrative
\$1,000 cost. That distinction is exactly the distinction a banking proposal
must preserve when discussing a profitable offer or servicing intervention.

\section{The population is part of the question}
The author archive supplies separate files for 185 treated and 260 control
observations with earnings in 1974, 1975 and 1978. The original paper explains
that the subset is drawn from male experimental participants for whom 1974
earnings can be recovered. Selection uses pre-intervention information,
including assignment month and employment history. The authors explicitly
condition the retained experiment's interpretation on the original
randomisation being independent of those pre-intervention covariates.
\citep{gap29dehejia,gap29data}

The distinction matters. These 445 people are neither the full demonstration
nor a sample of bank customers. The public files do not contain the original
assignment logs or a complete site-by-month randomisation history. We retain
the paper's selection argument as a substantive premise. We do not infer it
from balance tests. Treatment assignment, rather than an independently
identified effect of treatment receipt, defines the contrast. Consistency,
absence of interference and preservation of the observed cohort are additional
premises.

For participant $i$, let $Y_i(1)$ and $Y_i(0)$ denote 1978 earnings under
assignment to the programme and control. The finite-population target is
\[
 \tau_S=\frac{1}{445}\sum_{i\in S}\{Y_i(1)-Y_i(0)\},
\]
where $S$ is the retained subset. The realised data reveal one potential
outcome per participant. The calculation therefore has sampling uncertainty
even though every row in the extract is used. It neither observes individual
causal effects nor establishes an effect for an unobserved population.

The original data files contain all required variables without missing values.
Comparison with the previously retained teaching mirror finds a maximum
absolute difference of 0.00125 across matched fields, consistent with the
different numeric storage precision. We use the author's text files for the
reported calculations and retain their exact identities. The current archive
states attributable non-commercial terms; commercial redistribution or product
embedding requires a separate rights decision. The page was accessed after
the literature cutoff; its current bytes are not represented as a historical
snapshot. \citep{gap29data}

\section{Start with the simple contrast}
The primary estimator is the difference between treated and control means:
\[
 \widehat\tau_U=\overline Y_1-\overline Y_0,\qquad
 \widehat V_U=\frac{s_1^2}{185}+\frac{s_0^2}{260}.
\]
Here $s_a^2$ is the sample variance within assignment group $a$. Under the
complete-randomisation idealisation, the variance of the difference also
contains a subtraction for the unobserved variation in individual treatment
effects. Omitting that term provides the usual conservative variance
construction. The interval uses a normal approximation; it is not an exact
finite-sample statement. The actual site's assignment mechanism and selection
history remain qualifications on applying that idealisation.

Adjustment uses eight documented pre-intervention fields: age, education,
race and ethnicity indicators, marital status, degree status and earnings in
1974 and 1975. The comparison fixes this list before fitting; it does not
select variables to obtain a favourable result. For numerical conditioning,
each field is centred at its full-sample mean and divided by its full-sample
standard deviation.

The common-slope regression fits an intercept, assignment and these controls.
The interacted regression additionally includes every assignment-by-control
interaction. At the centred covariate origin, its assignment coefficient is
the difference between the two arm-specific fitted outcomes averaged over
the same pooled covariate distribution. In the design-based analysis of
\citet{gap29lin}, the fully interacted estimator has no worse asymptotic
precision than the unadjusted estimator under a fixed number of covariates,
bounded moments, a nonsingular limiting design and treatment proportions
bounded away from zero and one. This asymptotic result does not order the
estimated standard errors in one finite dataset.

For a design matrix $Z$, residuals $\widehat e_i$ and leverages $h_i$, the
reported regression covariance is
\[
 \widehat V_{HC2}=(Z'Z)^{-1}
 \left(\sum_i z_i z_i'\frac{\widehat e_i^2}{1-h_i}\right)(Z'Z)^{-1}.
\]
The HC3 sensitivity replaces $1-h_i$ by $(1-h_i)^2$. Neither adjustment
repairs a false causal model. Sandwich variance theory supplies asymptotic
support under the declared design conditions; small samples and influential
observations still warrant scrutiny. \citep{gap29lin}

\begin{table}[htbp]
\centering\small
\begin{tabular}{lrrl}
\toprule
Estimator & Estimate & Std. error & Approx. 95\% interval \\
\midrule
Difference in means & 1,794 & 671 & [479, 3,109] \\
Common-slope adjustment & 1,676 & 677 & [349, 3,003] \\
Fully interacted adjustment & 1,622 & 695 & [260, 2,983] \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{New calculations on the 445 retained experimental observations.
Intervals use normal critical values and HC2 covariance, equivalent to
separate-arm variance for the unadjusted estimator. This single dataset
establishes neither finite-sample coverage nor estimator superiority.}
\end{table}

The adjusted point estimates are somewhat smaller, and their estimated
standard errors are somewhat larger. This dataset provides no basis for
declaring a more elaborate estimator superior. It also does not refute an
asymptotic theorem: estimated precision in a realised sample and repeated-
assignment variance are different objects. An honest software comparison
reports both the target and the uncertainty convention before discussing
numerical agreement.

\section{Precision, influence and the spending threshold}
About 30.8\% of observed 1978 earnings are zero; the largest is about
\$60,308. The largest leverage is 0.346 for the interacted fit. Its HC3
standard error is about 717, compared with 695 under HC2. Deleting one
observation at a time moves the unadjusted point estimate between about
1,501 and 1,929. This sensitivity is reported without selecting a preferred
sample or substituting a trimmed estimand.

The predeclared split by zero versus positive 1975 earnings gives similar
point estimates, about 1,711 and 1,691, but very different uncertainty. The
respective intervals are approximately [263, 3,159] and [-875, 4,258].
These are descriptive subgroup contrasts. Their comparison neither
establishes equal effects nor justifies choosing a subgroup after seeing
its significance. A targeted policy would require its own evaluation.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=.94\textwidth]{scientific-gap-closure/2026-10-29/decision-intervals.pdf}
\caption{Estimated earnings contrasts and approximate 95\% intervals. The
dashed line is an illustrative cost of 1,000 in the archive's earnings units.
It is not an observed programme cost.}
\label{gap29:intervals}
\end{figure}

Let $c$ be a stipulated per-person cost in the same units. Subtracting $c$
from the estimated earnings contrast gives a deliberately limited accounting
comparison, $\widehat\tau-c$. At $c=1,000$, the unadjusted point comparison
is positive, about 794, but its interval is approximately [-521, 2,109].
A rule requiring the lower confidence bound to exceed cost therefore cannot
support spending at that threshold. At $c=2,000$, even the point comparison
is negative. Choosing the relevant rule requires a decision-maker's loss
function; statistical significance alone does not supply one.

Earnings gains are not automatically fiscal savings, bank revenue or social
surplus. Programme costs, displacement, persistence, discounting and the
distribution of benefits would all matter in a full economic appraisal.
The illustration asks whether the effect is large enough relative to an
explicit hurdle; it supplies no measured return on investment.

Sampling uncertainty is also distinct from a failure of the design premises.
If an analyst supplies a credible bound $B$ on the absolute discrepancy
between the estimated target and the target of interest, the interval can be
expanded from $[L,U]$ to $[L-B,U+B]$. With $B=500$, the unadjusted lower
endpoint falls to about -21. This is a conditional sensitivity calculation.
The data do not identify $B$, and the expansion is not a universal correction
for hidden confounding.

\section{What software agreement establishes}
The same rows and specifications were fitted independently with NumPy least
squares and R 4.1.2's \texttt{stats::lm}. R uses its QR-based fitting route;
the HC2 covariance was constructed explicitly rather than silently using a
default homoskedastic standard error. Point estimates, variances and standard
errors agree to within $10^{-6}$ in absolute units. The unadjusted covariance
also agrees with direct group-variance arithmetic, and the interacted
coefficient agrees with separate-arm standardisation. \citep{gap29r}

This result supports reusing existing linear-model machinery for this
specified calculation. It does not establish agreement with every causal
package, validate an R adapter, or qualify missingness, survey weights,
dependent records or other models. The proposal's integration should preserve
the choice of target and covariance explicitly. A language boundary is a
manageable engineering problem; an unrecorded change of statistical meaning
can invalidate the economic conclusion.

The fitted estimates and covariance summaries were then passed through the
existing library, command-line interface and local MCP service. Each returned
the same interval. In this construction the numerator is the estimated effect,
the denominator is the fixed value one, and the supplied covariance is
$\operatorname{diag}(n\widehat V,0)$. The service's Gaussian residual
inversion consequently reduces to the stated normal interval. This is an
executed path from public data to fitted summaries to consistent inference
and a local decision report. Raw-data estimation and report generation are
still local scripts, not newly implemented service endpoints.

Marking the assignment premise contradicted produces a refusal. Keeping it
unverified preserves conditional inference rather than certifying truth.
These behaviours make the worked example useful to an economist: uncertainty
and missing evidence survive the change of interface. They do not qualify a
bank platform or a sibling repository.

chapters.title: A shared service for economic analysis

segments.text:
\chapter{A shared service for economic analysis}
\label{r3:product}

A banking study connects a feasible action to its financial consequence
through a defensible account of customer behaviour. The underlying event
records have changing identities and reporting delays. An economist supplies restrictions on
assignment or shocks; a learner estimates conditional distributions; a
validator needs a sampling argument; a decision maker needs the value of
a feasible policy. A shared product is useful when it preserves the
meaning of the question across those transformations.

The proposed product is a library and a standalone analytical workspace
built around the same definitions of populations, interventions and outcomes. Its first release should expose
a bounded collection of well-defined operations. More general discovery,
inverse problems and latent control remain important research capabilities,
but their outputs must retain the assumptions and unresolved alternatives
developed in the preceding chapters. The construction below derives this
boundary; it is a specification, not a claim that the entire product
already exists.

\section{Define the study before choosing an estimator}
\label{r3:request-type}

Write a request as
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal Q=(\mathcal M,\mathcal K,g,\nu,\theta,\mathcal E,\mathcal F),
 \label{r3:request}
\end{equation}
where $\mathcal M$ is a class of causal models, $\mathcal K$ the observation
operator, $g$ the intervention, $\nu$ the target population, $\theta$
the requested functional, $\mathcal E$ the sampling experiment and
$\mathcal F$ the information available to the decision rule. For a model
$M\in\mathcal M$, the observed law is $P=\mathcal K(M)$ and the causal
answer is $\theta(M;g,\nu)$. The observation operator includes selection,
measurement, clocks, aggregation and record linkage when relevant.
The sampling experiment specifies independent households, randomized
branches, a dependent calendar series, or another explicit design.

For deposit retention, the request might ask for the difference in
six-month discounted net funding contribution under two invitation
rules for households eligible on a specified date. It must distinguish
invitation from receipt, and baseline eligible households from eventual
activators. If the action is instead an increase in offered interest,
both customer balances and the price paid on existing balances change.
These are different interventions and financial functionals even when
the same table is used.

The target needs a measurable definition before computation. For example,
with monthly contribution $R_t$ in a declared currency and discount
factor $d_t$, use
\[
 \theta(M;g_1,g_0,\nu)
 =\E^\nu_M\!\left[\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}d_tR_t^{g_1}\right]
  -\E^\nu_M\!\left[\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}d_tR_t^{g_0}\right].
\]
Here $R_t$ includes the agreed funding, servicing, incentive and expected
loss components without counting the same balance benefit twice.
An average balance effect is an input to this account, not already its
answer. Currency conversion, discounting, exposure weights and eligibility
are part of the target rather than invisible formatting options.

Several request fields can be inferred syntactically from data, but the
scientific restrictions cannot. Software can detect a duplicate decision
or a covariate first recorded after action. It cannot infer that a pricing
instrument has no direct effect or that all private underwriting
information has been measured. The workspace should let an analyst draw
and explain the model, compare plausible alternatives, and attach empirical
diagnostics to particular restrictions. A single numerical validity score
would erase the distinction between those obligations.

\section{Identification returns a mathematical object or an explicit limit}
\label{r3:identification-interface}

Define the identified set
\[
 \Theta_{\mathcal Q}(P)=
 \{\theta(M;g,\nu):M\in\mathcal M,\ \mathcal K(M)=P\}.
\]
An identification routine receives the model and observation declarations;
it does not receive permission to add whichever assumptions make a preferred
estimator available. A singleton set can be represented by an observed-law
functional $\Psi(P)$. A non-singleton set may admit bounds, a union of
functionals, or only a nonidentification witness. The useful result types
are therefore distinct.

\begin{description}[style=nextline,leftmargin=0pt,labelwidth=0pt,labelsep=0pt]
\item[Identified expression.] An expression for $\Psi$ together with the
assumptions and transformations that derive it. Numerical evaluation may
still be unsupported.
\item[Identified set or outer bound.] A set with its model class, support,
restrictions and sharpness status. A conservative outer bound is useful,
but must not be labelled sharp without a compatible-model construction.
\item[Nonidentification witness.] Two allowed models with the same observed
law and different targets, or a valid source-specific failure certificate
such as a hedge in the applicable ID model.
\item[Unsupported query.] The registered algorithm does not handle the
graph class, intervention, observation process or requested target.
This makes no claim that the target is unidentified.
\item[Incompatible specification.] The declarations are logically
inconsistent or violate a deterministic support/schema requirement.
A statistical model-check rejection should separately carry its test
and error level.
\end{description}

These types follow from Chapter~\ref{r3:graphs} and the ID/IDC construction
of \citet{id2006}. Failure to find a back-door set is not a
nonidentification certificate. Nor is failure of an optimizer. For
example, the front-door expression is identified under its restrictions,
but a backend implementing only covariate adjustment should return
an identified expression with no available estimator. Conversely, the
two invitation models of Section~\ref{r3:late} agree on all observed
records and disagree on the population ATE. Increasing an estimator's
iteration budget cannot supply that missing information.

For an initial implementation, observed-law expressions can use a small
typed language: conditional probability kernels, products, integrals or
finite sums, substitutions, and ratios on declared positive support.
A kernel records its random arguments, conditioning arguments, units,
dominating measure and observation regime. The type of
$p(y\mid a,x)$ differs from $p^g(y\mid x)$; a density in currency units
differs from a probability mass. Marginalization removes a random argument;
it must not accidentally integrate a fixed intervention value.

Each allowed transformation should produce a trace. In ordinary adjustment,
that trace names the adjusted variables, explains why their predecision
status and separation condition apply, and yields
$\int p(y\mid a,x)p(x)\,dx$. In recursive ID, it records ancestors,
districts, extracted kernels and support restrictions. The trace certifies
the consequence of the supplied assumptions. It cannot certify that
the graph supplied by a bank economist is the true graph.

\section{Adapters must preserve targets and statistical experiments}
\label{r3:adapter-inference}

The target-preservation identity
$\Psi(P)=\Psi_B(T_\#P)$ in Section~\ref{r3:software-types} is necessary
for converting data through $T$ to backend $B$. It also constrains
uncertainty. Suppose, for this paragraph, that observations $O_i$ are
independent and identically distributed, $T$ is fixed and applied
separately to each unit, and $Z=T(O)$. Let $P_\varepsilon$ be a regular
submodel with score $S(O)$. Differentiating the pushforward density gives
the reduced score
\[
 S_Z(Z)=\E[S(O)\mid Z].
\]
If $\phi_B(Z)$ is a gradient for the reduced functional, then
\begin{align}
 \left.\frac{d}{d\varepsilon}\Psi(P_\varepsilon)\right|_0
 &=\E[\phi_B(Z)S_Z(Z)]\nonumber\\
 &=\E[\phi_B(T(O))S(O)].
 \label{r3:gradient-pullback}
\end{align}
Thus the pulled-back score is a gradient for the original target.
In an unrestricted original model it is the canonical gradient when
the stated differentiability conditions hold; in a restricted model
projection onto the model's tangent space may improve efficiency.
This is a project consequence of the pathwise argument in
Chapter~\ref{r3:learning}, not a theorem for arbitrary preprocessing.

The qualifications explain common failures. A learned encoder is random
and may need independent training and a remainder analysis. Demeaning
over a panel is not a fixed transformation of each independently sampled
row. Expanding one household into transactions changes the sampling
units. Discarding a component of history may destroy target preservation.
An adapter must therefore declare both its mathematical transformation
and its mapping of sampling units, weights and information sets.

A backend estimator should return sufficient information for the
specified inference route. For a regular scalar moment this includes
unit-level scores, the Jacobian, target normalization, fold assignments
and nuisance estimates or their immutable references. For an identified
set it includes bound objectives and constraint certificates. For a
weak-IV inversion it includes the accepted set, including disconnected
or unbounded components. For a likelihood model it includes the exact
factorization, numerical approximation and parameter restrictions.
Forcing all of these outputs into an estimate/standard-error pair would
discard information that changes the bank decision.

\label{r3:protocol}
The companion scientific protocol gives this separation a concrete design
form. A request binds the model, observation, target and sampling
specifications by content hash. A result separately records computational
completion, identification and inferential availability. A scalar
confidence set is an ordered union of intervals, including empty,
disconnected and unbounded sets; posterior credible sets have a different
type. Derivations, bounds and failure witnesses have distinct artifact
roles. The supplied schema fixtures check these representation invariants.
They do not execute an identification algorithm or establish coverage.
The following versioned extension supplies explicit vector, curve and graph-set
types for the bounded constructions developed in this monograph. A general
graph probability distribution remains a different object.

\section{A bounded mathematical language and a concrete lowering rule}
\label{s4:scientific-language}
The specification must be stronger than a collection of file hashes. A
variable declaration contains its name, support, physical unit, causal role
and clock. A population declaration identifies the economic unit and the
role of its weights. An observation declaration identifies the immutable
view, revision relation, availability convention and sampling frequency.
The model specifies a structural class and an assumption set. A target
specifies the action, outcomes, fixed horizons or policies, normalization
and population. These declarations together determine a statistical
experiment; no single field can substitute for the others.

For finite mechanisms an executable expression grammar is particularly
transparent. A mass kernel has ordered parent variables $U$, ordered child
variables $V$, declared finite supports and an array of shape
$|\mathcal X_U|\times|\mathcal X_V|$. Every parent slice must be
nonnegative and sum to one over the child axes. A generative product
$\prod_jK_j(x_j\mid x_{\operatorname{pa}(j)})$ requires one mechanism
per child and a topological order. Marginalization sums named random axes;
substitution fixes an axis without summing it. Replacing an action mechanism
by $g(a\mid h)$ requires that its information variables precede the action.
This operation evaluates the supplied causal factorization; it does not
establish that an arbitrary observed kernel can be intervened upon.

The local finite-mass interpreter implements product, marginalization and
mechanism replacement, checking support, normalization and information order.
For a binary confounded example it recovers the interventional mean $0.5$
and rejects a policy using a future outcome. A general expression language
would additionally need density measures, positive-denominator restrictions
and numerical integration error. The initial lowering rules do not pretend
that this finite interpreter implements continuous ID or general latent
identification. Instead they recognize the complete constructions already
derived and reject mismatched target/sampling combinations.

\begin{longtable}{P{.13\textwidth}P{.38\textwidth}P{.42\textwidth}}
\toprule Regime & Scientific input & Lowering and inferential output\\\midrule\endhead
Stationary response & Fixed horizon, stable Gaussian linear law, external
instrument and nonzero impact normalization. & Joint direct moments,
Bartlett covariance and residual-test interval unions; a proxy VAR is a
challenger only with its additional dynamics restriction.\\
Integrated response & Stationary changes, same shock restriction, cumulative
level target. & Difference, fit common-origin moments, transform their full
covariance, then invert. No stationary-level shortcut.\\
Observed history & Independent whole trajectories, sequential identification,
fixed feasible policies and the finite observed-state fitting family. &
Cross-fitted augmentation or backward targeting; within-customer policy
contrast scores and trajectory variance.\\
Controlled latent & Randomized logger, binary informative emission model,
identified transitions/rewards and regular likelihood. & Scaled EM plus
observed-score refinement; fixed-policy value and information/refit uncertainty.
Boundary or failed fits retain an unavailable inference status.\\
Gaussian graph class & Three observed variables, iid Gaussian sample,
causal sufficiency and optional background order. & Joint covariance region,
retained DAGs and outer effect union. No probability attached to a DAG.\\
Temporal graph class & Stable VAR(1), known lag bound, independent innovations,
no contemporaneous causal edges. & Coefficient box, unresolved zero/nonzero
edges and its fixed-horizon response image.\\\bottomrule
\end{longtable}

These are conditional method choices, not six interchangeable backends.
The standalone reference runner checks the request and data identities,
dispatches these bounded numerical recipes and validates their typed result.
Its two servicing families retain their stated reward, state and policy
semantics; a new family requires a new mathematical and numerical qualification.
The separated-block sparse IV construction is available as a reproducible
study recipe with declared learner settings. General controlled continuous
states, unrestricted temporal discovery and policy optimization remain
separate extension requests.

\subsection{Results that can carry the actual uncertainty}
Protocol version 0.4 supplements the historical scalar protocol. A scalar
is a one-coordinate result; vectors and response curves have named ordered
axes and one physical unit per flattened coordinate. A response curve orders
outcome before horizon. Its covariance has that same coordinate order and
already includes the sample-size divisor. A confidence object carries its
method, level, coverage target and an interval union for each coordinate.
For a simultaneous rectangular set, the Cartesian product of these unions
is the confidence region. Empty, disconnected and unbounded coordinate sets
remain representable; an unbounded endpoint is a typed null, not a JSON
infinity or a large arbitrary number. Pointwise coverage cannot be relabeled
simultaneous by an adapter.

A graph result retains ordered nodes and its graph class. A DAG set stores
directed binary adjacency matrices. CPDAG/PAG endpoint matrices use zero
for absence, one for a tail, two for an arrowhead and three for a circle;
the latter is permitted only for a PAG. Basic endpoint validation is not
a complete PAG-recognition algorithm. The temporal reference instead stores
lower and upper coefficient matrices with edge marks ``present'' or
``zero or nonzero''. Its graph class is not a posterior distribution over
graphs. The effect union is explicitly an outer set, and uncertainty about
the causal-sufficiency assumption is not encoded as its confidence level.

Computational completion, conditional identification and inference have
separate status fields. Numerical error bounds, when available, use the
same output units. A null numerical bound means no certified bound was
provided; it must not be interpreted as zero error. Solver diagnostics and
all requested failed repetitions remain attached evidence. Hashes bind
those arrays and declarations to a computation, while scientific validation
determines whether their asserted premises are plausible.

\subsection{Allowed conversions and explicit rejection cases}
For a fixed known diagonal scale matrix $S$, the converted effect and
covariance are $S\widehat\theta$ and $S\widehat V S'$. Interval endpoints
reverse when a scale is negative; the order of disconnected components
also reverses. A rate denominator changing from percentage points to basis
points divides a normalized response by 100. A fixed currency multiplier
can be applied in the same way. A time-varying exchange rate generally
changes the reward functional and requires rebuilding it; a monthly stock
cannot be converted into daily flows by relabeling an axis.

Population weights, inverse behavior probabilities, inverse observation
probabilities and bootstrap frequencies have different mathematical roles.
The request validator rejects their substitution. It also rejects an iid
row experiment for the dependent response route, a split inside a purportedly
independent trajectory, inclusive availability when the request requires
strict predecision information, and a learned policy supplied to fixed-policy
inference. A valid clock conversion can preserve timestamp/sequence order
exactly; changing that order requires a new observation analysis. These
checks enforce declared meaning, not the truth of exchangeability or
instrument exclusion.

\section{Concrete sibling boundaries and the standalone study}
\label{s4:sibling-mappings}
Read-only inspection of the actual sibling APIs changes the integration
design. FinMarketing's \texttt{CausalData.from\_record} requires pretreatment
features, mature outcomes, binary actions and independent groups. Its
\texttt{FeatureSnapshot} orders availability, cutoff and decision by
timestamp/sequence pairs. The local mapping preserves those pairs, horizon
and dependence unit. It does not coerce a dynamic curve into FinMarketing's
scalar \texttt{Estimate}; that requires a richer result consumer. A causal
response to a macro shock also cannot inherit its independent-group standard
error merely because the source rows are account records.

dataml's \texttt{LineageGraph.append} accepts run, dataset, partition and
metadata, while its correction schema requires a resolvable assumption and
a numerical confidence field. Observation candidates therefore map to
lineage metadata with their assumptions and alternatives. An uncalibrated
hint score does not populate correction confidence, and ambiguous candidates
do not generate an automatic correction. This preserves dataml's distinction
between an original source and an assumed overlay.

BayesFilter's \texttt{SSMStaticShape}, \texttt{SSMDataSignature} and
\texttt{BayesianSSMProblem} can record dimensions, data/mask identities and
parameter coordinates. For the binary controlled family, the local mapping
adds action identity, randomized-logger semantics, reward, finite state
support and the full observation order to its model manifest. A generic
Bayesian SSM descriptor alone does not supply those causal meanings or a
controlled categorical filter implementation. Its numerical target and
derivative still need to refer to the same likelihood, as required by
Chapter~\ref{r3:controlled-identification}.

MacroFinance's \texttt{DirectedPairMeasurement} and
\texttt{ObservationContract} distinguish directed quote pairs, maturity,
observed rows and derived diagnostics. Its convention is $x_m=-\chi$;
reversing a pair reverses the quoted wedge sign. The local mapping preserves
these identities and requires a separate causal role for the measured
variable. A triangle diagnostic is not automatically an identified structural
cycle intervention. The inspected MacroFinance BayesFilter facade also
references a different import root from the workspace checkout, so inspection
alone cannot establish runtime compatibility between them.

The same scientific request/result files support an independent study:
choose the economic target and observation plan, inspect the identifying
assumptions, select a supported regime, execute its estimator and mandatory
comparison, and publish the result with its uncertainty and source trace.
Local examples exercise the mappings and numerical operations here. Sibling
checkouts remain unchanged; accepted adoption, shared release management and
institutional data access remain separate implementation work.

\section{A bounded catalogue of scientific operations}
\label{r3:operation-catalogue}

The first supported catalogue should be selected by mathematical closure
and banking demand. Table~\ref{r3:operations} defines seven operation
families. Support means a particular target, observation representation,
estimator and inference construction have been qualified together;
it does not mean every method within that family is implemented.

\begin{longtable}{P{.16\textwidth}P{.38\textwidth}P{.39\textwidth}}
\caption{Proposed operation families and their required scientific outputs}
\label{r3:operations}\\
\toprule
Operation & Input and identification route & Output and essential rejection\\
\midrule\endfirsthead
\toprule Operation & Input and identification route & Output and essential rejection\\
\midrule\endhead
Adjusted effect &
One decision, baseline covariates, explicit exposure/population weights;
consistency, conditional exchangeability and support. &
Regime mean or ATE functional, cross-fitted score and declared cluster
inference. Reject a descendant adjustment or an unsupported action.
CATE surfaces need their own local inference route.\\
Invitation/IV &
Separate assignment/receipt; randomized or justified conditional instrument;
linear moments, monotone compliance or a stated inverse model. &
ITT, homogeneous coefficient or weighted complier target. Preserve weak-IV
test sets; do not relabel a LATE or regularized response as an ATE.\\
Adoption and panel contrasts &
Entity/calendar records; cohort, comparison group, anticipation and
parallel-trend specification, or a distinct structural moment model. &
Group--time ATT and declared aggregation, or the named panel coefficient.
Reject conversion of reversible actions into first-adoption dates.\\
Observed-history policy &
Finite horizon, ordered histories, feasible actions, intervention density,
event/censoring definitions and sequential identification restrictions. &
Policy value/contrast with its recursive estimator and trajectory score.
Differentiate propensity-dependent policies; retain horizon/support limits.\\
Dynamic shock response &
Observation frequency, moment restrictions, shock instrument and scale,
dependence regime and a finite set of horizons. &
Normalized response vector with stacked inference or weak-normalization
sets. Reject an unidentified historical-shock interpretation.\\
Controlled latent analysis &
Initial, transition, emission, reward and logging laws; policy information
and a target-specific identification argument. &
Model-conditional fit/filter, identified value or value ambiguity.
Planning requires the interventional law, not only a fitted likelihood.\\
Discovery-to-query &
Clock, graph class, background constraints, CI/functional assumptions and
the observation operator. &
Endpoint-preserving equivalence graph, then a common functional, effect set
or unresolved query. Retain uncertainty about discovery itself.\\
\bottomrule
\end{longtable}

For adjusted and longitudinal means, the product can initially support
the scores derived in Chapters~\ref{r3:learning} and \ref{r3:longitudinal},
with finite categorical actions and fixed horizons. This is a useful
construction boundary: it permits both simple randomized comparisons and
repeated collections policies while keeping the intervention density
explicit. A continuous deterministic intervention under a continuous
observed action law is not automatically absolutely continuous; density
ratios for point masses require a different identification/estimation
route. Modified policies and smooth stochastic shifts can supply one,
under the assumptions in Chapter~\ref{r3:policy-targets}.

Panel support should begin with specified cohort estimands and strong
linear-moment baselines, not an unrestricted auto-panel operation.
The equal-weight branch target, household target and balance-weighted
target require different aggregations. Temporal shock support should
likewise identify a normalized response under the stated instrument
exclusions, with the fixed-horizon inference of
Section~\ref{r3:series-inference}. Structural breaks and weak impact
normalizations should produce an explicit alternative analysis.

Controlled latent support can be valuable before a general latent causal
identification engine exists. The same workspace can compare a randomized
logging model, a private-logging model and an observed-history policy
value, displaying which conclusions require which assumptions. The
known-emission inversion in Section~\ref{r3:known-emission} supplies a
finite validation case; it is not a general theorem for learned emissions.
Proxy-value routes should be registered with their bridge and rank
conditions rather than offered through a generic hidden-state option.

\section{Estimation and uncertainty form one qualified composition}
\label{r3:inference-contract}

An inference contract has five parts: the target and its differentiability
class; an estimator expansion; the statistical sampling units; the
covariance or test construction; and the conditions controlling nuisance
and numerical error. For a regular vector target one common form is
\[
 \widehat\theta-\theta
 =-\widehat J^{-1}\frac1n\sum_i\psi_i(\theta,\eta_0)
   +R_n,\qquad \sqrt n R_n=o_p(1),
\]
where the meaning of $n$ and the scaling must match the experiment.
Independent trajectories, independent clusters with variable sizes,
crossed arrays and a long time series imply different normalizations
and limit arguments. A covariance option alone cannot establish them.

For one-way independent clusters, reduction of all score contributions
within each cluster precedes forming outer products. For crossed
entity/date dependence, inclusion--exclusion of cluster covariance
components requires the appropriate crossed-array assumptions; a large
entity count does not compensate for a fixed handful of macro dates.
Multiway cross-fitting must prevent training/evaluation overlap in the
relevant coordinates \citep{cluster2021}. A simple entity split is not
automatically a multiway construction.

For a time series, keep the time order, outcome window, separation gap
and score bandwidth as distinct fields. Overlapping outcomes can extend
dependence past disjoint origin blocks. When a stationary mixing
argument is invoked, its mixing and moment restrictions must be named.
A user selecting a HAC option has specified an estimator family, not proved
that a structural-break or unit-root score obeys the required CLT.
Simultaneous bands require a joint horizon construction.

Uncertainty for weakly identified parameters, nonsmooth bounds and
selected policies needs separate operations. Ratios with weak
denominators should use a qualified test inversion; graph ambiguity
requires a union or other defensible set operation. Learned-policy
evaluation must distinguish a frozen policy on an independent evaluation
sample from a data-adaptive optimal-value target. Bayesian posterior
intervals require their likelihood, prior and numerical diagnostics;
they cannot inherit frequentist coverage merely because they are called
credible.

The result should consequently carry several evidence dimensions:
identification conditional on stated restrictions, numerical convergence,
sampling inference, sensitivity to disputed restrictions and decision
adequacy. A converged point estimate can coexist with unsupported
uncertainty. A wide but valid confidence set can be adequate for a decision
if every contained model favors the same affordable action.

\section{Policy evaluation has a separate information boundary}
\label{r3:planner-interface}

A controlled-state adapter must expose the observational and interventional
laws separately. In the finite model, a pre-action belief is
$b_t(s)=P(S_t=s\mid H_t)$. Under a private logger, after seeing the
historical action it becomes proportional to
$b_t(s)q_\eta(A_t\mid s,H_t)$ before the transition, reward and next
signal update. Under an intervention using only the recorded history,
the action density $g_t(A_t\mid H_t)$ is constant across hidden states
and cancels in normalized filtering. Replacing the logger changes the
law, not simply one input tensor.

The planner receives a distribution over the information it is allowed
to use. A smoothed posterior $P(S_t\mid H_T)$, $T>t$, includes future
evidence and is not an online policy state. A retrospective smoother is
useful for fitting and diagnosis, while prospective evaluation must
reconstruct the predecision filter. The adapter must also specify whether
reward is observed before the next signal and whether reward carries
additional information about the state.

For a supplied causal model the finite-horizon value recursion is
\[
 V_t(b)=\max_{a\in\mathcal A_t(b)}
 \left\{r_t(b,a)+
 \gamma\int V_{t+1}(\tau_t(b,a,o',r))\,
                 p_t(do',dr\mid b,a)\right\}.
\]
The belief update $\tau_t$ and predictive observation/reward law must
use the same factorization. This is the information-state construction
of \citet{kaelbling1998} specialized to the declared timing.
For this display all decision-relevant recorded context is assumed to
be included in the belief state or its explicit arguments. Action
constraints can depend on recorded eligibility, customer consent
and a specified budget. An estimate of a hidden risk state does not
authorize using unavailable information in those constraints.

Model ambiguity creates another decision problem. If $\mathcal M_P$
contains several observationally compatible causal models, a robust
policy may maximize $\inf_{M\in\mathcal M_P}V_M(\pi)$. In general the
same $M$ must govern the whole trajectory. A stagewise minimization
that freely chooses a new adverse model at each date solves a larger,
rectangular uncertainty problem. Its result can be conservative and
need not be the sharp value bound for persistent hidden types. The
dynamic-bound analysis of Section~\ref{r3:dynamic-bounds} shows why
the uncertainty-set type must accompany the planning algorithm.

For a two-date fixed policy with no discount, suppose the allowed
reward vectors are $(0,1)$ and $(1,0)$, with one model applying at
both dates. Worst-case total value is one. Independently choosing
the worse component at each date instead gives zero, a vector absent
from the original model class. This exact example isolates the extra
freedom introduced by rectangularization; it is not a claim that a
bank's ambiguity set contains those two models.

Finally, solver error needs its own budget. The Bellman residual bound
in Section~\ref{r3:value-errors} controls numerical error for the
specified contraction. Parameter uncertainty, model ambiguity, reward
accounting and policy support remain separate. A planner can report
a precise solution to a scientifically weak model; the user needs
enough information to recognize that situation.

\section{Discovery should improve a decision-relevant model class}
\label{r3:discovery-product}

The discovery workspace begins with mechanisms and timing. It proposes
variables and lags from the available data, records business restrictions,
and returns a DAG, CPDAG, PAG or named functional-model object with its
endpoint semantics intact. Metadata lineage is displayed separately
from causal ancestry. An upstream database dependency does not establish
an economic intervention edge.

The next operation asks a specific causal query across compatible models.
For the chain example of Section~\ref{r3:graph-effects}, the observed
Gaussian covariance and CPDAG imply effects $\{0,1/4\}$ within the
declared linear causally sufficient class. The product should expose
both values, explain the orientations that produce them, and show
which credible timing information or intervention would distinguish
them. Returning the effect of one arbitrarily oriented representative
would turn an unresolved scientific question into a spurious estimate.

General PAG completion is expensive and may still leave latent
nonidentification within each completion. The first bounded route
should therefore use verified generalized-adjustment criteria on
supported graph classes \citep{perkovic2018}, small enumerated classes
for exact examples, and unresolved results beyond those capabilities.
Search limits, CI test assumptions, variable screening and lag windows
must be retained. A timeout is computationally unresolved, not a
certificate that no adjustment set exists.

A useful experiment recommendation should name the ambiguity it resolves.
For deposit pricing, a randomized encouragement may distinguish a price
response from latent liquidity selection. For collections, a new
predecision signal may improve a bridge's measurement rank. For treasury,
a higher-frequency observation may remove an aliasing ambiguity. Their
cost and decision value can be compared; edge-count improvement alone
is not the economic objective.

\section{Acceptance is a collection of scientific obligations}
\label{r3:product-acceptance}

Each registered operation needs a reviewable construction dossier. It
contains the exact target and restrictions, an identification derivation
or witness, an estimator/inference derivation, the qualified backend
version and transformation, and reproducible positive and negative
examples. Exact finite laws should be used when they expose semantic
errors that a large benchmark can conceal.

For adjustment, compare the estimator's population expression with
explicit intervention enumeration, and include a confounded pair of
models that observation cannot distinguish. For IV, hold the observed
law fixed while changing the unobserved outcomes of never-takers; ensure
that the requested ATE remains unresolved although LATE is returned.
For longitudinal analysis, verify the recursive score under feedback,
then change the policy's dependence on the propensity and require the
corresponding gradient change.

For controlled states, enumerate hidden paths to check the likelihood,
filter and sufficient counts with and without the logger; compare
interventional value against independent dynamic programming. For
discovery, round-trip all endpoint marks and propagate every supported
completion into its effect set. For data organization, delay and revise
events across the decision boundary and verify exactly which history
the policy receives. For distributed inference, repartition the same
scores across workers and preserve folds, cluster sums and accepted
uncertainty sets.

Repeated-sample experiments then assess bias, coverage or policy regret
under named laws, including failures of support, rank, stationarity
and model specification. Their purpose is to test the implemented
construction and characterize its operating range. They do not prove
that the bank's unobserved confounding assumption holds. Bank data
validation subsequently evaluates the actual information, process
and financial account.

This division makes a staged product possible without shrinking its
scientific ambition. A bank can use rigorous observed-history analyses
while researchers develop controlled latent and discovery-to-effect
routes in the same representations. Promotion of a method then requires
