must reproduce the declared aggregation order rather than substitute a familiar
formula.~\citep{exec24_longcxx_reference}

\subsection{Integration, adoption and justified rejection}

The proposed first route retains original engines behind typed workers. XGBoost
and CatBoost are conditional boosted-prediction alternatives once their objective,
endpoint, margin, weight, tie and environment contracts pass selected fixtures.
ranger's standalone C++ library or CLI and its R wrapper are separate packaging
choices; the inspected build declares C++14 and library/CLI targets. Its primary
headers explicitly distinguish the MIT C++ core from the GPL-3 R package.
XGBoost and CatBoost have Apache-2.0 root declarations. aorsf declares MIT and
R/Rcpp/RcppArmadillo dependencies. These direct declarations do not clear every
dependency, model artifact or redistribution. Rights review must bind the actual
chosen distribution.~\citep{exec24_longcxx_xgboost,exec24_longcxx_catboost,exec24_longcxx_ranger,exec24_longcxx_aorsf}

For aorsf, an original R worker preserves the formula, validation and prediction
semantics while using its C++ core. Extracting that core into a new standalone
port would require recreating the R-side contract and numeric dependencies;
the proposal has not demonstrated a benefit sufficient to justify that work.
For ranger, direct C++ embedding remains an alternative to an R worker when
deployment requirements and rights justify the separate interface. Whole-library
rewrites are rejected for the present proposal because they add parity and
maintenance obligations without demonstrated need. Native workers, a dedicated
longitudinal R/Python estimator and an independent finite-law reference remain
substantive alternatives, selected according to the target rather than language
preference.~\citep{exec24_longcxx_aorsf,exec24_longcxx_ranger}

The CLI and MCP proposal should expose a versioned request containing population,
time zero, availability clock, event dictionary, competing-event interpretation,
entry/censoring representation, treatment history, weights and their meaning,
sampling units, horizons, options and artifact hashes. The result must preserve
accepted and rejected row identities, objective and output type, baseline or
distribution parameters, convergence/numerical warnings, uncertainty method,
timing and complete request costs. Refusal is a typed result. A finite output,
successful process exit or replayed artifact must not be promoted to causal
identification or qualified uncertainty. These are proposed interfaces; no new
native adapter or sibling integration is implemented by this review.

The method owner must first decide whether a public or generated study can
identify the proposed target. The adapter owner then freezes version, wrapper
and conversion fixtures; the rights owner resolves the actual distribution;
the evaluation owner preregisters held-out targets, ties, censoring and competing
events, row permutations, dependent units, failure denominators and full costs.
No purchase, vendor trial or expensive bank experiment is necessary to write
those contracts. Candidate aliases, unreturned discovery tails, uninspected
delegates, cluster-calibrated uncertainty and native performance remain recorded
follow-ups. This bounded comparison improves the proposal's executable evidence
and actions without declaring C++ longitudinal coverage complete.

\section{Julia and Rust survival components: preserving the clock and the estimand}
\label{sec:exec24-longitudinal-other}

A collections decision is defined by its clock before it is defined by its software language.
Consider accounts eligible for a payment holiday at the start of a month. The bank may
compare initiation within a grace period against continued ordinary servicing, follow
default and prepayment, and value interest receipts during a fixed horizon. A program
that returns a survival curve has solved only one part of this problem. The eligibility
date, treatment strategy, event definition, observation mechanism and sampling unit
must survive the translation from the business request to the estimator. This section
examines six concrete Julia and Rust alternatives at commits preceding the client
cutoff of 7 October 2026. Their role is conditional reuse or reference, not evidence
that a native causal product has already been qualified.

\subsection{A target and an observation contract}
Let $T^a$ denote event time under strategy $a$, measured from eligibility, and let
$S_a(t)=\Pr(T^a>t)$. Two possible targets are the event-risk contrast
\begin{equation}
 \Delta_F(\tau)=\Pr(T^1\leq\tau)-\Pr(T^0\leq\tau),
 \qquad
 \Delta_M(\tau)=\int_0^\tau\{S_1(t)-S_0(t)\}\,dt.
\end{equation}
The first is a probability difference; the second is a restricted-mean survival-time
difference and has time units. If the event is default, prepayment needs an explicit
competing-event or hypothetical-intervention interpretation. Treating prepayment as
ordinary independent censoring changes the question unless the necessary assumptions
are supplied. These definitions do not by themselves identify either counterfactual
curve. Consistency, treatment and censoring exchangeability under the specified
history, positivity and an appropriate observation law remain substantive conditions.

Write $L_i$ for entry, $C_i$ for right censoring and $\widetilde T_i$ for observed exit.
For a continuous clock with a declared boundary convention, a risk indicator might be
$Y_i(t)=\mathbf1\{L_i<t\leq\widetilde T_i\}$. By contrast, an interval-censored
record $(u_i,v_i]$ says that the event occurred somewhere in that interval; it does not
say that observation began at $u_i$. Three otherwise eligible accounts, one entering
after the first observed event, give a first-event increment $1/2$, while ignoring
entry gives $1/3$. This exact example concerns data meaning, not numerical speed.
The independent reference also constructs two deterministic event times, four and
two months, with horizon five. Their restricted means differ by two months while
their event risks at the horizon are both one, so the risk difference is zero.
Multiplying the time scale by thirty changes the mean contrast to sixty days and
leaves the probability contrast unchanged.~\citep{exec24_survivalother_reference}

The proposed command and MCP request must therefore bind population, eligibility
clock, intervention strategy, history availability, entry, censoring, competing events,
horizon, output units and sampling unit before selecting an engine. A convenient
two-column schema is insufficient evidence that two engines implement the same target.

\subsection{Julia alternatives and their distinct contracts}
The JuliaStats Survival.jl snapshot declares version 0.3.3 and Julia 1.10 compatibility,
with a direct MIT licence. Its exported event type contains a time and a Boolean
event/right-censoring indicator. The event-table constructors, Kaplan--Meier component
and Cox fitting component provide useful building blocks for a narrow right-censored
worker. They do not, through that response type alone, encode entry or a treatment
history. The inspected Cox objective uses fractional removal of tied event risk
scores, an Efron-style convention.~\citep{exec24_survivalother_juliastats}

Even this narrow candidate needs explicit boundary fixtures. In the inspected
zero-time helper, the first nonzero index is $i$ and the deletion interval is
$\texttt{start}:(\texttt{start}+i-1)$. For a conventional one-based vector
with times $(0,1,2)$, the abstract trace removes indices one and two, leaving only
time two. If all times are zero, the first-nonzero search has no result and the
deletion branch is not entered. The already-sorted event-vector constructor also
passes its vector into this mutating helper; its comment that the input is unaffected
does not settle aliasing. These are source-local concerns with inspected constructor
and export paths, not reported outcomes from a Julia execution. The safe proposal
route is to reject unsupported zero-time inputs until the intended rule and a native
regression fixture are agreed; silently adding a small epsilon would change the
clock and conceal the question.~\citep{exec24_survivalother_juliastats,exec24_survivalother_reference}

SurvivalAnalysis.jl supplies another architecture. Its pinned version 0.1.0 declares
Julia compatibility \texttt{\^{}1.2} and MIT licensing. Its response hierarchy contains
right-, left- and interval-censored forms, but the inspected documentation explicitly
says that only right-censoring methods are included. In particular,
\texttt{Surv(start,stop)} represents interval censoring. The parametric fitting
dispatch takes a right-censored response and admits Weibull or exponential baselines.
The Hessian inverse and standard-error calculation have exception paths producing
NaNs. An adapter must report those outcomes as unavailable uncertainty, not replace
them with zero standard errors. PH prediction distinguishes a linear predictor from
a transformed survival distribution, which is useful for a typed output contract.
The stated candidate role is an original Julia parametric worker, subject to baseline,
optimisation and uncertainty checks; its response classes do not justify a universal
censoring claim.~\citep{exec24_survivalother_juliaanalysis}

SurvivalModels.jl, at its pinned 0.1.6 declaration with Julia 1.11 compatibility and
MIT licensing, develops parametric general-hazard alternatives and Cox and
nonparametric components. The inspected CoxDefault implementation groups tied times
before subtracting $d\log R$ from the log likelihood: this is a Breslow-style tied
denominator. It should not be expected to agree numerically with the preceding
Efron-style path for every tied data set. With risk scores $(1,2,3)$ and the first
two subjects failing together, the numerator is two and the total risk score is six.
The Breslow partial-likelihood contribution is $2/6^2=1/18$, whereas fractional
removal gives $2/[6(6-3/2)]=2/27$. A parity fixture must name its tie convention
before classifying a difference as a failure.~\citep{exec24_survivalother_juliamodels,exec24_survivalother_reference}

Its Kaplan--Meier constructor forms event increments at stored event/censor times.
The vector survival prediction takes their cumulative product; scalar prediction
uses only times strictly less than the requested time. For one event at time two
among two accounts, with the other censored at four, the abstract boundary values
are $S(2-)=1$ and $S(2)=1/2$. The inspected scalar and stored-grid routes thus encode
different sides of the jump, despite documentation describing the usual less-than-or-equal
product. The proposed wrapper must explicitly distinguish left limits from survival
after the event and test scalar/vector agreement under the chosen meaning. A package
name or a successful fit cannot resolve this discrepancy. Delegated SurvivalBase and
SurvivalDistributions behaviour remains a separate inspection obligation.
\citep{exec24_survivalother_juliamodels,exec24_survivalother_reference}

JointSurvivalModels.jl offers a different reuse candidate: constructing distributions
from hazards linked to a longitudinal process. Its version 1.0.0 snapshot declares
Julia 1 compatibility and MIT licensing. The inspected structure combines a baseline
hazard with covariate and linked-process effects. This can help formulate a stipulated
joint model of servicing history and event time, but a model of association does not
identify a payment-holiday intervention. Numerical support defaults to a positive
lower endpoint $10^{-4}$ and upper endpoint $10^4$; hazard integration begins at
the configured lower endpoint. The sampling method accepts a random generator but
the inspected uniform draw calls the unqualified global random function. Integration
tolerance, tail support and generator routing must therefore be inspected and tested
before reproducibility or distributional accuracy is claimed. A conditional modelling
worker is plausible; a blanket port would import these unresolved semantics.
\citep{exec24_survivalother_juliajoint}

\subsection{Rust causal labels require method-level inspection}
The Cameron-Lyons survival repository declares version 2.0.0, edition 2024,
Rust 1.94 and MIT licensing at the pinned commit. These are declarations in the
snapshot, not evidence of a tested toolchain or supported release. Its public Rust
module path re-exports target-trial, marginal-structural-model and TMLE-named
functions. Python registration is delegated and is not established merely by a
Rust export. This explicit distinction matters because an integration proposal must
name the entrypoint whose behaviour is being assessed.~\citep{exec24_survivalother_rustcore}

In the inspected target-trial function, a treated clone initiating within the grace
period receives follow-up $\min(\widetilde T-t_A,\tau)$, while the control clone
uses a clock censored at treatment initiation. With eligibility zero, treatment at
month two, event at month ten and grace period three, the untruncated treated duration
is eight rather than ten months from eligibility. With maximum follow-up five, the
treated duration becomes five but its event flag retains the original event status.
The authored trace is $(5,1)$, while an origin-clock observation administratively
censored at five would be $(5,0)$. This does not establish runtime behaviour of
every wrapper; it establishes why a native admission fixture must bind origin,
grace-period strategy, censoring time and event status jointly.
\citep{exec24_survivalother_rustcore,exec24_survivalother_reference}

The inspected censoring-weight routine ignores its censoring-covariate arguments,
assigns protocol-censored clones a constant based on the trimming option and can
then normalise the weights to mean one. It is not a fitted conditional censoring
model in this path. If two hypothetical conditional observation probabilities are
$1/2$ and $1/4$, their inverse weights are two and four and their mean-normalised
weights are $2/3$ and $4/3$. Giving both records ten and normalising yields one
and one; normalisation cannot create the missing conditioning information.
Likewise, a longitudinal weight's numerator model has a meaning distinct from mean
normalisation. Two treatment probabilities $1/4$ and $1/2$ give an unstabilised
weight eight; numerator probabilities $1/2$ and $1/2$ give a stabilised weight two,
whereas mean normalisation of a single weight gives one.
\citep{exec24_survivalother_rustcore,exec24_survivalother_reference}

Output and uncertainty contracts need equally close attention. The inspected
\texttt{risk\_difference} field is assigned the difference between restricted means,
which has time units. The main calculation weights clones and uses one hundred
grid points; its subject-resampling bootstrap recreates clones without the inspected
censoring-weight call and uses fifty grid points. Fewer than two bootstrap results
trigger a fixed pair of 0.5 standard errors. The sequential-trial helper skips
small eligible sets and retains successful results from a conditional call, so a
delivery wrapper must preserve attempted, skipped, failed and returned trial counts.
These findings motivate rejection of direct causal admission for these entrypoints
at this snapshot, not rejection of every component in the repository.
\citep{exec24_survivalother_rustcore}

The inspected survival-TMLE function assigns outcome one to observations surviving
beyond a horizon, zero to prior observed events and one half to observations censored
before that horizon. A half is an assumption about an unresolved outcome. With one
known survivor, one known event and two unresolved records among four subjects, the
finite-cohort survival fraction can range from $1/4$ to $3/4$; imputing one half for
each unresolved record chooses $1/2$. It does not identify that value. The inspected
function fits a propensity and an outcome regression but contains no explicit
censoring-model adjustment for that assignment. Its restricted-mean integration starts
at the first supplied horizon, while its reported mean-time standard error is an
unweighted combination of pointwise errors without time widths or cross-horizon
covariances. Rescaling months to days must rescale a time-valued standard error;
the abstract expression without time widths does not do so. A method name cannot
substitute for these checks, and no conclusion here extends to uninspected censoring
or TMLE alternatives elsewhere in the repository.
\citep{exec24_survivalother_rustcore,exec24_survivalother_reference}

\subsection{An interval-data candidate and a justified refusal}
The small Rust turnbull snapshot declares version 0.1.0 and edition 2021. No licence
grant was located in the inspected Cargo declaration or complete root tree, so
adoption or redistribution cannot be presumed. Its response type includes interval
and entry information, but the inspected estimator constructs support only from
uncensored exact-event times and an infinity point; handling truncation and variance
is marked unfinished. With only finite intervals $(1,2]$ and $(2,3]$, this abstract
support construction supplies only infinity. Neither interval contains that point,
so both membership rows have zero sum. The normalisation step then has no positive
denominator. This is a reproducible support witness, not a native Rust test result.
The visible convergence loop also lacks an explicit iteration cap.
\citep{exec24_survivalother_rustturnbull,exec24_survivalother_reference}

The defensible proposal disposition is reference-only pending source, rights and
algorithmic repairs. A qualified interval-censoring worker would need an appropriate
support construction, a declared truncation likelihood, finite-iteration and
nonfinite-value handling, and an uncertainty contract. A zero variance placeholder
must not become a claim of certainty. An interval-only fixture is especially valuable
because ordinary exact-event examples can succeed without exercising the capability
named by the package.

\subsection{Adoption choices, public prototypes and full costs}
The preferred architecture preserves selected original engines behind typed,
versioned workers. JuliaStats is a candidate for narrowly specified right-censored
estimation after boundary qualification; SurvivalAnalysis for its declared parametric
response family; SurvivalModels for explicit tie and prediction contracts; and
JointSurvivalModels for a stipulated joint distribution after numerical and random
generator checks. Rust components can be reference or future worker candidates,
but the inspected causal entrypoints require semantic repair before admission.
The interval-data prototype remains reference-only while its licence and support
questions are unresolved. Whole-library ports are not justified by language
preference alone: a port transfers maintenance, rights, numerical and semantic
obligations without supplying identification.

A generated/public prototype can test the merit of this architecture before an
expensive bank experiment. Register exact-event, all-censored, zero-time, delayed-entry,
interval-only, tied-event, competing-event, administrative-censoring and malformed-input
fixtures; match each fixture to a target-specific oracle. Compare scalar and vector
outputs, time-unit rescaling, row permutations, random-seed routing and complete
estimator resampling. Separately evaluate uncertainty under a declared independent
or clustered sampling law. Finite-law examples establish those exact laws; public
data establish only the observable behaviours and assumptions they actually support.
Neither silently supplies counterfactual bank truth.

The CLI/MCP result should carry the source snapshot, environment and rights profile,
original row and subject identities, target and clock, tie/boundary options, diagnostics,
refusal reason, uncertainty method and complete costs. Preserve unsuccessful requests
and human repairs in the denominator. In a stipulated accounting example, twelve
initiated requests costing USD 36 and producing three accepted numeric deliveries
cost USD 3 per initiation but USD 12 per accepted delivery. Correct refusals should
be scored separately from accepted numeric results; deleting them would distort
both reliability and cost. These amounts are authored examples, not vendor prices
or measured performance.~\citep{exec24_survivalother_reference}

The six selected profiles constitute a contrastive review, not exhaustive
other-language coverage. The Julia discovery tail, Rust alternatives, failed
target-trial search and uninspected delegates remain explicit follow-ups. The method
owner must approve the target and observation law; the adapter owner must preserve
units, failures and identities; the rights owner must clear the exact distribution;
and the evaluation owner must preregister public/generated comparisons. This gives
concrete next actions while leaving native, exhaustive and bank acceptance unestablished.


The chapter's common requirement is to preserve the same account history
through every stage of the calculation. Changing the time origin, event
priority, policy law, averaging population or unit of uncertainty can change
the financial decision while leaving a plausible curve on the screen. The
mathematical references and source-specific failures show which distinctions
a proposed worker must expose. The next treatment compares regimes,
heterogeneous effects and continuous doses using those requirements, rather
than assuming that one longitudinal label makes the methods interchangeable.

chapters.title: Longitudinal regimes, heterogeneous effects and continuous doses

segments.text:
\chapter{Longitudinal regimes, heterogeneous effects and continuous doses}
\label{v13:sw-regimes}

The detailed comparisons distinguish complete policy evaluation from components
that estimate heterogeneity or a dose curve. This chapter brings those choices
back to a small set of servicing and incentive requests. Its finite examples
show why the same data field or output name cannot determine which component
the bank needs. The preceding source studies supply the implementation limits;
the task here is to preserve them when composing the workflow.

\section{A sequence of decisions changes the software contract}

Servicing involves repeated decisions. A customer may receive a reminder, a
repayment plan and later a restructuring offer, with delinquency and contact
history changing between actions. An operation for a single binary treatment
does not become a longitudinal estimator by adding a time column. The target
must state which histories the policy observes, when actions occur, what ends
follow-up and how default or account closure changes the outcome.

Let $L_t$ be information available before action $A_t$, and let
$H_t=(\bar L_t,\bar A_{t-1})$ denote the observed history. A deterministic regime
$d$ supplies $A_t=d_t(H_t)$. For a terminal outcome $Y$, its value is
$V(d)=\mathbb E(Y^d)$. Under the required consistency, sequential
exchangeability and positivity conditions, a g-computation construction can
integrate an outcome regression against the covariate transition laws induced
by the intervention. Schematically,
\[
 V(d)=\int m(\bar l_T,\bar d_T)
             \prod_{t=0}^{T}p(l_t\mid\bar l_{t-1},\bar d_{t-1})
             \,d\bar l_T.
\]
The notation suppresses censoring and competing events, which must be specified
in an actual application. The product follows the intervention history; it is
not the factual joint distribution with treatment columns overwritten afterward.

The software comparison should therefore examine covariate transitions,
intervention callbacks, history updates, horizon conventions, simulation error
and sampling uncertainty. It should also compare parametric g-computation with
weighting and longitudinal targeted estimation on the same policy and population.
Disagreement over a default horizon or competing event can dominate any
difference in optimization speed.

\section{pygformula exposes the history and event choices}

The inspected \texttt{ParametricGformula} class accepts individual and time
identifiers, time-varying covariate names/types/models, custom histories, custom
fit/prediction functions and intervention descriptions. Its outcome options
include survival, continuous end-of-follow-up and binary end-of-follow-up.
Separate arguments address competing events, whether to treat them as censoring,
and a censoring model used for natural-course comparisons. \cite{v13_sw_pygformula}

For servicing, default and account closure should not be casually interchanged.
If default prevents later repayment, a default-free survival probability and a
cumulative incidence of repayment are different targets. If closing an account
merely hides future payment information, a censoring argument is needed. Asking
software to treat a competing event as censoring changes the scientific
experiment; the decision requires substantive justification and must survive
the library, CLI and agent interfaces.

The class documentation sets the number of bootstrap samples to zero by
default. The selected fit path invokes separate bootstrap work when samples
are requested. Thus the presence of bootstrap support does not imply that a
particular invocation produced sampling intervals. The helper review in
Section~\ref{sec:exec24-longitudinal-python} establishes whole-subject history
resampling and documents the failed-replicate handling discrepancy. That source
finding does not qualify arbitrary calendar dependence or the fitted intervals.
The adapter must retain the actual sampling unit and complete failure counts.
\cite{v13_sw_pygformula}

Simulation size and bootstrap size address different uncertainties. Conditional
on fitted transition laws, additional simulated trajectories reduce numerical
integration error. They do not provide new bank observations or reduce the
uncertainty in estimated transition parameters. A report should distinguish
the number of observed independent sampling units, simulated histories and
bootstrap replications. Treating simulated histories as additional observed
customers would greatly overstate precision.

The first useful adapter contract therefore preserves customer identity, event
and availability clocks, action timing, history definitions, horizon, competing
events and intervention semantics. It records whether uncertainty was requested
and actually obtained. Natural-course reproduction is a diagnostic: matching
factual outcomes does not prove that intervention predictions are valid.
Unsupported actions, missing positivity and impossible history combinations
should remain explicit, even if simulation can generate a numeric outcome.

The inspected MIT license supports considering reuse. Adoption still needs the
complete simulation and bootstrap paths, environment and dependency terms, and
matched comparisons with R implementations and other longitudinal estimators.
The retained source studies resolve selected simulation and bootstrap questions;
they do not replace those native qualification requirements.
Evaluating supplied regimes also does not establish that an optimal regime has
been learned. Policy selection and its evaluation are additional operations.

\section{grf: binary heterogeneity and continuous slopes are different targets}

The inspected \texttt{causal\_forest} documentation defines a binary-treatment
conditional effect and, for continuous treatment, describes the conditional
covariance ratio
\[
 \tau(x)=\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(Y,A\mid X=x)}
                    {\operatorname{Var}(A\mid X=x)}.
\]
The interface accepts nuisance predictions, clusters and equal cluster
weighting, honesty, subsampling, tuning, grouped trees for uncertainty and a
seed for its native random-number generator. Defaults include 2,000 trees,
honesty enabled and no tuning. These options define a specific statistical and
computational operation; they are not optional metadata for a reproducible
comparison. \cite{v13_sw_grf}

For binary treatment, an effect conditional on $X=x$ differs from a population
average unless it is integrated over the desired population. For continuous
treatment, a slope-like summary differs from a finite contrast
$\mu(a_1,x)-\mu(a_0,x)$. Calling both outputs ``uplift'' obscures the decision.
A bank deciding whether to increase an incentive from one specified amount to
another needs the latter contrast, or a justified approximation to it.

An exact project example makes the discrepancy visible. Suppose the stipulated
mean outcome, in CNY, is
\[
 \mu(a)=20a-3a^2,\qquad A\sim\operatorname{Unif}[0,2].
\]
This is a synthetic response curve, not a fitted bank relationship. Its
covariance slope is
\[
 \frac{\operatorname{Cov}(A,20A-3A^2)}{\operatorname{Var}(A)}
 =20-3\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(A,A^2)}{\operatorname{Var}(A)}=14.
\]
The finite change from dose one to dose two is instead
\[
 \mu(2)-\mu(1)=28-17=11.
\]
Exact moments of the uniform distribution verify both calculations. The
difference is a target difference, not a forest error. Multiplying the slope
by a unit change would overstate this stipulated finite benefit by three CNY.
Neither number includes incentive cost unless that cost is already part of the
outcome definition. \cite{v13_project_exact}

Cluster options require a similar question about the averaging measure. Giving
each branch equal total weight is different from giving each customer equal
weight when branch sizes differ. The chosen measure affects both the target
and the interpretation of heterogeneity. An adapter should require an explicit
population-weight policy and record the effective cluster structure; it should
not silently translate a customer population into an equal-branch population.

The R wrapper's seed, threading and native interface make an R/native adapter
a natural candidate. This inspection does not qualify the C++ training,
prediction or variance implementation. The observed repository GPL text also
requires a complete licensing and distribution review before a port or embedded
binary decision. A rewrite is not automatically preferable to a well-specified
boundary around the original implementation. \cite{v13_sw_grf}

\section{A generalized propensity score is a density component}

CausalGPS's inspected \texttt{estimate\_gps} function accepts continuous
exposure and covariates, a formula, normal or kernel density mode and a
SuperLearner library selection. In its normal branch, the fitted exposure mean
and a residual standard deviation enter a normal density. Its kernel branch
fits exposure and residual scaling and calls a separate density helper. Returned
fields include identity, exposure, generalized propensity score, fitted mean
and scale, and residuals. \cite{v13_sw_causalgps}

For continuous $A$, a generalized propensity score is a conditional density
$r(a,x)=f_{A\mid X}(a\mid x)$, not a probability in $[0,1]$. Its units depend
on the treatment scale. If $B=cA$ for $c>0$, then
\[
 f_{B\mid X}(b\mid x)=\frac1c f_{A\mid X}(b/c\mid x).
\]
Thus converting an incentive from CNY to hundreds of CNY changes the density
numerically. A bridge that normalizes every ``propensity'' into a binary
probability can corrupt continuous-treatment calculations. Exposure units and
the exact density evaluation points belong in the contract.

The observed-density function alone does not provide a dose-response estimator.
To compare feasible doses one needs densities or another identified construction
at the relevant counterfactual doses, an outcome model or weighting/matching
procedure, support diagnostics and an uncertainty argument.
Section~\ref{sec:exec24-dose-response-reuse} follows the density delegate,
transformation factors and downstream weighting. It identifies the selected
kernel branch's residual-density export and the conditions needed for an
original-scale density interpretation. Those restrictions must survive any
cross-package conversion. The retained source analysis establishes a component
and concrete qualification cases; it does not establish the complete causal
workflow.

A useful banking support diagnostic asks whether both proposed incentive levels
occur with adequate conditional support among the intended customers. The
normal model can assign positive density far beyond observed incentive choices;
mathematical positivity of a parametric density is not evidence of practical
overlap. Reporting density values together with observed range, local support
and model sensitivity is more informative than presenting a successful fit as
permission to extrapolate. The observed package declaration is GPL-3; complete
dependency and redistribution choices remain part of adoption review.

\section{causaldrf describes a full response surface, with different limits}

The inspected \texttt{hi\_est} documentation describes fitting a treatment
model, a GPS-adjusted outcome response surface, and predictions averaged over
customers at requested dose-grid values. It lists Normal, LogNormal, transformed
normal, Poisson, negative-binomial, Gamma and Binomial treatment models, and
returns fitted model and parameter records. This supports a documented
response-surface comparison; it is not an execution result or a review of every
internal estimator~\citep{v13_sw_causaldrf}.

Writing a fitted response surface as $\widehat m(a,r)$, the described averaging
operation is of the form
\[
 \widehat\mu(a)=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n
                      \widehat m\{a,\widehat r(a,X_i)\}.
\]
The GPS is evaluated at the proposed dose for each customer, rather than simply
reusing every customer's density at their observed dose. A finite effect then
requires a specified comparator, $\widehat\mu(a_1)-\widehat\mu(a_0)$.
A curve ordinate is an expected outcome, and labeling it as an effect without
the comparator misstates the answer.

The choice of dose grid also matters for decision support. If a business
constraint permits only three incentive levels, interpolation at arbitrary
levels has no immediate operating interpretation. If the optimum is selected
from a dense grid using the same fitted surface, uncertainty in that selection
is not the same as pointwise uncertainty at a fixed dose. A package comparison
should therefore distinguish fixed contrasts, whole curves and policy
optimization, and explain which one is actually supported.

The observed DESCRIPTION declares MIT plus a separate LICENSE file. The
initial documentation review did not include that accompanying notice or a
complete implementation review~\citep{v13_sw_causaldrf}. The later source
review recovered and inspected the notice, identifying the year and copyright
holder~\citep{v131_sw_causaldrf}. The appropriate decision remains a provisional
reference or adapter candidate: full implementation, interval behavior and
transitive dependency terms still require qualification. A recovered notice
is not a complete dependency inventory, and documented point estimation is
not evidence of qualified confidence intervals.

\section{A common servicing and incentive benchmark}

These components should be compared through a small set of declared banking
queries. One query fixes a two-period servicing regime and a terminal repayment
outcome. Another fixes a binary offer and asks for heterogeneity. A third fixes
two continuous incentive levels and asks for their net financial difference.
Each query has its own sampling unit, support requirements, feasible actions
and reference functional. A tool may be appropriate for one and unsupported
for another; that is useful information for architecture.

The comparison should retain a model that fits factual outcomes but fails an
intervention assumption, a weak-support population, a changed event definition
and a changed treatment unit. It should separately measure statistical error,
simulation error, numerical failure and computation. For longitudinal work,
the complete cost includes fitting transitions and histories, simulating
interventions, obtaining uncertainty and reporting diagnostics. Timing one
prediction call omits most of the workflow the bank would operate.

An eventual selection can combine components: symbolic identification, a
longitudinal engine, a heterogeneous-effect estimator and a dose-response
component can coexist behind one semantic contract. The common contract must
preserve their distinct assumptions and outputs. It should make unsupported
requests explicit rather than coercing every query into the nearest available
estimator.

chapters.title: Longitudinal treatment, monitoring and mediation

segments.text:
\chapter{Longitudinal treatment, monitoring and mediation}
\label{sw:longitudinal}

Policy choice also determines what the bank observes. Monitoring can change
record availability, and a recorded engagement measure may become a mediator
rather than a baseline control. The compact example here connects these roles
to the detailed longitudinal and mediation comparisons, so that an interface
preserves the question before routing it to an R estimator.

\section{The history is part of the intervention}

The servicing problem is naturally sequential. An initial action \(A_0\), such
as an early contact, can change a later financial condition \(L_1\). A second
action \(A_1\) is then chosen using that condition, and a later account cost
\(Y\) is observed. The variable \(L_1\) can be both a consequence of the first
action and a determinant of the second. Treating it as an ordinary baseline
control erases that temporal structure. Treating both actions as one binary
indicator can erase the policy being evaluated.

Consider a finite project mechanism in which \(A_0,L_1,A_1\) are binary and
\[
 \Pr(L_1=1\mid\operatorname{do}(A_0=0))=0.8,
 \qquad
 \Pr(L_1=1\mid\operatorname{do}(A_0=1))=0.4.
\]
Conditional mean cost, in CNY per account over a fixed horizon, is specified as
\[
 m(a_0,l,a_1)=100l-50a_1l+20a_0+10a_1.
\]
The initial action costs 20 and reduces the chance of the adverse condition.
The later action costs 10 and reduces adverse-condition cost by 50 when that
condition is present. These numbers define the example; they are not estimates
of actual bank effects.

For a second-stage rule \(d\), replacing the two action equations gives
\begin{equation}
 V(a_0,d)=\sum_{l=0}^{1}m(a_0,l,d(l))
             \Pr(L_1=l\mid\operatorname{do}(A_0=a_0)).
 \label{sw:finite-policy}
\end{equation}
Equation~\eqref{sw:finite-policy} follows by enumerating the two possible
conditions under the specified intervention. It yields
\[
 V(0,0)=80,\qquad V(1,l\mapsto l)=44,\qquad V(1,1)=50.
\]
The adaptive policy is better than always giving the later action because it
avoids paying for that action in accounts without the adverse condition.
No policy-learning or global-optimality theorem is needed for this comparison
of three explicitly specified rules. A proposed general optimizer would have
additional obligations.

Now hold \(A_0=0\) and consider an observed logger that gives \(A_1=1\) with
probability 0.9 when \(L_1=1\), and 0.1 otherwise. The observed treated group
contains a disproportionate share of accounts with the adverse condition.
Direct enumeration gives
\[
 E[Y\mid A_1=1,A_0=0]=58.64865\ldots,
 \qquad E[Y\mid A_1=0,A_0=0]=30.76923\ldots.
\]
The observational difference is approximately \(+27.88\). Yet the intervention
contrast that treats everyone at the second stage, at \(A_0=0\), is
\(V(0,1)-V(0,0)=50-80=-30\). The sign reversal is selection by an observed
time-varying condition in this mechanism. It shows why an interface must retain
the treatment history and the distribution over which the policy is valued.

In an application, evaluating an expression like
\eqref{sw:finite-policy} from observations requires substantive assumptions
connecting observed conditional distributions to the intervention model. It
also requires that relevant histories and actions have support. The example
supplies its structural law directly; it does not demonstrate that a bank's
logger, monitoring or missingness mechanisms satisfy those assumptions.

\section{Point treatment and sequential software have different contracts}

The selected tmle interface concerns binary point-treatment effects with
missingness and subject-ID options. It is a candidate for a suitable static
effect question; that does not make it an arbitrary longitudinal policy engine.
The versioned documentation also contains a treatment-missingness wording
difference between DESCRIPTION and the selected Delta argument.
Section~\ref{exec20:rfx-scope} resolves the selected implementation's contract:
missing treatment and baseline covariates are rejected, while the no-variation
route estimates an outcome mean. Section~\ref{sec:exec24-tmle-reuse} retains
the additional interval and resampling restrictions. A convenient argument
name cannot extend those admitted meanings. \cite{v12_sw_tmle}

stremr's selected sequential g-computation and TMLE documentation is closer to
the servicing problem. It accepts time points, sequential outcome-model
formulas, treatment intervention probabilities, monitoring intervention
probabilities and related weighting choices. Treatment and monitoring are
separate intervention components. A bank that increases contact may also
increase the chance that financial stress is recorded; holding monitoring
fixed and changing it are different policy questions. The interface should
name which of these is being evaluated. \cite{v12_sw_stremr}

The same documentation makes several operational qualifications explicit.
The documentation labels \texttt{Qstratify} nonfunctional and an error source,
while the source review in Section~\ref{sec:exec23-longr-workers} finds a
corresponding branch. That discrepancy remains a qualification question;
it is not evidence of failure in every native call. The proposed profile
withholds that option pending qualification. Weight truncation and stabilization
are choices, and the reviewed stopping loops can differ from the requested
cap. A wrapper should report the effective weights, actual updates, final
residuals and warnings after execution. A truncated weight or stopped numerical
iteration is not evidence that positivity or statistical accuracy has been
established. It is part of the approximation and diagnostic record.

survtmle addresses another closely related but distinct problem: right
censoring, competing failures and cumulative incidence. Its selected interface
supports two treatment values. A competing failure must not be recoded as
ordinary censoring simply to fit a common input schema. In a banking setting,
default, repayment, restructuring and account closure can correspond to
different outcome or observation events, depending on the question. The
adapter must preserve the cause, horizon and target, and the analyst must
justify their interpretation. \cite{v12_sw_survtmle}

The initial software decision is to evaluate separate R operations for static
TMLE, sequential g-computation/TMLE, and competing-risk cumulative incidence.
One common transport envelope can contain their inputs and outputs, but it
should not imply scientific substitutability. The proposed tests include
treatment-confounder feedback, monitoring-dependent recording, administrative
censoring, absent action support, and the distinction between a failure event
and a missing observation. These trials must assess the specific estimand and
sampling law; a successful fit on complete independent records does not
qualify a dynamic bank panel.

The age of a saved distribution is recorded as evidence about that distribution,
not as a verdict on project maintenance. In particular, older stremr and
survtmle snapshots do not prove abandonment. Conversely, a recent version
string does not demonstrate correctness of every documented feature. Build
compatibility and method validity require their own observations.

\section{Mediation changes the target again}

A servicing team may want to decompose an action's effect into a part operating
through customer engagement and a part operating through other channels. This
is a different question from the total effect of an adaptive policy. The
mediator's definition and observation time matter, and a missing engagement
record may itself be affected by contact intensity.

medflex supplies a natural-effect-model interface based on expanded data. Its
selected documentation explains that the original mediator is excluded from
the final natural-effect formula and that a full bootstrap refits working
models. Both details affect integration. Expanded records must retain their
link to the original account, and a bootstrap operating on those records
independently would not generally reproduce a bootstrap of the original
subjects and fitting procedure. Reusing a fixed first-stage fit would also
change the documented full-bootstrap operation. \cite{v12_sw_medflex}

The proposed adapter should therefore export an expansion identity, the
original sampling unit, the effect scale, the mediator definition and the
models refitted in each resample. Section~\ref{exec23:medflex-scope} traces
the expansion, full refitting and original-subject covariance, including the
cross-derivative contribution. That review does not make expanded rows new
independent information. The adapter should not market data expansion as a
solution to unmeasured mediator--outcome confounding. Sensitivity summaries
can accompany the decomposition, but they remain conditional analyses of
assumptions. A total-effect engine and a mediation engine can both be useful
without their outputs being interchangeable.

\section{What an R boundary must preserve}

An R process boundary is a plausible first integration route because it permits
evaluation of the existing estimator with its native dependencies. It is not
yet a selected or qualified deployment. The input should contain a stable
account identifier, the information and action clock, event/availability
times, the observation convention, the intervention specification and the
target's units. Serialization must distinguish absent values from absent
records and preserve factor levels, censoring codes and repeated-subject
structure.

The output needs more than an estimate. It must identify the exact target,
weights and truncations, nuisance-model choices, fitted sample, uncertainty
procedure and unavailable quantities. A bridge may fail before the estimator
runs, during fitting, or while translating a result. These failures require
different remedies. The first remedy is an environment or transport repair;
the second may require numerical diagnostics or revised assumptions; the
third requires correction of the adapter. None is a causal conclusion about
the underlying servicing policy.

Porting is an alternative only after the complete method boundary is clear.
Reimplementing a final regression while omitting its expansion, sequential
weighting, model-refitting bootstrap or stopping conditions would create a
different procedure. The advantage of a native port must be demonstrated on
the full workflow, including data transfer, model fitting, uncertainty and
failure handling. A faster final matrix multiplication is not enough.

chapters.title: Choosing repeated actions

segments.text: \chapter{Choosing repeated actions}

A repeated servicing decision changes both cash flows and the information
available for later decisions. Choosing software therefore begins with the
policy question: evaluate a fixed rule from logged experience, learn a rule
and evaluate it separately, or plan within a supplied model. A numerical
answer can be accurate for one of these questions and misleading for another.

The chapter first examines learned policies and their evaluation populations,
then R methods for learning and evaluating dynamic rules. The detailed Python
comparisons distinguish sequential scores, one-time offers and hidden-state
planning before bringing those choices together. Java and C++ provide
contrasting learning, inference and planning implementations. The final Julia
studies connect interface semantics to concrete model evaluation and
partial-history weighting. Their worked examples keep policy selection,
information loss, monetary scaling and uncertainty visible throughout.

\section{d3rlpy: learning a policy without losing its evaluation target}
\label{exec15:d3rlpy-contract}

A collections team wants to choose the next contact, restructuring offer or
referral from a borrower's history. A library that learns actions from logged
episodes is an attractive challenger to a manually specified rule. The
proposal must nevertheless say which policy is evaluated, whose starting
states define value, when money is received, and which unobserved alternatives
the historical data can support. These choices belong to the scientific
interface. They cannot be delegated to an algorithm name.

The selected d3rlpy source is revision \texttt{38c34b6f99fd}, dated
10 September 2025 and declaring version 2.8.1. It supplies offline and online
reinforcement-learning interfaces, episode and transition objects, and fitted
Q evaluation (FQE). The separately observed PyPI release also has the label
2.8.1; a matching label alone does not establish equality between a released
distribution and a later repository snapshot. The proposal selects these
pinned interfaces as a reference and prospective challenger. An enabled bank
adapter remains conditional on the concrete acceptance cases developed here.
\citep{exec15_d3rlpy_package,exec15_d3rlpy_value,exec15_d3rlpy_contract}

\subsection{From a loan history to a value target}

Let \(H_t\) contain information available before action \(A_t\), and let
\(S_t=f(H_t)\) be the state supplied to a learner. Let \(R_{t+1}\) be net
cash flow from that decision interval, including contact cost and any
specified credit loss. For a policy \(\pi\), a starting distribution \(\mu\),
and a declared period discount \(\gamma\), the proposed target is
\[
 V^{\pi}(\mu)=E_{S_0\sim\mu}^{\pi}
       \left[\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\gamma^t R_{t+1}\right].
\]
This is a definition of the desired policy value. Recovering it from logs
requires that the state/history and observation process support the relevant
conditional transitions and rewards, that action assignment is adequately
accounted for, and that the policy does not require unsupported histories and
actions. A convenient compressed state need not preserve these conditions.
A feature constructed from a later recovery cannot be included in a state
available to an earlier collections decision. The adapter therefore needs
timestamps, lineage and a declared information set as well as arrays.
\citep{exec15_d3rlpy_contract}

FQE fits a separate action-value approximation for a supplied policy. In
the selected implementation, the update obtains the next action through
\texttt{predict\_best\_action}, passes the observed terminal indicator to the
Q-loss calculation, and discounts a transition spanning \(k\) intervals by
\(\gamma^k\). The public learner distinguishes a greedy prediction from a
sampled action. That distinction matters: the inspected FQE update does not
average its continuation over the actions of an arbitrary randomized policy.
No claim about all possible custom implementations follows from this selected
path. \citep{exec15_d3rlpy_value}

Consider a one-decision model with stipulated rewards USD~2 and USD~10 for
actions zero and one. A policy choosing these actions with probabilities
\(1/4\) and \(3/4\) has value USD~8. A deterministic policy always choosing
action one has value USD~10. Evaluating the latter cannot certify the former,
even if both are stored in the same learner object and agree on which action
has the largest score. The proposed contract must freeze whether deployment
uses a greedy rule, a sampled rule, an exploration mixture or a constrained
postprocessor. For a stochastic target, it must either supply a verified
policy-integrated Bellman update or refuse this FQE route. These are exact
target distinctions, not empirical claims about learner quality.
\citep{exec15_d3rlpy_exact,exec15_d3rlpy_contract}

\subsection{Ending an episode changes which observations are learned from}

The pinned episode generator separates terminal flags from timeout flags.
If both are set, it gives priority to termination by setting the overlapping
timeout entries to zero. The source assignment modifies the supplied timeout
array. It then emits episodes at marked boundaries. If no termination or
timeout is present it raises an assertion; if a final segment after an earlier
boundary is unclosed, that segment is not emitted. The selected episode
representation counts all rows as transitions when terminated and one fewer
when truncated. A basic terminal transition receives a zero successor, whereas
a nonterminal transition needs the next stored observation.
\citep{exec15_d3rlpy_episode}

These conventions are reasonable only after mapping the bank's observation
scheme. A default may be terminal for a loan-lifetime objective; an extract
ending on a reporting date is not evidence that no later recovery will occur.
A refinancing event may end one contract while preserving a customer-level
relationship. Each target needs an explicit event dictionary. Treating all
extract boundaries as terminal substitutes zero future value for an unresolved
continuation. Treating an actual end as truncation can omit the final reward.
\citep{exec15_d3rlpy_contract}

For an exact row-accounting example, three stored rows provide three
transitions when the episode is terminal but only two when it is truncated:
the latter's final observation can be a successor, while its final action and
reward have no successor transition in the basic picker. In a six-row input
with a timeout only at row index two, the generator emits indices zero through
two and leaves indices three through five outside emitted episodes. The
adapter should retain the original six-row count, identify this final segment
and require a declared disposition. Silently relabelling the tail as a
completed episode would conceal missing information. A separate boundary
fixture with both flags true must verify the declared precedence and preserve
the caller's original arrays. \citep{exec15_d3rlpy_exact,exec15_d3rlpy_contract}

The inspected upstream test has an additional qualification limit. Its
parameter named ``overlap'' sets timeout flags, but the assignment to terminal
flags occurs only in the separately named terminal branch. Consequently that
parameter does not exercise simultaneous true flags. This is a direct
source-control-flow observation, not an upstream test execution or a claim
that the precedence code fails. A prototype must construct an actual overlap,
check input immutability at the wrapper boundary and verify row disposition
across terminal, truncated and unclosed episodes. The presence of a suitably
named test is insufficient evidence that the intended case is covered.
\citep{exec15_d3rlpy_episode,exec15_d3rlpy_contract}

\subsection{An initial-state score must actually use the initial population}

The selected \texttt{InitialStateValueEstimationEvaluator} is documented as
averaging value at initial states. Its implementation iterates through batches
of each episode and takes the first observation of every batch. The batch
window is 1,024 rows. For sufficiently long episodes, later batch starts
therefore enter the reported mean. Episode duration also changes the number
of contributions. This cannot be treated as one starting observation per
borrower merely because of the evaluator's name.
\citep{exec15_d3rlpy_value}

Take two terminated episodes with 2,048 and one rows. Stipulate predicted
values USD~10 and USD~30 at the long episode's first and second batch starts,
and USD~20 at the short episode's initial state. Equal weighting of the two
initial borrowers gives
\[
   \widehat V_{\mathrm{starts}}=(10+20)/2=15.
\]
The literal selected batching calculation gives
\[
   \widehat V_{\mathrm{batch}}=(10+30+20)/3=20.
\]
The five-dollar difference arises even when every supplied prediction is
exact. It is population substitution, not approximation error. This exact
control-flow reference has not executed the native package.
\citep{exec15_d3rlpy_exact}

A repaired wrapper should extract exactly the declared start state for every
eligible target unit and average with prespecified population weights. It
should separately report exclusions and zero-transition episodes, including
batch-boundary tests at 1,023, 1,024, 1,025 and 2,048 rows. A continuing
portfolio might instead require a calendar-date state distribution; that is
a valid different target and needs an explicitly different scorer. The
package's average-value metric over logged transitions is useful as a scale
diagnostic, while its SoftOPC score contrasts values in episodes selected by
a return threshold with values across all episodes. Neither is automatically
the requested incremental collections value.
\citep{exec15_d3rlpy_value,exec15_d3rlpy_contract}

\subsection{Calendar time and monetary units survive preprocessing}

The basic transition picker assigns interval one. The multistep picker uses
row offsets to discount intervening rewards and to construct the continuation
interval. A physical calendar is not supplied by those row offsets. If a
state is recorded monthly until delinquency and daily thereafter, identical
row discounts express different economic preferences in the two regions.
The contract must choose a fixed grid or a verified clock-aware conversion;
the learner and evaluator must then use the same convention.
\citep{exec15_d3rlpy_episode,exec15_d3rlpy_contract}

Suppose cash flows USD~10 and USD~20 occur at months zero and two, with a
stipulated monthly discount of 0.9. The calendar value is
\(10+0.9^2(20)=26.2\), whereas treating the second stored record as the next
month gives \(10+0.9(20)=28\). This discrepancy is deterministic. More
training cannot resolve a clock the input has failed to represent.
\citep{exec15_d3rlpy_exact}

Reward preprocessing raises a related issue. The selected source includes
clipping, affine standardization and scaling by a range of episode returns.
The public \texttt{predict\_value} applies observation and action
transformations but does not apply an inverse reward transformation.
A transformed Q-value must therefore retain its transformed-objective label.
Moreover, applying a one-step inverse to a cumulative value is generally
incorrect when preprocessing shifts rewards. If \(r'=a r+b\), then
\[
 V'^{\pi}=a V^{\pi}+b E^{\pi}
                 \left[\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\gamma^t\right].
\]
The additional term depends on the discounted horizon and potentially the
policy. A shift can change preferences when policies alter episode length.
This equation is an authored algebraic identity for the declared transform,
not a theorem about a fitted neural approximation.
\citep{exec15_d3rlpy_value,exec15_d3rlpy_exact}

For two adjacent periods with rewards ten and twenty, \(\gamma=0.9\), and
\(r'=(r-5)/5\), the original value is USD~28 and the transformed value is
3.7. Applying the one-step inverse gives \(5(3.7)+5=23.5\). The correct
horizon-aware inversion gives \(5(3.7)+5(1+0.9)=28\). Clipping is more
severe: rewards one hundred and one thousand both become one at an upper
clip of one. No inverse call can recover their original magnitudes from that
output alone. The original cash-flow records must remain available for
evaluation. If a return-range scaler has an equal minimum and maximum, the
selected division also needs an explicit invalid-scale outcome rather than a
nonfinite monetary score. \citep{exec15_d3rlpy_value,exec15_d3rlpy_exact}

\subsection{Conservative learning cannot create missing intervention evidence}

The discrete CQL path combines its temporal-difference loss with a penalty
formed from log-sum-exp action values minus the logged-action value. This is
a specified learning objective. Its name and penalty do not establish the
bank's action-assignment mechanism, recover omitted confounders or turn a
never-observed action into an identified policy comparison.
\citep{exec15_d3rlpy_value}

In a one-state example, suppose logging always chooses action zero and
observes reward zero. Two admissible models agree on every logged record.
Under action one, their rewards are respectively USD~100 and minus USD~100.
The value of always taking action one is different in these models, although
no observed-data fitting criterion can distinguish them using the specified
logs alone. A conservative learner may prefer the supported action; that is
a defensible decision rule under additional preferences or ambiguity
restrictions. It is not recovery of the missing reward. The proposed output
should retain unsupported action mass and any imposed structural assumptions,
and refuse an unconditional causal-value certificate.
\citep{exec15_d3rlpy_exact,exec15_d3rlpy_contract}

Evaluation requires a further separation among sources of uncertainty. A
return distribution describes variation in what happens under a fixed policy
and model. Variation among fitted critics or random seeds describes another
object. Neither automatically supplies sampling coverage for an estimated
mean, uncertainty from unsupported actions or the effect of searching over
many policies. The selected FQE configuration exposes a critic count, but the
inspected update is not by itself an inference procedure for all those
targets. \citep{exec15_d3rlpy_value,exec15_d3rlpy_contract}

For example, a return equally likely to be zero or one hundred has mean fifty
and variance 2,500 square dollars. Under an explicitly independent sample of
one hundred such returns, the sample mean has variance twenty-five and
standard error five dollars. The return standard deviation is fifty dollars.
Reporting one as the other confuses individual risk with precision of a mean.
If two equal-value policies instead receive independent, unbiased score
errors of plus or minus ten, selecting the larger score gives errors
\(-10,10,10,10\) across the four equally likely possibilities: expected
optimism is five dollars. These stipulated calculations motivate customer-level
evaluation splits and selection-aware protocols; they are not measured FQE
coverage or a prediction of a particular bank's bias.
\citep{exec15_d3rlpy_exact}

\subsection{A bounded reuse decision and its next experiment}

The root source has an MIT license with notice-retention and warranty terms.
Its package declaration requires Python at least 3.9 and eleven direct
dependencies, including PyTorch at least 2.5, Gym at least 0.26 and Gymnasium
exactly 1.0.0. Several other requirements are unpinned. The inspected CI
configuration uses Python 3.10 on Ubuntu and macOS and temporarily omits
Windows from its active matrix. These are declared inputs and configuration,
not a resolved installation, a successful CI observation or a commitment to
future support. A deployment decision also needs dependency notices,
checkpoint compatibility and a reviewed update policy.
\citep{exec15_d3rlpy_package}

Direct adoption is deferred. Narrow integration is a plausible later route
because it can retain upstream learners while making population, episode,
policy, clock, scale and failure semantics explicit. Porting the neural
learners is not selected: it would create a second implementation and its
numerical-equivalence burden without a demonstrated benefit. Rejecting all
reference use is also unwarranted; the identified issues admit specific
constraints, fixes and generated acceptance cases. The detailed SCOPE-RL and
Open Bandit Pipeline reviews in Sections~\ref{exec23:scope-rl-scope}
and~\ref{exec23:obp-scope} retain reference dispositions, with native workers
conditional on their own qualifications. This reference does not qualify
those engines or their different sequential and contextual-bandit targets. \citep{exec15_d3rlpy_contract}

The next justified experiment is a small generated environment with an exact
tabular value and direct independent rollouts. It should first verify the
native observations and repaired conversions above, then compare learned
policies against the tabular reference while removing an action from logging
support. Training, tuning and final evaluation should have explicit episode
identities; repeated configurations, failed fits, unsupported requests and
nonfinite scores stay in the denominator. Runtime, review time, data
reconstruction and maintenance cost belong beside performance. Bank-specific
losses, authentic customer validation and measured return on investment are
later inputs. This sequence permits a concrete product proposal now while
making the evidence required for a future adapter precise.
\citep{exec15_d3rlpy_contract}

\label{exec15:d3rlpy-contract-end}

\section{R policy learning: what is optimised, what is evaluated, and what remains unknown}
\label{sec:exec24-policies-r}

A servicing policy should be judged by the value of the decisions it will make after selection.
Consider a bank choosing between a reminder, a payment holiday and ordinary servicing at
successive monthly decisions. A shallow decision tree can describe an interpretable allocation;
a backward regression can construct a sequence of actions; and a policy evaluator can estimate
the value of a supplied rule. These are related services, but they have different targets and
failure modes. This section compares policytree, DynTxRegime, DTRreg and polle at pinned
commits preceding 7 October 2026. It develops conditional original-R-worker choices from
inspected technical sources. Native behaviour, the original methodological papers referenced
by those packages, complete rights and exhaustive R coverage remain separate obligations.

\subsection{Three targets that an interface must distinguish}
Let $H_t$ be the information available before the stage-$t$ action $A_t$, and let
$d=(d_1,\ldots,d_K)$ be a policy with $A_t=d_t(H_t)$. For a stipulated utility $U$,
write $V(d)=\mathbb E[U^d]$. The value of a fixed rule $d$, the value of a
data-selected rule $\widehat d$, and the best value
$\sup_{d\in\mathcal D}V(d)$ over a declared policy class $\mathcal D$ are different
objects. Exact empirical optimisation within shallow trees establishes neither
population optimality nor optimality over unrestricted policies. An estimated value
for rules trained on subsets also need not be the value of the final rule refitted
on all observations. The request must identify which of these is intended.

Selection alone can create apparent value. Suppose two policies each have true value
zero, and their independent development-value errors are equally likely to be minus
one or plus one dollar. Selecting the larger estimate has development expectation
$\mathbb E[\max(\epsilon_1,\epsilon_2)]=1/2$ dollar: the maximum is minus one
only when both errors are negative, with probability $1/4$. The selected policy's
fresh expected value is still zero in this stipulated law. No defect in the optimiser
is needed. A held-out evaluation or a justified design for adaptive-policy evaluation
addresses a different question from improving the empirical search.
\citep{exec24_policiesr_reference}

The familiar one-stage augmented score also exposes the assumptions that a software
label can hide. For action $a$, define
\begin{equation}
 \Gamma_a=m_a(X)+\frac{\mathbf1\{A=a\}}{\widehat e_a(X)}
                      \{Y-m_a(X)\}.
\end{equation}
Conditional on $X$ and fixed fitted nuisance functions, let $e_a=\Pr(A=a\mid X)$
and $\mu_a=\mathbb E[Y\mid A=a,X]$. Direct conditioning gives
\begin{equation}
 \mathbb E[\Gamma_a\mid X]-\mu_a
 =\left(1-\frac{e_a}{\widehat e_a}\right)(m_a-\mu_a).
\end{equation}
Thus either correct nuisance function removes this conditional mean error, where
the propensity denominator is positive and the expectations exist. Interpreting
$\mu_a$ causally still requires the relevant consistency and exchangeability
conditions. Conditioning on fixed nuisance fits is also not a licence to reuse
the same observations adaptively without further analysis. With $\mu_a=10$,
$m_a=8$, $e_a=1/4$ and $\widehat e_a=1/2$, the expected score is nine, not ten;
correcting either nuisance gives ten in this exact example.
\citep{exec24_policiesr_reference}

When an action has no logging support, neither optimisation nor a fitted propensity
creates evidence for its reward. A logger that always takes action zero with reward
zero is compatible with both minus ten and plus ten dollars under action one.
These worlds have the same observed data but different optimal decisions. A bank
must supply additional justified structure, new information or an experiment;
there is no universal software repair for this unrestricted gap.

\subsection{policytree: a useful optimiser with an upstream score obligation}
The inspected policytree declaration is version 1.2.5, requiring R at least 3.5.0,
with MIT plus its licence file and dependencies including grf and Rcpp. Its main
interface accepts a feature matrix $X$ and an action-reward matrix $\Gamma$. The
documentation describes exhaustive shallow-tree search and explains the substantial
dependence on depth, feature count and distinct feature values. The optional
\texttt{split.step} skips candidate splits; hybrid search builds a deeper tree using
limited lookahead. The latter is a different optimisation procedure, not an
unqualified certificate of the same global optimum.
\citep{exec24_policiesr_policytree}

The inspected R wrapper checks numeric matrix/data-frame inputs, missing entries,
matching row counts, nonnegative depth and positive integer split and node-size
controls. It passes the matrices to an Rcpp binding, which invokes the C++ tree
search. The inspected leaf routine maximises sums of supplied rewards, retaining
the earlier action on exact reward ties because its update uses a strict greater-than
comparison. Recursive paths check interrupt requests and split eligibility. These
details make an original R worker a plausible proposal choice, but they do not
establish runtime bounds on an arbitrary input or causal validity of the supplied
reward matrix. The wrapper needs explicit finite-value, depth/resource and action-ID
policies, with native tests of the exact entrypoint before admission.
\citep{exec24_policiesr_policytree}

The binary causal-forest score adapter constructs the two conditional mean estimates
from forest predictions and forms the augmented scores using observed treatment
propensities. In the inspected function, the inverse propensity is calculated
directly; support and any upstream grf safeguards therefore need to be matched
explicitly. An adapter should record whether the supplied scores are out-of-sample,
which nuisance version produced them and which observations were used to select
the policy. It should not label an arbitrary matrix as doubly robust evidence.
The package's train/test example is useful documentation, but a complete learning
procedure must also account for nuisance and feature-selection dependencies.
\citep{exec24_policiesr_policytree}

Prediction adds a mundane but material banking risk: feature meaning can change
without changing matrix dimensions. The R method checks the column count, while
its documentation requires the training order. The C++ prediction path follows
numeric split-column positions. A CLI/MCP worker should bind names, order, units
and preprocessing to the fitted artifact, and refuse a schema mismatch. Action
indices similarly need a stable mapping to reminder, holiday and ordinary servicing.
The proposed choice is to integrate the original optimiser behind a schema-aware
worker and an independently qualified scoring/evaluation layer. A whole C++ port
is unnecessary unless a measured deployment constraint justifies its maintenance.
\citep{exec24_policiesr_policytree}

\subsection{DynTxRegime and DTRreg: sequential structure is an explicit modelling choice}
DynTxRegime's pinned 4.16 declaration identifies Q-learning, interactive Q-learning,
weighted learning and value-search families, with GPL-2 licensing and dependencies
including modelObj, kernlab and optimisation packages. Its \texttt{qLearn} interface
performs a single backward step. A numeric response starts the recursion; a prior
\texttt{QLearn} object passes the preceding estimated value into the next step.
The inspected dispatch verifies model objects, the data frame, response and feasible
action-set interface, then delegates regression and prediction. A sequence of calls
therefore needs a declared stage order, available histories and reward convention;
the existence of the object hierarchy does not prove that the chosen regression
models identify the bank's optimal strategy. The documented training-set value
must be kept distinct from an external evaluation of the resulting rule.
\citep{exec24_policiesr_dyntx}

This is a reasonable original-R-worker candidate where its model and action-set
interfaces match the question. The alternatives are to use a different qualified
sequential estimator, to retain it as a mathematical/design reference, or to defer
a family whose delegates and assumptions have not been inspected. The package-level
listing of methods must not close every method-specific coverage cell. In particular,
the selected Q-learning dispatch does not establish a universal outcome-weighted,
value-search or hidden-state capability.

DTRreg version 2.4 declares GPL-2 and provides dynamic weighted least squares,
G-estimation, Q-learning and survival-related families. The inspected DTRreg
documentation specifies treatment, treatment-free and blip models at each stage;
it restricts continuous-treatment blips to a quadratic form. Its direct consistency
claims depend on model conditions and should be assessed against the methodological
originals before inheritance as a theorem. In the inspected dispatcher, multinomial
G-estimation is explicitly rejected. Backward stage fitting is followed by forward
recalculation of selected treatments and renewed pseudo-outcome construction.
That is a substantive sequential algorithm, not a collection of unrelated stagewise
regressions.~\citep{exec24_policiesr_dtrreg}

The continuous-action domain illustrates why an apparently precise optimum can
exceed the evidence. For a stipulated benefit $u(a)=8a-2a^2$, the nonnegative
unrestricted optimum is $a=2$ with value eight. If observed actions cover only
$[0,1]$, the supported optimum is $a=1$ with value six. A second response curve
can equal this quadratic on $[0,1]$ and continue as $6-100(a-1)$ beyond one;
the observed action range cannot distinguish it, but its optimum remains one.
Choosing the first curve's extrapolated optimum requires the quadratic restriction
outside support. Clipping a recommendation is a policy constraint, whereas asserting
the extrapolated optimum is an identification claim.~\citep{exec24_policiesr_reference}

DTRreg's inspected weight dispatcher distinguishes inverse probability, capped inverse
probability, overlap and other paths. The capped path uses the empirical 99th
percentile. Trimming can control extremes, but it changes the estimating expression
and does not restore unsupported actions. In an exact four-stage example with
probability $1/10$ of the required action at each stage, the target path occurs with
probability $1/10{,}000$ and has inverse weight $10{,}000$. With unit reward and a
cap of one hundred, the expectation of the capped path contribution is $1/100$
instead of one. This is an authored illustration of the tradeoff, not a benchmark
of DTRreg's default settings.~\citep{exec24_policiesr_dtrreg,exec24_policiesr_reference}

Its selected bootstrap resamples participant rows, reconstructs the object and
reruns the stage procedure. An interruption returns an explicit aborted result;
NA parameter draws trigger an error before covariance construction. An optional
tail replacement modifies bootstrap draws before variance calculation. These
are observable source contracts that a worker should preserve. They do not
establish finite-sample coverage, justify treating correlated bank accounts as
independent, or remove nonregularity near tied optimal actions. The documentation
warns about nonunique optimal treatment only when a variance-estimation option is
selected; absence of that warning otherwise is not evidence of a unique optimum.
\citep{exec24_policiesr_dtrreg}

\subsection{polle: separating training, evaluation and history restrictions}
The pinned polle 1.6.5 declaration describes policy learning and evaluation, requires
R at least 4.1 and lists an Apache License at version two or later. Its dependencies
include policytree, DynTxRegime, survival and targeted; this declaration is not
transitive rights clearance. The inspected evaluator accepts either a fixed policy
or a learner, and distinguishes value evaluation from a restricted single-stage,
binary-action subgroup effect. It accepts separate action, outcome, censoring and
terminal-outcome models. Source checks request censoring models when relevant
censoring events occur and a terminal-outcome model for the specified missing
terminal-utility case. These are useful refusal semantics for a proposed worker.
\citep{exec24_policiesr_polle}

The default evaluator has \texttt{M=1}. In that branch, training and validation
objects are the same. For \texttt{M>1}, the inspected routine constructs folds,
splits by the policy-data IDs and passes distinct training and validation objects
to the evaluation function. That function sends the training object to
\texttt{fit\_functions}; when no fixed policy is supplied, the inspected delegate
invokes the learner on that training object before evaluating on validation data.
This establishes a concrete source path for outer evaluation separation. It does
not by itself prove independence of related accounts, prevent leakage through
externally supplied fitted nuisance objects, or validate every delegated learner.
The choice of a fixed policy, training algorithm, training sample size and final
refit must appear in the reported target.~\citep{exec24_policiesr_polle}

History compression is another explicit restriction. The inspected interfaces have
separate full-history flags for action, outcome and censoring models and for the
policy itself, with state-like histories as defaults. In a stipulated example,
an earlier binary observation $H$ is fair, the present state is constant, and utility
is $\mathbf1\{A=H\}$. A rule retaining $H$ achieves value one; every fixed action
using only the constant state achieves one half. A smaller state representation is
not harmless merely because an API accepts it. The bank must explain why the
retained state suffices for the causal and decision questions, or preserve the
history and evaluate the larger model.~\citep{exec24_policiesr_polle,exec24_policiesr_reference}

The learning interface offers distinct Q-learning, doubly robust Q-learning, tree
and weighted-learning choices, with method-specific restrictions and delegates.
Nested nuisance-fitting folds and outer policy-evaluation folds are different
controls. An adapter must preserve both, record any supplied prefit models and
avoid translating a method name into a blanket calibration claim. Source comments
about the orientation of one weighted-learning solver require inspection of that
delegate before they are inherited as established behaviour. For the present
proposal, polle is a conditional original-R-worker candidate with named method,
history, support and evaluation contracts.~\citep{exec24_policiesr_polle}

\subsection{Qualification through public and generated tasks}
The package comparisons lead to a practical prototype rather than an immediate
whole-library rewrite. Use a small finite-state servicing generator with known
