Enterprise Edition and above; transient and temporary objects have different
limits. Extending retention does not restore versions already outside Time Travel.
Retention also consumes storage. These are material deployment and cost
distinctions, although no price quote or commercial entitlement is established
here. A storage snapshot can preserve what a warehouse held at a particular time;
the correspondence between that state and what an operational decision-maker knew
still requires ingestion and availability evidence~\citep{exec22_obs_snowflake_time}.

The SQL boundary rules must survive the adapter. \texttt{AT} includes changes at
the specified boundary; \texttt{BEFORE} a statement means immediately before its
completion, and can include another transaction committed after that statement
started. Timestamp casts, time zones and the statement-ID age limit also affect
replay. Historical queries use the current table definition, including added
columns and defaults, and current access requirements apply retroactively.
Consequently a stored query alone is insufficient to reconstruct every historical
semantic or authorization decision. Preserve the relevant schema, dictionary,
transformation, query boundary and permission evidence alongside the snapshot.
An expired historical query should remain a refusal rather than fall back to
current data~\citep{exec22_obs_snowflake_at}.

\subsection{Inclusion, evaluation and a conditional integration decision}
\label{exec22:obs-selection}

Linkage failures can alter the estimand even when retained links are correct.
Suppose a randomized study has two equally common strata with causal effects 6
and 2. Let retention into the linked analysis sample be 1 in the first stratum
and $1/4$ in the second, independent of treatment and potential outcomes within
stratum. The population effect is 4, but the linked sample has stratum proportions
$4/5$ and $1/5$, giving
\begin{equation}
 \tau_{\rm linked}=\frac45\,6+\frac15\,2=\frac{26}{5}.
 \label{exec22:obs-inclusion}
\end{equation}
Weighting retained records by the inverse of their stipulated inclusion
probabilities returns 4 after normalization. This correction needs positive
inclusion probabilities and conditional transport of potential outcomes. It does
not automatically apply when matching depends on unobserved outcomes or on
post-treatment information. An audit selected only from easy, successfully linked
customers cannot establish performance in the excluded population~\citep{exec22_obs_reference}.

These distinctions support conditional reuse. AWS and QualityStage are candidates
for obtaining documented matching outputs; Databricks is a candidate for explicitly
versioned feature retrieval; Snowflake is a candidate for retained storage history.
The proposal's additional obligation is to connect those outputs to units,
information sets, target populations and causal assumptions. It currently has the
exact authored examples and design contracts described here, not qualified native
adapters. There is no basis for a blanket superiority claim over any platform.

A shared library, CLI and MCP request should declare the observational unit,
relationship type, source keys, decision time, event and availability fields,
mapping vintage, intended population and query purpose. Its result should retain
native workflow and version identifiers, alternative links or explicit absence of
them, score granularity, null/stale behavior, excluded/error records, schema and
replay evidence. Sampling uncertainty, linkage uncertainty and structural causal
ambiguity must remain distinguishable. An agent can propose schema mappings,
retrieve documentation and explain conflicting timestamps; it cannot certify
identity, ownership, causal assignment or calibration from those texts alone.
Missing availability, incompatible score semantics and expired history need typed
refusals shared by all three interfaces.

A public prototype can test these requirements without private bank data. Generate
customer histories with hidden known identities, separate household relations,
controlled name/address corruption, late corrections and known treatment effects.
Keep the truth out of the matching inputs. Compare raw exact-key joins, a declared
probabilistic matcher, corrected-clock retrieval and the proposed wrapper under
matched information. Report false merges and splits, exclusion rates by stratum,
future-information violations, effect bias, uncertainty coverage where a justified
procedure exists, and decision loss under explicit monetary scenarios. Separate
calibration from final evaluation and include abrupt population shifts. Native
vendor trials require pinned editions, rights and a reviewed budget; mathematical
examples do not substitute for them. Public prototype merit should determine
whether a later experiment with costly bank evidence is justified.

\section{Commercial missing-data workflows and transfer between bank populations}
\label{exec21:transport-scope}

A bank may obtain a credible intervention estimate in a pilot and still make a
poor decision when it extends the intervention to another branch. Customers may
differ, follow-up outcomes may be missing, and the software used to complete
the records may report uncertainty for a different quantity from the proposed
decision. A useful commercial comparison therefore follows the complete
question: which population receives which action, when is the outcome measured,
why is it unobserved, and which assumptions connect the observed records to the
decision? Imputation, uncertainty combination and population transfer are
separate steps. A feature called ``missing values'' establishes none of those
connections by its name alone.

The selected primary documentation provides concrete comparators. Stata's
\texttt{mi} family manages multiple completed datasets and their analysis;
SAS/STAT's MI and MIANALYZE procedures separate generation and combination;
IBM SPSS Missing Values exposes imputation and output-specific pooling.
The inspected IBM edition is 31.0.2. The SAS HTML identifies version 14.1,
whereas the Stata manuals contain release-19 example-data paths and July 2026
PDF metadata. These identities delimit the comparison; later retrieval does
not authenticate every byte as the edition available at the literature cutoff.
Exact licensed builds, current entitlements and broader commercial coverage
remain unresolved. EViews, Mplus and commercial graphical tools remain leads
requiring matched technical originals for this particular target.
\cite{exec21_transport_stata_mi,exec21_transport_sas_mi_intro,exec21_transport_spss_missing}

\subsection{Missingness assumptions precede record completion}
\label{exec21:transport-missingness}

Let $A$ be a binary action, $X$ covariates recorded before that action, $Y(a)$
the monetary outcome under action $a$, and $R$ an indicator that the outcome is
observed. The record contains $(X,A,R,RY)$, with a separate missingness mask so
that an absent outcome is never mistaken for a zero. Consistency connects an
observed outcome to $Y(A)$; treatment exchangeability and positive treatment
probability are additional causal assumptions. For the particular problem in
which only $Y$ is missing, a conditional mean restriction sufficient for response
adjustment is
\begin{equation}
 E[Y\mid X,A,R=1]=E[Y\mid X,A],\qquad
 P(R=1\mid X,A)>0.
 \label{exec21:transport-mar}
\end{equation}
The stronger familiar MAR restriction makes response independent of the missing
outcome conditional on the observed variables. When covariates are also missing,
the pattern-specific observed information and imputation model must be specified
again; equation~\eqref{exec21:transport-mar} is not a general multivariate recipe.
Administrative censoring, a variable undefined for a customer, and an outcome
lost through nonresponse need distinct observation models.

Stata's substantive manual and the SAS assumptions chapter distinguish MAR
from MCAR and describe ignorability using MAR together with distinct parameters
for the data and missingness models. They also explain why an assumption about
unobserved values cannot be verified by inspecting only the observed values.
The SAS profile adds distributional restrictions for particular regression and
MCMC procedures. These restrictions must accompany a procedure name. A good
fit to observed records, a plausible-looking imputed distribution or rejection
of an MCAR diagnostic does not establish MAR.
\cite{exec21_transport_stata_substantive,exec21_transport_sas_assumptions}

An exact example makes the investment consequence visible. Let a latent response
type $H$ be equally likely to be zero or one, randomize $A$ independently of
$H$, and set $R=H$. All customers have $Y(0)=0$. Responders have $Y(1)=10$.
In one complete-data law, nonresponders have $Y(1)=-10$; in a second they have
$Y(1)=10$. The observable joint distribution of $(A,R,RY)$ is identical in
both laws: each action-response cell has probability $1/4$, and observed treated
outcomes equal 10. Yet the complete-population effects are respectively 0 and
10. At an assumed action cost of USD 4, the margins are USD $-4$ and USD 6.
More imputation draws from one selected model cannot distinguish these worlds.
The project reference enumerates the complete laws and verifies equality of
their observed distributions. It does not assert that either law describes
actual bank records. \cite{exec21_transport_reference}

A transparent sensitivity parameter writes the unobserved treated mean as
$10+\delta$, keeping the control mean zero. The resulting target is
\begin{equation}
 \tau(\delta)=10+\tfrac12\delta,\qquad
 V(\delta)=6+\tfrac12\delta.
 \label{exec21:transport-sensitivity}
\end{equation}
For the illustrative restriction $\delta\in[-20,0]$, value ranges from $-4$
to 6 and changes sign at $\delta=-12$. The interval is supplied as a sensitivity
restriction, not learned from the missing outcomes. The SAS sensitivity chapter
documents a pattern-mixture approach in MI and explicitly says that the
selection-model approach is not supplied by that procedure profile. A result
that changes under a plausible MNAR scenario establishes dependence of the
decision on assumptions; it does not establish which scenario is true. Exact
syntax and later-release capabilities need their own evidence.
\cite{exec21_transport_sas_sensitivity,exec21_transport_reference}

\subsection{What the three documented workflows preserve}
\label{exec21:transport-workflows}

Stata offers four MI storage styles while retaining the original data as
$m=0$ and the completed datasets as $m=1,\ldots,M$. Variables can be regular,
imputed or passive, with passive variables representing algebraic functions
of other variables. The introduction also states that extended missing values
\texttt{.a} through \texttt{.z} persist as hard missing in the documented
profile. An interchange layer that maps every absent value to an ordinary
numeric null could therefore change what the engine is asked to impute.
Maintaining the missingness reason and role is part of the statistical contract.
\cite{exec21_transport_stata_mi}

For chained equations, Stata documents a default burn-in of ten iterations,
ordering from the most to the least observed variable, configurable conditional
models and saved trace summaries. Perfect prediction produces an error unless
an explicit augmentation option is requested. The manual discusses
incompatible conditionals and dependence of results on specification, order
and burn-in. These are useful controls, but a chosen default is not a proof of
convergence or of adequacy for a causal estimand. For example, an imputer that
omits a treatment interaction needed by the analyst can erase the heterogeneity
needed for the branch-transfer decision even if marginal summaries look
reasonable. \cite{exec21_transport_stata_chained,exec21_transport_stata_substantive}

There is a stronger reason to retain the conditional specifications themselves.
Consider binary $U,V$ with proposed conditionals
\begin{equation}
 \begin{aligned}
 P(U=1\mid V=0)&=P(U=1\mid V=1)=\tfrac12,\\
 P(V=1\mid U=0)&=\tfrac14,\qquad P(V=1\mid U=1)=\tfrac34.
 \end{aligned}
 \label{exec21:transport-conditionals}
\end{equation}
For any positive binary joint distribution, the odds ratio calculated from
either pair of conditionals must agree. Here the first specification requires
odds ratio 1 and the second requires 9, so no such joint distribution exists.
Nevertheless, alternating draws can have stable distributions. In the cell
order $(0,0),(0,1),(1,0),(1,1)$, a scan updating $U$ then $V$ has stationary
law $(3,1,1,3)/8$; reversing the scan has stationary law $(1,1,1,1)/4$.
Direct multiplication verifies each invariant distribution. Thus an apparently
stable trace does not demonstrate compatibility of the supplied conditionals.
This exact constructed example is a diagnostic design, not an observed failure
of a particular vendor's implementation. \cite{exec21_transport_reference}

SAS supplies a related but separately versioned workflow. Its MI overview
distinguishes sequential methods for monotone patterns from multivariate-normal
MCMC and fully conditional specification for arbitrary patterns. FCS uses
separate conditional models rather than beginning with an explicit common
multivariate model. The completed datasets are analyzed using the relevant
complete-data procedures, and MIANALYZE reads parameter estimates together with
standard errors or covariance matrices. It notes an additional assumption for
multivariate Wald inference and special treatment for quantities such as
correlations and ratios. The proposal therefore needs a typed collection of
estimates and covariance matrices, not just a filled table. The recovered HTML
contains equations as images that are outside this text inspection; the numerical
pooling formulas below are grounded in the readable Stata manual.
\cite{exec21_transport_sas_mi_intro,exec21_transport_sas_mianalyze_intro,exec21_transport_sas_combining}

IBM's manual makes another important distinction. Multiple Imputation accepts
analysis weights in summaries and imputation models, but it does not explicitly
handle strata, clusters or other complex sampling structures. The manual also
says that Complex Samples procedures do not automatically analyze MI datasets
in this profile. Frequency weights and analysis weights have different
semantics; noninteger frequency weights are rounded. Passing a final sampling
weight therefore does not establish a cluster-aware covariance calculation.
Stata documents a survey-prefix analysis route, but that alone also leaves
the imputation model's treatment of the sampling design to be justified.
\cite{exec21_transport_spss_missing,exec21_transport_stata_estimate}

SPSS chooses a monotone method when the pattern permits it and otherwise uses
FCS. Automatic FCS uses ten iterations; the manual provides history output
for convergence assessment. Main effects are the automatic specification,
with optional categorical two-way interactions under selected settings.
Scale variables can use linear regression or predictive mean matching, whose
documented default donor count is five; categorical models use logistic
regression. Constraints can cause redraws, and excluding highly incomplete
variables removes them from both imputation and prediction. Reproducing a run
requires the same seed, case order, variable order and settings. These details
affect the implied procedure and belong in an adapter request.
\cite{exec21_transport_spss_missing}

The output variable \texttt{Imputation\_} distinguishes original data from
the $M$ completed versions, and split-file settings control how those versions
are analyzed. IBM distinguishes naive combination, which supplies a pooled
parameter, from univariate combination, which can also supply standard errors,
effective degrees of freedom, intervals and missing-information diagnostics.
Support is specific to each output; an unsupported procedure returns no pooled
output. An integration must preserve that unavailability rather than attach a
generic confidence interval to every pooled number.
\cite{exec21_transport_spss_missing}

\subsection{Combine uncertainty on the declared estimand scale}
\label{exec21:transport-pooling}

For a fixed scalar estimand $Q$, let $\widehat Q_m$ and $U_m$ be the estimate
and its completed-data variance from imputation $m$. The documented combination
rule is
\begin{align}
 \overline Q&=M^{-1}\sum_{m=1}^M\widehat Q_m,&
 \overline U&=M^{-1}\sum_{m=1}^M U_m,\nonumber\\
 B&=(M-1)^{-1}\sum_{m=1}^M(\widehat Q_m-\overline Q)^2,&
 T&=\overline U+(1+M^{-1})B.
 \label{exec21:transport-poolformula}
\end{align}
The between-imputation term reflects missing-data uncertainty under the
specified imputation model, and $B/M$ reflects using finitely many imputations.
Neither accounts automatically for uncertainty about an unverified MAR or
population-invariance assumption. Valid completed-data inference and suitable
imputation remain premises. For vector parameters the covariance matrices,
including their off-diagonal terms and common coefficient identities, must be
preserved. \cite{exec21_transport_stata_estimate,exec21_transport_stata_substantive}

For the authored values $(\widehat Q_1,\widehat Q_2,\widehat Q_3)=(0,2,4)$
and $U_m=1$, equation~\eqref{exec21:transport-poolformula} gives
$\overline Q=2$, $B=4$ and $T=19/3$. Retaining only the within variance gives
1. Incorrectly treating the three completed-data estimates as independent
replicate measurements would give $\overline U/M=1/3$. Neither is the MI
variance. The documented large-complete-sample degrees-of-freedom approximation
uses $r=(1+M^{-1})B/\overline U$ and
$\nu=(M-1)(1+1/r)^2$, giving $361/128$ here. A small complete-data sample
requires the further adjustment documented by the manual; the arithmetic is
not a universal coverage result. \cite{exec21_transport_stata_estimate,exec21_transport_reference}

The estimand scale also matters. If two log-odds estimates correspond to odds
ratios 1 and 9, exponentiating their average coefficient gives 3, whereas
averaging the odds ratios gives 5. Stata documents coefficient-scale pooling
followed by an optional exponentiated display; it also has explicit requests
for transformed coefficients. A declared transformed estimand needs its own
completed-data uncertainty and suitable pooling justification. Neither 3 nor
5 is a bank's average profit or a marginal treatment effect merely because it
was returned after imputation. \cite{exec21_transport_stata_estimate,exec21_transport_reference}

Failure handling is part of the same argument. Stata normally stops when an
imputation's estimation fails or the estimation sample changes. Its
\texttt{errorok} and \texttt{esampvaryok} options permit different behavior.
An automatic wrapper must expose such choices and retain the failing
imputation and sample identities. Otherwise it can silently pool different
populations or select only successful fits. The appropriate number of
imputations should be chosen using stability and Monte Carlo error diagnostics
for the requested inference; high relative efficiency of a point estimator
does not guarantee stable intervals or decision thresholds.
\cite{exec21_transport_stata_estimate,exec21_transport_sas_mi_intro}

\subsection{Transport needs an explicit population bridge}
\label{exec21:transport-target}

Let $S=1$ denote the source pilot and $S=0$ the target branch, and define
$p_s(x)=P(X=x\mid S=s)$ and
$\tau(x)=E[Y(1)-Y(0)\mid X=x,S=1]$. One sufficient route assumes consistency,
source treatment exchangeability, positive source treatment and response
probabilities, valid response adjustment within source covariates, and equality
of conditional potential-outcome means across $S$. It also requires source
support wherever $p_0(x)>0$. Under these restrictions, iterated expectation gives
\begin{equation}
 \tau_0=\sum_x p_0(x)\tau(x)
       =E\left[\left.\frac{p_0(X)}{p_1(X)}\tau(X)\right|S=1\right].
 \label{exec21:transport-standardize}
\end{equation}
This is a project derivation for a declared finite-covariate regime. Equality of
conditional means is extra scientific information; it is not established by
the existence of a weight column or by the imputation procedure.
\cite{exec21_transport_reference}

For clarity, write $e_a(x)=P(A=a\mid X=x,S=1)$ and
$r_a(x)=P(R=1\mid A=a,X=x,S=1)$. Under the same response restriction and
positivity, each source conditional mean can be written
\begin{equation}
 \mu_a(x)=E\left[\left.
       \frac{\mathbb{1}\{A=a\}RY}{e_a(x)r_a(x)}
       \right|X=x,S=1\right].
 \label{exec21:transport-response}
\end{equation}
Condition first on $A=a$ and $R=1$, cancel the treatment and response
probabilities, then apply the mean restriction and source causal assumptions.
Substitution into equation~\eqref{exec21:transport-standardize} gives a
combined population, treatment and response-weight expression. It is not a
variance estimator: estimated nuisance models, sampling the target covariates,
clustering and any use of MI require a jointly justified inference procedure.
Weights for these different purposes must remain separately named.

Suppose the source proportions of two customer strata are $(4/5,1/5)$ and the
target proportions are $(1/5,4/5)$. Conditional intervention effects are USD
10 and USD $-10$. The pilot's average effect is 6, the target's is $-6$, and
the population weights are $1/4$ and 4. At an assumed cost of USD 2, the pilot
margin is USD 4 and the target margin is USD $-8$. The exact reference also
enumerates randomized treatment and four positive response rates, verifying
that the combined weighting expression recovers the stipulated target.
No software error is needed for the naive deployment decision to reverse:
the wrong population suffices. \cite{exec21_transport_reference}

If the source instead contains only the first stratum, the second effect is
unobserved and no finite reweighting creates its information. With the explicit
restriction that the second effect lies in $[-10,10]$, the target effect is
$2+(4/5)\tau(1)\in[-6,10]$, giving margin $[-8,8]$ at cost 2. Without such
a justified bound, even that interval cannot be asserted. An adapter should
report the support defect and any defensible identified set. Silently trimming
the second stratum changes the target population; silently predicting into it
adds extrapolation assumptions. \cite{exec21_transport_reference}

\subsection{Competitive position and a public qualification route}
\label{exec21:transport-integration}

The documented commercial systems already provide substantive imputation,
analysis and diagnostic workflows. The proposal has not demonstrated a native
replacement or superior estimation performance. Its proposed contribution is
to preserve the causal question and its restrictions across those workflows:
source and target populations, observation clocks, missingness reasons,
imputation identity, covariance semantics and explicit refusal. Licensed
isolated execution is a candidate integration route; public manuals do not
grant redistribution rights for the engines. EViews, Mplus and graphical-tool
profiles cannot be ranked without the missing originals, and prices remain
unknown. \cite{exec21_transport_stata_estimate,exec21_transport_sas_mianalyze_intro,exec21_transport_spss_missing}

A useful first prototype would compare a selected licensed procedure and an
already reviewed open implementation on the same generated population,
missingness law and estimand. Complete-record analysis, complete-case analysis,
single imputation, proper multiple imputation and an explicitly specified
response-weight procedure supply substantive alternatives. Fix the causal
target, sample law, interaction structure, number of imputations, diagnostic
and refusal rules before evaluation. Include MAR and MNAR cases, complete and
missing source support, compatible and incompatible imputation models, cluster
sampling, changing coefficient sets and unsuccessful fits. Report bias,
coverage under the claimed regime, interval width, unavailable requests,
simulation error and full workflow cost. A sensitivity grid evaluates
robustness; it is not a device for choosing whichever assumption makes a
preferred intervention profitable.

The library, CLI and MCP interfaces should carry the same request and result
meaning. Original and imputed data need stable unit and imputation identifiers,
measurement types, category references, passive transformations and sampling
design. Results need per-imputation estimates and covariance, pooled scale and
degrees of freedom, convergence diagnostics, population support and retained
failures. An assistant can help locate technical passages, propose models and
explain sensitivity; it cannot infer the unobserved outcomes or authorize a
scientific assumption from fluent text. These public comparisons can establish
whether the proposed integration merits a more expensive bank experiment.


\subsection{What must be preserved from the audit to the decision}

The chapter's alternatives answer different information problems. Joint audits
can distinguish relationship laws that separate-edge labels cannot. Coordinated
actions can sometimes avoid an unresolved graph moment. Population adjustment
uses justified invariance and support; imputation uses an observation and
analysis model; historical retrieval uses identity and availability rules.
Neither a completed table nor a precise conditional calculation establishes
all of those premises.

A defensible recommendation therefore retains the missing information and its
monetary consequence. It may call for an additional joint audit, a different
allocation, a restricted target population, sensitivity analysis or refusal.
The software choices matter because their score, covariance, mask, clock and
failure behavior can preserve or change that recommendation. The next chapter
examines hidden-state and Bayesian computations as further conditional tools,
with their assumptions carried into the comparison.

chapters.title: Hidden states and Bayesian comparisons

segments.text:
\chapter{Hidden states and Bayesian comparisons}

An uncertain customer state can be useful for a banking decision only if its
meaning, observation law and action mechanism are specified. This chapter first
examines state filtering and probabilistic model surgery through Dynamax, PyMC
and NumPyro. It then compares the resulting requirements across languages and
commercial engines. The comparison keeps causal identification, parameter and
state uncertainty, predictive variation and numerical approximation distinct.
Similar finite examples provide common tests of those distinctions; their
repetition is not additional empirical evidence about a package or a bank.

\section{Dynamax reuse requires a declared conditional law and information clock}
\label{exec19:dynamax-scope}

A servicing team may infer a borrower's unobserved repayment propensity from
payments, contacts and changing account conditions. A state-space engine is a
natural computational component, but its likelihood must describe the experiment
that generated those observations. Treating an adaptive contact as an ordinary
input can omit information carried by the contact decision itself. Replacing an
online filter by a full-history smoother can introduce information unavailable
when the bank acted. These are distinct scientific errors even when both calls
return finite arrays.

The selected Dynamax revision is commit
\texttt{5098927f2c377c0dd548cda750e6f1436220aac6}, dated 29 September 2026.
Twelve original files at that revision supply the present comparison: the
project description, root notice, dependency metadata, HMM abstraction,
filtering and smoothing implementation, standard transition component,
state-space fitting wrapper, version helper, selected tests and parameter/shape
helpers. This is a historical source inspection. The inherited PyPI version
1.0.2 is a separate release observation; the selected dynamic version helper
has not been executed to establish release equivalence.~\citep{exec19_dynamax_source}

\subsection{An input-conditioned model is not a logger-aware causal model}
\label{exec19:dynamax-logger}

The inspected HMM wrapper supplies initial-state probabilities, transition
matrices and emission log likelihoods to its filter. Its marginal-probability
method returns the filter's marginal log likelihood. No separate observed-action
likelihood is automatically inserted. For externally fixed inputs this is a
reasonable computational representation of a declared conditional experiment.
For an action selected using a private state, the joint law generally also needs
the action mechanism. Merely passing the realized action as an input does not
establish that the omitted factor is ignorable.~\citep{exec19_dynamax_source}

Consider an authored one-period construction. Let latent repayment propensity
$Z$ be Bernoulli with probability $1/2$. Conditional on $Z$, let action $A$
match $Z$ with probability $9/10$, and outcome $Y$ match $Z$ with probability
$4/5$. The action and outcome noises are conditionally independent. The outcome
has no structural dependence on the action. The observed law therefore factors as
\begin{equation}
 p(z,a,y)=p(z)\,p(a\mid z)\,p(y\mid z).
 \label{exec19:dynamax-law}
\end{equation}
Exact enumeration gives
\begin{equation}
 \begin{gathered}
 P(Y=1\mid A=1)=\frac{37}{50},\qquad
 P(Y=1\mid A=0)=\frac{13}{50},\\
 E[Y\mid\operatorname{do}(A=1)]-E[Y\mid\operatorname{do}(A=0)]=0.
 \end{gathered}
 \label{exec19:dynamax-contrast}
\end{equation}
The observational contrast is $12/25$, although acting has no effect in the
stipulated structural model. Given $A=1,Y=1$, the posterior probability of
$Z=1$ is $36/37$. Omitting the logger and conditioning only through the outcome
factor gives $4/5$ instead. Both calculations are coherent for their respective
information sets; only the former uses the observed informative action under
this law. They are exact project calculations, not Dynamax execution results.
\citep{exec19_dynamax_reference}

Suppose a unit improvement in repayment probability is assigned USD 200 of
value and an action costs USD 20. These are assumptions. Substituting the
observational contrast gives USD 76, whereas the stipulated causal effect gives
minus USD 20. No model-fitting improvement can make those two targets equal
without additional assumptions or information. A proposed adapter must either
justify the conditional-input experiment, provide the logger-aware law, or
return a clearly described unsupported causal request.~\citep{exec19_dynamax_reference}

\subsection{Preserve the observation and transition clocks}
\label{exec19:dynamax-clocks}

The source distinguishes predicted, filtered and smoothed probabilities.
Filtering at time $t$ conditions on the observation prefix; smoothing can use
all observations through the end of the sequence. The distinction belongs in
the product's result type and availability timestamp. An online decision cannot
silently consume the smoother because it is more concentrated or easier to
compute. Retrospective state reconstruction is a legitimate but different task.
\citep{exec19_dynamax_source}

For a separate exact example, let $Z$ persist across two dates, with prior
probability $1/2$, and let two conditionally independent signals each match $Z$
with probability $4/5$. Observing $Y_1=0$ gives
\begin{equation}
 P(Z=1\mid Y_1=0)=\frac15,\qquad
 P(Z=1\mid Y_1=0,Y_2=1)=\frac12.
 \label{exec19:dynamax-filter}
\end{equation}
Suppose a decision between the two signals earns USD 100 when $Z=1$ and costs
USD 30. Under that explicitly assumed response rule, the legitimate first-date
expected net is minus USD 10. Using the later signal would report USD 20 for
the same first-date decision. This is an information-clock violation, not an
observed advantage of smoothing or evidence about real servicing returns.
\citep{exec19_dynamax_reference}

Input indexing is equally consequential. The generic HMM transition helper
constructs its time-varying transition matrices from \texttt{inputs[1:]},
consistent with the inspected model abstraction's destination-time input.
The low-level filter description instead writes its transition using the
source-time input. A wrapper must declare the mapping rather than infer it from
an argument name. The standard transition class accepts an input argument but
returns its fixed transition matrix without using that argument. Passing a
contact sequence therefore does not ensure that the selected transition model
actually responds to contacts. A deterministic indexed-sequence reference
should compare sampling, model wrappers and low-level calls before admission.
\citep{exec19_dynamax_source}

\subsection{Numerical completion and parameter learning need separate checks}
\label{exec19:dynamax-numerics}

The inspected normalizer preserves exact zeros, floors very small positive
entries and substitutes one for a zero denominator. An all-zero input consequently
remains all zero rather than becoming a valid probability distribution. The
emission update subtracts the maximum log likelihood without a dedicated
all-minus-infinity branch. The smoother masks near-zero predicted probabilities
using a closeness test before another normalization. These are local source
observations motivating native conformance cases; they are not measured defect
rates or a claim about every reachable backend execution. Invalid support,
nonfinite arithmetic, unsupported laws and valid negative scientific findings
must not collapse into the same output status.~\citep{exec19_dynamax_source}

The fitting wrapper exposes a specified iteration count and an objective trace.
For nonpositive iteration counts it returns the supplied parameters with an
empty trace. The reviewed path does not make a general convergence or
identification guarantee. Selected parameter helpers also distinguish fully
frozen groups from partially frozen groups that certain joint EM updates
reject; the inspected tests compare that boundary with SGD support. A caller
must retain initialization, trainable flags, shapes, optimization settings and
failures. A state posterior conditional on fitted parameters is not automatically
a confidence statement about parameter estimates or a selected policy.
\citep{exec19_dynamax_source}

Selected upstream tests compare filtering and smoothing with explicit finite
latent-path sums, exercise nonstationary transitions and inspect fitting
behavior. They provide useful candidate conformance specifications, but none
was executed here. A future native suite should include impossible emissions,
zero support, one-step and empty sequences, input shifts, frozen parameters,
multiple starts and device synchronization. Resource and timing claims must
include compilation, conversion and failed requests.~\citep{exec19_dynamax_source}

\subsection{Prefer a narrow original-engine comparison; defer executable admission}
\label{exec19:dynamax-choice}

The selected root notice is MIT. The project metadata requires Python at least
3.10 and eight direct runtime dependencies: JAX, JAXlib, TFP-nightly,
fastprogress, Optax, jaxtyping, typing-extensions and NumPy. Those declarations
are unversioned; build and optional groups are separate. A complete distribution,
transitive notices and resolved backend/precision environment remain necessary
before executable admission. Root license text alone does not qualify the whole
installed stack.~\citep{exec19_dynamax_source}

The proposal should retain the original engine as a conditional-state-space
comparator behind a narrow adapter. A small exact enumerator remains the
transparent baseline for finite cases; it does not offer a scaling solution.
A complete port would duplicate numerical, differentiation and maintenance
obligations without a demonstrated platform need. A causal policy optimizer
built solely from a conditional likelihood is outside the initial profile.
Scientific ownership must cover the target, logger and clocks; engineering
ownership must cover the environment, conversions and failure contract; release
ownership must cover the actual distribution and notices.

This is a bounded reuse recommendation with executable admission deferred.
Public sources and generated examples suffice to specify the first comparison.
Native conformance, parameter uncertainty and measured full-workflow cost remain
prototype work; authentic bank assignment and value remain later institutional
questions. Neither the package name nor an API returning a posterior closes
those distinct obligations.

\section{Bayesian model surgery needs a separate prediction contract}
\label{exec23:pymc-scope}

PyMC is a plausible worker for bank-specific probabilistic models, including
hierarchical likelihoods and explicitly modeled latent quantities. The proposed
product, however, needs to distinguish three questions: which model is being
conditioned on data, which mechanism is replaced by an intervention, and which
variables are subsequently regenerated. The inspected repository revision is
dated 7 October 2026 and is identified by its immutable commit and twelve
authenticated source, documentation and test files. Its version is dynamically
resolved; this review does not assert that the selected development revision is
a named stable release. Its metadata requires Python at least 3.12 and below
3.15, and a specified PyTensor compatibility range. Those requirements, the
root Apache license and the actual dependency artifacts must be part of a
future worker contract rather than inferred from an older installed environment.
\citep{exec23_pymc_sources}

\subsection{Conditioning does not replace a treatment mechanism}
\label{exec23:pymc-intervention}

The inspected \texttt{observe} transformation converts selected random or
deterministic variables into observed variables, with compatible shape and
type. The \texttt{do} transformation instead replaces named model variables
by intervention expressions in a cloned graph. An expression depending on
random variables is represented as a deterministic; a constant intervention
is shared data by default. These operations provide useful model construction
machinery. They do not establish that the supplied graph correctly represents
assignment, latent common causes, information timing or a bank's feasible
interventions.
\citep{exec23_pymc_sources}

For an exact example, let hidden borrower type $U$ be Bernoulli with probability
$1/2$, let observed treatment $A$ agree with $U$ with probability $3/4$, and let
the outcome be $Y=2A+4U$. Then
\[
 E[Y\mid A=1]=5,\qquad E[Y\mid A=0]=1,
 \qquad E[Y\mid\mathrm{do}(A=1)]-E[Y\mid\mathrm{do}(A=0)]=2.
\]
The association is four, while the intervention effect is two because changing
$A$ leaves the population law of $U$ unchanged. At a stipulated value of
USD 100 per outcome unit and action cost USD 250, the association-based decision
reports net USD 150 but the causal calculation gives USD $-50$. The numerical
example is an authored finite-law calculation; it is neither a package
benchmark nor estimated bank economics.
\citep{exec23_pymc_reference}

Even a perfect posterior computation cannot resolve every causal ambiguity.
The structural models $A=U,Y=A$ and $A=U,Y=U$, with a fair binary $U$, induce
the same observed law for $(A,Y)$ but treatment effects one and zero.
Under equal observational likelihoods, posterior odds between these models
remain their prior odds. A narrower posterior obtained by choosing one model
is conditional on that choice, not evidence that observations distinguished
the models. A useful separate computational oracle is the conjugate update
from a uniform beta prior after six successes and four failures: the posterior
is beta$(7,5)$ with mean $7/12$ and variance $35/1872$. Agreement with this
oracle checks a declared probability calculation; it does not validate a
causal interpretation of those successes.
\citep{exec23_pymc_reference}

The transformation API also allows interventions that reference the original
variable. The inspected code warns and gives the replacement a new name with
a \texttt{do\_} prefix. Such an expression needs an explicit scientific
interpretation, for example a declared shift policy; it must not be silently
described as a fixed assignment. Optional pruning removes variables detached
from observed variables, and its helper explicitly refuses models containing
Potentials because their prior-versus-likelihood role is ambiguous. Therefore
pruning cannot substitute for reviewing the target and retained information.
\citep{exec23_pymc_sources}

Graph cloning has concrete limits. The inspected conversion refuses
nondefault initial values and nested submodels, and warns that reusing old
Gaussian-process objects can reintroduce variables from the original model.
It copies shared random generators, data and symbolic dimension lengths.
A worker must therefore bind the original and transformed model identities,
coordinates and initialization choices, and inspect rejected conversions.
These source operations are a basis for a future isolation test; source
inspection alone does not certify a concurrent service or a complete snapshot.
\citep{exec23_pymc_sources}

\subsection{Stored draws, regenerated variables and changed expressions}
\label{exec23:pymc-prediction}

The selected forward-sampling implementation separates output selection from
regeneration. \texttt{var\_names} controls what is returned; it does not request
a fresh draw. \texttt{sample\_vars} identifies variables to regenerate, while
\texttt{freeze\_vars} preserves trace values. Random variables present in the
trace and not explicitly selected for regeneration are automatically frozen.
Missing random variables, including ordinary observed outcomes absent from
the trace, are regenerated. The code detects some changed-ancestor cases and
issues an implicit-freeze warning, but warning availability does not establish
that the chosen predictive experiment is appropriate.
\citep{exec23_pymc_sources}

Suppose a stored draw contains $X=1,Y=1$ from a model with
$Y\mid X\sim N(X,1)$. After changing $X$ to three, retaining the stored $Y$
returns one, whereas regenerating $Y$ from the changed model has conditional
mean three. Both operations can be intentional, but they answer different
questions. A policy simulation must identify which parameter draws remain
conditioned on the original evidence and which post-intervention variables
are generated anew. Otherwise an apparently successful transformation can
leave precisely the outcome of interest tied to the old experiment.
\citep{exec23_pymc_sources,exec23_pymc_reference}

Changed deterministic expressions require their own attention. The inspected
documentation explicitly describes replacing a deterministic expression without
changing any random variable or data value: the predictive machinery can then
reuse its stored value unless regeneration is requested. For two illustrative
trace points $X=1,2$, replacing $X^2$ by $X^3$ changes the desired values from
$(1,4)$ to $(1,8)$ and their mean from $5/2$ to $9/2$. A model digest must
therefore identify expressions, not just variable names and current data.
Name-based trace matching with compatible shapes and coordinates is a software
matching rule, not proof of causal or semantic equivalence between models.
\citep{exec23_pymc_sources,exec23_pymc_reference}

Predictive handling of Potentials adds another boundary. The inspected prior
and posterior predictive routines warn that their direct effect on other
parameters is ignored during forward sampling. A fair binary generator with
a hard weight excluding zero has weighted probability one of a positive value,
whereas the unconstrained forward generator still has probability $1/2$.
This witness explains why a density factor cannot automatically be treated
as a generative rule. It does not imply that all effects of a Potential vanish:
posterior ancestors supplied by the trace may already reflect that factor.
The worker must identify the factor's role, whether it enters the inferential
posterior, and how the requested predictive law is constructed.
\citep{exec23_pymc_sources,exec23_pymc_reference}

The selected upstream tests include intervention, self-reference, dimensional
and predictive cases, as well as a constant-intervention predictive case marked
as an expected failure. These are useful conformance leads, not executed results
in this project. The proposed fixture set must exercise both shared and constant
interventions and inspect the actual result and warning, without converting
an upstream test marker into a claim that failure was reproduced here.
\citep{exec23_pymc_sources}

\subsection{Computation and diagnostics must remain visible to the caller}
\label{exec23:pymc-decision}

Sampler identity cannot safely be left implicit. At the selected revision,
the default dispatch can choose nutpie when the installed environment, model,
compilation mode and arguments permit it, otherwise the PyMC sampler. The
external paths impose restrictions on variable types and supplied steps,
and reject custom trace backends and per-draw callbacks. Consequently,
partial-trace persistence described for a PyMC trace backend cannot be
advertised for every sampler choice. Persisting draws also does not by itself
establish resumable chain state, independent restarts or distributed recovery.
\citep{exec23_pymc_sources}

The inspected convergence routine reports missing posterior data, too few
draws, a single chain and fewer than four chains separately. It checks
reported divergences and tree-depth statistics; missing statistics return no
corresponding warning. Its inspected thresholds include an $\widehat R$
warning above 1.01 and an effective-sample-size warning below 100 per chain.
These are the package's conditional diagnostics, not a theorem of convergence
or a guarantee that an intervention model is correct. NUTS source documentation
also describes energy, trajectory-depth and timing statistics and distinguishes
CPU from wall time. The product must preserve missing, unavailable, adverse
and satisfactory diagnostics as different states, rather than flatten them
into a single successful API status.
\citep{exec23_pymc_sources}

A posterior credible interval is conditional on the declared prior,
likelihood and model class. Its numerical stability does not establish
frequentist coverage across a bank's data-generating processes, nor account
automatically for selecting a model or policy after examining the same
outcomes. Those uncertainty questions need their own assumptions and evaluation
law, including sensitivity to the indistinguishable models above.
\citep{exec23_pymc_reference}

The current disposition is a source-qualified reference with a conditional
native Python worker route. A blanket port to other languages would reproduce
graph rewriting and predictive rules at considerable maintenance cost without
a demonstrated advantage. A concrete prototype should instead pin the release
or commit, Python, PyTensor, compiler, sampler and dependencies; register exact
conjugate and finite latent-model oracles; exercise intervention/freeze/sample
semantics, Potentials, dimensions and warnings; and measure compilation,
effective samples, memory, predictive cost and recovery together. Scientific
owners must justify model and intervention meaning, while maintainers own
conversion conformance and operators own budgets and persistence. Library,
CLI and MCP should expose the same target and refusal conditions. LLM-generated
models can be proposed for review, but cannot certify their own causal graph,
identification assumptions or scientific validity. Native qualification,
general causal identification and bank adoption remain open.
\citep{exec23_pymc_sources,exec23_pymc_reference}

\section{Commercial Bayesian and hidden-state engines: what a posterior can justify}
\label{exec22:state-scope}

A servicing decision may depend on a credit state that the bank cannot directly
observe. A missed payment, account balance and contact history provide evidence
about that state, but the proposed action changes a mechanism rather than merely
revealing another measurement. A useful commercial comparison must therefore
separate four questions: what state is plausible given information available now;
what parameters are plausible within a specified model; which model restrictions
the observations identify; and what happens when the bank changes an action.
An accurate answer to the first two questions need not answer the last two.

The relevant commercial landscape includes graphical-model engines, statistical
estimators and general numerical environments. Three complete Stata command
manuals add detail to the previously inspected GeNIe/SMILE, Netica, BayesiaLab and
Mplus profiles. These five supported families allow a substantive comparison,
while SAS, EViews, HUGIN, Bayes Server and commercial numerical environments
remain candidates requiring further matched technical evidence. The comparison
retains the 7 October 2026 literature cutoff. The Stata copies have July 2026 PDF
metadata and release-19 example routes, but later retrieval does not authenticate
their exact cutoff-era bytes or an installed licensed build. The older sources
retain their stated manual families and mutable-page limitations. None of these
qualifications licenses a claim that an unevaluated product lacks a feature.

\subsection{Supplied-model computation and the missing causal restriction}
\label{exec22:state-identification}

Let $A\in\{0,1\}$ denote a servicing action and $D\in\{0,1\}$ a subsequent
default. Consider two deliberately small, fully specified mechanisms. In the
selection mechanism, $U\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(1/2)$ is an unobserved
favourable credit state, $N\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(1/5)$ is independent noise,
and
\begin{equation}
 A=U\mathbin{\oplus}N,\qquad D=1-U.
 \label{exec22:state-selection}
\end{equation}
The exclusive-or operation flips its first binary argument when $N=1$. In the
causal mechanism, an independent action $A\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(1/2)$
replaces the first equation, and $D=(1-A)\mathbin{\oplus}N$. Both mechanisms give
exactly the same observable table:
\begin{equation}
\begin{array}{c|cc}
 &D=0&D=1\\ \hline
A=0&1/10&2/5\\
A=1&2/5&1/10
\end{array}
\label{exec22:state-table}
\end{equation}
Consequently, both yield $P(D=1\mid A=0)=4/5$ and
$P(D=1\mid A=1)=1/5$. Under an intervention that replaces only the action
equation, however, the selection mechanism retains default risk $1/2$ for
either action. The causal mechanism has risks $4/5$ and $1/5$. The identified
contrast within each stipulated mechanism is therefore different even though
every observable cell agrees. This is a project derivation by complete finite
enumeration, not a finding about actual customers.~\citep{exec22_state_reference}

With an assumed loss of USD~1,000 per default and action cost USD~100, the net
value of universal action relative to no action is USD~$-100$ under selection
and USD~500 under the causal mechanism. More observations from this same law
cannot distinguish those values. If $w$ is the prior probability of the causal
mechanism in a two-model analysis with these fixed parameters, equal likelihoods
leave its posterior probability equal to $w$ for every observed sample. The
posterior expected margin is
\begin{equation}
 V(w)=600w-100\quad\text{USD},\qquad V(w)>0\ \Longleftrightarrow\ w>1/6.
 \label{exec22:state-prior}
\end{equation}
Priors $w=1/10$ and $w=9/10$ imply USD~$-40$ and USD~440. These numbers expose
the decision's sensitivity to a causal assumption that the likelihood cannot
learn in this example. They do not prohibit Bayesian decisions under declared
assumptions; they require the source and consequences of those assumptions to
remain visible.

BayesiaLab's inspected documentation distinguishes observation from intervention
and names graph surgery and likelihood matching. Its identification discussion
requires causal information expressed in a DAG before estimation. This is a
useful conceptual strength for an adapter. It does not mean that drawing the
action arrow or invoking graph surgery establishes that the bank's graph is
true.~\citep{exec13_ct_bayesia_inference,exec13_ct_bayesia_identification}
An agent could help enumerate the two mechanisms, identify which records might
distinguish them and draft a public experiment. It must retain both until justified
restrictions or new information resolve their difference. A natural-language
statement of confidence cannot replace that missing evidence.

\subsection{State inference must preserve the decision clock}
\label{exec22:state-clock}

The supplied state model may nevertheless be valuable for prediction and decision
support. GeNIe's inspected DBN overview represents a stationary discrete-time
stochastic process. Its discrete-DBN learning page fits parameters by EM in an
already specified structure; the selected page explicitly excludes learning the
dynamic structure. Time-indexed columns must match node identifiers, and existing
network evidence is ignored during that parameter-learning operation. These are
concrete semantic requirements, not interchangeable user-interface details.
\citep{exec13_ct_genie_dbn,exec13_ct_genie_learning}

SMILE's C++ tutorial distinguishes initial and transition conditional-probability
tables, temporal lag order, the number of unfolded slices and integer outcome
indices. A flattened belief array is ordered by slice and outcome. A proposed
Python, Java or R wrapper must preserve those mappings before its output can be
compared with a native model. A matching array shape is insufficient if the
meaning of outcome zero or the initial slice changes.
\citep{exec13_ct_smile_tutorial}

Stata's documented \texttt{sspace} procedure estimates linear state-space
parameters by maximum likelihood using Kalman or diffuse-filter likelihoods.
Its general form separates a latent state $z_t$, measured variables $y_t$,
exogenous inputs $x_t,w_t$ and disturbances:
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
 z_t&=Fz_{t-1}+Bx_t+C\varepsilon_t,\\
 y_t&=Hz_t+Gw_t+J\nu_t.
\end{aligned}
\label{exec22:state-model}
\end{equation}
The coefficient matrices are time invariant in this documented profile.
The stated likelihood uses Gaussian, serially uncorrelated disturbances with
state and observation errors uncorrelated with each other. The documented robust
variance option and stationary/nonstationary initialization methods address
different statistical and numerical choices; they do not certify that a bank
action placed among the regressors is exogenous. A proposed adapter must retain
the declared covariance structure, model constraints and initial-state method.
\citep{exec22_state_stata_sspace}

The postestimation interface makes an especially important distinction:
one-step predictions use past information, filtered states use past and current
information, and smoothed states use all sample information. Its prediction
sample can change the recursive state estimates. The bank's information set
must therefore include availability times, not merely a date column.
\citep{exec22_state_stata_sspace_post}

For an exact example, let a hidden distress state $H$ remain constant for two
dates, with $P(H=1)=1/2$. Conditional on $H$, independent indicators $X_0,X_1$
equal $H$ with probability $3/4$. On observing $X_0=1$, the filtered probability
is $3/4$. If the later observation is $X_1=0$, retrospective smoothing gives
\begin{equation}
 P(H=1\mid X_0=1,X_1=0)
 =\frac{(3/4)(1/4)}{(3/4)(1/4)+(1/4)(3/4)}=1/2.
 \label{exec22:state-smoothing}
\end{equation}
Suppose a separate, stipulated causal model says an action prevents default with
probability $1/10$ when $H=1$, has no effect otherwise, costs USD~60 and avoids
USD~1,000 when successful. Its filtered expected margin is USD~15; using the
later smoothed probability gives USD~$-10$. The latter is a legitimate
retrospective calculation, but it was unavailable when the action was chosen.
The example assumes that the causal benefit law is known; filtering does not
identify that law.~\citep{exec22_state_reference}

Observability is another distinct obligation. In a noise-free two-state model
with $F=(9/10)I$ and $H=(1,1)$, the observability matrix formed by $H$ and $HF$
has rank one. The initial states $(1,0)$ and $(2,-1)$ generate the same output
$(9/10)^t$ at every date, but their first-minus-second component contrasts are
one and three. The null direction $(1,-1)$ remains invisible. Adding a prior
can regularize or select a state representation; it does not make the contrast
observable from these measurements. New measurements, constraints justified by
the application, or a decision defined only on observable combinations are
substantive alternatives. State observability, parameter identification and
causal identification each require their own argument.

\subsection{A posterior, a prediction error and a simulation error answer different questions}
\label{exec22:state-uncertainty}

Stata's \texttt{bayesmh} provides adaptive Metropolis--Hastings estimation with
explicit likelihoods and priors. Its manual cautions that allowed combinations
need not produce a proper posterior, and that no single diagnostic establishes
convergence. Multiple starting points, all model parameters and requested
functions need attention; apparent mixing can conceal multimodal
pseudoconvergence. Chain count, burn-in, adaptation, thinning and random seeds
must therefore be retained in a reproducible specification. The documented
defaults are starting configurations, not universal adequacy guarantees.
\citep{exec22_state_stata_bayesmh}

Netica's inspected learning text instead describes counting, EM and
conjugate-gradient parameter fitting, with prior information supplied through
preexisting tables and experience. Its objective includes both data likelihood
and prior terms, and local optima remain possible. A fitted table should not be
relabeled a sample from a full parameter posterior.~\citep{exec13_latent_netica_algorithms}
The Mplus 8.1 addendum supplies a complementary Bayesian dynamic-SEM profile,
including latent centering and outcome versus residual lag distinctions. Its
missing-covariate rule can remove observations unless the covariate is modeled
as an outcome. A servicing comparison must preserve that modeling decision and
its observation set. The addendum alone does not supply a complete selected
release's prior, sampler and licensing specification.~\citep{exec13_ct_mplus81}

Uncertainty must be named before being compared. For a parameter $\theta$,
training information $\mathcal D$ and a future outcome $Y$, total variance is
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
 \operatorname{Var}(Y\mid\mathcal D)
 &=E[\operatorname{Var}(Y\mid\theta,\mathcal D)\mid\mathcal D]\\
 &\quad+\operatorname{Var}(E[Y\mid\theta,\mathcal D]\mid\mathcal D).
\end{aligned}
\label{exec22:state-variance}
\end{equation}
The first term describes conditional outcome variation; the second propagates
parameter uncertainty. For $\theta\sim\operatorname{Uniform}(0,1)$ and
$Y\mid\theta\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(\theta)$ with no data, these terms
are $1/6$ and $1/12$, totaling $1/4$. For two future outcomes conditionally
independent given their shared $\theta$, the variance of their count is
$2(1/6)+4(1/12)=2/3$. Treating the probability as fixed at its posterior mean
$1/2$ gives $1/2$ instead. The shared unknown parameter induces dependence.
\citep{exec22_state_reference}

The selected \texttt{sspace} postestimation manual explicitly states that its
reported prediction RMSE includes disturbance variation but does not account
for parameter-estimation error. It must therefore be labeled accordingly.
An adapter could add a justified parameter-propagation layer, but its result
would be an additional construction requiring its own assumptions and tests.
Neither layer automatically represents graph uncertainty or uncertainty about
the action mechanism.~\citep{exec22_state_stata_sspace_post}

Monte Carlo error is separate again: it measures finite simulation error in a
posterior summary. The \texttt{bayesmh} manual distinguishes effective-sample-size
and batch-means MCSE calculations. Its saved dataset also compresses repeated
states into rows with chain, iteration and frequency fields. Frequencies are
required when summarizing these rows.~\citep{exec22_state_stata_bayesmh}
For values $0.1$ and $0.9$ with frequencies nine and one, the posterior-sample
mean is $0.18$, whereas the unweighted row mean is $0.5$. A CSV conversion that
retains parameter values but drops frequencies silently changes the result.
This exact arithmetic is an export-contract example, not a native execution
test.~\citep{exec22_state_reference}

\subsection{From numerical tolerances to a conditional decision bound}
\label{exec22:state-approximation}

An approximate belief need not support the same action as its reference. Suppose
the exact and approximate probabilities of a beneficial state are $0.61$ and
$0.59$, an action produces USD~100 in that state and costs USD~60. The expected
margins are USD~1 and USD~$-1$. A small probability discrepancy can matter near a
decision threshold even when average predictive scores look similar.

A conditional bound clarifies what an approximation contract would need. Let
$b_t$ and $\widetilde b_t$ be exact and approximate marginal state laws under
the \emph{same fixed policy}. Define total variation as
$\|b-\widetilde b\|_{\rm TV}=\frac12\sum_s|b(s)-\widetilde b(s)|$.
If the reward at each date has range at most $R$, and the marginal discrepancy
is at most $\epsilon_t$, then
\begin{equation}
 |V-\widetilde V|\leq
 R\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\gamma^t\epsilon_t,\qquad 0\leq\gamma<1.
 \label{exec22:state-bound}
\end{equation}
To see this, subtract the reward minimum, bound each expected-reward difference
by its range times total variation, and apply the triangle inequality to the
discounted sum. With $R=100$ dollars, $\epsilon_t=0.02$, $\gamma=0.9$ and
$T=12$, the bound is
$2(1-0.9^{12})/(1-0.9)$, approximately USD~14.3514.
\citep{exec22_state_reference}

This argument assumes the marginal error bounds. A one-step transition
approximation, a sampler stopping rule or agreement on one benchmark does not
establish them. Nor does a bound for one fixed policy automatically cover the
regret of a different policy selected using approximate beliefs. Deriving
propagation under a specified transition law, verifying it on known-law public
examples, and separating policy-selection error are the next scientific steps.
The proposed product should report these limits instead of attaching an
unqualified confidence label to the action value.

\subsection{Commercial comparison and an executable proposal route}
\label{exec22:state-comparison}

The vendors have different documented strengths. Stata supplies explicit
state/observation equations, initialization options, information-set choices,
Bayesian diagnostics and persistent simulation exports. GeNIe/SMILE supplies
graphical DBNs and concrete native temporal representations. Netica supplies
parameter-learning alternatives with latent or incomplete data. BayesiaLab
distinguishes observation, intervention and identification assumptions. Mplus
supplies a Bayesian dynamic-SEM modeling route. The proposal currently has
exact authored references and semantic requirements; it has no qualified native
adapter for these profiles. Its proposed contribution is to preserve causal
meaning and refusals consistently across the library, CLI and MCP, including
the agent's translation of a business question into a model.

The appropriate reuse route is a conditional, isolated licensed worker with a
versioned exchange contract. A request must identify its task, decision time,
outcome horizon, units, observed and latent variables, action mechanism and
admissible information. A returned result must distinguish filtered from
smoothed states, process from parameter uncertainty, and posterior from Monte
Carlo variation. It must preserve native diagnostics, chain frequencies,
parameter names, initialization and failed calculations. Replacing a vendor's
engine or porting its mathematics is a separate rights and validation decision;
public documentation is not a redistribution entitlement. Prices, commercial
deployment rights and measured operating costs remain unavailable in this
comparison, so no saving or superiority is asserted.

SAS's selected MCMC PDF transfer was incomplete; EViews and HUGIN technical
endpoints failed. Those attempts neither establish their capabilities nor
prove absence. Complete selected-release MCMC/SSM manuals, official state-model
help, HUGIN DBN and intervention documentation, Bayes Server's versioned SDK
contracts, and MATLAB/Wolfram toolbox-specific originals are concrete recovery
targets. Broader complementary searches must also test whether the shortlist
misses a product family. These source obligations can proceed independently of
public prototype design.

The first prototype comparison can use the finite laws above, supplied-state
models with known parameters, and deliberately misspecified alternatives.
Before execution, freeze the query, information clock, causal assumptions,
uncertainty components, monetary inputs and admissible errors. Compare exact
enumeration with a licensed native inference path; test a timestamp violation,
an unobservable contrast, a frequency-loss export, posterior impropriety and a
policy near its decision threshold. Record both correct answers and justified
refusals. Only after such comparisons show merit should the proposal request
costly bank-specific experiments. This route develops useful public evidence
while retaining the unresolved assumptions and commercial terms.


\subsection{From a conditional calculation to a defensible banking action}

The chapter supports conditional use of these engines, with a separate argument
for the action being evaluated. A justified likelihood and a well-behaved
sampler answer computational questions within a model. An intervention requires
an account of which mechanism changes; a prospective decision requires the
information actually available at that time. Posterior averaging, state decoding,
conditional prediction and cross-world simulation remain different requests.
Their numerical and scientific failure states belong in the recommendation.

The next chapter adds another source of dependence: one customer's action can
affect another customer's outcome. A precise individual-state calculation does
not by itself define that allocation problem. The relevant joint policy,
exposure mapping and population must be supplied before comparing its value.

chapters.title: Interference, allocation policies and software adoption

segments.text:
\chapter{Interference, allocation policies and software adoption}
\label{v13:sw-networks}

The preceding relationship analysis showed why a policy may require joint
graph and action information. This chapter examines the allocation problem
itself. It distinguishes network and grouped targets, develops the two initial
software references, and compares spatial, experimental, learned-policy and
simulation alternatives. The recurring small graphs and cost denominators are
matched comparison devices; each implementation's different assumptions and
failure conditions remain part of the argument.

\section{The unit receiving treatment need not be the independent unit}

A household member's offer can influence another member's borrowing, and an
outreach campaign can affect connected firms. In such settings a potential
outcome depends on more than the individual's own action. Writing only
$Y_i(a_i)$ hides the policy being evaluated. A more explicit representation is
$Y_i(a_i,\mathbf a_{-i})$, often restricted through an exposure mapping of
other units' actions. The mapping and the network are scientific inputs;
neither is established merely by finding matching customer identifiers.

Two broad software constructions appear in the inspected sources. MossSpider
uses a network and exposure summaries in a network-targeted estimation
workflow. Inferference uses grouped formulas, allocation probabilities and
inverse-probability weighting. These constructions have different observation
laws and potentially different targets. Their package names do not establish
interchangeability. \cite{v13_sw_mossspider,v13_sw_inferference}

An allocation policy illustrates the target. Suppose two linked borrowers have
binary outreach actions $A_1,A_2$, independently assigned with probability $p$
under the proposed policy. Stipulate the synthetic financial outcome
\[
 Y_i(a_i,a_j)=100a_i+40a_j-30a_i a_j
\]
in CNY. The first term represents the own-action contribution, the second a
spillover and the last diminishing combined benefit. These are hypothetical
structural values, not bank estimates. Averaging under the allocation gives
\[
 V(p)=140p-30p^2.
\]
For $p=0.2$ the mean is 26.8 CNY; for $p=0.8$ it is 92.8 CNY. The allocation
contrast is 66 CNY per borrower. Exact enumeration of the four assignments
checks the formula. \cite{v13_project_exact}

The direct effect of changing only the individual's own action is instead
$100-30a_j$, or $100-30p$ when the neighbor is independently treated with
probability $p$. This differs from the total allocation contrast. Reporting
one as the other can misprice the campaign even when every arithmetic
calculation is correct. The bank must specify whether it changes one action,
the neighborhood's allocation or an entire branch policy, and which costs
are included in the outcome.

\section{MossSpider: network semantics are part of the estimand}

The inspected \texttt{NetworkTMLE} documentation describes expected incidence
under a treatment plan, with Monte Carlo integration over allocations for
stochastic plans. It states a direct-contact interference assumption. The
constructor rejects self-loops, noninteger node identities and nonbinary
exposure, creates a relabeled network while retaining original identities,
and constructs an unweighted adjacency matrix. \cite{v13_sw_mossspider}

These details matter for bank graphs. A weighted guarantee network is not the
same as an unweighted adjacency graph. Removing weights can turn a small
guarantee into the same exposure contribution as a large one. Relabeling nodes
is harmless only when results can be mapped back to the correct identities.
A linkage error can attach the correct numerical estimate to the wrong firm.
Semantic conformance therefore needs an identity roundtrip and an explicit
policy for unsupported weighted relationships.

Direction requires particular review. The documentation initially describes an
undirected graph but also explains a directed influence convention opposite
the graph arrow, and the selected constructor includes directed handling. This
combination requires a concrete test with an asymmetric small graph. One should
not infer direction from a diagram's appearance or assume that every library
uses source-to-target influence. A two-node one-way example with distinguishable
covariates can determine which neighbor contributes to each exposure summary.
Section~\ref{sec:exec24-interference-reuse} develops the selected mapping,
policy and variance paths. Their inspected direction convention still needs
matched native tests; directed bank-network adoption remains a proposed use. \cite{v13_sw_mossspider}

Degree restrictions also change the target. The documentation treats nodes
outside a requested degree range as background, with their exposures unchanged
by the intervention. This can be scientifically useful, but it is not the
same as deleting those nodes from the graph or intervening on all customers.
The response must state which nodes are in the target population, which remain
background and how their factual exposure affects the intervention outcome.

The source disclaims a missing-data procedure. Missing node attributes,
uncertain links and omitted customers are common in banking, but the existence
of an exposure-mapping function does not solve those observation problems.
One must either supply defensible complete data in the declared regime or
develop a separate missingness/linkage construction. Network-targeted estimation
does not automatically qualify ownership or inclusion truth.

The observed MIT text makes a restricted adapter worth considering. Full adoption
requires qualification of the exposure-model and mapping code, targeting step,
Monte Carlo integration and variance calculation, together with actual
dependency/runtime checks. The developed study retains deterministic-policy
refusals, background-node treatment and a potentially negative variance
quadratic; these restrictions belong in any proposed adapter. A claim of general contagion, dynamic financial-network equilibrium or
arbitrary spillovers would go beyond the selected implementation evidence.

\section{Inferference: grouped allocation and numerical integration}

The inspected \texttt{interference} function uses a formula that identifies
outcome, exposure, optional participation, propensity covariates and a grouping
variable. It accepts allocation probabilities and propensity-model choices
including \texttt{glm}, \texttt{glmer}, \texttt{HLfit} and an oracle route.
Its documented causal-estimation path is IPW with naive or robust variance
options. The selected code sorts records by group and checks group count,
allocation range and the variance option. \cite{v13_sw_inferference}

A group-based model can be appropriate when the scientific design justifies
within-group interference and the required between-group sampling assumptions.
It does not become a model of arbitrary connected borrowers by assigning
everyone a group label. Cross-group guarantees or shared market shocks can
violate the intended observation law. The grouping decision needs domain
evidence and should be subjected to sensitivity analysis where boundaries
are uncertain.

The default logit integrand is restricted to a single random effect in the
documented implementation. The code rejects more than one when that integrand
is selected. Thus a proposal with household and branch random effects needs a
different justified integration path; silently dropping one random effect is
a model change. An oracle propensity option is useful for synthetic reference
calculations, but supplied true parameters cannot be counted as evidence that
an estimated-propensity workflow is calibrated.

There is also a reproducibility issue visible directly in the source. The prose
describes \texttt{integrate\_allocation} as defaulting to false, while the
inspected function signature sets it to true. The proper response is to specify
and record the argument explicitly. Section~\ref{sec:exec24-interference-reuse}
traces the downstream ratio and derivative paths; their flag propagation,
allocation-mass and missing-group restrictions still require matched native
qualification. It is not appropriate to select whichever default gives a more
favorable result after comparing outputs. \cite{v13_sw_inferference}

For large groups, multiplying many probabilities can create numerical problems.
The documentation discusses an allocation-integration option in this context.
Qualification should include large and uneven groups, boundary allocation
probabilities, integration tolerances and variance derivatives. A successful
floating-point result does not prove adequate support; an underflow error does
not prove nonidentification. These are different failure modes and need
different diagnostics.

The observed DESCRIPTION declares GPL version 2 or later and a dated version.
That informs a dependency review but does not establish the license status of
every linked component or distribution arrangement. A candidate grouped-policy
reference should remain distinct from a decision to embed or port it.

\section{A common comparison must distinguish network and group assumptions}

The two packages can be compared on a common small allocation problem only
after their target, exposure mapping and sampling assumptions are aligned.
For the two-borrower example, the exact four-assignment enumeration supplies a
transparent functional reference. A larger benchmark should vary degree,
group size, allocation probability, support, observation errors and dependence.
It should include examples where a direct-contact or group restriction is false.

Metrics should separate the target mean, direct and spillover contrasts,
coverage, finite availability, Monte Carlo integration error and total cost.
Increasing simulated allocations reduces integration error conditional on a
fitted model. It does not create independent groups or validate the graph.
Uncertainty must follow the actual sampling unit; counting nodes as independent
merely because the graph is stored in a table can produce misleading precision.

The implementation contract should retain the original graph, its direction
and weights, the identity map, intervention population, allocation rule,
background nodes and exposure mapping. A result should be rejected as
semantically incompatible if a proposed bridge silently changes any of these.
This requirement is shared by library calls, command-line jobs and agent tools.
An interface can make a scientific restriction visible; it cannot make it true.

\section{Provisional reuse choices and the evidence needed to change them}

The inspected software supports a portfolio of candidate components rather
than a single universal engine. The following choices describe potential uses and qualification conditions,
not accepted integrations or benchmarks. The earlier functional and
longitudinal chapters develop the corresponding source findings
(Chapters~\ref{v13:sw-functional} and~\ref{v13:sw-regimes}); the table retains
the conditions that must survive implementation rather than treating those
studies as still absent.

\begin{longtable}{P{0.18\textwidth}P{0.34\textwidth}P{0.39\textwidth}}
\toprule
Component & Candidate role & Conditions to preserve and qualify\\
\midrule
\endhead
DirectLiNGAM & Functional discovery adapter & Reviewed base-class behavior, prior orientation,
functional assumptions and adverse latent/Gaussian cases\\
y0 & Symbolic ID/IDC adapter & Reviewed recursive paths, conditional-path restriction,
graph validation, expression roundtrip and nonidentification references\\
delicatessen & Equation and numerical reference & Solver, Jacobian, covariance,
sampling unit and complete dependency contract\\
statsmodels & Point-treatment GMM baseline & Matched population, propensity bounds,
actual covariance behavior and dependent-data limits\\
pygformula & Longitudinal-regime adapter & History/event meaning, simulation,
bootstrap unit, diagnostics and policy scope\\
grf & R/native heterogeneous-effect component & Native algorithms, variance,
aggregation measure, ABI and license/distribution review\\
CausalGPS & Continuous-density component & Density/transformation helpers,
counterfactual doses, support and downstream estimation\\
causaldrf & Dose-response reference & Full function, interval procedures,
support, recovered holder notice and dependency terms\\
MossSpider & Restricted network-policy component & Direction, mapping, identity,
targeting, variance and observation restrictions\\
inferference & Grouped-allocation reference & Integrands, numerical defaults,
variance, group law and dependency terms\\
\bottomrule
\end{longtable}

An integration decision is stronger than identifying a promising function.
Direct adoption needs a stable, compatible dependency and scientific contract.
An adapter needs semantic parity and error preservation. A port needs the right
