mean of twenty-five dollars. A planning cohort of ten thousand customers
turns the five-dollar difference into fifty thousand dollars in a naive
projection. That calculation exposes the target change; it does not
justify applying an equal-branch mean to an arbitrary customer
portfolio.

The R interface documents that equal cluster weighting changes both
training sampling and average-effect weights, and disallows user sample
weights in that mode. Replacing the final mean alone cannot reproduce
training under that option. A native port would have to preserve both
mechanisms. The initial independent-customer profile therefore rejects
cluster and weight options; the independent-cluster extension is
specified for later qualification and must name whether customers or
clusters define its target \cite{exec13_grf_rpath}.

\subsection{Sampling uncertainty is not a numerical decoration}

For independent clusters indexed by \(g\), define
\(S_g=\sum_{i\in g}q_i(\Gamma_i-\widehat\theta)\), \(Q=\sum_iq_i\), and
let \(G\) count positive-weight clusters. The inspected all-sample
augmented average-effect path computes the variance expression \[
 \widehat V_{\rm cl}=\frac{G}{G-1}\frac{\sum_g S_g^2}{Q^2}.
\] This specifies a computation. Asymptotic validity needs an
appropriate independent-cluster experiment, sufficient effective
clusters and nuisance conditions; no fixed small cluster count
guarantees it. Dependence shared across branches through a calendar
factor lies outside that law.

For the six scores above, treating all rows as independent gives
variance forty dollars squared. Preserving two branch clusters while
retaining the customer target gives \(1600/9\) dollars squared. Giving
the two branches equal total weight gives variance 225 dollars squared
around the changed target of twenty-five dollars. The standard errors
are approximately 6.325, 13.333 and 15 dollars. Two clusters make a
useful arithmetic counterexample and supply no empirical
confidence-coverage qualification. A single positive-weight cluster is
refused. Zero total weight is separately refused
\cite{exec13_grf_oracle,exec13_grf_rpath}.

Conditional prediction variance is another quantity. The native
prediction strategy estimates it using grouped trees and a
variance-debiasing calculation; the binding copies the variance values
into \texttt{variance.estimates}. The R average-effect operation instead
returns \texttt{std.err}, already square-rooted. Squaring the wrong
field or taking its square root twice changes the units. The proposed
adapter keeps the raw field identity, method and units, then creates any
reported interval only under a declared inference profile. Pointwise
conditional intervals cannot become a simultaneous customer band or an
interval for their average through serialization. Likewise
\texttt{excess.error}, a finite-forest error diagnostic, is not a
substitute for sampling uncertainty
\cite{exec13_grf_native,exec13_grf_rpath}.

\subsection{Memory ownership, coordinates and model persistence}

The inspected \texttt{Data} class is a read-only view of a borrowed
contiguous column-major buffer. Element \((r,c)\) is read at offset
\(cn+r\), where \(n\) is the number of rows. Constructing the view from
a temporary vector does not transfer ownership. The host must keep the
allocation alive until all training or prediction threads have finished;
it must validate shape, index ranges and multiplication overflow before
the call. A three-row, two-column example has columns \((1,2,3)\) and
\((10,20,30)\). Correct layout reads twenty at zero-based coordinate
\((1,1)\); passing row-major bytes to the same index formula reads
three. Neither value is a memory error, so a mere successful call cannot
detect the scientific corruption
\cite{exec13_grf_memory,exec13_grf_oracle}.

Role coordinates must remain separate from predictor coordinates. The
native setters mark outcome, treatment, instrument and weight columns as
disallowed split variables. The host records the ordered covariate
dictionary, row identifiers, role indices and training/query
distinction. It cannot infer those roles from whichever columns happen
to be numeric. Missing values in covariates are supported by inspected
package paths, but are excluded by the initial profile so that an
undocumented imputation or missingness assumption is not introduced.
Conversion to double precision must preserve identifier strings
separately and refuse nonfinite numerical values rather than silently
dropping affected customers.

Model serialization also has ownership semantics. The inspected Rcpp
helper iterates by moving the unique pointer to each native tree into
its serialized representation. The header explicitly says the original
forest cannot be used after that operation. A direct embedding that
serializes and then predicts on the consumed forest is therefore
invalid. Either serialize an explicitly supported copy, or deserialize
the saved representation into a new object. Retain the engine commit,
ordered feature map, original training-data identity, nuisance vectors,
options and format version beside the forest. The selected source does
not establish a stable C++ ABI or a portable standalone model format.
These are admission questions for a native route, not problems solved by
choosing a file extension \cite{exec13_grf_memory}.

\subsection{A concrete request and result contract}

The operation is \texttt{estimate.effect}. Its generic parameter schema
accepts an engine identifier and estimator identifier, so the proposed
profile uses \texttt{grf-r-native-2.6.1} and
\texttt{binary-iid-aipw-all-v1} there. Detailed settings reside in an
immutable configuration artifact, carried through the existing artifact
list. That artifact binds the exact source commit, treatment contrast,
outcome/horizon, row and column roles, seed, thread count, tree options
and target. The adapter validates its own profile before dispatch;
generic JSON acceptance alone does not validate these scientific
restrictions \cite{exec13_grf_design}.

Library, CLI and MCP surfaces must resolve identical authorized data and
configuration identities. The context digest retains the estimand,
population, units, information clock, assumptions, sampling declaration
and graph. The full request identity additionally binds data bytes,
configuration, engine environment and numerical settings. Changing the
target population or turning branch weighting on produces a different
request; transport names cannot cause reuse of a previous result. Graph
endpoint marks and unresolved sets remain intact. A forest is not a
graph-identification service: if a retained model class gives different
effects and the query has no accepted identification argument, this
profile cannot silently select a graph.

Before runtime admission, discovery of this engine returns unavailable.
A recognized but unsupported sampling regime, continuous treatment,
dynamic policy request or unresolved graph requirement returns
unsupported with an actionable explanation. Nonfinite output, failed
subprocess execution or an invalid model artifact is a failure; no
finite effect accompanies it. A reviewed identification failure can
return not-identified with its evidence, but the adapter's inability to
analyze a model is not an impossibility proof. An overlap alarm produces
a refusal under the declared profile. Trimming or switching to an
overlap population requires a newly reviewed target and request.

After engineering admission, a computed scalar estimate keeps its dollar
unit, signed offer-minus-no-offer contrast and target identifier. A
diagnostic conditional-prediction artifact retains query-row coordinates
and explicitly denotes conditional means, not individual counterfactual
differences. The initial engineering result carries execution-only
qualification and no confidence claim. Conditional inference needs its
own reviewed uncertainty construction and evidence. A mathematically
unbounded or disconnected result from another method must be returned
with its topology; this forest profile does not approximate it by a
large finite interval.

\subsection{Deployment choices and the next informative comparison}

The package description requires R at least 3.5.0, C++17 and GNU make,
links Rcpp and RcppEigen, and imports additional packages including
Matrix, DiceKriging, lmtest and sandwich. These declarations are
minimum/source requirements, not a tested environment lock. The proposed
R process must record the installed R and dependency versions, source
and binary hashes, compiler and flags, thread settings and runtime
options. The inspected native CMake file collects both source and test
files into an executable; its presence does not supply a ready
production shared library or a reviewed installed ABI. Package metadata
declares GPL-3 and the inspected source headers state GPL version 3 or
later. Preserve file and dependency terms and review distribution
obligations before shipping; a subprocess boundary alone settles neither
licensing compatibility nor distribution duties
\cite{exec13_grf_runtime}.

The parent process bounds wall time, memory and output size and
publishes only a complete validated result atomically. Standard output
is the protocol channel; diagnostics have a bounded separate log. A
crash or timeout leaves a typed failure and its input identities. No
mid-tree recovery is promised. Replaying an immutable request starts
from its recorded seed and environment; bitwise equality across
different compilers or thread settings remains a measured property. One
worker per isolated R process is the conservative initial choice because
the inspected binding also writes global runtime context. Concurrency
inside a shared embedding requires its own review.

The proposal recommends the R/native route first because it retains the
inspected nuisance, score and aggregation paths. Direct native embedding
may later reduce interface overhead or fit a host's deployment
constraints, but would transfer those statistical and ownership
responsibilities to the host. A full algorithm port has the greatest
maintenance and conformance burden. Reject direct embedding for the
initial profile until it reproduces the R path; this is a scoped
engineering choice, not a claim that native integration is impossible.

The next comparison should freeze one environment and the complete
workload: data conversion, nuisance estimation, forest training,
average-effect scoring, serialization, output validation and failure
handling. Compare the maintained R route with a direct-native candidate
only under identical inputs, target, options and estimator formulas.
Exact fixtures first check coordinates, residualization, score
aggregation and refusal behavior. A separately registered generated-data
study can then examine coverage, availability, heterogeneity recovery
and resources, retaining weak-overlap and dependent cases in its
denominator. Pure arithmetic agreement cannot replace that study, and
local runtime cannot establish bank workflow savings. The useful
investment question is whether a native route improves the complete
workload enough to justify owning the additional statistical and
deployment machinery. \label{exec13:grf-adapter-end}

\section{A common interface preserves differences that matter}

The adapter comparison supports a common request and result vocabulary with deliberately different admitted operations. The Python route returns a symbolic functional under a supplied graph and explicit conditional-path restrictions. The Java route proposes a graph class under a specified discovery model and must retain failed tests before publication. The R/native route estimates a defined customer effect while preserving nuisance adjustment, aggregation and uncertainty conventions. A single effect field cannot stand in for these three services.

The local trials show why preservation extends beyond the estimator. A coordinate permutation, rounding at an integer boundary, a changed context, corrupt replay or incomplete publication can alter or conceal the scientific result. The observed refusals and successful recoveries establish particular behavior; the descriptor, input-access and error-classification findings identify repairs still needed for those versions. The next service design must carry both kinds of evidence forward. Its value is that a caller can tell what was computed, under which assumptions, what remains uncertain and which next action could resolve the limitation.

chapters.title: The library, command line and MCP service

segments.text:
\chapter{The library, command line and MCP service}
\label{in:surfaces}
\label{exec13:i2-start}

\section{An interface must preserve a scientific question}

A servicing analyst asks whether an offer would improve the next twelve
months' net value for accounts eligible today. A notebook, a scheduled command
and an agent can all transmit this question. They should receive the same
conditional answer when they submit the same declaration, inputs and method.
They should also retain the same unresolved assumptions. A successful call
which replaces the target population, changes the sign or drops an unbounded
component of an uncertainty set has failed as a scientific interface even if
its JSON is valid. The preceding chapter establishes the exchange contract;
this chapter develops the actual access paths and the client behavior needed
to preserve it.

The implemented library entry is
\texttt{causalbank.runtime\_v12.Runtime.invoke}. The command-line adapter and
local MCP server use that runtime, its artifact store and the scientific
dispatcher. This shared implementation reduces divergence among surfaces.
It does not prove their equivalence: parsing, version negotiation, error
handling and asynchronous state can still alter the result seen by a client.
Consequently an interface comparison must examine complete canonical responses,
including negative findings, rather than compare only the estimated coefficient.
The inspected source and recorded local trials support this narrow architecture
claim~\citep{v12_in_runtime,exec13_i2_examples}.

The tested runtime revision advertises nine operations. Capability inspection reports the
implemented subset. Graph review checks a supplied declaration's syntax.
Identification attempts a supplied-DAG back-door expression for independent
units and a binary contrast. Estimation inverts a Gaussian residual test using
supplied moments and covariance. Sensitivity solves supplied quadratic
inequalities. Observation auditing checks declared timestamps. Report building,
job status and job cancellation provide the remaining three operations.
Automatic problem formulation, data-driven graph discovery and design
comparison have no engine in this runtime. They belong to the proposed
architecture, and are absent from this revision's advertised MCP tool list. The later bounded fitted studies elsewhere in the book do not establish that those methods are available through this historical interface.

These distinctions matter when an agent chooses a tool called
\texttt{estimate.effect}. The name identifies an operation family; the supported
engine and estimator identifiers determine what can actually run. An agent
cannot turn the supplied-moment engine into a fitted causal forest by changing
its description. Nor does the graph syntax operation establish that a graph
represents the bank's assignment mechanism. Capabilities should be inspected
at the start of a client session and retained with its results, because a
proposed method and an installed method are different inputs to a decision.

Write a canonical request as $Q=(o,C,A,p,B,k)$, where $o$ is the operation,
$C$ the scientific context, $A$ the artifact references, $p$ the operation
parameters, $B$ the resource budget and $k$ an optional replay key. The separate
request identifier correlates a reply with a call. For deterministic synchronous
examples, the desired transport property is
\[
 R_{\mathrm{library}}(Q)=R_{\mathrm{CLI}}(Q)
 =R_{\mathrm{MCP}}(Q),
\]
after decoding each transport's wrapper. This is a scoped design property,
tested on selected cases. For jobs, compare stable handles and the same
observed terminal state; two polls at different times need not report the same
intermediate state. Neither equality proves that $C$ is causally correct.

\section{A complete request for an offer decision}

Let $A$ denote a binary offer, $Y$ twelve-month net value in USD and $X$ a
pre-decision risk score. The generated example declares the arrows
$X\to A$, $X\to Y$ and $A\to Y$. Its target is the offer-minus-no-offer average
effect for eligible accounts. These are example declarations, without bank
observations or independently verified graph truth. An explicit
\texttt{unverified} assumption is more useful than silently treating the graph
as known.

The following Python file creates a complete request. Save it as
\texttt{offer\_request.py} and run it with Python; its only output file is
\texttt{request.json}. The example uses a loop to retain the same evidence and
review fields on each edge. There is no hidden inference step in that loop.
\begin{lstlisting}[language=Python]
import json
from pathlib import Path

edges = [
    {"left_node": a, "right_node": b,
     "left_mark": "tail", "right_mark": "arrow",
     "evidence_type": "assumption", "evidence_refs": [],
     "review_status": "unverified"}
    for a, b in [("risk", "offer"), ("risk", "net_value"),
                 ("offer", "net_value")]
]
context = {
    "target": {"kind": "average_effect", "outcome": "net_value",
               "treatment": "offer", "contrast": "1-versus-0"},
    "population": {"definition": "Generated eligible accounts at decision",
                   "unit": "account"},
    "variables": [
        {"id": "offer", "role": "action", "unit": "binary"},
        {"id": "net_value", "role": "outcome", "unit": "USD"},
        {"id": "risk", "role": "adjustment", "unit": "score"}],
    "intervention": {"kind": "set", "value": "offer=1"},
    "horizon": {"value": 12, "unit": "months"}, "units": ["USD"],
    "sign_convention": "offer-minus-no-offer",
    "observation_clock": {
        "event_time": "event_at", "available_time": "available_at",
        "decision_time": "decision_at", "rule": "strict_before_decision",
        "alternative_justification": None},
    "sampling": {"law": "independent_units", "unit": "account",
                 "fold_unit": "account"},
    "assumptions": [{
        "id": "graph_truth",
        "statement": "The supplied graph represents this generated example",
        "status": "unverified", "evidence": []}],
    "graph": {"kind": "DAG", "edges": edges}, "source_evidence": []
}
request = {
    "schema_version": "causalbank.request/1.0.0", "request_id": "backdoor",
    "operation": "identify.effect", "artifact_inputs": [],
    "budget": {"wall_seconds": 12, "memory_bytes": 1073741824,
               "max_output_bytes": 100000, "model_calls": 0},
    "parameters": {"method_id": "backdoor"},
    "scientific_context": context, "idempotency_key": None
}
Path("request.json").write_text(json.dumps(request, indent=2) + "\n")
\end{lstlisting}

The budget declares a twelve-second worker limit, one GiB of worker address
space and a 100,000-byte output limit. It requests zero model calls because
this runtime has no model backend. The observation clock names three fields;
it does not assert that real records satisfy the ordering. Actual row checks
are a separate operation. Likewise, the sampling law records independent
accounts; repeated monthly observations do not become independent simply
because the client uses this string.

This request is deliberately an identification request, with no data artifacts.
Its answer is an expression and the conditions under which that expression
identifies the target. Converting that expression into a numerical estimate
requires an appropriate estimator and data construction. The current moment
engine is not a general next stage which accepts arbitrary account rows. A
client must identify a supported numerical path instead of treating a common
operation vocabulary as a guarantee of automatic end-to-end composition.

\section{Calling the library and the command line}

For the inspected installation, run Python with \texttt{PYTHONPATH=src} from
the causal repository root. The local environment is
\texttt{.runtime/in04/bin/python}. The library use is small enough to expose
the whole boundary:
\begin{lstlisting}[language=Python]
import json
from pathlib import Path
from causalbank.runtime_v12 import Runtime

request = json.loads(Path("request.json").read_text())
runtime = Runtime(Path.cwd() / ".runtime" / "offer-client")
response = runtime.invoke(request)
Path("response.json").write_text(json.dumps(response, indent=2) + "\n")
\end{lstlisting}
The runtime root is an operator configuration inside this repository's
\texttt{.runtime} tree. The scientific request has no field for choosing an
arbitrary directory, Python module or shell command. The library can still
raise validation exceptions for malformed requests before producing a
canonical response; the caller must retain those as invocation failures.
The example assumes its displayed valid request~\citep{exec13_i2_examples}.

The corresponding CLI call takes the operation name and the same JSON file:
\begin{lstlisting}
PYTHONPATH=src .runtime/in04/bin/python -m causalbank.cli_v12 \
  operation identify.effect --input request.json
\end{lstlisting}
The command's operation must agree with the request. Standard input is used
when \texttt{--input} is omitted or is \texttt{-}. To share the library's
operator store, set \texttt{CAUSALBANK\_STATE\_ROOT} in the launching
environment to its absolute path. The path is launch configuration, rather
than text supplied by an agent in the scientific request. Without this
setting the CLI uses its documented default local store.

A notebook should save the complete response before displaying a concise
interpretation. In this example, the useful interpretation is ``conditional
adjustment expression, no fitted dollar estimate.'' Displaying only
\texttt{result.estimate} would show null and omit the successful identification
result. Conversely, replacing null with zero would falsely assert that the
offer has no effect. The result's \texttt{kind}, \texttt{disposition} and
\texttt{qualification} determine what presentation is appropriate.

A scheduled consumer should retain both the process return code and parsed
JSON. It must first determine whether it received a canonical response or an
adapter error object; the latter need not contain \texttt{result} or
\texttt{scientific\_context}. Blindly indexing a nonexistent estimate can
convert a well-explained input failure into an opaque client crash. These
practical distinctions are part of the proposed common client library:
validated decoding, faithful storage and an explicit outcome for each branch.
They are not supplied by printing an arbitrary JSON scalar.

\section{Conditional identification and a useful refusal}

For the declared graph, adjustment for $X$ blocks the back-door path
$A\leftarrow X\to Y$. Let $Y(a)$ be the potential net value under offer
state $a$. Consistency, conditional exchangeability
$Y(a)\perp A\mid X$, positivity on the target population's support, and the
declared sampling interpretation give
\begin{align*}
 \E\{Y(a)\}&=\int \E\{Y(a)\mid X=x\}\,dP_X(x)\\
 &=\int \E\{Y\mid A=a,X=x\}\,dP_X(x),\\
 \tau&=\int\left[\E\{Y\mid A=1,X=x\}
                 -\E\{Y\mid A=0,X=x\}\right]dP_X(x).
\end{align*}
The first equality averages over the target risk distribution. The second
uses the identifying assumptions. The resulting units are USD per account
over the declared horizon. This derivation explains the returned
\texttt{adjustment\_contrast}: integrate over \texttt{risk}, take the
one-versus-zero contrast, and retain the outcome unit and independent-unit
sampling declaration. It is an application of the identification argument
developed earlier in the monograph; the execution confirms the expression
and its metadata, not the causal premises~\citep{exec13_i2_examples}.

Two counterexamples clarify the consumer's next action. If the sampling field
is changed to dependent months, the local identification routine returns
\texttt{unsupported}. It is refusing a request outside this implementation's
scope; it has not proved that a panel estimand is unidentified. The appropriate
next step is a reviewed longitudinal or dependent-sampling path. Changing the
field back solely to make the call succeed would conceal a scientific problem.
If a declared premise is marked \texttt{contradicted}, identification instead
returns \texttt{refused}, with no scientific result. The premise or target
must then be reconsidered; an automatic retry with unchanged information has
no scientific benefit.

Even within a supplied DAG, failure of the selected back-door attempt is not
a general nonidentification theorem. An alternative graph assumption or
identification strategy may succeed, while another query may require only a
bound. The service states the failed method's boundary in its result when
available. A proposed agent should preserve that explanation, route the case
to a substantive alternative, and label any new assumptions. It should never
replace ``this adjustment attempt failed'' with ``causal analysis is
impossible.''

\section{Uncertainty sets are part of the result type}

A response may carry a set without a scalar estimate. To understand why the
client must preserve its topology, consider the explicitly generated
inequality $a b^2+c b+d\leq0$, where $b$ is a scalar effect coordinate.
Coefficient units are understood to make the terms commensurate; the example
uses a fixed normalized USD coordinate. The deterministic sensitivity
operation returns the solution set. Four elementary choices give independent
algebraic checks of the numerical representation:
\begin{center}
\begin{tabularx}{\textwidth}{P{.20\textwidth}P{.29\textwidth}X}
\toprule
Inequality & Real solution & Canonical interval array \\
\midrule
$b^2-4\leq0$ & $[-2,2]$ & \texttt{[[-2,2]]} \\
$b^2+1\leq0$ & $\varnothing$ & \texttt{[]} \\
$-b^2-1\leq0$ & $\mathbb R$ & \texttt{[[null,null]]} \\
$-b^2+4\leq0$ & $(-\infty,-2]\cup[2,\infty)$ & \texttt{[[null,-2],[2,null]]} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}
\end{center}
The first and fourth follow by comparing $b^2$ with four. The second is empty
because $b^2+1$ is strictly positive; the third is the whole line because
$-b^2-1$ is strictly negative. In these interval arrays null denotes an
unbounded endpoint according to position, not missing data. An unknown set
has a different representation: unknown topology and null intervals.
All four arrays agreed between the library and CLI and with these independent
calculations. Their uncertainty kind is \texttt{sensitivity}, coverage is
\texttt{none}, and the probability level is null~\citep{exec13_i2_examples}.

An empty result is not a numerical failure and is not evidence of a zero
effect. It can mean that the stipulated restrictions have no joint solution.
A whole-line result supplies no finite restriction on this coordinate. For
the disconnected result, taking the convex hull discards the excluded central
region; truncating the tails fabricates information. A client chart should
retain the two rays and label their interpretation. A lending decision that
requires a guaranteed positive net benefit cannot infer it from a set containing
an unbounded negative ray.

The moment engine supplies a second reason for preserving these objects.
Suppose a moment relation is $m_Y-bm_A=0$. Under the supplied Gaussian
approximation, test inversion compares
\[
 (\widehat m_Y-b\widehat m_A)^2
 \quad\hbox{with}\quad
 \frac{c_\alpha}{n}
 (\widehat\Omega_{YY}-2b\widehat\Omega_{YA}
                      +b^2\widehat\Omega_{AA}),
\]
where $n$ and the covariance matrix $\widehat\Omega$ are supplied inputs and
$c_\alpha$ is the squared normal critical value. For $m$ coordinates the
simultaneous option uses $c_\alpha=\{\Phi^{-1}(1-\alpha/(2m))\}^2$,
with $\Phi$ the standard normal distribution function; the pointwise option
uses $m=1$ in that formula. Rearrangement produces a quadratic
inequality in $b$. A weak or zero denominator moment can make its accepted
set disconnected or unbounded. The generated input
$\widehat m=(1,0)$, $\widehat\Omega=\operatorname{diag}(0.01,1)$ and $n=100$
indeed produces two unbounded components in the reference engine. The
supplied covariance and Gaussian approximation are assumptions of this
calculation; this fixture does not establish coverage for an arbitrary bank
estimator.

The client must also retain pointwise versus simultaneous interpretation,
sampling law, probability level, numerical limitations and construction
evidence. A simultaneous collection of coordinate sets does not by itself
describe the full joint geometry. Downstream portfolio aggregation therefore
needs an explicitly justified construction, rather than treating separately
reported endpoints as a joint distribution. Changing transport cannot supply
the missing dependence information.

\section{Four different meanings of success}

Transport success, invocation completion, scientific disposition and
qualification answer different questions. The first says a reply arrived.
The second says the operation finished. The third distinguishes a computed
object from an unsupported, refused or unavailable scientific result. The
fourth records what evidence supports using that object. A proposed client
must preserve all four, because none is a substitute for the next.

The observed examples illustrate the distinction without a hypothetical
failure rate. The back-door request completed with a computed expression and
conditional-inference qualification. The unimplemented discovery request and
the dependent-sampling request completed with an unsupported disposition.
The contradicted-premise request completed with a refused disposition. All
four returned CLI exit zero. In contrast, changing the sign convention while
reusing an artifact bound to the old context produced a failed canonical
response, \texttt{invalid\_or\_unavailable\_input}, and exit four. Adding an
undeclared request property produced an adapter validation error and exit
two~\citep{exec13_i2_examples}.

\begin{center}
\begin{tabularx}{\textwidth}{P{.19\textwidth}X X}
\toprule
CLI outcome & What the adapter establishes & What the client must inspect \\
\midrule
Exit 0 & Canonical status is completed, queued, running or cancelled &
Disposition, result kind, qualification, and job payload state when present \\
Exit 2 & Request parsing, schema or semantic validation reached an adapter error &
Error object and its actual origin; caller input and corrupt saved state need different repairs \\
Exit 3 & A missing-file or permission exception reached the adapter &
Which operator input or local artifact was unavailable \\
Exit 4 & Failed/rejected canonical response or another execution failure &
Canonical error if present; otherwise the adapter error object \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}
\end{center}
This is an adapter rule, not a universal classification of root causes. The
runtime catches some artifact access failures itself, returning a failed
envelope that leads to exit four. Thus ``artifact problem'' does not imply
exit three. A client should branch on the actual response and record the
underlying cause, instead of guessing it from a coarse return code. Section~\ref{exec16:semantic-parity} supplies a concrete counterexample: corrupt saved replay reaches the broad input-error handler even though the scientific request is valid.

For decision use, a conservative proposed display sequence is: validate and
retain the response; check operation and context identity; inspect execution
status; interpret scientific disposition; then render the typed result with
its assumptions, uncertainty and qualification. A computed timestamp
diagnostic can contain failed rows. A computed set can be the whole line.
A completed identification operation can leave estimation entirely undone.
The user-facing conclusion should express these facts directly, rather than
use a green success icon as a surrogate for a supported financial decision.

The same distinctions constrain automated repair. Malformed dates may admit
a documented format correction. Missing causal assumptions require new
information or an explicitly changed problem. An unsupported engine may
require another implementation. A weak-information set may be the correct
answer. A loop that retries until it obtains a positive scalar would replace
scientific reasoning with selection on favorable outputs.

\section{Context binding, artifacts and observation time}

Large or reusable inputs enter through the local artifact store. An operator
can import a JSON document with the CLI's \texttt{artifact put} command,
declaring its schema version and role. For example, a prepared
\texttt{moments.json} can be imported as follows:
\begin{lstlisting}
PYTHONPATH=src .runtime/in04/bin/python -m causalbank.cli_v12 \
  artifact put --schema-version moment-summary/1 \
  --role moment_summary < moments.json
\end{lstlisting}
The returned descriptor goes into \texttt{artifact\_inputs}; the complete
descriptor, not merely a guessed path, supplies the artifact identity and custody declaration checked by the local runtime. It is not independent authentication of an authorized requester. The file must contain the supplied means,
covariance, sample-size and uncertainty settings required by that operation,
including its context digest. Other input roles have different schemas.
This import operation checks bounded JSON and identity; it does not certify
that moments were correctly estimated or that an operator chose a truthful
schema label~\citep{exec13_i2_examples}.

Let $J(C)$ be the deterministic finite JSON serialization used by the
implementation and $h_C=\operatorname{SHA256}(J(C))$. An input moment,
quadratic or observation artifact carries $h_C$; the operation compares it
with the digest of the submitted context. The digest binds target,
population, variables, intervention, horizon, units, sign, clock, sampling,
assumptions and graph together. Object-key order is normalized; ordered
arrays remain ordered. This is byte-level declaration identity, not a proof
of semantic equivalence between two differently expressed targets.

Suppose a numerical provider prepared moments for offer-minus-no-offer.
A client then changes the displayed question to no-offer-minus-offer and
reuses those moments. The context check refuses that mismatch. To perform
a legitimate sign conversion, the provider must actually transform the
numerical object and issue a new bound declaration. Simply copying a new
digest into unchanged input bytes can satisfy a structural check while
lying about the computation; the local system does not claim to defeat a
dishonest operator. Its guarantee is that an unnoticed declared mismatch
is detected, with provenance available for review.

The artifact identifier also includes the content hash and descriptor,
including schema, role, byte count and custody label. Reads compare the
submitted descriptor with saved metadata and verify bytes and hash. Files
must be bounded nonsymlink regular files. These rules detect accidental
mutation and prevent request-specified filesystem traversal within the
implemented boundary. They do not establish a multi-tenant authorization
service. Every caller using the same operator store is operating inside
the same local custody model. Section~\ref{exec14:artifact-custody} further qualifies these checks: the inspected reader does not recompute the descriptor-derived handle, and opening a named pipe can block before its regular-file check. The proposed repairs must be tested before these ordinary-case checks support a broader custody claim.

The clock example shows why metadata retention has scientific consequences.
The implemented diagnostic requires timezone-aware timestamps satisfying
\[
 t_{\mathrm{event}}\leq t_{\mathrm{available}}<t_{\mathrm{decision}}.
\]
An event that happened yesterday but became available after the offer decision
cannot support a claim that its measured value was a baseline covariate.
The three generated rows contain a valid earlier observation, availability
exactly at the decision, and a missing availability field. The latter two
are flagged. Passing this check establishes timestamp consistency only;
source ownership, measurement truth and inclusion mechanisms remain unverified.
The proposed client should therefore retain both the row diagnostics and the
causal declaration explaining why a field is an admissible adjustment variable.

\section{MCP negotiation and client interpretation}

The real local MCP adapter uses Python SDK~1.27.0 and protocol
\texttt{2025-11-25} over standard input/output. Its launch command is
\begin{lstlisting}
PYTHONPATH=src .runtime/in04/bin/python -m causalbank.mcp_server_v12
\end{lstlisting}
A compatible client launches the process, negotiates the protocol and sends
protocol messages. The command is not a natural-language console. The
inspected specification reserves stdout for newline-delimited JSON-RPC
messages and allows diagnostic text on stderr. Mixing a startup banner with
stdout would corrupt the transport even if the causal dispatcher were
correct~\citep{v12_mcp_legacy_stdio}.

Initialization is the first exchange. The client sends its supported version
and capabilities; the server returns its version and capabilities; the client
then sends \texttt{notifications/initialized}. A server that cannot use the
requested version can return another supported version. If the client cannot
use the returned version, the specification says it should disconnect.
Normal operations must respect the negotiated capabilities~\citep{v12_mcp_legacy_lifecycle}. The local adapter restricts negotiation to its
tested legacy revision. Receiving a response to initialization is therefore
insufficient: the client must inspect what version was actually selected.

After initialization, \texttt{tools/list} exposes only the nine implemented
operations, with input and output schemas. For this example,
\texttt{causal\_identify\_effect} accepts the complete canonical request as
the \texttt{arguments} member of a \texttt{tools/call} request. The protocol
request identifier correlates that exchange; the canonical request identifier
inside the arguments correlates the scientific operation. They need not be
equal. The tool name must map to the operation inside the request. Changing
only the outer name does not relabel an identification request as a discovery
request~\citep{v12_in_runtime}.

The server returns the canonical response in \texttt{structuredContent} and
as serialized JSON in a text-content block, following the inspected tool
specification's compatibility recommendation. A client that supports
structured content should validate it against the output schema and retain
the scientific fields. A client using the text copy must parse that JSON,
rather than ask a model to invent a convenient summary of it. A discrepancy
between representations is an interface defect to investigate~\citep{v12_mcp_legacy_tools,v12_in_runtime}.

There are three distinct negative-result layers. An unknown tool is a
JSON-RPC protocol error, with the recorded adapter returning code $-32602$.
A tool execution or input-validation failure is a tool result with
\texttt{isError=true}. A scientifically unsupported or refused request can
be a successful tool execution whose canonical disposition explains that
no requested effect was computed. The inspected legacy tool specification
distinguishes the first two layers; the third is the causal service's own
typed scientific meaning. A client which interprets
\texttt{isError=false} as ``causal conclusion accepted'' discards that meaning~\citep{v12_mcp_legacy_tools,exec13_i2_examples}.

Resources have a similarly explicit boundary. The protocol supports resource
listing and reading; the local adapter exposes only reports, evidence
summaries and canonical responses no larger than 65,536 bytes. Raw input
roles are excluded. Reads use opaque \texttt{causal-artifact} identifiers
and repeat identity, role and size checks. An external model can nevertheless
receive sensitive information if the calling client sends it a readable
summary containing that information. Excluding raw roles is not content
redaction, consent management or a proof that a report contains no customer
data. Those policies belong in any proposed bank-facing wrapper~\citep{v12_mcp_legacy_resources,v12_in_runtime}.

The separately inspected protocol revision \texttt{2026-07-28} changes
discovery and per-request metadata handling. Those newer paths and HTTP
transport are not implemented here~\citep{v12_mcp_versioning,v12_mcp_basic}.
A future adapter should be selected against the intended client's exact
revision and tested on initialization or discovery, tool schemas, errors,
resource custody and cancellation. The implementation does not invoke a
language model, even when its caller is an agent. Any model provider, data
egress and model-call budget are properties of that external workflow and
need separate evidence.

\section{Replay, report jobs and cancellation}

A client can lose a response after the work has completed. Retrying without
an identity may duplicate work; reusing an identity for a changed question
may return a scientifically irrelevant result. The implemented synchronous
replay cache binds the optional idempotency key to a digest of the request,
excluding its correlation identifier and the key itself, and to the source
and selected execution environment: Python and the recorded numerical/schema
package versions. It is not an identity of every installed package or the
host operating system. Inputs, operation, context, parameters and budget
remain part of that identity~\citep{exec13_i2_examples}.

The generated capability example changes only the request identifier and
recovers the same response with the new correlation identifier. It then
changes the wall budget from twelve to eleven seconds under the same key;
the runtime rejects the request with \texttt{idempotency\_conflict}.
This result is deliberate: a changed execution contract is not an exact
retry. A revised analysis should use a new identity and explicitly state
which earlier result it supersedes. The cache can also preserve a failed
response, so a client should not expect repeated use of the same key to
perform fresh attempts until one succeeds.

Report building has a durable lifecycle. An operator supplies one to one
hundred distinct canonical-response artifacts. The runtime validates their
schemas and creates a job bound to input hashes, request, source, environment
and budget. Submission returns a queued handle even if the worker has
already finished by the time the client receives it. The client uses the
handle in a \texttt{job.status} request. The returned envelope can itself
be completed because the status query succeeded, while
\texttt{result.payload.state} says that the report is queued, running,
failed, cancelled or completed. The latter field determines the report's
state; the outer status determines the query's state.

The executed report example summarizes the computed back-door response,
the unsupported discovery response and the refused premise. It preserves
those three declarations and labels verification as
\texttt{schema\_only\_not\_causal\_or\_external\_review}. Resubmission with
the same identity returns the original handle and a queued submission
envelope. It does not create a new scientific review or promote the
unsupported input~\citep{exec13_i2_examples}. The proposed user interface
should display the final report only after a completed payload state exposes
its result reference, and should inspect each input's declared status before
presenting a combined conclusion.

Recovery is bounded. Completed work identifiers form an ordered prefix of
the frozen input list; checkpoints bind that prefix and the accumulated
summaries to the execution identity. The local runtime uses atomic state
publication and a worker lease, allows at most three spawn attempts, and
retains the original declared deadline and checks code and checkpoint identity. The wall-clock adjustment example in Section~\ref{exec17:continuity-jobs} shows why that deadline arithmetic is not yet a clock-robust elapsed-time guarantee. These mechanisms support local report
recovery. They do not establish distributed consensus, platform failover or
universal exactly-once side effects in another system. Historical fault
trials, including interruption after a checkpoint, supply the existing
bounded engineering evidence~\citep{v12_in_runtime}.

Cancellation also has two scopes. The protocol's optional cancellation
notification concerns an in-progress protocol request and admits races with
completion~\citep{v12_mcp_legacy_cancellation}. The causal service's
\texttt{job.cancel} operation concerns an already submitted local report
job; it is not an implementation of MCP's separate task API. Closing a
client connection or cancelling a tool request must not be assumed to undo
a durable report. The job operation requests cooperative cancellation,
after which the client must read the observed state. In the generated
example, cancellation after completion leaves the completed report intact.
For a bank-facing workflow that actually sends offers, cancellation and
compensating actions would require a further design: this report service
does not send offers or reverse financial transactions.

\section{Resource limits and deployment alternatives}

Resource limits belong in the client contract because a mathematically
well-formed request may be infeasible in its launch environment. The local
runtime bounds requests to one million bytes, stored artifacts to eight
MiB, worker address space to between 64 MiB and four GiB, and worker wall
time to at most 300 seconds. Artifact reads also respect the request's
memory declaration. The worker runs a fixed internal entry point, with
single-thread numerical settings; the request cannot select arbitrary
executable code. A small control error may exceed an unrealistically tiny
output limit so that the refusal remains explainable~\citep{exec13_i2_examples}.

These are implementation bounds, not service-level guarantees. The worker's
address-space limit does not cover the resident coordinator or MCP SDK.
End-to-end elapsed time includes validation, process startup, transport and
client handling. A process can fail while importing dependencies under a
small memory allocation. The client should report the actual execution
failure instead of claiming that the causal problem has no answer. A future
service needs measured admission limits for the chosen workload and its
whole process tree, together with a storage-retention policy and failure
handling for exhausted capacity.

Library use is the natural first option for a Python research workflow: it
avoids protocol negotiation and keeps canonical objects accessible to local
code. It also places runtime dependencies and exception handling in the
consumer's environment. The CLI provides a process boundary and a simple
JSON exchange for schedulers and language wrappers, with explicit parsing
and exit handling. It incurs process startup and requires artifact custody
to be arranged between invocations. MCP provides discovery and typed tool
access for a compatible agent client, but introduces protocol-version,
transport and model-exposure questions. These are different operational
tradeoffs over the same scientific dispatcher.

An R, Java or C++ consumer can in principle launch the CLI and preserve the
JSON contract without importing Python into its process. That is a proposed
integration route, not evidence that every such client works. A foreign
function interface could reduce serialization costs for intensive numerical
work but couples runtimes and memory management. An HTTP service could
centralize dependencies and custody but adds authentication, network
failures, multi-user resource management and remote artifact authorization.
The prototype recommendation is to begin with the simplest surface matching
the consumer's actual needs and verify a complete workflow before adding
another boundary. The remaining study in this chapter develops the consumer's admission and interpretation rules; the following chapter then examines named research consumers and their scientific mappings.

\section{What the evidence supports and what the next client must show}

The historical local trial compared eleven scientific fixtures across the
library, CLI and real MCP transport, including both structured MCP output
and its text copy. It also exercised report and resource behavior; nine
separate fault cases addressed local recovery and rejection. Those results
remain scoped to the inspected source, environment and cases. The SDK's
thread wakeup hung in the managed sandbox, while the recorded approved local
environment outside that sandbox passed the diagnostic and conformance
harness. An installation proposal must test its actual launch environment,
because importable packages do not establish a functioning service~\citep{v12_in_runtime}.

The additional thirteen deterministic examples in this chapter compare
library and CLI behavior only. They include a risk-adjusted expression,
scope and premise failures, four independently derived set shapes, weak
moments, changed-context rejection and strict observation clocks. Separate
lifecycle checks establish replay conflict handling, report declarations,
terminal-state interpretation and non-rollback after completion. They add
reader-usable demonstrations; they are neither a rerun of MCP conformance
nor a statistical performance study~\citep{exec13_i2_examples}. A separate later suite, discussed in Section~\ref{exec16:semantic-parity}, did compare thirteen scientific requests and three lifecycle calls through the real library, CLI and MCP surfaces. These are distinct retained trials; their counts and scopes should not be merged.

For the next actual consumer, the useful acceptance example is a complete
decision trace. Start from its target and data dictionary, retain the
population, unit, sign, horizon, clocks and assumptions in the request,
select an implemented method, and examine both a supported and a
decision-relevant negative case. Verify that the consumer preserves
uncertainty topology and qualification when storing, plotting and exporting
the result. Include an interrupted or lost-response scenario with a stable
identity, and check that recovery neither repeats an external action nor
silently changes the scientific problem. External actions remain outside
this reference implementation and require their own contract if introduced.

This evidence would justify a scoped prototype connection. A claim of bank
deployment would additionally need the bank's data and access policies,
the intended platform's operating evidence, independent scientific review
and acceptance of the actual financial workflow. The proposal can already
specify the connection and its decisive tests without pretending that those
later observations have occurred. The design contribution here is concrete:
one scientific object survives three access paths, and every client has
explicit obligations for recognizing what that object does and does not say.
\label{exec13:i2-end}

\section{Admission precedes interpretation in a causal client}
\label{exec17:i2-admission}

The three surfaces become useful to a consumer only when the consumer can
decide what kind of reply it has received. Consider a scheduled lending
report that asks for a conditional adjustment expression, saves the reply,
and later displays it through an agent. The numerical estimate is correctly
absent. If the final client converts that absence to zero, the report now
asserts a null monetary effect that no component calculated. If it displays
only a successful process status, the unsupported and refused cases look
equally favorable. The missing product component is therefore a reviewed
client interpretation contract, with an explicit boundary between receiving
bytes, admitting a response, and deciding how that response may be used.

A proposed client session should retain its launch configuration and admitted
server identity, the negotiated protocol where applicable, the operation
catalogue and schemas, and the exact scientific request. The catalogue is
evidence about available operations in that session. It is not a warranty
that every graph class or estimator mentioned in a description is supported.
Admission needs the operation, method identifier and declared scientific
domain together. In the inspected local implementation, the outer MCP tool
name must agree with the operation inside the canonical request; discovery
is absent from the available mapping. These are actual source boundaries
\citep{exec13_i2_examples}. The more detailed consumer decision procedure
below is a proposed extension, evaluated by a separate finite reference
rather than installed as a new production client.

\subsection{A narrow decoding profile with explicit failure states}

First establish the transport boundary. A CLI consumer has process exit,
stdout and stderr as separate observations. A protocol consumer has a
correlated protocol reply or a transport failure before any causal response
exists. Diagnostic output should be retained separately from the object to
be decoded. Stripping an arbitrary prefix until some braces can be parsed
would hide a corrupted channel and could select the wrong object from a
mixed output stream. The proposed local profile accepts one complete JSON
value at the expected boundary, subject to its byte allowance. It rejects a
banner or trailing unrelated text. This is a deliberate consumer restriction,
not a claim that every possible transport framing uses one JSON document.

The profile also rejects duplicate object keys, nonfinite numeric tokens and
numeric overflow that becomes nonfinite after parsing. Duplicate keys matter
because two parsers can choose different values for the same field. A reply
containing both a completed and a failed status under the same key has no
single admitted meaning in this profile. Permitting a nonfinite number as a
point estimate would also bypass the explicit representation of unbounded
sets. The decoder consequently checks both the lexical input and the parsed
numeric tree. A finite byte limit reduces the amount of accepted input but
does not by itself bound all parsing memory or nesting depth; a deployment
must add and measure those resource boundaries.

After decoding, validate the full request and response schemas and the
semantic relation between them. The local semantic validator checks request
and operation identity, the context digest, units, result state, interval
topology and uncertainty interpretation. For example, a result marked
uncomputed cannot carry a numerical estimate, and a sensitivity result has
no sampling-confidence level. These are testable declared relationships.
They do not establish that the graph or supplied covariance is true
\citep{exec13_i2_examples}. The proposed client should keep schema admission
and semantic admission as separate diagnostic steps so that a missing field
does not become a scientific claim of nonidentification.

The finite reference applies the existing semantic validator to eleven
preserved library/CLI fixtures and classifies their meanings. It separately
rejects duplicate keys, a nonfinite token, overflow, trailing text, a banner,
an excessive byte count, a wrong request identifier, a wrong operation,
a wrong context, inconsistent set topology and an unsupported response
carrying a numerical result. A twelfth adverse case compares conflicting
structured and text representations. The exercise uses local stored
responses and deliberate copies; it makes no network call and does not
constitute a new MCP transport trial. Its scope is the proposed semantic
consumer, not complete schema, SDK, parser-resource or deployed-client
qualification \citep{exec17_integration_review_reference}.

\subsection{Two representations must describe one admitted response}

The inspected MCP adapter returns structured content and a serialized text
copy of the same canonical response. A proposed client that consumes both
should decode them separately and compare their canonical finite JSON
representations before interpreting either. Object ordering and whitespace
can vary without changing the declared fields, while ordered arrays remain
ordered. The reference uses the project's explicit serialization convention;
it does not claim a universal JSON-equivalence theorem. In particular, the
chosen identity need not treat every numerically equivalent spelling as
interchangeable. Any normalization beyond that convention must be justified
as part of the admitted profile.

A disagreement in qualification is consequential even when the estimated
coefficient agrees. One copy might say execution-only while another says
conditional inference. A disagreement in interval topology or context can
be still more serious. The proposed response to any such conflict is an
integrity failure with both originals retained. Choosing whichever copy gives
a convenient answer would make the consumer an unreviewed arbiter of
scientific meaning. If a permitted protocol profile supplies only one
representation, the client can use that representation after its own checks;
absence of a second copy is not automatically a conflict. The local reference
checks agreement under changed whitespace and rejection after changing a
qualification field \citep{exec17_integration_review_reference}.

This decision also specifies when a language model should see the result.
A deterministic admission layer should first establish which object exists
and what fields it contains. The model can then explain a supported typed
object with links to its assumptions and evidence. Asking the model to repair
a malformed response before preserving the original creates an additional
unmeasured transformation. A corrected result must instead have its own
identity and a recorded reason for the change. This is a design obligation
for the proposed client, not an assertion that the current local service
already implements a complete user interface.

\subsection{The decision table for a lending report}

Once the response is admitted, its interpretation follows the result type.
The following branches are deliberately separate because their remedies
require different information.
\begin{center}
\begin{tabularx}{\textwidth}{P{.24\textwidth}X}
\toprule
Admitted outcome & Proposed consumer behavior \\
\midrule
Execution failed or rejected & Retain error and request identity; publish no scientific answer. \\
Scientific unsupported & Show the unsupported domain or method; preserve the requested target. \\
Scientific refused & Show the contradictory or unmet premise; do not retry it as a numerical failure. \\
Identification expression & Display the expression and assumptions; do not manufacture an effect estimate. \\
Effect set & Preserve every component and its uncertainty interpretation, including empty or unbounded results. \\
Job reply & Read the payload's job state; expose a report only through its admitted completed result reference. \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}
\end{center}
This table is a display and routing rule. It cannot promote execution-only
evidence to scientific qualification. The preserved fixtures demonstrate
conditional expressions, unsupported sampling, contradicted premises,
finite/empty/whole-line/disconnected sets and context rejection. The proposed
consumer keeps these outcomes distinct
\citep{exec13_i2_examples,exec17_integration_review_reference}.

For an effect set, the display should show the monetary coordinate, sign,
horizon and the construction of the set. An empty sensitivity set means that
the supplied restrictions have no joint solution in that coordinate; it does
not mean a zero effect or zero uncertainty. A disconnected set cannot be
displayed as its central gap, and an unknown set cannot be converted to the
whole line merely because both are inconvenient to plot. The mathematical
distinctions are developed in the interchange chapter. The additional client
obligation here is to make each distinction survive storage, filtering,
sorting, plotting and export. For example, dropping rows with a null scalar
estimate would remove correctly computed identification expressions and
unbounded effect sets from the report denominator.

A completed job-status query is another important branch. The query can
finish successfully while the job payload says running. The local reference
constructs two semantic job replies with the same completed query status
and payloads running and completed, and obtains different display states.
These are authored semantic fixtures, not submitted report jobs. A full
client must additionally validate the job request schema, result-reference
presence, role, size, custody and bytes before opening a completed report.
It must then inspect the report's individual declarations. The inspected
report builder summarizes qualification; it does not supply a new causal
review of its inputs \citep{exec13_i2_examples}.

\subsection{Lost replies, stale observations and consumer state}

The client needs its own durable record of an attempt. A timeout after
submission does not establish that the server did no work. If a stable
idempotency identity was supplied, the consumer can use the permitted replay
or status path and retain the original request. Changing the scientific
context or budget while keeping the same identity requests a different
computation and should follow the conflict branch. The current implementation
binds the selected execution environment as well as the request, so replay
after a source change can be rejected even when the business sentence is
unchanged. That rejection is evidence about compatibility, not a failure to
understand the user's wording \citep{exec13_i2_examples}.

Polling introduces observation order. Suppose one status request begins
before completion but its response arrives after a later request that saw
the completed state. A naive display that overwrites its state with every
arriving reply can regress from completed to running. The proposed client
should associate observations with the exact job and request identity and
apply a declared terminal-state rule. Under an immutable job identity, a
terminal observation is not replaced by a later-arriving nonterminal
observation. Conflicting terminal states require reconciliation with the
authoritative job record; choosing the more favorable state is not a repair.
This is a proposed consumer rule and an adverse case for a future real
transport test, not a claim that the finite semantic reference simulates
network ordering or distributed consistency.

Cancellation has the same distinction between a request and an observation.
Recording that the user requested cancellation is compatible with a final
completed job when publication won the race. The client should preserve both
facts and label the resulting report accordingly. It must not equate closing
a window, cancelling a protocol call, requesting job cancellation and undoing
an external financial action. The actual service exposes report jobs and
does not perform those external actions. A consumer that later adds them
needs a separate authoritative reconciliation contract, not just another
status string.

\subsection{Capability negotiation determines a feasible workflow}

A proposed workflow planner should admit a chain of operations only when
each step's typed output can satisfy the next step's input domain. A
back-door expression is not a moment-summary artifact; a graph suggestion
is not a validated causal DAG; a successful timestamp diagnostic is not an
assignment mechanism. Therefore operation-name agreement alone cannot
establish composability. The current common runtime is useful precisely
because it exposes those narrow boundaries. The consumer should show the
unsupported bridge explicitly and retain an analyst path when no admitted
bridge exists.

For each candidate route, the planner should compare the declared target,
graph class, observation law, input artifact role, supported method and
result interpretation. If any component is absent, it can propose an
alternative route or ask for the missing scientific choice. It must not
silently replace a dependent panel by independent rows to gain admission.
For a source or protocol upgrade, the consumer's recorded capability snapshot
helps identify which prior route may have changed. Re-admission requires a
semantic comparison and selected adverse fixtures; a changed version string
neither proves compatibility nor automatically invalidates every earlier
scientific result.

The practical prototype deliverable is thus a small deterministic consumer
with a visible admission trace, followed by an optional explanation layer.
Its evaluation should pair each supported result with an appropriate
negative case and inspect the stored and exported objects, not merely the
screen caption. The finite reference already makes specific decoding and
interpretation errors reproducible. Completing an actual client would add
full schema validation, bounded parser resources, live transport ordering,
artifact retrieval, custody policy and launch-environment trials. These are
known engineering steps justified by the proposal. They remain separate
from expensive bank experiments, which should follow only after the
prototype demonstrates useful preservation of the scientific question.
\label{exec17:i2-admission-end}

chapters.title: Using the analysis in other research applications

segments.text:
\section{What a complete connection must preserve}

A treasury analyst may obtain a state estimate from one package, an intervention
contrast from another and a value calculation from a third. The final number
answers the original question only if these exchanges preserve its meaning.
An exposure measured in millions, a rate expressed in basis points, an outcome
available after a decision and a value computed under a different continuation
policy can each change that meaning while leaving a syntactically valid table.
The integration problem therefore begins with the banking decision and ends
with the consumer's displayed result. Successful transfer of a numeric array
is one intermediate condition.

Let the target declaration be
\[
 \mathcal T=(\mathcal P,\pi,\pi_0,t_0,H,\mathcal F,u,c),
\]
where $\mathcal P$ is the population, $\pi$ and $\pi_0$ are the intervention
and comparator, $t_0$ is the decision origin, $H$ the outcome horizon,
$\mathcal F$ the available information, $u$ the measurement unit and $c$ the
cash-flow convention. This is a proposed semantic record, rather than a claim
that every inspected repository already serializes these fields. A target also
needs its scientific premises: the observation and assignment laws, graph or
model class, sampling units, and the evidence supporting any restrictions.
Those premises are referenced alongside $\mathcal T$; a short tuple is not a
replacement for their mathematical definition.

Write $D$ for a consumer's data and $M(D)$ for the representation sent to the
causal operation. A correct adapter must give a declared mapping $g$ for which
\begin{equation}
 \tau_{\mathrm{consumer}}(D;\mathcal T)
   =g\{\tau_{\mathrm{provider}}(M(D);\mathcal T')\}
 \label{exec13:i3-target-map}
\end{equation}
under the stated model. For a unit conversion, $g$ may be a fixed affine
function. For a population change, time aggregation or policy substitution,
there is usually no such automatic identity. The adapter must then require a
new analysis or an additional argument. This requirement is useful even when
both packages use identical field names: an ``effect'' can denote an
association, a structural response or a policy-value difference.

The result mapping must preserve uncertainty as well as the target. For a
fixed known function $g$ and a confidence set $C$ for $\tau$, the event
$\{\tau\in C\}$ implies $\{g(\tau)\in g(C)\}$. Thus applying $g$ to the
whole set preserves the coverage lower bound. This elementary implication
does not make a supplied interval a valid confidence set, and it does not
apply to unaccounted uncertain exchange rates, estimated exposure weights or
a transformation chosen after inspecting the result. A joint confidence
region for all uncertain inputs, or an explicitly conditional scenario, is
needed in those cases. An identified set, a sensitivity range and a confidence
set must keep different result types even when each happens to be printed as
two endpoints.

Three connections consequently need separate judgments. Source inspection can
establish that a field or command is declared. An author-operated trial can
establish that a selected version transports and interprets a fixture
correctly. Acceptance by a consumer or an institution requires its own
decision and evidence. The cases below use inspected interfaces, existing
local runtime evidence and the transparent calculations developed in this chapter at their respective levels. The fitted studies elsewhere in the book provide additional evidence for particular statistical regimes, but do not qualify these proposed consumer mappings. They do not claim that sibling maintainers have adopted this library.

\section{The workspace as a set of scientific roles}

The dated inventory observed eighteen top-level directories and inspected
fifty-three source records on 12 October 2026. It recorded three MacroFinance
directories as one project family with distinct revisions. Its observation
date is later than the 7 October literature cutoff, so it establishes a local
environment snapshot rather than a retrospective software census~\citep{v12_in_inventory}. Selected declarations for FinMarketing, CardNPV,
BayesFilter and dataml were inspected again on 13 October. A comparison of all
fifty-three historical identities found ten changed files; the four selected
technical declaration files retained their recorded bytes. Historical
descriptions of the other projects therefore remain dated observations, not

Table~\ref{exec13:i3-workspace} gives a disposition for every observed

summary stand in for a primary source. The default location for new mappings
is the causal project, where their scientific restrictions can be reviewed
together. No cross-repository import is required merely to describe a proposed
exchange.

\section{Information clocks before feature exchange}

A transaction can occur before a decision and still be unavailable to the
decision maker. Let $v_j$ be the event time for feature $j$, $a_j$ its
availability time and $d_t$ the action time. The relevant information set is
generated by records available before $d_t$, not by every record whose event
time precedes it. Late corrections, external bureau arrivals and retrospective
entity resolution all create this distinction. Reconstructing the final
database as though it were visible at every earlier date gives a different
policy from the one the bank could have used.

FinMarketing's inspected \texttt{FeatureSnapshot} compares timestamp and
sequence pairs and requires
\[
 (a_{\max},s_a)\leq(c,s_c)<(d_t,s_d),
\]
where $c$ is the feature cutoff and $s$ is a within-timestamp sequence.
Its selected records also distinguish training, validation, test and serving
partitions, bind a fitted transformation to a snapshot, and keep outcome
names separate from feature names. The inspected \texttt{SourceBatch}
includes owner, use basis, permission and source digest, with a declared
synthetic or licensed-public boundary~\citep{exec13_i3_inspection}. These
declarations give a concrete proposed mapping. They do not establish that
the supplied timestamps or ownership claims are true.

Consider an illustrative decision pair $(100,4)$ and cutoff $(100,3)$.
Availability at $(99,9)$ or $(100,3)$ is admitted; availability at $(100,5)$
or $(101,0)$ is rejected. The four exact checks are reproduced with the other
chapter examples~\citep{exec13_i3_examples}. Dropping the sequence field makes
the third case appear simultaneous and loses the needed ordering. Converting
UTC to a local display time must not change the comparison. When a source
does not supply the required ordering, the adapter should request a coarser
defensible decision clock or report unavailable information, rather than
inventing the missing sequence.

Filtering introduces the same issue at a less visible boundary. A state
estimate using observations through $t$ can support a decision after those
observations arrive. A smoothed state using later observations cannot be
substituted into that historical policy without changing its information
set. Both arrays can have the same dimensions and plausible values. The
consumer therefore needs the conditioning horizon and observation-availability
rule, in addition to a state name and numeric uncertainty. This requirement
connects the workspace interfaces directly to the longitudinal assumptions
developed earlier in the monograph.

\section{Funding: from a structural rate response to value}

Suppose treasury asks for the value of a ten-basis-point reduction in a
funding action over four quarters. Three objects are required. The consumer
must specify the action and exposure. A scientific analysis must establish
what change in paid funding rate that action would cause under its model.
A valuation step must then translate that response into dated cash flows.
A forecast of market rates alone supplies neither the intervention response
nor the exposure response to the bank's decision.

The inspected MacroFinance inventory directs active numerical work to
BayesFilter and describes the root migration adapter as a compatibility
facade~\citep{v12_in_inventory}. In the re-inspected BayesFilter declarations,
\texttt{BayesianSSMProblem} binds the model manifest, data signature, static
shape and coordinate convention; \texttt{FilterProgram} separately names the
filter, required model capabilities, target policy and approximation
semantics~\citep{exec13_i3_inspection}. A proposed funding adapter should retain
these distinctions. An exact structural model, a deterministic approximate
filter and a fixed-randomness numerical procedure need not imply the same
likelihood or uncertainty. Importing a historical local sampler because it
returns a familiar array could bypass the selected authority entirely.

For a transparent conditional example, fix exposure $B=100$ million USD,
action $a=-10$ basis points, annual effective discount rate $r=0.04$ and an
initial implementation cost $K=40{,}000$ USD. Let $\theta$ denote paid-rate
pass-through in basis points per action basis point, held constant across
four quarters. Assume balances are invariant to the action, cash accrues
uniformly within each quarter and is paid at quarter end, and no additional
fees or risk effects occur. The present value of savings is then
\begin{equation}
 V(\theta)=-B\frac{a}{10{,}000}\theta
      \sum_{q=1}^{4}\frac{1/4}{(1+r)^{q/4}}-K
       =97{,}584.369097\theta-40{,}000.
 \label{exec13:i3-funding}
\end{equation}
The sign is explicit: a negative rate change decreases cost and produces a
positive saving. The factor $10{,}000$ converts basis points to a decimal
rate, while $1/4$ converts an annualized rate into quarterly accrual. The
fractional discount exponent is required because $r$ is annual effective.
Replacing it with a quarterly rate would require a different parameterization.

For an assumed pass-through range $[0.6,0.9]$, the resulting value range is
$[18{,}550.62,47{,}825.93]$ USD; at $\theta=0.75$ the value is
$33{,}188.28$. The break-even coefficient is approximately $0.409902$.
These figures reproduce both by the affine formula and by summing the four
cash flows, including a dollars-to-millions round trip. They are generated
planning calculations with supplied inputs, not bank estimates or a
confidence interval~\citep{exec13_i3_examples}. The coefficient range could
instead be an identified set or a fitted confidence set, but only if a
scientific analysis justified and labeled that interpretation.

The example makes several adverse exchanges visible. Treating each quarter
as a full year of accrual changes the midpoint value to $252{,}753.11$.
Reading ten basis points as ten percentage points changes the rate scale by
a factor of one hundred. Reading millions as dollars changes the exposure
scale by a factor of one million. These are semantic errors even if the
downstream computation is numerically exact. A consumer acceptance fixture
should assert the declared dimensions and the independently computed cash
flows, not only compare two calls to the same valuation function.

More consequentially, an action may change the balance itself. With
action-dependent balance $B_q(a)$ and funding rate $s_q(a)$, the cost
contrast is based on
\[
 \sum_q d_q\Delta_q
       \{B_q(a)s_q(a)-B_q(0)s_q(0)\},
\]
where $d_q$ discounts the cash flow and $\Delta_q$ is the accrual fraction.
Equation~\eqref{exec13:i3-funding} follows only under its fixed-exposure
restriction and the specified rate contrast. Multiplying a rate effect by
the observed balance does not account for endogenous deposit attrition,
replacement funding or interaction between amount and price. A useful
adapter therefore either retains this restricted target or asks for the
joint structural response. It does not silently convert a restricted
scenario into a general treasury value claim.

The first proposed workflow is consequently modest and complete: a
MacroFinance question supplies target and exposure declarations; a selected
numerical output supplies its model and approximation identities; a causal
analysis accepts or refuses the intervention meaning; and a value object
retains the transformation and the complete uncertainty object. A simpler
baseline is a manually reviewed exported result with the same declarations.
Only a measured reduction in repeated translation errors or effort, with
equivalent scientific output, supports replacing that baseline with an
automated connection. No general MacroFinance--BayesFilter--causal adapter
has been qualified by the arithmetic example.

\section{Numerical authority and the error in a value transformation}

A connection to a state-space provider also needs a mathematical account of
approximation. Suppose, conditional on an explicitly declared model and
available history, the provider's target distribution over a finite state
$S$ is $P$ and its numerical approximation is $\widetilde P$. Let $f(S)$
be the value contribution, with known bounds $m\leq f(s)\leq M$.
Define total variation by
\[
 \operatorname{TV}(P,\widetilde P)
     =\frac12\sum_s|P(s)-\widetilde P(s)|.
\]
Then a supplied bound $\operatorname{TV}(P,\widetilde P)\leq\epsilon$
implies
\begin{equation}
 |E_Pf-E_{\widetilde P}f|\leq(M-m)\epsilon.
 \label{exec13:i3-tv}
\end{equation}
For a direct proof, let $\delta_s=P(s)-\widetilde P(s)$. The sum of the
positive $\delta_s$ and minus the sum of the negative $\delta_s$ both
equal total variation, since $\sum_s\delta_s=0$. Subtract the constant
$m$ from $f$, and bound the positive contribution by
$(M-m)\sum_{\delta_s>0}\delta_s$. Interchanging $P$ and $\widetilde P$
gives the other direction. This bound is a project derivation for the
specified finite problem, not a claim that an inspected filter supplies
$\epsilon$ automatically.

In the funding example, let the low and high states have coefficients
