server. The earlier question about a complete terminal-state schema remains
open: a successful mock does not enumerate every server terminal state.
\citep{exec23_workflow_delegates_dominopy}

For the proposal, preserve the client's useful restart and revision controls
and add an explicit result contract at the worker boundary. Keep transport
retry, reauthentication, remote restart and a new scientific attempt as
different events. Before any resubmission with external effects, reconcile
the remote attempt and use an application identity whose idempotency
semantics are actually supported. This is a proposed protocol, not a claim
that Domino duplicates jobs or lacks an idempotency facility. Porting the
whole client would reproduce the unresolved schema and dependency questions
without yet demonstrating better causal fidelity.

\subsection{Posit: terminal state, exit code and conformance coverage}

The Launcher SDK gives a particularly useful typed distinction. Its
\texttt{Failed} status means the job could not be launched; its
\texttt{Finished} status includes a process that launched and exited with
a nonzero exit code. Canceled, Failed, Finished and Killed are terminal.
The job object carries status, optional reason/code and a separate optional
process exit code. A causal CLI or MCP consumer should preserve these fields
instead of translating every terminal or Finished record into scientific
success. A successful refusal artifact may be an acceptable scientific
answer, but that acceptance must be explicitly bound to its request and
contract.
\citep{exec23_workflow_delegates_positgo}

To expose the accounting consequence, suppose four supplied attempts yield
Finished with exit zero and a valid bound artifact; Finished with exit seven;
launch failure; and cancellation. All four are terminal. Only the first
satisfies a stipulated acceptance predicate requiring the allowed state,
allowed exit and artifact binding. At a supplied cost of USD 3 per attempt,
USD 12 has been spent. Reporting USD 3 per terminal event and USD 12 per
accepted artifact answers different questions. Neither number proves causal
validity, which remains another contract, and neither is a Posit price or a
bank ROI estimate. This exact example shows why a proposal comparison must
use the same accepted-output definition and failed-request denominator for
every execution alternative.
\citep{exec23_workflow_delegates_reference}

The scheduler example offers a reusable separation between Launcher protocol
handling and a \texttt{SchedulerClient} backend that submits, observes,
cancels, kills and retrieves output. Its illustrative state mapper sends
unrecognized native values to Pending. That default is an example, not
evidence that all scheduler states are known or that a supplied plugin is
production ready. A bank worker should retain the native value and use an
explicit unresolved mapping until the chosen backend profile justifies it.
Reusing the SDK boundary is a narrower candidate than reimplementing the
execution service, but the backend and supported product versions must be
selected before qualification.
\citep{exec23_workflow_delegates_positgo}

The source conformance facilities strengthen the proposed qualification
design when their coverage is kept explicit. A profile requires job
factories and expected stop/kill states and exit codes. Network, output and
suspend switches determine which workflow assertions run. The
\texttt{NetworkAvailable} comment says default true, while the inspected
\texttt{applyDefaults} function sets only durations. An omitted Go boolean
remains false. A prototype must therefore record the actual profile and set
the required switch explicitly, instead of assuming that a documented
default caused a network check to execute. This is a discrepancy between
selected source comments and defaults, not an observed deployment failure.
\citep{exec23_workflow_delegates_positgo}

Two further qualifications prevent overstatement. The terminal-regression
invariant compares a terminal result with one revisit 200 milliseconds
later. Agreement at those times is useful evidence for that run, not a proof
of permanent stability: an authored history can agree at times zero and
one fifth second and change at one second. The cancellation scenario skips
when the API returns an error, explaining that the job may already have
started. That branch does not first demonstrate the proposed start race.
A registered adaptation should inspect state and error identity before
classifying a race, retain every skipped or unsupported case, and avoid
counting a skip as successful cancellation. No upstream conformance suite
has been executed here.
\citep{exec23_workflow_delegates_positgo,
exec23_workflow_delegates_reference}

\subsection{A bounded integration choice and the remaining comparison}

These delegates support a coherent prototype choice. Preserve vendor job
dispatch and resource management behind typed workers, with a common causal
request and result contract above them. Record request, attempt, code,
dataset, environment, information date and native state separately. Bound
observation and transport time; reconcile a remote attempt after a timeout;
freeze audit membership; and validate the expected artifact and its
scientific meaning independently of process completion. This is a proposed
integration architecture. The exact authored timing, sampling and cost
witnesses explain why its contracts are needed; they do not qualify the
implementation.

The remaining market comparison has specific inputs. The next treatment adds SAS's historical REST examples, a declared-range HTTP dependency profile for Domino and Posit's concrete Local backend. Those resolve specific source questions. SAS still needs a complete supported server contract, Domino its terminal and error schema, and Posit a supported product/backend combination with an explicit conformance profile. Immutable Dataiku 15.0.2 cutoff technical bytes remain a
separate historical-source omission. Client licensing, commercial server
rights, dependency notices and actual prices must be assessed separately.
Public or synthetic fault trials can justify a later costly prototype study
once its environment is fixed. Until then, these are source-based comparison
and integration choices; native capability, whole-market coverage and bank
acceptance remain open.

\section{From workflow submission to a scientifically acceptable artifact}
\label{sec:exec24-workflow-contracts}

A restarted causal batch needs an account of what was requested, what
actually ran and which result answers the banking question. A collections
team might request a monthly policy comparison, receive a trigger
acknowledgement, and later find either a completed simulation or no run at
all. A funding analyst might receive a Finished job whose process exited
unsuccessfully. Neither an acknowledgement nor a terminal state establishes
that the requested intervention contrast, population and information date
survived execution. The following historical source profiles supplement the
earlier client comparisons with immutable Dataiku client text, SAS REST
examples, a declared-range HTTP dependency profile and a concrete Posit
Local backend. They establish source contracts, not observed performance of
licensed installations.~\citep{exec24_workflow_contracts_dataiku,
exec24_workflow_contracts_sas,exec24_workflow_contracts_domino,
exec24_workflow_contracts_posit}

\subsection{Dataiku: the trigger denominator precedes the run denominator}

The authenticated Dataiku client identifies version 14.7.3. Its scenario
interface explicitly distinguishes a trigger firing from a scenario run.
A manual firing may be cancelled because a scenario is already running or
another trigger fires. The firing's run identifier is the trigger-run
identifier; it is not automatically the eventual scenario-run identifier.
The proposed adapter should retain both identities and their relation,
including the legitimate outcome that no scenario run is created. This
historical client cannot authenticate the separately requested DSS 15.0.2
server behavior or a complete supported client/server matrix.
\citep{exec24_workflow_contracts_dataiku}

The distinction matters even in convenience methods. The inspected
trigger-wait method with \texttt{no\_fail=True} returns \texttt{None}
when a trigger is cancelled. The surrounding \texttt{run\_and\_wait}
method passes that option into the trigger wait, then constructs a waiter
without checking whether a run exists. The waiter's next loop dereferences
\texttt{scenario\_run.run}. Under the documented cancelled-trigger
condition, this composition therefore has an unguarded \texttt{None} path.
This is a conditional static finding; no native execution, deployment
prevalence or observed customer failure is claimed. A wrapper should handle
a cancelled-before-start event explicitly instead of promising that the
permissive flag suppresses every exception. It can do so without porting
the whole scenario engine.~\citep{exec24_workflow_contracts_dataiku}

Once a run exists, the client treats the presence of its result as the end
of running. It exposes SUCCESS, WARNING, FAILED and ABORTED outcomes.
The strict completion path accepts only SUCCESS; WARNING is not silently
equivalent to it. A permissive return still needs an explicit consumer
decision about outcome and artifact validity. Backoff begins at 200
milliseconds, grows by a factor of 1.1 and caps each sleep at 15 seconds.
This per-sleep ceiling does not bound the number or duration of requests.
The inspected DSS HTTP delegate does not pass a timeout argument. These
facts motivate a separate observation deadline and transport policy; they
do not establish that every customized client session behaves identically.
\citep{exec24_workflow_contracts_dataiku}

For an authored example, suppose four requested triggers produce one
cancellation before a run, one successful accepted result, one warning
result outside the acceptance contract, and one failed run. There are four
requests, three actual runs and one acceptable artifact. If $A$ is the
number accepted, $N$ the number requested and $R$ the number started,
\begin{equation}
  \widehat p_{\mathrm{request}}=A/N=1/4,
  \qquad \widehat p_{\mathrm{started}}=A/R=1/3.
  \label{eq:exec24-workflow-denominator}
\end{equation}
Both rates are legitimate when labelled, but only the first retains the
cancelled request. With stipulated costs of USD 2, 4, 3 and 3, total cost
is USD 12: USD 4 per started run and USD 12 per accepted artifact. These
invented amounts demonstrate a denominator effect, not vendor prices or
bank economics. Three stipulated backoff sleeps total $331/500$ seconds.
With three two-second requests, observation takes $3331/500$ seconds before
other overhead. A sleep schedule is not a whole-workflow time guarantee.
\citep{exec24_workflow_contracts_reference}

The same distinction protects statistical evidence. Public-data evaluations
that retain only successful runs describe performance conditional on
execution and acceptance. They cannot represent all requested cases without
accounting for exclusions. The proposed CLI/MCP result should expose request,
trigger and run identities, whether execution began, native outcome,
exception and acceptance decision. A caller can then require strict success
or inspect a warning while retaining the original denominator.

\subsection{SAS: an execution example is not a supported server schema}

The pinned SAS repository describes its contents as preview REST examples.
Its Job Execution text describes asynchronous execution of a job definition,
submission through \texttt{/jobExecution/jobs}, and polling the created
job's state link. It distinguishes completed from failed and directs the
consumer to an error member on failure. Artifacts occupy a provider-specific
results map; the log location is separate. Without a supplied expiration,
the example assigns cleanup to the client. A workflow-origin submission
can identify its submitting application. These details support an adapter
that follows resource links and preserves provider identity, execution
state, artifacts and lifecycle actions separately.
\citep{exec24_workflow_contracts_sas}

The page identifies document version 5 and an update date of 26 November
2019, not a SAS server release. A cutoff repository revision authenticates
the bytes without making the examples a complete supported API schema.
The separate Visual Investigator workflow text concerns BPMN case management
for investigation and threat analysis. It must not be substituted for the
analytics workflow service used by an earlier Python client. Supported
editions, complete state/error enumerations, prompt schemas and timezone
behavior still need normative technical originals.
\citep{exec24_workflow_contracts_sas}

For the proposal, a narrow worker can bind the scientific target and data
revision to the definition, submission, provider and returned artifact
before remote cleanup. Reimplementing the REST stack would not remove
the missing server evidence. Public examples justify prototype interfaces
and test cases; they cannot supply licensed-deployment conformance results.

\subsection{Domino: method and failure class govern retry behavior}

The earlier Domino HTTP manager supplies a retry policy without overriding
its allowed-method set. Package setup permits Requests at least 2.4.2 and
urllib3 at least 1.26.19 but below 3; the requirements file narrows Requests
to the 2.31 line. A selected historical profile of Requests 2.31.0 and
urllib3 1.26.20 fits these inspected ranges, including Requests' own range.
It is a source-review profile, not a solved environment or deployment lock.
A separately acquired cutoff development revision cannot replace this
declared-range distinction.~\citep{exec24_workflow_contracts_domino}

Requests retains the supplied Retry object and passes it to the connection
pool. In the selected urllib3 profile, default allowed methods are HEAD,
GET, PUT, DELETE, OPTIONS and TRACE. POST and PATCH are absent. The response
retry predicate checks the method before its status list; the read-error
path also applies a method gate. Thus a retryable status list alone does
not imply that a submission POST is retried on those statuses. The
connection-error branch differs: it does not apply that gate. The source
classifies connection failures as cases in which the server is thought not
to have received the request, whereas read errors can follow processing.
A blanket claim that POST can never be retried would also be too broad.
\citep{exec24_workflow_contracts_domino}

A transport retry, authentication refresh, restart of a known remote job
and new scientific attempt must therefore remain distinct. After an
ambiguous submission, the proposed worker retains the unresolved remote
identity and reconciles it under an actual server idempotency contract.
HTTP defaults and response codes do not prove exactly-once execution.
The pinned public \texttt{api-docs} repository does not close this gap:
its original README and index redirect to a mutable latest guide rather
than storing a versioned \texttt{v4/jobs} schema. Complete terminal/error
semantics and the meaning of every conflict response remain unresolved.
\citep{exec24_workflow_contracts_domino}

The open client remains a plausible integration boundary because it already
exposes identities and job actions. A wholesale port would create a second
implementation with the same unresolved server assumptions. A prototype
should first lock full dependencies and register response-status,
connection, read, credential and reconciliation cases. No native trial or
claim that an installation duplicates or loses requests is made here.

\subsection{Posit: preserve a concrete backend's unsupported actions}

The C++ SDK's sample Local backend supplies a concrete execution contract.
It launches an asynchronous child, stores its process identifier and
publishes Pending. On exit it records the process exit code, then changes
every non-killed job to Finished without requiring zero. A quickly exiting
Pending job can first receive a Running notification. This backend explicitly
does not support cancellation. Kill, stop, suspend and resume use separate
signals and state paths. A proposed adapter must report unsupported Cancel
explicitly instead of turning it into a successful or merely skipped test.
\citep{exec24_workflow_contracts_posit}

Two stipulated records can both say Finished while one has exit zero and
a valid artifact and the other has exit seven and no acceptable artifact.
Acceptance needs the appropriate native state, an allowed exit code where
the contract uses one, a request-bound artifact and scientific validation.
A valid refusal may itself be an acceptable scientific answer if the contract
declares that possibility. The example describes invented records, not
observed bank jobs.~\citep{exec24_workflow_contracts_reference}

Historical documentation limits remain material. The prerequisite guide
mentions Workbench 1.4, later says 1.4 or greater, and requires a launcher-enabled
license and test scheduler. That statement is not a current support matrix.
The build specifies C++11, default Boost 1.83.0 and OpenSSL 1.1.1, which need
reconciliation with the older prerequisite table before building an environment.
The Local three-second setting concerns inter-node connections, not a global
causal-job deadline. The SDK notice distinguishes public permissive terms
from software received under a commercial agreement; it does not license
Workbench itself.~\citep{exec24_workflow_contracts_posit}

The smoke-test guide explicitly says its utility does not replace integration
testing with Launcher and the consuming product. It varies privilege and
configuration and requires manual verification of printed responses. Its
informal description of Finished as without failure must not erase the
executable exit-code distinction. A future profile should name exact product
and Launcher builds, SDK revision, backend, privilege mode, network/output
switches and allowed exit codes. Unsupported Cancel, races, missing artifacts
and failures each retain their own accounting. This is a testable prototype
plan, not completed conformance.~\citep{exec24_workflow_contracts_posit}

These comparisons favor small typed workers around existing execution
contracts. The causal library owns the intervention target, assumptions,
observation clock, artifact validation and failure accounting; platforms
retain their native execution vocabulary. Public evidence now supports a
more precise trigger/run distinction, retry classification and exit-code
contract. Historical server manuals, complete schemas, supported product
profiles, rights and measured costs still need their stated evidence. These
limits guide the next prototype without claiming complete commercial-workflow
coverage.

\section{Dataiku as a workflow reference with explicit scientific acceptance}
\label{sec:exec25-dataiku-reuse}
Dataiku supplies a concrete orchestration reference for the proposed causal
library. The selected evidence concerns the Python API client at revision
\texttt{de83b58cc2d5e1b539fd}\allowbreak\texttt{44797778d56e20f1d367},
committed 3 August 2026, whose package declaration is version 14.7.3. It also
includes retained official DSS 14 and DSS 15 documentation. The immutable
client predates the 7 October 2026 cutoff; the subsequently acquired mutable
documentation is qualified by branch and acquisition date, and does not prove
an exact cutoff server patch or current commercial offer. The reference choice
separates the open client, its dependencies and the commercial server profile.
A client license notice is not a server entitlement, compatibility guarantee
or causal engine qualification.~\citep{exec24_workflow_contracts_dataiku,exec23_dss_dss14_flow,exec23_dss_dss14_releases,exec23_dss_latest_flow,exec23_dss_latest_releases}

This treatment consolidates the preceding Dataiku source findings into an adoption choice; it is not an additional native trial. A useful banking application is a recurring branch-policy analysis. A scenario
can coordinate preparation, fitting, diagnostics and delivery, but a completed
scenario cannot alone establish that the treatment definition, observation
clock, adjustment set and uncertainty calculation are appropriate. Suppose a
monthly analysis is replayed after a data correction. The proposed library
must bind the question version, eligible branch-periods, treatment adoption
record, data and schema digests, method configuration and output identity.
An output from the previous data version is not an accepted answer to the new
request merely because the scenario has a successful execution status. This
scientific acceptance layer is a proposed responsibility of the causal library,
not a claim that the orchestration product lacks a particular undocumented
feature.~\citep{exec25_dataiku_choice}

\subsection{Trigger, run and result are separate objects}
The selected client distinguishes firing a trigger from obtaining a scenario
run. Its \texttt{run} method returns a trigger-fire object; the waiting path
polls for the run or cancellation. Cancellation can return \texttt{None} when
\texttt{no\_fail=True}. In the inspected \texttt{run\_and\_wait} composition,
that result is passed to a waiter without a local \texttt{None} guard, and the
waiter dereferences the scenario-run object. This identifies a conditional
static path to qualify and handle in an adapter; no native cancellation trial
or observed server failure is claimed. The proposed adapter should keep
\emph{trigger cancelled before run creation} distinct from \emph{run aborted}
and from \emph{request completed with a scientific refusal}.~\citep{exec24_workflow_contracts_dataiku}

Completion and outcome also differ. One inspected path regards the presence
of a result as completion, while its strict outcome check accepts
\texttt{SUCCESS} and raises for other outcomes. The documented outcome set
includes \texttt{WARNING}, \texttt{FAILED} and \texttt{ABORTED}; the selected
waiter can return non-success when \texttt{no\_fail} is enabled. Official DSS 14
step-control documentation permits selected failures to be downgraded to
warnings and provides conditional steps, including steps that run regardless
of earlier failure. A proposed causal adapter must retain both the original
outcome and the configured exception policy. A warning permitted by workflow
configuration may still be scientifically disqualifying, while a deliberately
completed refusal can be a valid service response. Neither should be silently
recoded to a successful effect estimate.~\citep{exec24_workflow_contracts_dataiku,exec23_dss_dss14_flow}

The orchestration boundary must therefore expose a logical request identifier,
trigger identity, run identity and attempt identity separately. Consider an
authored example with requests A, B and C: A has two attempts and two created
runs, B has one attempt cancelled before a run, and C has one attempt and one
run. There are three logical requests, four attempts and three runs. The same
run count as request count is accidental; reporting only that count hides both
A's duplicate execution and B's cancellation. No idempotence guarantee is
inferred from the selected client. The proposed replay contract reconciles
existing run identities and accepted artifacts before retrying, and records a
new execution attempt without creating a second scientific request.~\citep{exec25_dataiku_choice}

\subsection{A bounded observer does not prove a stopped computation}
The selected backoff helper starts at 200 milliseconds, multiplies by 1.1 and
caps each sleep at 15 seconds. A cap on an individual polling delay does not
bound the sum of delays. Once the cap is reached, $n$ further waits consume
$15n$ seconds before any HTTP or server time is added. The inspected HTTP call
does not supply a timeout argument, so this source path does not establish a
whole-operation deadline either. These observations are restricted to the
selected source; they are not an assertion about all server or deployment
controls.~\citep{exec24_workflow_contracts_dataiku,exec25_dataiku_choice}

The proposed contract distinguishes a caller's observation deadline from a
confirmed server cancellation. In a stipulated timeline, a trigger fires at
second 0, a run is created at second 3, observation stops at second 10 and the
run completes at second 12. At second 10 the honest state is completion
unknown. An automatic retry could overlap the original run unless the adapter
reconciles its identity and effects. Conversely, a server acknowledgement of
a cancellation request is not accepted as proof that every side effect has
been rolled back. The candidate integration needs bounded client calls,
monotonic total budgets, authenticated terminal-state reconciliation and an
explicit policy for late results. The library must be able to decline a stale
artifact while preserving the costs incurred by the original attempt.~\citep{exec25_dataiku_choice}

\subsection{Conditional integration and the public qualification route}
The present choice is reference use of the selected client and documented
scenario semantics. Conditional integration would wrap a supported and
entitled server/client combination, retain the distinct states above, and
connect completed artifacts to the library's causal question contract. Direct
adoption as a causal engine is not established by orchestration evidence.
Porting selected client logic requires a component and dependency rights
review and reproduces the responsibility for protocol compatibility; porting
proprietary server internals is not authorized by the client notice. Rejection
is specific to unsupported semantic shortcuts, such as equating a successful
scenario with identified causal effect, or treating a local observation timeout
as confirmed remote termination. Other product functionality is outside this
selected-source assessment.~\citep{exec24_workflow_contracts_dataiku,exec25_dataiku_choice}

Before spending on a bank deployment, a public qualification study should
freeze a permitted server profile, compatible client, project and scenario
versions, generated data law, effect query, artifact digests, acceptance rules
and complete cost categories. Generated branch-period fixtures can carry known
causal truth; permitted public datasets can exercise data preparation and
workflow without supplying unobserved assignment truth. The exact scientific
oracle must be supplied by the selected causal method, separately from the
orchestration checks. Fault fixtures include a trigger cancelled before run
creation, a warning-producing step, late completion after an observer deadline,
a stale output digest, duplicate delivery, a failed diagnostic, a scientifically
valid refusal and a changed question version. A fixed direct-library workflow,
the permitted upstream scenario and the proposed adapter should receive the
same scientific task and information. No trial in this protocol has been run
as part of the reference decision.~\citep{exec25_dataiku_choice}

Scientific owners would approve the query, assumptions and acceptance rule;
workflow owners would maintain scenario-to-artifact identity; platform and
procurement owners would establish server rights, compatibility and support;
evaluators would control the fault and causal oracles; maintainers would
review version drift. These remain proposed responsibilities. An illustrative
USD 1,200 preparation cost, USD 1,800 for all attempts, USD 2,400 for scientific
review and USD 600 maintenance allocation total USD 6,000. Across 120 attempted
requests, 90 completions and 60 admissible outputs, the corresponding costs
are USD 50, USD $200/3$ and USD 100. These authored amounts establish accounting
semantics, not a quote or return on investment. The commercial decision requires
actual entitlements, measured complete costs and accepted causal outputs from
the selected supported deployment.~\citep{exec25_dataiku_choice}

chapters.title: Runtime uncertainty and institutional evidence

segments.text:
\chapter{Runtime uncertainty and institutional evidence}
The following treatments support the completed studies in the main argument.
They retain version-dependent uncertainty behavior, recovery restrictions
and the scope of institutional evidence. These facts qualify an operating
claim; they do not replace the economist's identification or value calculation.

\section{Evidence required for institutional adoption}
\label{exec17:signed-adoption}

The evaluation object must identify what was assessed. A proposed release
manifest binds the reader PDF and source audit; canonical schemas and operation
registry; runtime and adapter builds; dependency and protocol versions; the
consumer decoder; the scientific target and sampling law; the declared
platform; and the acceptance criteria. A change to any item starts an impact
review. Prior receipts may be carried forward only when their owner records
which claims remain applicable and why. A hash establishes byte identity, not
who signed those bytes, whether that person had authority, or whether the
scientific statement is true.

The exact authored gate table contains six assumed conditions: independent
scientific review; authorized bank data and truth; actual consumer acceptance;
target-platform acceptance; a matched economic case; and a sponsor decision.
There are $2^6=64$ Boolean combinations, but only the all-true combination is
eligible for scoped adoption under the stated conjunction. This is a logic
check on a proposed rule. It supplies zero authentic receipts, identifies no
signer, and performs no cryptographic verification. Institutional acceptance additionally requires identifiable responsible
owners and authentic evidence for scientific review, bank truth, platform,
consumers, workflow economics and the sponsor decision.~\citep{exec17_continuity_reference,exec17_continuity_contract}

Local preparation can still be complete enough to hand over. The package
should contain an exact-release manifest, a criterion-by-criterion evaluation
protocol, a custody-safe bank data manifest, the consumer and platform test
plans, a full-cost ledger, a conflicts statement, and a receipt schema with
review scope, owner role and organization, evidence identity, criteria,
unresolved findings, and assessed release. The intake script can verify
required fields and hashes. It explicitly cannot authenticate a signature,
establish legal access, validate bank truth, or decide scientific adequacy.
Those determinations belong to the authentic responsible owner and reviewer.
The existing external-input contract states this boundary directly.
\citep{exec17_continuity_contract}

The six-field release example changes the reader, core, adapter, consumer,
scientific context, or platform one at a time. Every change breaks exact
release equality and triggers impact review; it does not automatically erase
all prior evidence. A scoped owner may establish that an earlier test remains
applicable, but the evaluator must bind that judgment to the successor
release. Otherwise the stale receipt is not evidence for the changed system.
The proposal deliberately has no success branch that manufactures the missing
owner, signature, bank history, or institutional decision.
\citep{exec17_continuity_reference,exec17_continuity_contract}

A prototype comparison can test whether the same scientific context survives
library calls, command-line decoding, protocol transport and declared job or
storage failures. Its record needs full request, response, cost and refusal
denominators. Success under constructed failures supports a scoped consumer
and platform trial; it supplies no authentic bank truth or institutional
approval. The economic decision to fund that trial depends on its information
value and a meaningful precision requirement, as developed in
Chapter~\ref{rewrite:investment-decision}.
\label{exec17:integration-continuity-end}

\part{Public evidence and banking studies}
\label{reading:part-evidence}
Public observations expose real measurement problems; controlled
experiments reveal errors when the causal truth is known. Neither replaces
the other. The studies compare useful quantities, preserve adverse results,
and ask whether another measurement changes the decision more than another
method applied to the same records.
\hypertarget{pd15:evidence}{%

chapters.title:
Public evidence for a causal banking
proposal

segments.text:
\chapter{Public evidence for a causal banking
proposal}\label{pd15:evidence}}

A bank should invest in a causal-analysis service only when there is a
credible account of the decisions it could improve, the methods worth
assembling and the experiments worth funding. Public evidence can establish
technical promise and identify consequential uncertainties before a bank
pays to collect private assignment histories or commission a larger trial.
The proposed studies follow that investment sequence. This chapter distinguishes the evidence classes and the original survey's coverage; the next compares dataset families, and the following chapter maps them to a bounded study portfolio. Later completed studies are linked explicitly so that a historical acquisition decision is not mistaken for the current state of the scientific evidence.

Public data can provide much of the evidence for that first decision. It
can expose realistic variable definitions, missingness, reporting
clocks, financial magnitudes and computational workloads. Public
experiments can exercise estimation under a documented assignment
design. Semi-synthetic data can combine empirical covariates with
generated treatment assignments and potential outcomes, making error
measurable. Entirely synthetic histories can isolate feedback,
confounding, graph equivalence and observation errors. These sources
complement one another because no single source supplies realistic bank
operations, observed counterfactual truth and unrestricted reuse at
once.

Public studies can establish technical merit and identify a worthwhile
next experiment without estimating the effect of a policy in the adopting
bank. An effect measured in another population is not the bank's effect.
A negative comparison, an informative finding of nonidentification, or a
narrower useful capability can still improve the investment decision.

\hypertarget{what-constitutes-evidence}{%
\section{What constitutes evidence}\label{what-constitutes-evidence}}

Let \(S=1\) denote membership in a public study and \(S=0\) membership
in the future bank population. A public randomized study may identify

\[
\tau_1=\mathbb E[Y(1)-Y(0)\mid S=1].
\]

It does not by itself identify \(\tau_0\). One possible transport
argument would require comparable interventions and outcomes, sufficient
effect modifiers \(X\), overlap between populations, and stability of
the conditional causal response. Under those additional assumptions,

\[
\tau_0=\int\{m_1(x)-m_0(x)\}\,dP(x\mid S=0),
\qquad m_a(x)=\mathbb E[Y\mid A=a,X=x,S=1].
\]

The expression explains the later data requirement: a target population
distribution and a credible account of effect modification. It is not a
finding that these assumptions hold. A banking example makes the
distinction concrete. Learning how advertising holdouts support an
incremental-conversion estimate can validate treatment coding and an
estimator's workflow. It does not show the deposit value of a bank
telephone campaign, whose product, population, contact policy and
financial payoff differ.

Five evidence classes are kept distinct throughout this survey.

\begin{longtable}[]{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{\dimexpr 0.22\linewidth-2\tabcolsep\relax}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{\dimexpr 0.36\linewidth-2\tabcolsep\relax}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{\dimexpr 0.42\linewidth-2\tabcolsep\relax}@{}}
\toprule
\begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Evidence class\strut
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
What it can demonstrate\strut
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
What it cannot establish alone\strut
\end{minipage}\tabularnewline
\midrule
\endhead
\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Public financial observations\strut
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Data semantics, empirical associations, support, sensitivity, realistic
workflows and resource use\strut
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Random assignment, omitted-information absence or target-bank
effects\strut
\end{minipage}\tabularnewline
\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Public randomized or designed studies\strut
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Effects in the documented study population under its design; estimator
comparisons with appropriate uncertainty\strut
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Individual counterfactual labels, automatic transport or bank ROI\strut
\end{minipage}\tabularnewline
\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Semi-synthetic benchmarks\strut
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Error against generated truth on realistic covariates, with the
generator disclosed\strut
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Truth of the generated response model in a bank\strut
\end{minipage}\tabularnewline
\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Controlled synthetic histories\strut
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Failure mechanisms, refusal behavior, exact references and
repeated-sampling calibration in a specified law\strut
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Empirical prevalence of those mechanisms or authentic audit
accuracy\strut
\end{minipage}\tabularnewline
\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Public reasoning and linkage tasks\strut
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Logical consistency, handling ambiguity, provenance and observation
construction\strut
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Business ownership, real customer identities or live-model reliability
without actual evaluation\strut
\end{minipage}\tabularnewline
\bottomrule
\end{longtable}

For an observational file, a fitted model is not an assignment
mechanism. For a randomized experiment, the difference in sample means
is an estimate with uncertainty, not the true individual treatment
effect. For a semi-synthetic file, both potential outcomes may be
available, but they were generated. These distinctions determine which
metrics are meaningful: prediction accuracy for a repayment label,
interval coverage only when truth or a valid evaluation construction is
available, and effect identification only under explicit substantive
assumptions.

\hypertarget{survey-method-and-coverage}{%
\section{Survey method and coverage}\label{survey-method-and-coverage}}

The survey inspected 24 dataset families using custodian descriptions,
author-maintained benchmark documentation, data dictionaries and
selected loader/generator source. It covers funding and bank panels;
household finance and marketing; lending and mortgage histories;
experimental and semi-synthetic estimation; discovery; linkage; and
language-model reasoning. A source register preserves exact downloaded
bytes, SHA-256 identities, inspected passages, supported claims and
access limitations. Dataset documentation supports dataset descriptions;
this survey does not infer a scholarly result from a paper title or
repository abstract.

The publication cutoff is 7 October 2026. Eight benchmark documentation
files and the CFPB historical schema are pinned to repository commits at
or before that cutoff. Other web pages are acquisition snapshots from 12
October; their current text is not represented as an archived 7 October
page. Older survey and data releases described by those pages remain
candidates, but their exact selected files must be frozen before
analysis. The SCF page provides a concrete trap: some summary extracts
were updated on 9 October 2026, after the cutoff. Those extracts are
excluded from a cutoff-respecting study until a prior version is
recovered. The full 2022 dataset is described separately with an earlier
release date \citep{pd15_scf}.

This is a structured, bounded survey. It is strongest for US regulatory
and mortgage data, two commonly used non-US bank datasets, and public
methodological benchmarks. It is not an exhaustive international census.
China-specific supervisory and household panels, European credit
registers, financial inclusion and microcredit trial archives, and
detailed commercial panel providers need separate custodian and access
reviews. Their absence does not establish that no suitable public source
exists. No registration-gated mortgage account was created, no
commercial data agreement was accepted, and no linked external benchmark
code was executed during this survey.

\hypertarget{evidence-already-available}{%
\section{Evidence already available}\label{evidence-already-available}}

The repository already contains a reproducible public 401(k) analysis
and a quarterly monetary analysis, alongside its synthetic banking
studies. The 401(k) extract contains 9,915 households, eligibility,
participation, financial assets and nine declared controls. The existing
analysis distinguishes an eligibility average effect from a
participation instrumental-variable target and compares score algebra
with DoubleML under identical fitted inputs. The extract lacks
survey-design fields sufficient to establish design-valid covariance;
conditional exchangeability, instrument assumptions and bank transport
are unresolved. These are informative prototype limitations, not reasons
to discard the example \citep{public401k}.

The monetary example uses 203 quarterly observations from 1959Q1 through
2009Q3. It reproduces local-projection coefficients and Bartlett
covariance against a numerical reference, and makes the
information-clock ambiguity explicit. An aggregate money-stock response
to a Treasury-bill rate change is not a bank's deposit-offer effect. It
is nevertheless a useful public demonstration of time-series
conventions, dependence-aware computation and sensitivity to period and
control choices \citep{public_macrodata_dynamic}.

A new descriptive inspection downloaded the UCI Bank Marketing archive,
checked its four CSV files and preserved their identities. The two full
datasets contain 41,188 and 45,211 observations; their smaller files
contain 4,119 and 4,521. The 41,188-row version has 4,640 subscriptions
and 36,548 non-subscriptions. Its \texttt{default} field contains 8,597
\texttt{unknown} values and \texttt{education} contains 1,731.
Empty-cell counts alone would therefore conceal missing information. The
full and smaller versions overlap and must not be used as independent
replications \citep{pd15_uci_bank,pd15_profile}.

That inspection is a completed data-profile exercise. It is not a new
treatment-effect estimate, a fitted benchmark or a preregistered
experiment. It establishes that an openly licensed, modest-size
financial dataset is immediately usable for schema, timing and refusal
demonstrations. The subsequent public NSW analysis in Chapter~\ref{gap29:public} supplies a fitted experimental comparison under its stated selection and design premises. The panel, servicing and linkage studies in Chapters~\ref{gap29:funding}, \ref{gap29:servicing} and~\ref{gap29:observation} instead use generated laws. These additions extend the evidence without changing the original survey's acquisition record or supplying bank transport and audit truth.
\hypertarget{pd15:datasets}{%

chapters.title: Dataset choices and their causal roles

segments.text:
\chapter{Dataset choices and their causal roles}\label{pd15:datasets}}

A dataset is useful for the information it contributes to a decision, not simply because its rows concern finance. The comparisons proceed from funding panels and household records to servicing histories, experimental and generated benchmarks, then discovery, linkage and reasoning tasks. Each choice states a usable role and the information it cannot supply. The recommendations retain the survey's dated acquisition scope; links to subsequent studies distinguish fulfilled comparisons from remaining source and implementation work.

\hypertarget{funding-responses-and-bank-panels}{%
\section{Funding responses and bank
panels}\label{funding-responses-and-bank-panels}}

\textbf{1. FDIC Summary of Deposits.} The custodian describes an annual
survey of branch-office deposits as of 30 June. Institutions with
branches submit the survey; institutions with only a main office are
exempt from that reporting requirement. The natural observational unit
is a branch-year, nested within an institution and local market. This
makes the source attractive for deposit concentration, branch-network
histories and a proposed event-study workflow. Before estimation, the
chosen release must establish identifiers, ownership changes, deposit
units and coverage. A branch closure or merger is not automatically an
exogenous treatment: local demand, financial distress and strategic
selection can drive both the event and deposits. Annual June
observations cannot recover a daily customer offer response.
\textbf{Decision:} shortlist for a public panel prototype, with causal
event-study claims conditional on a separately justified design
\citep{pd15_fdic_sod}.

\textbf{2. FDIC Bank Data API financial and structural series.} The
inspected API specification exposes institution, financial,
historical-change and deposits routes. This gives an acquisition route
for an institution-time dataset and the structural history needed to
avoid treating a merger as organic growth. Financial fields and history
must be joined using a frozen field dictionary and defensible continuity
rules. First compare accounting identities, dates and missingness; then
examine a declared event or exposure. Bank and calendar dependence
belong in the uncertainty design. No bank-quarter dataset or causal
effect was downloaded or estimated in this survey. \textbf{Decision:}
pair with the deposits source after a bounded schema and vintage
inspection; do not pool institution, holding-company and branch units
without an explicit aggregation map \citep{pd15_fdic_api_spec}.

\textbf{3. Federal Reserve FR Y-9C.} The report collects consolidated
holding-company balance sheets, income statements and supporting
schedules quarterly. The official description says microdata are public
with exceptions. The unit is a consolidated holding company, which is
different from an insured bank or a branch. It can support funding
composition and institution-level stress examples when thresholds,
reporting changes and consolidations are accounted for. It is not a
customer-level dataset and does not supply the bank's internal pricing
decision. \textbf{Decision:} reserve as a second panel source; prefer
one coherent institution panel initially and add holding-company
aggregation only for a question that requires it \citep{pd15_y9c}.

\textbf{4. Federal Reserve H.8.} H.8 supplies estimated weekly aggregate
commercial-bank balance sheets and bank-group series, with downloadable
data routes. It is inexpensive context for system-wide deposits, credit
and common-calendar shocks. The aggregation is useful for a forecasting
or conditional-response example, but it removes customer and institution
assignment information. Group composition, revisions and seasonal
adjustments need attention. \textbf{Decision:} adopt as a contextual and
time-series workflow source; require a separately documented shock
design before attaching a structural causal interpretation
\citep{pd15_h8}.

\textbf{5. Archived macroeconomic extract.} The existing 203-quarter
dataset is already local and has an executed, bounded projection study.
Its advantages are a fixed historical snapshot, small resource
requirements and an existing independent numerical comparison. Its
limitations are age, aggregation and unresolved policy information.
\textbf{Decision:} reuse this baseline now; a newer series can be a
versioned extension, with release vintages and units preserved.
Replacing it merely because newer numbers exist would not supply an
identification argument \citep{public_macrodata_dynamic}.

\hypertarget{households-acquisition-and-credit-decisions}{%
\section{Households, acquisition and credit
decisions}\label{households-acquisition-and-credit-decisions}}

\textbf{6. SIPP-based 401(k) extract.} Eligibility, participation and
financial wealth yield a compact financial example with two distinct
estimands. The existing workflow can show adjustment-set declarations,
orthogonal scores, overlap diagnostics and why a participation effect
needs stronger assumptions than an eligibility contrast. Unknown survey
design and variable timing remain explicit. Employer selection and
saving preferences are plausible unmeasured confounders.
\textbf{Decision:} retain as the principal existing public
household-finance example; add sensitivity and target-definition tests
without relabeling observational assumptions as verified randomization
\citep{public401k}.

\textbf{7. Survey of Consumer Finances.} The 2022 public file is
described as 4,595 families represented by 22,975 rows across five
implicates. The Federal Reserve supplies separate replicate weights and
warns that ignoring both imputation and complex sampling yields
incorrect standard errors. This is valuable for wealth, debt,
balance-sheet heterogeneity and the product's treatment of uncertainty
across completed datasets. It is normally a triennial cross-section, not
a customer transaction panel. A credible exercise would reproduce a
published descriptive quantity with proper imputation and survey
variance before attempting an assumption-dependent causal example.
\textbf{Decision:} shortlist for observation construction and household
heterogeneity, selecting a documented pre-cutoff file; do not
concatenate implicates and count them as independent families
\citep{pd15_scf}.

\textbf{8. UCI Bank Marketing.} The data concern telephone campaigns at
a Portuguese bank and term-deposit subscription. The full additional
version has 20 inputs, 41,188 examples and a documented date ordering
from May 2008 to November 2010; the older full version has 45,211 rows.
The custodian states CC BY 4.0 terms. Contact duration is an especially
clear timing test: it is not available when deciding whether to place
the call. The files do not establish a random treatment policy, a
representative uncontacted group or an entity key sufficient for a
repeated-customer causal panel. ``The client subscribed'' is an outcome;
it is not itself an intervention. \textbf{Decision:} adopt immediately
for data profiling, business-question translation, leakage detection and
principled refusal. Reject a claimed incremental campaign effect from
this file alone \citep{pd15_uci_bank,pd15_profile}.

\textbf{9. UCI Default of Credit Card Clients.} This 30,000-row Taiwan
dataset has 23 predictors, including credit limits, payment status,
bills and payments over April--September 2005, followed by a default
label. The custodian states CC BY 4.0. The histories are useful for
checking feature clocks, censoring assumptions and the distinction
between a repayment and a bank action. A payment is partly a customer's
response, not an assigned servicing treatment. The file does not
disclose the complete sequence of contact, limit-change or relief
decisions and their logging probabilities. \textbf{Decision:} use as an
openly reusable credit-history and prediction baseline; use its
admissible covariates in a clearly labeled generated-action study if
desired. It cannot establish the causal effect of a collection policy
\citep{pd15_uci_credit}.

\textbf{10. Public HMDA application records.} The inspected CFPB
historical public schema includes lender identity, year, geography,
application action, loan amount, income and pricing fields. It supports
a lending-funnel example: application, denial, origination and
conditional loan terms are distinct objects. Conditioning a rate
analysis on origination changes the selected population. Public
disclosure transformations, missing fields and policy-specific coverage
require the selected year's dictionary. The current publication endpoint
returned HTTP 403; the accessible, cutoff-pinned historical schema is
evidence about that schema, not proof of the 2024 file's contents.
\textbf{Decision:} shortlist for application and selection analysis
after current-year access is resolved. Do not present it as a monthly
repayment panel or individual discrimination ground truth
\citep{pd15_hmda_schema}.

\hypertarget{loan-servicing-and-repeated-outcomes}{%
\section{Loan servicing and repeated
outcomes}\label{loan-servicing-and-repeated-outcomes}}

\textbf{11. Freddie Mac Single-Family Loan-Level Dataset.} The official
page describes origination and monthly performance data, including
prepayments and credit events, and directs users to register and sign
in. It also states that data are unaudited and subject to change. Free
noncommercial, academic/research and limited uses remain subject to
terms; commercial redistribution requires an agreement. Longitudinal
loan histories can demonstrate competing events, outcome horizons,
cohort splits and incomplete observations. Modification flags do not
supply the full decision state, all feasible offers or known action
probabilities. \textbf{Decision:} strong conditional candidate for
realistic servicing histories. Review the permitted use and a small
fixed cohort before committing resources; use an unrestricted synthetic
history route meanwhile \citep{pd15_freddie}.

\textbf{12. Fannie Mae Single-Family Loan Performance Data.} The
custodian describes selected fixed-rate loans with origination and
dynamic monthly performance, alongside a HARP mapping between original
and refinanced loans. Its stated population excludes several mortgage
categories, so it is not the entire mortgage market. Registration is
required; third-party redistribution and external commercial uses are
restricted without written consent. The HARP mapping is valuable for
discussing how an apparent loan termination may be a linked refinancing,
but it does not resolve endogenous refinancing selection.
\textbf{Decision:} alternative to Freddie Mac, not a mandatory second
acquisition. Select one source by access, variable coverage and cohort
quality; retain the other as a robustness extension only when it answers
a consequential question \citep{pd15_fannie}.

\textbf{13. NHEFS observational follow-up.} The inspected causallib
loader distinguishes a smoking-cessation/weight-change analysis and a
survival variant with follow-up and censoring. It explicitly records
optional exclusion of missing outcomes and uses cessation as the
exposure. This is an adjacent-domain teaching example for baseline
treatment, observation restrictions and survival semantics. It is not a
series of randomized bank servicing decisions. \textbf{Decision:} keep
as an optional inexpensive survival comparison after checking upstream
data terms and cohort construction. Use a generated sequential decision
process for time-varying treatment feedback rather than pretending this
baseline-exposure example supplies it \citep{pd15_nhefs_pinned}.

For a sequential policy, histories \(H_t\), actions \(A_t\), subsequent
states and censoring need a declared order. Identification by a
longitudinal g-formula requires consistency, positivity and sequential
exchangeability given the available history. Monthly rows satisfy none
of those assumptions merely by being longitudinal. An observed
modification may follow a private hardship assessment absent from the
release. Therefore the first servicing prototype should combine
realistic public outcome histories, where access permits, with generated
actions and outcomes whose causal law is fully declared. Its empirical
and generated components must remain separately labeled.

\hypertarget{experimental-panel-and-semi-synthetic-benchmarks}{%
\section{Experimental, panel and semi-synthetic
benchmarks}\label{experimental-panel-and-semi-synthetic-benchmarks}}

\textbf{14. NSW experimental job-training extract.} The
\texttt{causaldata} documentation describes \texttt{nsw\_mixtape} as a
445-row experimental extract with earnings and baseline covariates. A
small public earnings experiment is useful for effect-versus-prediction
semantics and a design-based baseline. Before claiming an identified
effect, recover the original assignment and sample-selection description
and bind the exact version. The original survey acquired a public teaching mirror without fitting a study. Chapter~\ref{gap29:public} subsequently uses the author's treated/control files and original selection argument for a fitted comparison, retaining their numerical difference from the mirror and the missing original assignment records.
\textbf{Decision:} preferred small experimental candidate, conditional
on those provenance and rights checks \citep{pd15_nsw_docs}.

\textbf{15. MatchIt LaLonde comparison sample.} The similarly named
\texttt{lalonde} file documented by MatchIt contains 614 observations:
185 treated observations from NSW and 429 PSID comparison observations.
It is not the all-randomized experimental comparison. This is a valuable
adverse example for an agent asked to ``load LaLonde and estimate the
RCT effect'': the response must disambiguate the dataset first.
\textbf{Decision:} retain as a selection-bias and dataset-identity
challenge, not the randomized baseline \citep{pd15_lalonde_pinned}.

\textbf{16. ACIC 2016.} The inspected author documentation specifies
4,802 empirical covariate rows and 58 covariates from the Collaborative
Perinatal Project. Its generator creates a treatment mechanism, response
surfaces and observations, and can return both potential outcomes,
conditional means and propensities. The package describes 77 settings
and 100 indexed seeds in its example; an evaluation must state the
chosen grid rather than quietly select easy settings. The code package
states GPL terms, but empirical input-data rights need their own review.
\textbf{Decision:} preferred standardized semi-synthetic estimation
benchmark. Freeze a modest scenario grid spanning overlap, nonlinearity
and heterogeneity, then compare a simple baseline and the proposed
method with identical inputs. Error against generated truth is
meaningful within that generator \citep{pd15_acic_pinned}.

\textbf{17. IHDP benchmark distributed with CEVAE.} The inspected
documentation explicitly says the benchmark contains generated treated
and control conditional means and factual/counterfactual outcomes. It
also warns that its legacy code is unmaintained. The name of an original
intervention study must not turn a generated benchmark into observed
counterfactual truth. \textbf{Decision:} secondary semi-synthetic
robustness option; prefer ACIC initially because adding a legacy
software stack contributes little to the first proposal. Read data in a
supported environment if this option is later used
\citep{pd15_cevae_pinned}.

\textbf{18. \texttt{did} county teen-employment panel.} The documented
\texttt{mpdta} example has 500 counties from 2003--2007, 2,500 rows and
a first treatment year associated with state minimum-wage changes. Its
\texttt{treat} indicator is ever-treated, not period-specific exposure.
This offers a compact staggered-adoption example and a concrete
treatment-clock test. Parallel trends, anticipation, state-level
assignment and limited assignment clusters need discussion; observed
adoption is not randomized. \textbf{Decision:} use as an adjacent-domain
panel adapter/reference example, with comparisons across appropriate
estimands. A future bank panel needs its own design \citep{pd15_mpdta}.

\textbf{19. Criteo uplift data.} The custodian describes advertising
incrementality tests in which a random subset is withheld from
targeting. Its page specifies 25 million users, 11 features, a treatment
indicator and visit/conversion labels. Feature projection and population
adjustments mean the original incrementality level cannot be recovered.
The displayed license is CC BY-NC-SA 4.0. \textbf{Decision:} useful
randomized large-data candidate, but deferred for this commercial
product proposal until permitted use is established. A free download is
not sufficient. A small generated randomized campaign with known
propensities can exercise the same interface without this dependency
\citep{pd15_criteo}.

\hypertarget{discovery-observation-construction-and-language-models}{%
\section{Discovery, observation construction and language
models}\label{discovery-observation-construction-and-language-models}}

\textbf{20. CausalBench perturbational gene-expression data.} The
documented benchmark offers observational, partially interventional and
fully interventional regimes on large biological datasets. It is
attractive because intervention labels allow evaluations that pure
observational graph recovery cannot supply. Nevertheless, perturbations
are biological operations, measured expression is an imperfect system
representation, and validation resources do not amount to a complete
known causal graph. Different auxiliary resources carry different
licenses, including a noncommercial component. \textbf{Decision:}
optional external-domain discovery challenge after a small declared
synthetic graph suite. Use held-out intervention prediction or
explicitly scoped reference metrics; do not call a learned biological
network banking graph truth \citep{pd15_causalbench_pinned}.

\textbf{21. FEBRL linkage datasets.} The inspected loader describes
synthetic identity records and returns known links reconstructed from
generator identities. FEBRL1 has 500 originals and 500 duplicates;
FEBRL4 has two tables of 5,000 records each with known correspondences.
These can test duplicate handling, blocking recall, false matches and
propagation of uncertain identity. Generator IDs that encode
correspondence must be hidden from matching features. A financial
outcome or transaction history added to these names is an additional
synthetic construction. \textbf{Decision:} preferred optional linkage
benchmark once data-specific terms are checked; existing
project-generated identities remain sufficient for an immediate
prototype. Neither establishes the error rate of a real bank audit
\citep{pd15_febrl_source}.

\textbf{22. PaySim.} The author description explains that mobile-money
transactions are generated by a simulator, initially from a service
schema and later using aggregate transaction information. Realistic
financial-looking records are still synthetic. This source is useful for
workload shape and event-stream concepts, but its fraud labels do not
identify the effect of a bank intervention. Code and linked dataset
terms need separate checks. \textbf{Decision:} optional engineering
fixture, deprioritized because the existing project simulator already
provides transparent decision and observation mechanisms
\citep{pd15_paysim_pinned}.

\textbf{23. CLadder.} The benchmark documentation describes 10,112
balanced generated causal questions, underlying model metadata and
variants with ordinary, counterintuitive and nonsense variable names.
Those variants help distinguish causal reasoning from memorized domain
associations. Public model metadata can support a logical reference; it
cannot be allowed into the evaluation prompt when it contains the
answer. \textbf{Decision:} shortlist for offline task design and later
bounded live evaluation after dataset terms and contamination controls
are fixed. Public benchmark performance is a diagnostic, not evidence
that the model owns the business assumptions
\citep{pd15_cladder_pinned}.

\textbf{24. Corr2Cause.} The documented generator builds graphs,
conditional-independence statements and verbalized causal-relation
questions; a three-class supplement distinguishes entailed,
underdetermined and contradicted claims within an equivalence class.
Variable renaming and paraphrases offer useful robustness contrasts.
\textbf{Decision:} pair selected tasks with CLadder and new controlled
banking briefs. Require the system to retain equivalent diagrams and
request missing identifying information instead of forcing a direction.
Source review is complete for these descriptions; no live-model scores
were produced \citep{pd15_corr2cause_pinned}.

The surveyed datasets cover concrete components of discovery, but none
establishes a universal ``business text to true causal graph'' route. A
useful graph prototype should return candidate structures, provenance
for asserted edges, explicit temporal restrictions and the consequences
of ambiguity for the requested intervention. On generated examples,
structural metrics can be scored against the generator. On empirical
observations, equivalence and uncertain measurement must survive into
the effect analysis.

The resulting portfolio favors one source per evidential role before adding scale. Existing household and macro examples support inexpensive scientific-interface comparisons; documented experiments support their own assignment contrasts; generated studies expose known failure mechanisms; and financial panels contribute measurement and continuity questions. Gated mortgage data, broader geographic coverage and uncertain reuse terms remain specific alternatives or omissions. None is needed merely to inflate the number of datasets, and none can replace a missing assignment or observation argument in another source.
\hypertarget{pd15:portfolio}{%

chapters.title:
A bounded public-data prototype
portfolio

segments.text:
\chapter{A bounded public-data prototype
portfolio}\label{pd15:portfolio}}

\hypertarget{selection-rather-than-accumulation}{%
\section{Selection rather than
accumulation}\label{selection-rather-than-accumulation}}

Acquiring every dataset would create cost without proportionate
evidence. The recommended portfolio has six study families, each tied to
a product decision. Documentation, assumptions, a runnable baseline and
an explicit failure result are more valuable than an impressive count of
downloaded files. A source that is registration-gated or unsuitable for
one estimand must not block another family. This is a portfolio design, not a claim that every listed acquisition or native trial has occurred. The public NSW analysis in Chapter~\ref{gap29:public} develops the experimental branch; Chapters~\ref{gap29:servicing} and~\ref{gap29:policy-uncertainty} develop generated sequential-policy comparisons; Chapter~\ref{gap29:observation} develops generated linkage uncertainty. The generated institution panel in Chapter~\ref{gap29:funding} tests continuity errors but is not the proposed FDIC acquisition. These completed studies supply evidence for the corresponding choices while their broader extensions retain the requirements below.

\begin{longtable}[]{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{\dimexpr 0.22\linewidth-2\tabcolsep\relax}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{\dimexpr 0.36\linewidth-2\tabcolsep\relax}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{\dimexpr 0.42\linewidth-2\tabcolsep\relax}@{}}
\toprule
\begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright

\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright

\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Comparison and useful output\strut
\end{minipage}\tabularnewline
\midrule
\endhead
\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}\raggedright
P1: financial formulation and timing\strut
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Existing 401(k); downloaded UCI Bank Marketing\strut
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}\raggedright

\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}\raggedright

\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}\raggedright

\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}\raggedright

\end{minipage}\tabularnewline
\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}\raggedright

CLadder/Corr2Cause tasks\strut
