P1 and existing P2 examples can proceed with local inputs. P3--P6 have
project-generated routes that do not depend on external accounts, paid
model APIs or bank records. Their results must be labeled synthetic
where appropriate. Using public covariates in a simulator improves
distributional realism but does not validate its action or response law.
A proposal can include a live-model evaluation design before paying for
it; a claimed live-model capability requires an actual identified
backend and held-out execution.

\hypertarget{p1-demonstrate-that-the-problem-is-correctly-formulated}{%
\section{P1: demonstrate that the problem is correctly
formulated}\label{p1-demonstrate-that-the-problem-is-correctly-formulated}}

The first study asks whether the prototype preserves the scientific
question as data move through it. For 401(k), write two briefs: the
effect of eligibility on assets and the effect of participation. The
reference specification distinguishes their assumptions and estimands.
For Bank Marketing, ask for pre-contact subscription prediction and the
incremental effect of making a call. The former can be a prediction
exercise with an explicit information cutoff. The latter requires the
system to identify absent assignment/control information and propose a
design.

The baseline is a reviewed template plus deterministic schema/timing
checks. The proposed assistant must output the population, unit, time
zero, feasible action, outcome horizon, available covariates, candidate
diagrams, adjustment or instrument assumptions, and missing evidence.
Score each field separately and record whether uncertainty is retained.
Do not score an invented graph as correct merely because it looks
economically plausible. A deliberately misleading brief that proposes
controlling for call duration should trigger a clock objection.

The completed archive profile provides an input fixture, not final task
performance. Freeze the briefs and reference alternatives before
evaluating a model or agent. Public benchmark text may be familiar to a
model; use disjoint graph templates and new names/numerical mechanisms
for the held-out portion. Record prompted assistance and reviewer
intervention in the denominator of workflow cost.

\hypertarget{p2-make-dependent-financial-computation-reviewable}{%
\section{P2: make dependent financial computation
reviewable}\label{p2-make-dependent-financial-computation-reviewable}}

Retain the existing macroeconomic result as an inherited baseline. For
an FDIC extension, first select a release window whose final included
publication predates the cutoff, a bounded set of institutions and a
documented event definition. Acquire field dictionaries, structure
changes and release information before fitting. Separate branch-level
deposits from consolidated bank financials. Entity continuity, mergers
and geography should be reproducible transformations rather than
unrecorded analyst choices.

The first result should reproduce descriptive totals and a declared
conditional panel association. A causal event study is an additional
design: define event time, comparison units, anticipation, interference,
common shocks and the identifying assumption. A conventional two-way
fixed-effect coefficient and a group-time effect can target different
weighted objects under staggered adoption; matching only the formula
name is insufficient. Include a falsification or negative-control design
where justified, but do not interpret a nonsignificant pretrend as proof
of parallel trends.

Evaluate numerical parity, retained sample/unit counts, missingness,
memory, elapsed time and recovery from an interrupted local job. These
metrics support engineering feasibility. Bank service levels and network
recovery remain future target-platform questions. The local workload
must preserve the complete calculation, including reconstruction and
uncertainty, rather than reporting only a fast inner reducer.

\hypertarget{p3-check-effect-estimators-against-the-right-reference}{%
\section{P3: check effect estimators against the right
reference}\label{p3-check-effect-estimators-against-the-right-reference}}

Begin with a generated randomized experiment that has a declared
assignment probability and known response law. Compare a difference in
means, a prespecified regression adjustment and the proposed score
estimator. Under unequal assignment, a naive mean contrast can remain
interpretable under the actual design, while precision comparisons must
account for the allocation. In observational semi-synthetic cases,
require the declared adjustment information and vary overlap, response
nonlinearity and heterogeneity.

For ACIC, preserve real covariates and simulated quantities as separate
objects. Report ATE error, heterogeneity error when conditional truth is
supplied, interval availability, width, repeated-sampling coverage,
overlap and runtime. Never tune on evaluation potential outcomes. Use
the same scenarios, training information and splits for each method, and
retain failures as outcomes. The completed NSW comparison in Chapter~\ref{gap29:public} reports uncertainty and preserves its exact extract identity. Its estimate is not a noiseless label for another method. An ACIC extension still needs its separately selected scenarios and input-rights review.

Select scenarios and replication counts prospectively from the precision
needed to distinguish meaningful failure. For example, at nominal
coverage 0.95, 400 independent repetitions give a Monte Carlo standard
error near 0.011; that is a planning calculation, not proof that
observed 94\% coverage is acceptable. A simultaneous acceptance rule
across the selected scenarios must be specified before final runs.
Current open calibration findings are not erased by switching to a
public benchmark with unknown truth.

\hypertarget{p4-distinguish-realism-from-sequential-identification}{%
\section{P4: distinguish realism from sequential
identification}\label{p4-distinguish-realism-from-sequential-identification}}

A servicing prototype should represent a fixed policy and a policy
learned on independent training histories. At each decision time,
disclose the available state, chosen action, action propensity,
subsequent outcome and censoring. Include an adverse case with a private
hardship variable that affects both actions and repayment, and a case
with weak support for the proposed policy. A useful result may be a
refusal, a broad identified set or a warning that an off-policy value
cannot be estimated reliably.

Real mortgage histories, if lawfully acquired, improve the realism of
delinquency and termination clocks. They should initially support
descriptive transitions and competing-event handling. If actions are
then generated conditional on recorded histories, label the resulting
policy comparison semi-synthetic; if future outcomes are also generated,
disclose that response law. Policy value under that law is a simulation
result. The proposed bank experiment is justified only when an
unresolved assumption about genuine actions or response materially
changes the policy recommendation.

\hypertarget{p5-carry-ambiguity-through-graph-and-identity-operations}{%
\section{P5: carry ambiguity through graph and identity
operations}\label{p5-carry-ambiguity-through-graph-and-identity-operations}}

For discovery, use small graphs where observational equivalence classes
can be enumerated. The baseline returns the entire compatible class; a
discovery method or language model must not receive credit for an
unjustified single orientation. Evaluate orientation precision,
valid-class retention and the resulting intervention-effect set,
including empty, disconnected or unbounded answers when they are
mathematically appropriate. Add interventional information in a separate
condition to test whether it resolves the intended ambiguity.

For observation construction, start from known entity histories and then
corrupt identifiers, timestamps or links. Keep the hidden generator
mapping outside the analysis interface. Compare exact-oracle, hard-match
and uncertainty-aware routes. Report missed candidate pairs, false
matches and the change in a downstream financial target. High pairwise
matching accuracy does not guarantee a small monetary bias when the rare
high-value records are the ones mismatched. FEBRL can add a public
fixture; it cannot supply the error distribution of the future bank's
audit process.

\hypertarget{p6-evaluate-the-assistant-as-part-of-a-workflow}{%
\section{P6: evaluate the assistant as part of a
workflow}\label{p6-evaluate-the-assistant-as-part-of-a-workflow}}

Use public data and controlled problems for the sequence from business
brief to diagram, identification query, tool execution and explanation.
The baseline should be a competent low-cost workflow: a reviewed form, a
deterministic graph/identification solver where applicable, and the
selected statistical package. The proposed agent should be evaluated for
improvements over that workflow, including errors it introduces and time
spent correcting them.

Measure invalid assumptions, clock violations, unsupported orientations,
identification mistakes, tool/schema failures, hallucinated results,
uncertainty fidelity, successful abstention and end-to-end completion.
Record calls, tokens, elapsed time and human review effort only when
they are actually measured. Live backend identity, version, budget and
custody are necessary for a live performance claim; they are not
prerequisites for the literature survey, offline fixtures, architecture
proposal or protocol. If a live evaluation is unaffordable, narrow the
claim and retain a costed protocol rather than fabricating results.

\hypertarget{common-study-controls}{%
\section{Common study controls}\label{common-study-controls}}

Each new final study needs a prospectively frozen question, input
hashes, methods, splits, scenarios, estimands, assignment/observation
assumptions, numerical tolerances, resource limit and stopping rule.
Exploratory profiles such as the UCI row inspection remain exploratory
and may inform that registration. Existing fitted results cannot be
relabeled fresh evaluation data. A source-access failure blocks only the
affected dataset branch.

An initial resource envelope should be modest: local public files, one
selected data source per role, no paid API by default, bounded CPU jobs
and recorded memory/time. Exact limits should be set after an
input-profile pilot, before final outcomes are examined. The plan does
not attach invented calendar dates or currency costs to unmeasured work.
A baseline that performs as well as the proposed component is evidence
to reuse the baseline, simplify the design or reject that component.

The investment sequence therefore purchases information in stages. Start with the smallest study that can expose a consequential error or establish a useful restricted capability; retain its adverse outcomes; then identify what a new source, method or bank experiment would resolve. The following banking studies put those comparisons into mathematical and numerical detail. Their exact constructions, fitted experiments and local implementations must keep their distinct claims when they inform the common product decision.

chapters.title: What the banking studies establish

segments.text:
\chapter{What the banking studies establish}
\label{r3:banking-studies}

The preceding design becomes concrete when the same analysis is followed
from its intervention to its financial account. This chapter uses published
banking designs to explain which information is useful, and reproducible
synthetic studies to test selected estimators and interfaces. The simulated
populations and cash schedules are deliberately specified. None is data
from JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America, HSBC or another institution. The sequence moves from published identifying designs to deposit cash flows, sequential and hidden-state policies, lending comparisons and joint response uncertainty. Computational studies then separate complete workloads from small components, before the public household and monetary analyses show what remains unresolved when causal truth is unknown.

\section{What banking evidence can transfer}
\label{r3:banking-evidence}

Published estimates arrive with an institutional design and population.
In \citet[printed pp.2--4]{drechsler2017}, the deposits-channel argument
uses within-bank branch comparisons across local market concentrations.
Bank-specific lending opportunities are controlled through the comparison;
the interpretation relies on a bank being able to transfer funding across
its branches. The subsequent lending analysis compares banks within a
county and uses their deposit-market exposure. Those are different
aggregation levels and identifying comparisons. The design supports a
mechanism linking market power, deposit pricing and transmission, not
an effect for any new household retention offer.

Relationship banking adds endogenous selection. The mover design in
\citet[Section 4.2.1, equations (6)--(8)]{basten2026} instruments an
existing deposit relationship with the bank's market share in the
household's former municipality, while controlling current share in
the new location. It investigates stickiness and persistent preferences.
The exclusion that prior market availability affects later borrowing
through the relationship remains substantive; the mover population
also limits transfer. This is a useful banking connection to
Chapter~\ref{r3:instruments}, not a universally valid instrument recipe.

For credit supply, the preserved 2006 version of
\citet[Section III.B, equation (5)]{mian2006} compares lenders to the same
firm after differencing. Firm effects remove common borrower-demand
shocks. The paper explicitly discusses the multiple-bank population,
anticipated adjustments and bank-specific demand components that might
remain correlated with funding shocks. A same-borrower comparison is
therefore much stronger than a pooled lending regression, while still
requiring a defensible residual supply variation.

The HARP design of \citet[printed pp.2--3]{agarwal2020} compares program
exposure for similar agency and non-agency high-LTV mortgages. It
distinguishes selected refinancing outcomes from program-level
differences including take-up. The product lesson is to retain eligibility,
assignment, application, acceptance and closing separately, and evaluate
the original eligible population. A borrower cash-flow gain is not
automatically a gain to the bank that owns or services the old mortgage.

Finally, \citet[printed pp.112--113]{beraja2019} explains why regional
refinancing differences do not identify common aggregate responses:
those responses were differenced out. Its model adds collateral and
lender-income channels. \citet[pp.5--6]{benetton2021} combines
discrete-continuous mortgage demand with multiproduct lender pricing,
using capital requirements as cost shifters under additional exclusions.
These sources motivate a structural extension interface when the bank
asks about competitor responses or market-wide regulation. A local
causal estimate may discipline that model but does not determine its
entire equilibrium counterfactual.

\section{A deposit rollout with a complete contribution account}
\label{r3:deposit-study}

The first synthetic study has 96 branches and 30 months indexed from zero.
Twenty-four branches adopt in each of months $12,18,24$, and 24 never
adopt. In USD millions, untreated balances are
\[
 B_{it}(0)=30+\alpha_i+.07t+.4\sin(t/3)+\epsilon_{it},
 \qquad \alpha_i\sim N(0,3^2),
\]
with independent branch disturbances
$\epsilon_{it}=.65\epsilon_{i,t-1}+\eta_{it}$,
$\eta_{it}\sim N(0,.28^2)$. The first disturbance is drawn at the
innovation scale. Cohort labels are independent of these disturbances.
For adoption cohort $g$ and event month $k=t-g\ge0$, the stipulated
balance effect is
\[
 \tau_{gk}=\{.85+.025(g-12)\}(1+.14k).
\]
Untreated parallel trends hold by construction, while treatment effects
differ across cohorts and grow with exposure.

The estimator compares each treated cohort's change from $g-1$ with
the same change in never-treated branches, then averages all treated
cohort-month cells equally. Since cohort sizes are equal, this target
also equally weights treated branch-months. Earlier cohorts receive
more total weight because they contribute more treated months.
The challenger is a single treatment-indicator regression with branch
and calendar effects. Chapter~\ref{r3:panels} explains why its
heterogeneity weights need not equal the requested aggregation.

The financial account uses an annual funding margin $m=.025$, promotional
rate increment $r=.0025$, and monthly program cost $c=1800$ dollars
per treated branch. Let balances now be in dollars. Then
\[
 C(1)=\frac{m-r}{12}B(1)-c,\qquad C(0)=\frac m{12}B(0),
\]
so
\begin{equation}
 \Delta C=\frac{m-r}{12}\Delta B-\frac r{12}B(0)-c.
 \label{r3:deposit-account}
\end{equation}
The second term pays the higher rate on funds that would have remained.
At a USD\,30 million baseline, the additional balance needed to break
even is $(rB(0)+12c)/(m-r)=\$4.293$ million. Counting only the return
on new balances would omit a material cost.

the simple simulation does not model that displacement.

\section{Collections: cumulative histories and policy contrasts}
\label{r3:collections-study}

The collections model has three observed states: current, moderate
arrears and severe arrears. An assistance action is unavailable in the
current state. For no assistance and assistance, respectively, the
row-stochastic transition matrices are
\[
 P_0=\begin{pmatrix}.88&.10&.02\\.30&.50&.20\\.08&.22&.70\end{pmatrix},
 \qquad
 P_1=\begin{pmatrix}.88&.10&.02\\.50&.40&.10\\.18&.42&.40\end{pmatrix}.
\]
The initial state distribution is $(.6,.3,.1)$, and historical assistance
probabilities are $(0,.35,.60)$. Reward after transition is
$(20,-10,-160)$ dollars according to the next state, less $12$ for
assistance; terminal values are $(0,0,-100)$. The horizon is eight
decisions and the discount is $.99$. The unused action-one transition
in the current state is not empirically identified; no evaluated policy
uses it.

Fit transition rows using 3,000 training trajectories and evaluate
three fixed policies on 8,000 independent trajectories. The estimator
uses half-count smoothing on supported transition cells. The policies
give no extra assistance, assist only severe arrears, or assist every
eligible state. Backward dynamic programming computes the reference
values from the generating kernels, which are unavailable to fitting.

\section{Hidden states: fit the logger before evaluating its replacement}
\label{r3:latent-study}

A separate experiment has two hidden states and three observed signal
categories. The initial hidden distribution is $(.72,.28)$, with
transitions and emission probabilities
\[
 T_0=\begin{pmatrix}.93&.07\\.22&.78\end{pmatrix},\quad
 T_1=\begin{pmatrix}.94&.06\\.52&.48\end{pmatrix},\quad
 B=\begin{pmatrix}.78&.18&.04\\.16&.34&.50\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Actions either have constant probability $.4$, or private-state
probabilities $(.15,.80)$. Fitting receives only signals and actions
from 800 trajectories with 12 transitions. Four-start EM estimates
initial, transition and emission probabilities; the joint model also
estimates private logging probabilities. State labels are ordered by
their mean signal for reporting.

Compare a fixed reactive policy acting only on signal category 2 with
never acting. Its eight-decision reward is next-signal payoff
$(18,0,-90)$ less an $8$-dollar action cost, with discount $.99$.
The generating-model gain is $22.34$.

\section{Matched lending and shared macro shocks}
\label{r3:credit-dependence-study}

The credit-supply example has 600 firms, 24 banks and three distinct
lenders per firm. Draw bank shock $Z_b$ and firm demand $U_f$
independently, then choose relationships with probabilities proportional
to $\exp(.65U_fZ_b)$. Generated loan growth is
\[
 \Delta L_{fb}=2-3Z_b+4U_f+\eta_b+\epsilon_{fb},
 \quad \operatorname{sd}(\eta_b)=.45,\quad
 \operatorname{sd}(\epsilon_{fb})=1.5.
\]
Selection makes observed lender shocks correlate with firm demand.
Within-firm demeaning removes the common $4U_f$ term. The pooled
coefficient is $-1.080$, while the within-firm coefficient is $-2.923$
against a generating coefficient of $-3$. The illustrative bank-cluster
$t_{23}$ interval is $[-3.027,-2.819]$. This single simulation does
not establish network or few-cluster inference; it isolates the
identifying comparison. A single bank would need outside-lender data
to implement it faithfully.

For dependence alone, generate
$X_{it}=a_i+b_t+\epsilon_{it}$ with independent standard-normal
components, 96 entities and 36 dates. The standard error of the
grand mean is exactly
\[
 \sqrt{1/96+1/36+1/(96\cdot36)}=.19617.
\]
Across 1,200 replications, nominal 95\% interval coverage is about
$.227$ treating rows as independent, $.693$ clustering only by entity,
and $.944$ with entity/date inclusion--exclusion. The last Monte Carlo
standard error is $.0066$. The simulation's negative-variance
truncation rule was never activated; the reusable component instead
returns an explicit flag for indefinite covariance.

The structural-series example uses
$F=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}.7&0\\.15&.6\end{smallmatrix}\right)$
and reduced innovation covariance
$\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&.8\\.8&1\end{smallmatrix}\right)$.
Two recursive orderings have the same reduced law but normalized
funding-shock impacts $(1,.8)'$ and $(1,0)'$. Their lending responses
differ. The observational fit cannot determine which timing restriction
is economically appropriate. This complements the larger-sample
variance comparison: more accurate uncertainty about an observed law
does not eliminate structural ambiguity.

\section{Joint response inference, persistence and learned adjustment}
\label{s4:response-results}
The response experiments instantiate Section~\ref{s4:response-construction}
with two banking outcomes, 13 horizons from zero through twelve, and a
common set of origins. Each row of Table~\ref{s4:response-coverage} contains
500 independent replications. Whole-curve coverage requires all 26 true
coordinates to lie in their reported sets. Applying 95\% pointwise intervals
to every plotted horizon is therefore deliberately an adverse comparison.
Zero numerical failures occurred; failed replications, had they occurred,
would remain in the denominator.

\begin{table}[htbp]\centering\small

\caption{Whole-curve coverage of nominal 95\% procedures. ``Joint'' uses
Bonferroni; ``max'' uses the estimated Gaussian maximum; ``IV set'' inverts
the joint residual tests. Standard Monte Carlo errors near .95 are about
.010. These are synthetic experiments, not coverage guarantees.}
\label{s4:response-coverage}
\end{table}

Strong instruments have innovation loading one; the weak case has loading
$.06$. The reference system has spectral radius $.81$; the near-unit case
uses $.985$. Persistent instrument noise has AR coefficient $.85$, rising
to $.95$ in the near-unit case. Most experiments use 800 origins; the long
persistent case uses 5,000. The invalid instrument additionally loads on
another structural innovation by $.6$. The initial stationary law and
all generating matrices are fixed in the reproducible specification.

Several method decisions follow. Joint covariance matters because a
pointwise interval is not a curve guarantee. Yet a consistent HAC estimator
can still underestimate finite-sample uncertainty: the Gaussian-maximum
band covers only .886 and .876 in the two persistent strong-instrument
experiments, and .724 near the unit boundary. Bonferroni is more conservative,
but its .818 near-unit coverage also fails the preset adequacy threshold.
These failures prohibit presenting the default bandwidth as automatically
calibrated for persistent bank series. The statistical result remains
asymptotic under a fixed stability margin, not uniform near a unit root.

The proxy VAR has much smaller mean squared error in the correctly
specified finite-order generating law. That advantage is a consequence of
its propagation restriction. It does not establish that an economist should
replace direct moments when finite-order dynamics are misspecified. Weak
normalization makes the direct and proxy mean squared errors about 752
and 13.5; 96.4\% of runs yield an unbounded residual-test set in at least
one coordinate. A narrow decision recommendation would conceal the
information deficiency. Instrument invalidity defeats both routes, including
zero proxy-VAR coverage in this example.

A separately specified follow-up, with a new random seed, compares bandwidth
$L=\lfloor n^{1/4}\rfloor$ and $4L$ at 5,000 origins. Their whole-curve
coverages are .948 and .968, with mean widths .312 and .338. This new
experiment does not replace the original .926 finding or establish that
$4L$ is universally preferable. The selected workflow reports sensitivity
to the lag window, compares the structural challenger when justified and
withholds a calibrated finite-sample claim in regimes that fail the stated
qualification. Picking the more favorable seed or interval after observing
the answer would be a different, unqualified procedure.

The integrated experiment has one common random-walk trend and two stationary
spreads. Mapping stationary-change IV estimates to cumulative level responses
gives whole-curve coverage .966 and mean squared error .0479. Treating the
levels as stationary gives .586 coverage and error 55.66. Cointegration is
substantive here: it defines which components are stationary and which
intervention response is being summed. The comparison does not certify
unknown rank selection or arbitrary local-to-unit triangular arrays.

With 4,000 dates and 80 bounded controls, separated-block sparse IV gives
.942 coverage of the scalar effect $1.2$, compared with .950 for oracle
nuisances. A three-factor reduction and an unadjusted estimator both have
zero coverage, with mean squared errors about .058 versus .00102 for
sparse adjustment. The causal confounder is sparse in this generator and
need not align with its leading covariance components. Factor compression
requires an information-preservation argument, not only a prediction score.
The fixed penalty multiplier in this experiment establishes feasibility;
the required population nuisance rates remain assumptions to justify in
each application.

For a fixed 96-bank panel, the additional mean-score experiment separates
common and bank-specific Gaussian AR components. At 800 dates, row-iid
intervals cover in .116 of runs; date-aggregate HAC covers in .856; an
oracle using the exact finite-sample Gaussian variance covers in .938.
At 2,000 dates the corresponding values are .104, .890 and .946.
Correctly recognizing the date as the information unit removes a gross
variance error, but the short Bartlett lag window still underestimates
persistent uncertainty. More customer rows do not repair either problem.

\section{The implemented data and score components}
\label{r3:component-evidence}

Two small local components implement selected parts of
Chapter~\ref{r3:construction}. The temporal component constructs
Equation~\eqref{r3:revision-feature} under its declared inclusive
availability convention. In an adversarial fixture, the correct
early and later amounts are $160$ and $90$. Using the latest
retrospective values gives $90$ at the early decision; filtering
economic time before choosing the revision gives $110$ at the later
decision. Delayed data, voids and a moved economic date explain the
differences.

The component rejects duplicate event revisions, incompatible currencies,
unqualified feed completeness and naive timestamps. Reconstruction review
also added explicit rejection of empty or non-string event/decision
identities. Without it, a missing decision entity could return a
misleading zero. This is a per-decision semantic reference, not a
bank-scale temporal query engine.

The score reducer retains raw sums/counts for entities, dates and their
intersections, centers globally and computes the stated crossed
covariance. Independent batch calculations agree to numerical precision
for both unique and repeated entity/date cells. Partition merges preserve
the result. Invalid multidimensional cluster keys now fail before
changing accumulator state. The caller still owns the target weighting,
Jacobian, training split and dependence argument; duplicate-task
protection remains part of the proposed execution layer.

The synthetic and component evidence so far establishes several useful construction tests:
incorrect cash accounts can reverse a business conclusion, current-only
weights can answer the wrong dynamic question, omitted private logging

The additional constructions above qualify local study recipes and selected
package operations. Complete product workspaces, institutional validation
and accepted sibling adoption remain distinct engineering and review tasks.

\section{A public household-finance analysis with unknown causal truth}
\label{s5:public-finance}
Public data expose choices that a known-truth simulation cannot. The archived
401(k) application extract contains 9,915 observations from the SIPP 1991
design used in the DML literature \citep[Section 6.2]{dml2018,public401k}.
The outcome is net financial assets; eligibility and participation are
separate binary variables. The declared controls are age, income, education,
family size, marriage, two-earner status, defined-benefit pension status,
IRA participation and home ownership. All required fields are observed in
the retrieved extract, so no row is removed by the declared missingness rule.
The dollar values are those in the archive, without an inflation conversion.

The first question is the average effect of eligibility on assets under
conditional exchangeability given these controls. This is an identifying
assumption about employer/program selection and saving behavior, not a
consequence of fitting a flexible model. The second question is participation's
complier effect with eligibility as an instrument. It adds exclusion,
instrument independence and monotonicity. The ratio of the adjusted
eligibility effect on assets to its adjusted effect on participation yields
that target under those restrictions. Ordinary participation regression
would answer neither question without a different selection argument.
The graph and observation choices must also establish which controls are
appropriate pre-exposure covariates; the cross-sectional extract alone cannot
verify their timing or rule out unmeasured saving preference.

Two nuisance families are compared: standardized quadratic features with
ridge outcome regression and logistic propensity regression, and histogram
gradient boosting for both roles. Three folds and seeds 7101--7103 are fixed
in advance. The original paper's 100-split aggregation and learner collection
are not replicated numerically; this reproduces the design and score with
declared alternative learners. The matched DoubleML check isolates score
agreement from those learner differences.

not supply survey weights, strata or primary sampling units. Consequently
these intervals are a reproducible working analysis, not a design-valid
survey inference claim. Alternative control timing, employer selection,
survey design and weak support require sensitivity or additional data.
The result does not transfer automatically to a bank offer, a different
country or current wealth. The useful product behavior is to preserve the
eligibility/participation target distinction, identical matched-reference
inputs, overlap diagnostics, empirical uncertainty and unverified design
assumptions through the final result.

\section{Public monetary histories and the boundary of an empirical claim}
\label{s6:public-dynamic}
The archived statsmodels macroeconomic extract contains 203 quarterly
observations from 1959Q1 through 2009Q3, assembled from FRED and labor
statistics with source access dated 15 December 2009
\citep{public_macrodata_dynamic}. It includes an end-quarter M1 stock,
a quarterly average of monthly three-month Treasury-bill rates, output
and inflation. Its data, source notes and exact numerical implementation
are preserved. This is a real dynamic financial-data analysis with a known
historical snapshot; it is not a current bank deposit-offer dataset.

The fixed projection response is
$100(\log M1_{t+h}-\log M1_{t-1})$ per percentage-point change in
the quarterly-average bill rate. Two lags each of the rate change, money
growth, output growth and inflation enter every regression. Four
specifications are fixed before fitting: these lagged controls; adding
current output growth and inflation; a pre-1984 origin window; and a
post-1984 origin window. Horizons zero through four use common origins
within each specification. Bartlett lag four covariance is computed from
the complete OLS influence, including controls. An independent statsmodels
OLS/HAC call agrees in coefficient and covariance to below $3\times10^{-14}$.

At horizon four, the full-sample lag-control estimate is $-2.102$
percentage points of cumulative money growth, standard error .452.
Adding current output/inflation gives $-2.163$ (.453). The pre-1984
estimate is $-.997$ (.262), while the later window gives $-4.329$ (.685).
There are 196 common full-sample origins and 97/99 in the two windows.
The different windows define different projection populations; selecting
one after observing its significance would add a selection problem. Their
contrast is a registered sensitivity analysis, not proof of a known break
date or a homogeneous policy effect.

These numbers do not identify a bank's price intervention. A quarterly
average rate and end-quarter stock do not supply a within-quarter decision
clock; central-bank information and money demand can confound the
innovation; M1 is not one bank's retained deposits; structural and
measurement regimes can change over fifty years. Current output controls
may be post-policy variables under one causal ordering and predecision
information under another. The data alone cannot settle that ordering.
The inference reported is conditional projection uncertainty, not uncertainty
over all these causal interpretations.

The public-data investigation also inspects the Federal Reserve H.8
description \citep{fed_h8_dynamic}. Its aggregate bank balance-sheet
statistics are useful for surveillance, but do not reveal customer offers,
the private assignment information, first-available entity-linked histories
and representative audited matches required by the treasury brief. Neither
that feed nor the archived macro series identifies the stipulated bank
experiment. Obtaining a current bank-specific price/offer history and its
assignment evidence is therefore a genuine empirical requirement, rather
than an excuse to call any public time series causal.

The central known-truth evidence uses the realistic but explicitly synthetic
funding mechanism, common shocks and revision/linkage construction. At 360
and 1,440 dates, 400 repetitions give financial interval coverage .945 and
.9375; pretending the branches supply independent calendar information
gives .230 and .2175. The corresponding joint Bonferroni response coverage
is .9425 and .965. Binomial Monte Carlo error is approximately one percentage
point for coverage near .95 at 400 repetitions; these differences do not
certify exact nominal calibration. The pair-linkage and audited-servicing
experiments add separate observation and information failures. Taken
together, the public analysis challenges economic interpretation, while
the synthetic analysis checks statistical behavior when its assumptions
are known. Neither estimates a named banking group's causal benefit.

These studies favor different remedies for different failures. Correcting the repricing account changes the economic target; retaining cumulative policy weights changes the dynamic comparison; fitting the private action law changes the observed likelihood; and preserving shared calendars changes uncertainty. Public estimates add sensitivity to interpretation and population, while generated laws expose errors against known truth. The next chapter develops those reliability questions when customer identity, audits, calendars and fitted models are uncertain together.

chapters.title: Reliability when identities, calendars and models are uncertain

segments.text:
\chapter{Reliability when identities, calendars and models are uncertain}
\label{r8:reliability}

A deposit intervention can affect many customers on the same date, while one
customer's uncertain identity persists across dates. These are two different
sources of repeated information. Auditing the same identity every month does
not produce independent identity evidence, and adding customers on one calendar
does not remove uncertainty about a common funding shock. The scientific
question is therefore not simply whether a database has enough rows. It is
which independent dimensions inform the intervention target, what information
the audits buy, and whether the resulting interval is precise enough to support
the decision. This chapter develops selected extensions with those distinctions
intact. Its new arguments are project derivations; its known-truth examples are
synthetic. They do not establish a generally validated bank product. The argument first separates persistent pair information from calendar information and independent gold labels, then asks what audit spending can improve. Funding calibration, finite graph restrictions, nonlinear state models and richer learners test different ways to gain information or reduce error. Their comparison keeps the scientific law, numerical implementation and decision-useful precision separate.

\section{Persistent identity audits on a shared calendar}
\label{r8:joint}

Consider $N$ independently sampled persistent customer pairs observed on $T$
common dates. Let $A_{it}\in\{-1,1\}$ be a randomized signed action, with two
candidate outcomes $Y_{i0t},Y_{i1t}$. Randomization, the outcome model and the
fixed outcome units identify a response moment $U_{it}=A_{it}Y_{i,\mathrm{focal},t}$.
This identification premise is separate from the identity-audit calculation.
For example, if $Y=(\theta_i+C_t)A+e$ with $E[Ae]=0$, the moment averages the
customer response and common shock; multiplying it by a declared monetary
scale gives currency per signed action. An observational bank action cannot
inherit this interpretation merely by satisfying the input shape.

Write $V_{ikt}=A_{it}Y_{ikt}$ and $H_{it}=(V_{i0t}+V_{i1t})/2$.
A persistent audit $R_i$ has known conditional inclusion probability $q_i$,
bounded below by a positive constant. The accurate binary identity $M_i=1$
selects candidate zero. If $U_{it}$ is revealed by the audit, the augmented
moment is
\begin{equation}
 Z_{it}=H_{it}+\frac{R_i}{q_i}(U_{it}-H_{it}),\qquad
 E_R[Z_{it}\mid\text{complete pair history}]=U_{it}.
 \label{r8:audit-moment}
\end{equation}
The expectation follows by substituting $E_RR_i=q_i$. The full history shares
one audit indicator. Summing this identity over dates does not change the audit
sampling unit. In particular, correctness counts alone can be singular when
each alias is correct half the time, while actual audited outcomes can still
identify the response. The new information changes the experiment.

Suppose the observed audit label $L_i$ is an independently flipped version of
$M_i$, with symmetric error probability $\epsilon<1/2$. The corrected moment is
\begin{equation}
 U^*_{it}(\epsilon)=H_{it}
  +\frac{(2L_i-1)(V_{i0t}-V_{i1t})}{2(1-2\epsilon)}.
 \label{r8:label-correction}
\end{equation}
Conditional expectation over the flip replaces $2L_i-1$ by
$(1-2\epsilon)(2M_i-1)$, recovering the correctly selected moment. Substitute
$U^*$ into \eqref{r8:audit-moment}. This argument needs the flip law conditional
on the pair history and audit design, not just an average error frequency.
Selected or asymmetric errors can violate it. A shape validator cannot discover
such a scientific violation from supplied histories.

\subsection{A selected joint limit, rather than an arbitrary cluster rule}

Let the corrected score have the representation
$Z_{it}=h(W_i,C_t,E_{it})$. The persistent attributes $W_i$, including map,
audit and label randomization, are iid. The stationary calendar $C_t$ is
independent of those attributes and strongly mixing. Conditional innovations
$E_{it}$ are independent across cells. Assume a $2+\delta$ moment envelope and
summable mixing/covariance bounds sufficient for the calendar central limit
and the residual covariance sums below; for instance
$\sum_k\alpha_C(k)^{\delta/(2+\delta)}<\infty$ with a suitable uniform envelope.
Define $\theta=EZ_{it}$ and the projections
\[
 a(W_i)=E[Z_{it}\mid W_i]-\theta,\qquad
 b(C_t)=E[Z_{it}\mid C_t]-\theta,\qquad
 r_{it}=Z_{it}-\theta-a(W_i)-b(C_t).
\]
Both conditional projections of $r$ vanish. Thus
\begin{equation}
 \bar Z-\theta=\frac1N\sum_i a(W_i)+\frac1T\sum_t b(C_t)
                  +\frac1{NT}\sum_{i,t}r_{it}.
 \label{r8:joint-projection}
\end{equation}
Cross-pair residual covariances vanish conditionally on the calendar. Within a
pair, the assumed summable residual covariance bound gives variance of its
calendar sum of order $T$. Consequently the last term has variance
$O((NT)^{-1})$. The first two sums are independent, and the iid and mixing
central limits give leading variance
\begin{equation}
 V_{NT}=\frac{\sigma_a^2}{N}+\frac{\Omega_b}{T},\quad
 \sigma_a^2=\operatorname{Var}(a(W)),\quad
 \Omega_b=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}\operatorname{Cov}(b(C_0),b(C_k)).
 \label{r8:joint-variance}
\end{equation}
This is a first-order argument under comparable $N,T$ growth, with at least one
nonzero leading projection and nonzero total leading variance. Degenerate
interaction-only regimes need a different limit. The reference operation
requires a supplied nondegeneracy declaration rather than pretending to test
that population condition from a finite sample.

The independent multiway sampling framework of \citet{cluster2021} separates
exchangeability and dissociation. A serially dependent calendar does not
automatically satisfy those premises. Equation \eqref{r8:joint-projection}
uses a different selected representation, and the calendar limit is supplied
by its own assumptions. This distinction prevents a convenient two-way API
from substituting for a sampling theorem.

Estimate the pair term by the sample variance of pair means divided by $N$,
and the calendar term by the Bartlett long-run variance of date means divided
by $T$. For centered date means $x_t$, the latter numerator is
\[
 \widehat\Omega=\frac1T\left[\sum_t x_t^2+
 2\sum_{k=1}^{L}\left(1-\frac{k}{L+1}\right)
       \sum_{t=k+1}^{T}x_tx_{t-k}\right].
\]
The positive-semidefinite Bartlett construction is inherited from
\citet{newey1986}; consistency here also needs the new score's joint sampling
conditions. Sufficient selected rates include $L\to\infty$ and
$L^2/\min(N,T)\to0$, with summable covariance tails and moment bounds.
Pair and calendar estimates can both contain interaction noise. Its population
order is $1/(NT)$, so retaining both is compatible with the leading limit;
it is not an exact finite-sample conservative confidence guarantee. Truncated
serial covariance and other finite-sample errors can still cause undercoverage.

\subsection{The third independent sample}

Let $M$ independently sampled gold labels estimate $\epsilon$ by the observed
error fraction $\hat\epsilon$. Gold truth must be accurately adjudicated and
representative of the same symmetric flip law. Differentiate the score:
\[
 \partial_\epsilon Z_{it}
   =\frac{R_i(2L_i-1)(V_{i0t}-V_{i1t})}
          {q_i(1-2\epsilon)^2},\qquad
 g=E\partial_\epsilon Z_{it}.
\]
With $\epsilon$ bounded away from one half, and $M$ comparable to $N,T$, a
Taylor expansion adds $g(\hat\epsilon-\epsilon)$ to the leading error. Its
independent variance contribution is $g^2\epsilon(1-\epsilon)/M$.
The quadratic Taylor remainder is negligible at the stated joint rate.
Plugging in the grand-mean derivative and the gold error fraction gives the
third variance component. A gold-label confidence region reaching one half
prevents regular inversion and yields an explicit unqualified result. This
is neither a bound for arbitrary label contamination nor semantic proof that
the recorded customer is the economic unit of interest.

\section{What audit spending can and cannot buy}
\label{r8:audit-design}

Suppose a complete pair supplies an audit correction difference $D$. Conditional
on the complete history, the audit-randomization variance is
$(q^{-1}-1)D^2$. For strata with population proportions $\pi_s$, per-audit
relative costs $c_s>0$ and second moments $d_s=E[D^2\mid s]$, minimizing this
contribution at expected budget $\sum_s\pi_sc_sq_s=B$ gives the Lagrangian
first-order condition
\[
 -d_s/q_s^2+\lambda c_s=0,\qquad
 q_s=\min\{1,\max\{q_{\min},\kappa\sqrt{d_s/c_s}\}\}.
\]
The objective is convex for positive $q_s$, so the clipped rule with a budget
multiplier solves the stated finite-stratum objective. An independent fully
audited pilot estimates $d_s$ and freezes the allocation before evaluation.
It does not certify the unknown population optimum, and it must not use the
final coverage outcomes to choose the design.

In the synthetic two-stratum example, costs are $1$ and $3$ relative units,
proportions are one half and budget is $.6$ per pair. The independent pilot has
4,000 fully audited pairs, costing 7,936 relative audit units under its realized
strata. Conditioning on the supplied symmetric error probability $.15$, it
produces inclusions $.2282$ and $.3239$, against uniform inclusion $.3$ at the
same expected budget. Final evaluation uses new histories and independent
gold labels. The gold sample has 1,200 labels per request; its adjudication
price and the history-acquisition cost are additional, unmeasured economic
inputs. They are not assigned a zero price.

The realized mean audit costs are 144.50 and 144.76 per 240-pair evaluation for
uniform and pilot allocation, respectively. Their expected costs are matched
by design, not forced to match every random audit count. Mean joint standard
errors are 204.9 and 203.8 currency units, a small change which does not by
itself justify the pilot's expense. The optimization theorem concerns an audit
variance component; it does not guarantee an attractive whole-program return.

A common-calendar floor survives even perfect identity information. Under the
declared AR calendar with marginal standard deviation $.8$ and persistence $.65$,
the asymptotic calendar variance is
$.8^2(1+.65)/((1-.65)T)$. At $T=180$ and monetary scale $1,000$, its nominal
95\% halfwidth is about $253.75$. Halfwidth targets of $100$ or $200$ therefore
cannot be attained by purchasing more pair audits alone. A target of $400$
clears this calendar floor, but still has pair and validation uncertainty.
Changing the calendar, the target or a scientifically justified model is a
different experiment; the audit optimizer cannot make this limitation vanish.

\section{Calibrating the dynamic funding inverse}
\label{r8:calibration}

The earlier deposit construction transforms two candidate responses in each
stratum into sum/difference primitives $m$ and covariance $\widehat V$.
With correctness probabilities $p_0,p_1$, the financial response before direct
price cost is $c(p)^\top m$, where
\[
 c(p)=\left(\tfrac12,\frac1{2(2p_0-1)},
                  \tfrac12,\frac1{2(2p_1-1)}\right)^\top.
\]
The primitives are half-sums and half-differences of the horizon-weighted
candidate responses. This factor matters for both currency units and variance.
Independent binomial audits contribute the delta variance through
$j_s=-m_{2s+1}/(2p_s-1)^2$ and $p_s(1-p_s)/n_s$.
More audits stabilize this inverse when its rank is separated from zero;
they do not repair a truncated calendar covariance estimate or a wrong outcome
model. The weak-rank confidence-set alternatives remain available separately.

Fresh original-design replications retain 720 dates, 2,880 independent pilot
dates, 200 audits per stratum and correctness probabilities $.95,.8$.
Two larger designs have 1,200 or 4,800 dates, a 1,600-date pilot, 1,600 audits per
stratum and probabilities $.9,.85$. These changes alter several information
dimensions, so a favorable larger-design result is not a unique diagnosis of
the historical undercoverage. Within each design, prespecified Bartlett windows
with multipliers $2,5,10$ are compared on the same fresh samples.

Known-audit arms remove calibration uncertainty only for diagnosis. A separate
1,000-draw synthetic training sample estimates the primitive response covariance
for each design, including independently retrained nuisance fits. Its estimated
covariance is frozen before final evaluation. A Student multiplier acknowledges
finite reference training but is not an exact theorem for these non-Gaussian
estimated responses. These arms can expose a variance-estimation contribution;
they are not deployable oracle procedures and do not retroactively qualify the
earlier intervals. Finite coverage, bias, precision and the remaining inverse
assumptions must be assessed together.

The fresh original-design interval covers $468/500=.936$; the 1,200-date
design covers $474/500=.948$, whereas the 4,800-date design covers only
$459/500=.918$. Its pilot remains at 1,600 dates. Larger windows do not
consistently improve these arms. The independently trained covariance raises
the corresponding frequencies to $.954,.968,.930$, but still leaves the
largest design short of nominal coverage. Its empirical response standard
deviation is about $71,401$ currency units, versus mean default standard error
$64,424$, with positive mean error about $11,718$. Known-audit comparisons
likewise retain a shortfall. Thus audit-count uncertainty is not the sole
observed limitation. Finite-pilot and calendar-variance contributions need
separate further investigation; these comparisons do not uniquely identify
their causes or supply a generally calibrated replacement.

\section{Sharper confidence in a finite latent information class}
\label{r8:graphs}

Suppose independent Gaussian episodes have ordered variables $(Z,A,Y)$.
The information class is supplied scientifically. Under observed sufficiency,
the coefficient of $A$ in $E[Y\mid Z,A]$ is the causal target throughout the
declared finite class. Gaussian linear regression with intercept gives an exact
conditional $t_{n-3}$ interval when the design has rank three. This uses causal
invariance across the class, rather than selecting a graph and then ignoring
its uncertainty. A broad latent observational class still supports every real
effect through the earlier same-law witness. More precise computation cannot
remove that lack of information.

Under valid randomized encouragement and exclusion, the true null effect
$\theta$ makes $Y-\theta A$ have zero $Z$ regression slope. Its Gaussian
reduced-form error is independent of $Z$ even when the treatment residual is
confounded with outcome error. The exact null-test approach is the Gaussian
specialization of the weak-IV principle discussed by \citet{staiger1994}; no
lower bound on the first-stage coefficient is needed.

Center all three variables and write
$k=Z^\top Z$, $a=Z^\top A/k$, $y=Z^\top Y/k$. Let $e_A=A-aZ$,
$e_Y=Y-yZ$ and $S_{uv}=e_u^\top e_v$. Inverting the two-sided null test gives
\begin{equation}
 (y-\theta a)^2\leq
 \frac{t_{n-2,1-\alpha/2}^2}{(n-2)k}
       (S_{YY}-2\theta S_{AY}+\theta^2S_{AA}).
 \label{r8:weak-iv-inversion}
\end{equation}
To verify the pivot, regress $Y-\theta A$ on $(1,Z)$: its slope is $y-\theta a$,
residual sum of squares is the expression in parentheses, and residual degrees
of freedom are $n-2$. At the true null, normal slope and independent scaled
residual variance give the Student distribution. Membership of the true effect
therefore has probability $1-\alpha$, including at zero first-stage rank.
The confidence set can nevertheless be practically uninformative.

Equation \eqref{r8:weak-iv-inversion} is a quadratic sublevel set. A positive
leading coefficient gives the interval between real roots; a negative one can
give two rays; absent roots give the empty or whole-line answer according to
sign. Linear and constant cases must also survive. Stable root formulas,
extended-precision discriminants and outward endpoint rounding reduce numerical
error without providing a complete floating-point certificate. These are new
prespecified confidence procedures, not intersections with the earlier 95\%
covariance rectangle. Intersecting independent-looking 95\% answers would
require its own simultaneous confidence argument.

In 2,000 fresh strong-encouragement episodes, the new set is bounded throughout,
with median width $.2079$ in outcome units per action and coverage $.9525$.
Weak encouragement often yields whole-line or disconnected sets, while exact
zero first stage does not invalidate true-null coverage. Supplied sufficiency
has coverage $.954$ in its valid law. False exclusion has zero encouragement-set
coverage, and falsely supplied sufficiency under hidden confounding likewise
fails. An exact statistical pivot cannot make an incorrect causal restriction
true. General PAG confidence and dependent histories remain distinct problems.

\section{An audited action-dependent nonlinear transition variance}
\label{r8:nonlinear}

Extend the scalar private-logger model by
\[
 S_{t+1}=\rho S_t+\gamma\tanh(S_t)+\beta A_t+\sqrt{q(A_t)}\,\xi_{t+1},
 \quad q(A)=q_0(1-A)+q_1A,
\]
with $A\in\{0,1\}$, independent standard normal $\xi$, and
$|\rho|+|\gamma|<1$. Observation remains $O_t=S_t+\sqrt{o}\,\zeta_t$;
the private action probability is
$.05+.90\operatorname{expit}(\lambda_0+\lambda_sS_t+\lambda_oO_t)$.
Reward has conditional mean
$\eta_0+\eta_sS_t+\eta_aA_t+\eta_{sa}S_tA_t$ and independent normal noise.
The Gaussian initial distribution and all observation, logging and reward
parameters remain in the likelihood. Adding $\log q_1$ produces 16 parameters;
silently omitting logging probabilities would change the observed experiment.

Representative accurate state audits reveal complete trajectories. Conditional
transition means are identified by a full-rank regression on
$(S_t,\tanh S_t,A_t)$ over their support. Residual second moments in both action
groups identify $q_0$ and $q_1$. Full support and an open state range distinguish
the linear and nonlinear features. Observation variance, logger parameters,
reward coefficients/variance and initial moments follow from their corresponding
labelled conditional laws with full-rank designs. Without representative state
truth or both action groups this argument does not supply identification.

Main trajectories integrate states using the same model factors; audited
trajectories evaluate them directly. Their independent log-likelihood sums
share one parameter. The recursive predictive-likelihood principle is inherited
from \citet{sarkka2013}, while this audit/model identification and uncertainty
construction are project arguments. Two constrained local starts use the stable
domain $|\rho|+|\gamma|\leq .95$ and explicit parameter bounds. For an interior
fit, Hessian $H$ and separately centered main/audit score matrices give
$\widehat\Sigma=H^{-1}(\sum\tilde s\tilde s^\top)H^{-1}$.
The gradient of the fixed policy value maps this covariance into value
uncertainty. Both independently sampled trajectory counts enter; audits are
not treated as free parameter knowledge.

The policy uses time-specific observable-signal thresholds trained independently
in the earlier study, frozen here as $(-1,-1,0)$. Its value integrates the
observation-triggered action probability and each action's transition kernel,
discounting rewards by $.97$ per step and converting by $1,000$ currency units.
It is not an optimal full belief-history policy. The registered three-step
mechanism has $q_0=.35$, $q_1=.9$, 80 main and 640 audited trajectories.
Every available fitted interval passes likelihood, score and value refinement
from 61 nodes on $[-7,7]$ to 101 on $[-10,10]$. Independent checks include all
16 likelihood and value derivative directions, direct labelled likelihood,
equal-variance reduction and the exact Gaussian limit requiring both
$\gamma=0$ and $\lambda_s=0$. Agreement is evidence about these calculations,
not a uniform numerical-error certificate or global optimizer proof.

All 120 correct-model requests supply intervals and 115 cover the truth;
the Monte Carlo 95\% interval is $[.9054,.9863]$. A homogeneous-variance challenger
also covers 115 of 120; this selected target does not establish a material
value-inference advantage for the added parameter. The extension supplies an
explicitly identified model capability, not an empirically proven superiority.
Adding an omitted nonlinear transition term causes all 120 fits in each arm
to become unqualified. Retaining unavailable outcomes is more informative than
computing coverage only among favorable fits. General nonlinear state models,
uniform boundaries and global policy optimization remain open.

\section{A richer dependent learner that fits in chunks}
\label{r8:learning}

The partial-linear IV score retains the Robinson form of
\citet{dml2018}, with nuisance conditional means $(\ell,r,m)$:
\[
 \psi_t(\theta)=(Z_t-m(X_t))
       \{Y_t-\ell(X_t)-\theta(D_t-r(X_t))\}.
\]
The source's iid inference theorem is not a theorem for an arbitrary temporal
learner. Here the dictionary is fixed as $(1,X,X_0X_1)$, observations are bounded
and geometrically mixing, the population Gram and IV slope are separated from
singularity, and all three nuisance means lie in the dictionary. Fixed-dimensional
OLS then has root-sample error under these selected conditions. Orthogonality
leaves a product error of order $n^{-1}$; a growing temporal gap makes training
and evaluation coupling negligible, and a slowly growing Bartlett window with
the corresponding score-error rate supplies the covariance argument.

Two held-out blocks are separated by gap 100. Each trains on the other; windows
and feature availability are checked before fitting. The whole declared origin
is the sampling unit. Inference globally centers retained scores and computes
lag products within each evaluation block. Concatenating separated blocks and
forming lags across their missing calendar gap would create nonexistent adjacent
observations. The declared population mixing rate is supplied, not estimated
from a successful fit.

For chunked fitting, form each block of the augmented matrix
$[X_{\mathrm{dict}},Y,D,Z]$ and take its QR factor. Stack the small retained
$R$ with the next augmented block and repeat QR. Orthogonal transformations
preserve the least-squares objective; the final leading $R_{XX}$ and target
columns solve the same three nuisance problems as dense least squares.
Predictions use the identical fixed dictionary, folds and envelope clipping.
Rank loss is refused. This construction avoids the full expanded fitting
matrix; it still retains input storage and $O(n)$ residuals/scores. It does not
make arbitrary adaptive dictionaries or learners safe to fit out of core.

Fresh synthetic laws add the previously omitted interaction to outcome and
instrument conditional means. The old linear dictionary has zero coverage in
300 draws. The richer QR and independent dense SVD routes agree to floating-point
tolerance and remove that large bias, yet their original-window coverage is
only $271/300=.9033$. A separately registered larger 16,000-date design reaches
$282/300=.94$ with both the original and a longer window; its Monte Carlo interval
is $[.9068,.9641]$. Equal coverage counts do not show that the longer window is
unnecessary in general. A further omitted quadratic term gives zero richer-
dictionary coverage. Representation, numerical algebra and calibrated
uncertainty are separate achievements.
