\end{longtable}

The common worst-case bias envelope is 1.37243 utility units, exceeding
every realized bias in the table. That conservatism is the price of
using probability error bounds without favorable outcome cancellation.
These perturbations illustrate the error propagation formula; they are
not estimates learned from an executed training sample.

Even with \(B_t=2\), \(c_e=.25\), \(c_g=.65\), \(T=2\), \(n=1000\) and
\(\alpha_E=.025\), the evaluation radius alone exceeds eight utility
units. The entire stipulated value range is only eight units wide. A
mathematically valid bound can therefore be unsuitable for choosing
assistance. Increasing the nominal confidence level or adding more rare
history cells makes this tradeoff harder. This is a reason to seek
shorter questions, stronger information, sharper variance-sensitive
bounds or a reviewed sequential regression construction; it is not a
reason to remove the error budget.

Sequential doubly robust scores offer a substantive alternative when
continuation values are useful. They require a separate analysis of
fitted action/retention models, value-function errors and sampling
dependence. The known-logger variance reduction in Jiang and Li does not
automatically establish estimated-logger finite coverage. The earlier
synthetic collection results already show that mean protection and
normal-interval reliability differ. \citep{jiang2016}

\hypertarget{observational-equivalence-prevents-a-hidden-state-repair-by-prediction}{%
\section{Observational equivalence prevents a hidden-state repair by
prediction}\label{observational-equivalence-prevents-a-hidden-state-repair-by-prediction}}

Consider a single decision with no censoring. In world E, action is a
fair independent coin and \(Y=A\) with probability \(.8\), otherwise
\(Y=1-A\). The intervention values are \(V_E(1)=.8\), \(V_E(0)=.2\). In
world H, private hardship \(U\) is a fair coin, \(Y=U\), and
\(\Pr(A=1\mid U)=.2+.6U\). Here \(V_H(1)=V_H(0)=.5\).

Both worlds have exactly the same observed joint probabilities:

\begin{longtable}[]{@{}lrrrr@{}}
\toprule
Observed pair \((A,Y)\) & \((0,0)\) & \((0,1)\) & \((1,0)\) &
\((1,1)\)\tabularnewline
\midrule
\endhead
Either world & .4 & .1 & .1 & .4\tabularnewline
\bottomrule
\end{longtable}

Even the private-state assignment in world H has overlap: its
probabilities are .2 and .8. Infinite recorded data estimate
\(\Pr(A=1)=.5\) and \(\mathbb E[Y\mid A=1]=.8\) perfectly in both
worlds. Weighting by that observed probability returns .8, while the
hidden world's value is .5. No fitted logger, extra evaluation data or
language-model interpretation of these same records can distinguish the
worlds. The effect is .6 in one and zero in the other.

Observation selection has a separate obstruction. Suppose half the
cohort is observed and half of those observed have \(Y=1\). One
full-data world assigns zero to every missing outcome; another assigns
one. Both yield the same observed records and retention probability .5,
but their cohort means are .25 and .75. Accurately estimating the
retention probability does not recover the unobserved outcome law. The
complete-case mean .5 answers neither world's population question.

An additional randomized action design, a truthful relevant-state audit,
or a validated proxy/instrument model can distinguish some such worlds.
Each adds information or restrictions. The existing proximal and
partial-observation treatments explain specific routes and their rank,
exclusion and policy-information requirements; they do not authorize
arbitrary hidden-state inference.
\citep{bennettprox2023,tennenholtz2020}

\hypertarget{what-the-proposal-can-recommend-after-this-derivation}{%
\section{What the proposal can recommend after this
derivation}\label{what-the-proposal-can-recommend-after-this-derivation}}

The preserved selected17 study used truthful representative state audits
and supplied action probabilities. It passed its selected valid cells,
while wrong probabilities covered only one of 512 requests and policy
leakage returned no finite outputs. The present finite-table route makes
estimated-probability uncertainty explicit after restricting to
sufficient observed histories. It removes no hidden-state requirement
from that predecessor and claims no new repeated-sampling qualification.
\citep{exec13_servicing_predecessor}

The separate proposed continuous-state servicing experiment has Gaussian
innovations and a quadratic reward. Its rewards are unbounded and its
history table is not finite. Consequently it cannot use this
bounded-table theorem as written. A prospectively declared bounded
utility would define a different target; alternatively, a valid
tail/moment bound and a continuous-model estimation argument are needed.
Quietly capping realized losses after evaluating the results would
answer a changed question.

For the proposal, the executable next comparison is a declared
finite-state generated demonstration with known evaluator truth,
estimated training probabilities, independent evaluation and adverse
hidden/censoring cases. Its useful-width screen must be chosen in
utility units before final draws. A broad interval or correct refusal is
an informative demonstration outcome. A claim about real servicing
remains conditional on an information audit and a justified dependence
law, and an unknown optimal policy remains a separate research question.
These distinctions make a prototype experiment worth designing without
pretending that a bank trial or a universal hidden-state theorem has
already been supplied. The following temporal analysis asks a related question at the level of causal structure: which intervention can distinguish effects that the observed law leaves equivalent? The servicing examples show why that information question must precede a more elaborate probability fit.

\label{exec13:servicing-observed-end}

chapters.title: Continuous temporal uncertainty and an informative intervention

segments.text:
\chapter{Continuous temporal uncertainty and an informative intervention}
\label{exec13:temporal-region}

\hypertarget{the-banking-question-and-the-observation-law}{%
\section{The banking question and the observation
law}\label{the-banking-question-and-the-observation-law}}

A bank can observe a stable association between an offer and a
subsequent outcome yet remain unable to price the effect of changing the
offer. The missing information can persist even with an exactly known
observational distribution. This chapter develops a restricted temporal
confidence construction and shows what an additional direct intervention
would contribute. The mathematical construction and exact calculations
are project derivations, not a fitted bank result.
\cite{exec13_temporal_argument,exec13_temporal_exact}

In the preserved temporal graph study, all valid cells covered and
retained their declared true graph in 512 of 512 requests. Weak
relevance and unrestricted latent observation each produced 512
whole-line sets. The persistent cell produced 507 finite sets and five
whole-line sets. Under false exclusion, the true graph was retained zero
times despite numerical effect coverage. These findings distinguish
numerical coverage from informative effects and from a valid causal
restriction. \cite{exec13_temporal_predecessor}

Let \(X_t=(Z_t,A_t,Y_t)'\) satisfy \[
 X_t=\rho X_{t-1}+\varepsilon_t,\quad
 \varepsilon_t\mathrel{\mathop\sim^{\rm iid}}N_3(0,\Sigma),\quad
 \Sigma\succ0,\quad \rho\in I\subset(-1,1).
\] Here \(I\) is a declared closed interval, not an estimated selected
lag. Initial observations have the invariant distribution
\(N_3(0,\Sigma/(1-\rho^2))\), independently of future innovations. We
observe \(X_0,\ldots,X_n\), with \(n\ge2\). The scalar lag common to all
coordinates and the Gaussian independent innovations are substantive
restrictions. A general lag matrix, unknown lag order, nonstationarity,
hidden temporal state, selection and measurement errors are outside this
law.

A structural innovation model is \[
 \varepsilon_Z=E_Z,\qquad
 \varepsilon_A=k\varepsilon_Z+U,\qquad
 \varepsilon_Y=\tau\varepsilon_A+c\varepsilon_Z+V,
\] where \(E_Z\) is independent of the jointly Gaussian pair \((U,V)\).
Dependence between \(U\) and \(V\) represents latent action/outcome
confounding. The target \(\tau\) is the contemporaneous response to
changing \(A_t\) while holding the past fixed. In observed-coordinate
structural equations, the lag matrix is \(\rho(I-B)\), where \(B\)
contains the contemporaneous coefficients. It is not permissible to
change that lag matrix to \(\rho I\) in the structural equations and
claim the same target/law.

The declared graph family may include the exclusion model \(c=0\) and a
broad latent model with unrestricted \(c\). In the former,
\(\Sigma_{ZY}=\tau\Sigma_{ZA}\). In the latter that equality need not
hold. An exclusion is a scientific restriction, not a conclusion from
fitting a favorable covariance. The construction below accommodates a
finite declared family through a union over graph/parameter pairs; it
does not claim an exhaustive search over unrestricted causal structures.

\hypertarget{a-feasible-region-with-continuous-unknown-lag}{%
\section{A feasible region with continuous unknown
lag}\label{a-feasible-region-with-continuous-unknown-lag}}

For every candidate \(r\in I\), form residuals \(E_t(r)=X_t-rX_{t-1}\).
Use the nine fixed directions \[
 \mathcal V=\{e_1,e_2,e_3,e_1+e_2,e_1-e_2,
 e_1+e_3,e_1-e_3,e_2+e_3,e_2-e_3\},\quad K=9.
\] For each direction, let \(S_v(r)\) be the ordinary sample variance of
\(v'E_t(r)\), with divisor \(\nu=n-1\). At the true lag only,
\(\nu S_v(\rho)/(v'\Sigma v)\) is the sum of squares of \(\nu\)
independent standard normal variables. To see this, scale the vector of
independent normal residuals by its population standard deviation and
apply an orthogonal matrix whose first row is the normalized all-ones
vector. The remaining \(\nu\) coordinates are independent standard
normals, and their squared norm is the centered sum of squares.
Consequently \[
 E[S_v(\rho)]=v'\Sigma v,\qquad
 \operatorname{Var}(S_v(\rho))=2(v'\Sigma v)^2/\nu.
\] For a declared rational tolerance \(0<t<1\), Markov's inequality
applied to the squared relative error gives \[
 P\{|S_v(\rho)/(v'\Sigma v)-1|>t\}\le\frac{2}{\nu t^2}.
\] If \(2K/(\nu t^2)\le\alpha_O\), the union bound supplies simultaneous
coverage at least \(1-\alpha_O\) for \[
 L_v(r)=\frac{S_v(r)}{1+t}\le v'\Sigma v
 \le \frac{S_v(r)}{1-t}=U_v(r),\qquad v\in\mathcal V,
\] evaluated at \(r=\rho\). Dependence between the nine directions is
harmless for this bound. Residuals at an incorrect lag need not be
independent.

Define \(\mathcal C_O\) to contain every tuple \((r,G,\lambda,\Sigma)\)
for which \(r\in I\), \(G\) is in the declared family, its parameters
\(\lambda\) generate \(\Sigma\succ0\) under the stated innovation law,
and all nine inequalities hold. All nuisance coefficients and the
continuous lag remain in the region. Let \[
 \mathcal S_O=\{\tau(G,\lambda):(r,G,\lambda,\Sigma)\in\mathcal C_O\}.
\] On simultaneous variance inclusion, the true tuple belongs to
\(\mathcal C_O\); hence its effect belongs to \(\mathcal S_O\). Thus
\(P(\tau_0\in\mathcal S_O)\ge1-\alpha_O\), provided the declared family
contains the true structural model. No multiple-testing penalty over the
continuum of candidate lags is required: this proof uses a single
coverage event at the fixed true lag, and the union includes that lag.
It does not declare every wrong-lag confidence calculation valid or
justify discarding the true lag by a separate selector.

The construction is deliberately conservative. With \(t=1/4\), \(K=9\)
and \(\alpha_O=.02\), it needs \(\nu\ge14{,}400\). The predecessor used
240 transitions; this particular finite bound cannot give it the
displayed two-sided relative band. At smaller sample size this profile
returns the whole line and a bound-insufficient disposition, rather than
inserting an invalid finite interval. The exact chi-square pivot above
offers a sharper candidate using suitably certified quantiles, but its
numerical implementation would need separate validation. No improvement
in cost or useful width is claimed from replacing a lag grid with this
conservative continuum argument.

\hypertarget{numerical-outer-bounds-that-cannot-lose-a-lag-or-a-component}{%
\section{Numerical outer bounds that cannot lose a lag or a
component}\label{numerical-outer-bounds-that-cannot-lose-a-lag-or-a-component}}

Let \(u_t=v'X_t\) and \(w_t=v'X_{t-1}\). Center each series over the
same \(n\) transitions. Direct expansion gives \[
 \begin{aligned}
 S_v(r)&=a_vr^2+b_vr+d_v,\\
 a_v&=\nu^{-1}\sum_t(w_t-\bar w)^2,\\
 b_v&=-2\nu^{-1}\sum_t(u_t-\bar u)(w_t-\bar w),\\
 d_v&=\nu^{-1}\sum_t(u_t-\bar u)^2.
 \end{aligned}
\] For a closed lag cell \(J=[r_L,r_U]\), its maximum is at an endpoint
because \(a_v\ge0\); its minimum is at an endpoint or at \(-b_v/(2a_v)\)
if that vertex lies in the cell. The constant case is handled
separately. Rational coefficients and cell endpoints therefore give
exact bounds \([s^-_v(J),s^+_v(J)]\). A finite partition covering all of
\(I\), with shared endpoints retained, is a continuum enclosure, not an
evaluation grid. Refining cells can reduce excess width; stopping early
preserves validity.

For exact supplied numbers, a conservative directional variance interval
over the cell is \([s^-_v/(1+t),s^+_v/(1-t)]\). Polarization gives an
entrywise covariance box. For \(i\ne j\), use \[
 \Sigma_{ij}\in\frac14
 [L_{e_i+e_j}(J)-U_{e_i-e_j}(J),
  U_{e_i+e_j}(J)-L_{e_i-e_j}(J)].
\] Dropping positive-definiteness and shared-parameter consistency
enlarges this box. It can make results much wider, but cannot remove the
true covariance. Positive-definiteness or graph constraints may narrow a
later implementation only through certified feasibility exclusion, not
by failure of an optimizer.

Exact arithmetic on decimal data alone does not enclose unknown
rounding. Suppose every coordinate of the ideal input is enclosed within
absolute error \(\eta\) of the supplied value, and let
\(h=\|v\|_1\eta(1+\max_{r\in J}|r|)\). Residual error is at most \(h\)
and its centered error at most \(2h\). Cauchy--Schwarz then bounds the
change in sample variance by \[
 B_v(J)=4h\sqrt{n/\nu}\sqrt{s^+_v(J)}+4nh^2/\nu.
\] Use rational upward bounds for the square roots and replace the
variance enclosure by \([\max(0,s^-_v-B_v),s^+_v+B_v]\) before dividing
by \(1\pm t\). This is an input-conversion certificate conditional on a
valid input enclosure. Undocumented measurement error, noisy proxies or
incorrect entity matches are changes to the observation law, not
floating-point errors that this formula repairs.

In an exclusion cell, write the resulting intervals as \(N_J\) for
\(\Sigma_{ZY}\) and \(D_J\) for \(\Sigma_{ZA}\). Retain the full set \[
 \mathcal T_J=\{\theta:\exists (N,D)\in N_J\times D_J,
                      \ N-\theta D=0\}.
\] When \(0\notin D_J\), its endpoints are the extreme corner ratios.
When the denominator straddles zero and the numerator excludes zero, two
rays can result. For \(N_J=[1,2]\) and \(D_J=[-1,1]\), the set is
\(( -\infty,-1]\cup[1,\infty)\). When both intervals include zero, their
rectangle contains \((0,0)\), so every \(\theta\) is feasible. When
\(D_J=\{0\}\) and \(0\notin N_J\), the moment set is empty. That is a
constraint inconsistency, not evidence for a zero effect.

Union these components over every lag cell and every retained graph. The
broad latent graph below contributes the whole line whenever its
observational law is admitted. Keep disconnected components unless they
overlap; never replace a pair of rays by a finite interval. The exact
reference checks ratio sets against the independent criterion that
\(N_J\) intersects \(\theta D_J\), including zero denominators and exact
endpoints. Bounds include every continuous lag by the quadratic proof;
sampled checks alone are not the certificate. The reference is not a
general graph feasibility solver and supplies no bank-data result.

\hypertarget{an-equal-law-witness-and-what-an-exclusion-actually-buys}{%
\section{An equal-law witness and what an exclusion actually
buys}\label{an-equal-law-witness-and-what-an-exclusion-actually-buys}}

Let \(Z,U,E\) be independent standard Gaussian innovations and set \[
 \varepsilon_Z=Z,\quad \varepsilon_A=Z+U,\quad
 \varepsilon_Y=\tau\varepsilon_A+(2-\tau)Z+(1-\tau)U+E.
\] For every real \(\tau\), the observed innovation is exactly
\((Z,Z+U,2Z+U+E)'\), with covariance \[
 \Sigma=\begin{pmatrix}1&1&2\\1&2&3\\2&3&6\end{pmatrix},
 \qquad\det\Sigma=1.
\] The confounded disturbance has variance \(1+(1-\tau)^2\) and
covariance \(1-\tau\) with \(U\); its conditional noise variance is
always one. Every world is a coherent positive-definite Gaussian law.
Attaching the same scalar lag and invariant initialization makes the
entire observed temporal law identical for every \(\tau\), while a
contemporaneous intervention on \(A\) changes \(Y\) at slope \(\tau\).
The equality is algebraic for all real effects, not merely an equality
across the finite checked examples.

The restriction \(c=0\) reduces this family to \(\tau=2\); strong
observed relevance \(\Sigma_{ZA}=1\) then gives the familiar ratio. But
relevance alone does not establish exclusion: all other worlds have the
same strong observed correlation with \(Z\). Merely observing more of
this law, using a different discovery optimizer or asking an LLM to
orient an edge cannot choose among these effects. No theorem here rules
out all additional measurements; it states exactly what the declared
observational law omits.

At zero relevance, even exclusion can leave every effect feasible. Take
\(\varepsilon_A=U\) and
\(\varepsilon_Y=\tau\varepsilon_A+(1-\tau)U+E=U+E\), with \(Z\)
independent. Now \(c=0\), \(\Sigma_{ZA}=\Sigma_{ZY}=0\), and the effect
is still arbitrary. A weak-instrument ratio that quietly deletes zero
cannot solve this information problem.

\hypertarget{a-direct-intervention-that-separates-effects-without-identifying-every-edge}{%
\section{A direct intervention that separates effects without
identifying every
edge}\label{a-direct-intervention-that-separates-effects-without-identifying-every-edge}}

Consider independent experimental episodes at a common fixed pre-action
history. Replace the action equation by \(A=a_0+\delta R\), where
\(\delta>0\) is known and \(R\in\{-1,1\}\) is assigned with \(m\)
episodes per arm independently of innovation roots. Keep the other
structural equations unchanged. Under the restricted linear Gaussian
model and an invariant \(\tau\), the outcome has the form \[
 Y=\mu+\tau\delta R+\xi,\quad
 \xi\mathrel{\mathop\sim^{\rm iid}}N(0,\sigma_I^2),\qquad \sigma_I^2>0.
\] The unknown \(\mu\) absorbs the fixed history and baseline action;
the unknown variance absorbs the remaining contemporaneous causes. The
episodes must be independent; taking adjacent dates from one continuing
customer trajectory does not satisfy this experiment. Identical variance
in the two arms and a common transported effect are additional model
assumptions.

Let \(\widehat\tau_I=(\bar Y_+-\bar Y_-)/(2\delta)\), and let \(S_p^2\)
be the usual pooled within-arm variance with \(\nu_I=2m-2\) degrees of
freedom. Orthogonal Gaussian projections within each arm make its sample
mean independent of its centered residuals. Hence \[
 T=\frac{\widehat\tau_I-\tau}{S_p/(\delta\sqrt{2m})}
   =\frac{Z_0}{\sqrt{Q/\nu_I}},\qquad
 Z_0\sim N(0,1),\quad Q\sim\chi^2_{\nu_I},\quad Z_0\perp Q.
\] For \(m>2\), integrating the chi-square density gives
\(E[Q^{-1}]=1/(\nu_I-2)\), so \(E[T^2]=\nu_I/(\nu_I-2)\). Choose any
rational \(b^2\ge\nu_I/((\nu_I-2)\alpha_I)\). Markov's inequality proves
finite coverage at least \(1-\alpha_I\) for \[
 \mathcal S_I=\left[\widehat\tau_I-
  \sqrt{\frac{b^2S_p^2}{2m\delta^2}},\quad
  \widehat\tau_I+\sqrt{\frac{b^2S_p^2}{2m\delta^2}}\right].
\] This conservative alternative avoids unverified numerical tail
quantiles. A sharper Student pivot interval is possible with certified
quantiles. Nonpositive pooled variance or insufficient degrees of
freedom produces a refusal/whole-line result under the declared
algorithm, never zero-width certainty. A nonnormal outcome model needs
another uncertainty argument. If input numbers are enclosed rather than
exact, enclose the arm means and pooled variance as well before
projecting these endpoints.

Under a common effect parameter, report
\(\mathcal S=\mathcal S_O\cap\mathcal S_I\). The two component coverage
events need not be independent: the union bound gives at least
\(1-\alpha_O-\alpha_I\). Using outer numerical supersets preserves this
inclusion proof. An empty intersection is a retained
inconsistency/failure event, not an invitation to change the error
budget or delete a graph after seeing the result. If no observational
restriction is defensible, use \(\mathcal S_I\) alone under its own
experiment and target assumptions.

In the equal-law family, intervention changes the arm mean difference to
\(2\delta\tau\). Distinct effects are now distinguishable, although
several graphs can remain compatible. Identifying the decision-relevant
effect does not require identifying every edge. Randomizing a variable
that merely encourages the action is a different experiment: exclusion,
compliance and relevance then need their own argument.

\hypertarget{precision-costs-and-the-exact-remaining-scope}{%
\section{Precision, costs and the exact remaining
scope}\label{precision-costs-and-the-exact-remaining-scope}}

For a binary offer, take \(a_0=\delta=1/2\). A planning illustration
with \(m=200\) per arm, \(\alpha_I=.03\), a reported effect of twenty
dollars and \(S_p^2=100\) dollars squared gives \(b^2=9950/297\) and
half-width \(\sqrt{9950/297}\), approximately 5.788 dollars. The exact
reference uses a rational upward square-root enclosure. These are
supplied planning summaries, not observations from a completed trial.

For 3,000 eligible customers and fifteen dollars incremental
implementation cost per offer, the point scenario has fifteen thousand
dollars net benefit. Its conservative interval still includes a small
loss. Scaling an effect by population does not remove uncertainty, and
changing the intervention or customer population may invalidate
transport. A genuine next-experiment proposal should ask whether
resolving this decision is worth the experiment's cost, compare a
cheaper operational alternative, and include delayed outcomes,
noncompliance and treatment costs in the estimand. No measured bank ROI
is inferred from this illustration.

What is resolved is the mathematical route for one continuous scalar-lag
Gaussian family, a certified enclosure strategy, exact information
counterexamples and a separating intervention with an explicit finite
bound. What remains is a resource-profiled implementation and
prospectively registered study, tighter useful uncertainty, justified
input and model assumptions, actual interventions/measurements if the
proposal advances, and the general
unknown-lag-matrix/latent-state/non-Gaussian/heterogeneous-effect
problem. This argument establishes no general temporal-graph capability,
bank validation or independent acceptance. The computational and
information routes are concrete enough to design the next bounded
public/generated experiment. The following design analysis tests whether the displayed bounds could be informative at the predecessor's sample size and whether its qualification screen has adequate power. It keeps theorem validity, finite availability and a useful financial comparison as separate requirements.

\label{exec13:temporal-region-end}

\section{When a valid temporal region is still an unsuitable study design}
\label{exec13:temporal-design-review}

The restricted continuous-lag argument separates mathematical coverage
from decision-useful precision. At the true common scalar lag, invariant
Gaussian initialization and independent innovations justify the projected
variance argument. A union over candidate lags need only retain the true
lag on that event; incorrect lags need not themselves produce independent
residuals. This is a useful restricted result. It does not establish a
confidence procedure for an arbitrary lag matrix, unknown order,
nonstationary hidden histories or a general learned partial ancestral
graph. These differences also determine whether a proposed numerical
study is worth conducting \cite{exec13_temporal_design}.

Consider the displayed Chebyshev construction with nine variance
directions, relative tolerance $t=1/4$ and observational error allocation
$\alpha_O=.02$. For a Gaussian sample variance with $\nu$ residual
degrees of freedom, the relative variance is $2/\nu$. Chebyshev and a
union bound therefore give
\[
 \Pr(\hbox{at least one relative deviation exceeds }t)
 \leq \frac{18}{\nu t^2}.
\]
To make this bound at most $.02$ requires $\nu\geq14{,}400$, or
$14{,}401$ transitions under the stated residual convention. With $240$
transitions and $239$ degrees of freedom, the untruncated expression is
approximately $1.20502$ and gives no useful coverage bound. The specified
whole-line fallback is honest about this limitation. Increasing the number
of Monte Carlo replications cannot make that per-request fallback
decision-useful \cite{exec13_temporal_design}.

A sharper pivot is a concrete development route. At the restricted true
lag, an exact chi-square variance pivot can replace the Chebyshev band
while preserving the continuous union. Ordinary development quantiles
at $239$ degrees of freedom and the nine-way $.02$ allocation give
variance multipliers approximately $[.76731,1.34533]$. These values
indicate potential improvement; they are not certified release endpoints.
The implementation must enclose the tail quantiles, observable inputs
and propagated covariance constraints, preserve conservative fallback
under timeout, and profile the continuous-lag calculation. Sampling a
lag grid or accepting a point optimizer's failure does not certify the
whole continuum \cite{exec13_temporal_design}.

The preserved finite-lag study also requires a precise reading. Its
persistent cell returned $507$ finite sets among $512$ requests, so
$507/512=.990234375$ passes the original raw finite-fraction threshold
of $.99$. The five whole-line answers remain visible, but do not justify
declaring that particular threshold failed. Weak relevance and the
unrestricted latent observational cell each returned zero finite sets
and still fail it. False exclusion retained the true graph in zero
requests, despite wide effect sets covering the numerical effect.
These findings concern different obligations: availability, effect
coverage, and scientific validity of the graph class
\cite{exec13_temporal_design}.

A lower confidence-bound rule for availability would be a different
criterion. At family error $.05$ across sixteen comparisons, the
one-sided lower bound for $507/512$ is about $.97130$; even $512/512$
gives about $.98880$. The historical study used a lower-bound screen
for coverage, but a raw fraction for finite availability. They should
not be interchanged retrospectively. A prospective successor may
justify different criteria, provided it states them before final data
and keeps the predecessor's outcomes under their original definitions
\cite{exec13_temporal_design}.

The coverage screen has its own design-power issue. With $512$
independent final requests per cell and error $.05/16$, at least $500$
successes are required for the exact one-sided lower bound to exceed
or equal $.95$. Exact binomial-tail calculations give per-cell passing
probabilities approximately $.001849$, $.234929$, $.770054$ and
$.997670$ when true coverage is respectively $.95$, $.97$, $.98$ and
$.99$. Thus a nominal $.95$ method is very unlikely to certify a
lower bound of $.95$ using this screen. More replications improve
discrimination above the boundary; they do not create high power at
the boundary while retaining the same error control. No product of
these per-cell powers is a joint power calculation without an
across-cell dependence argument \cite{exec13_temporal_design}.

Useful precision also requires an information distinction. In the
unrestricted equal-law latent family, every real effect can produce
the same observed temporal law. No numerical improvement can create
a uniformly finite informative effect set from those unchanged
observations. A direct assigned-action experiment changes the
information available. The proposed Gaussian episode argument assumes
independent episodes, a common transported effect and equal arm
variances. Adjacent records from one trajectory or encouragement in
place of the action require different assumptions and derivations
\cite{exec13_temporal_design}.

The supplied-summary example makes the planning distinction concrete.
At $200$ episodes per arm, reported effect $20$ dollars, reported
pooled variance $100$ dollars squared and the specified conservative
bound, the half-width is about $5.78806$ dollars. For $3{,}000$
eligible customers and an incremental cost of $15$ dollars per offer,
the net-benefit lower endpoint is approximately $-2{,}364.19$ dollars.
Holding the same reported variance and effect fixed, $268$ episodes
per arm first reduce the half-width below $5$ dollars, while $400$
give about $4.08761$. In a future experiment both the estimated effect
and pooled variance would vary. These are conditional arithmetic
screens, not prospective power or recommended bank sample sizes
\cite{exec13_temporal_design}.

The next restricted study therefore needs a certified executable and
input-enclosure policy, measured resource limits, a fixed final grid
of observational and added-information regimes, and an explicit
useful-width or loss criterion. A generated experiment can develop
these elements now. It should preserve strong, weak and zero relevance,
false exclusion, latent equal-law cases and all interval topologies.
Final seeds, replication budgets and stopping rules must follow the
design review. General hidden-state, non-Gaussian, selection and
heterogeneous-transport questions remain unresolved beyond the
restricted claim; public observations alone cannot decide among
observationally equivalent causal worlds
\cite{exec13_temporal_design}. The next chapter adds fitted prediction to the information budget. Its pilot certificates can control specified nuisance errors, but the same questions about weak identification, dependence and useful width still determine whether a larger experiment is justified.
\label{exec13:temporal-design-review-end}

chapters.title: Learning with an explicit error budget before a dependent evaluation

segments.text:
\chapter{Learning with an explicit error budget before a dependent evaluation}
\label{exec13:dependent-pilot}

Consider an encouragement to take a bank offer. The bank observes information
$X$ before the encouragement $Z$, the eventual action $A$, and its subsequent
value $Y$. Flexible prediction is useful because accounts differ in their
pre-existing circumstances. It also creates a second estimation problem:
removing predictable variation imperfectly changes the instrument moment.
When the residual response to the encouragement is small, that change can be
large relative to the information identifying the effect. A narrow interval
computed after fitting a good predictor need not describe the uncertainty in
the bank's causal decision.

This chapter develops a restricted alternative. Learn on an independent pilot,
obtain an explicit bound on each prediction error, and carry that bound into
a joint region for two observable moments. Evaluate those moments on a bounded
sequence with a known dependence range. Project the region into the effect,
retaining disconnected and unbounded answers. The construction is a project
derivation with exact numerical references, rather than an implemented general
learner or a new repeated-sampling qualification~\citep{exec13_dependent_argument}.
Its restrictions are substantial; explaining them is part of deciding whether
the proposed product merits a larger experiment. After the derivation, a design analysis asks whether the bound can support a decision at plausible information levels. The final comparison considers geometric and hierarchical causal models as substantive alternatives: they change the dependence restrictions or intervention target and require their own estimation and uncertainty arguments.

\section{What the repaired predecessor did and did not establish}

The preceding sparse-learning experiment already has a repaired version. Its
first version selected penalties using evaluation outcomes, standardized with
all observations, included covariance products across an omitted calendar gap,
and ignored some scenario dimensions. The repaired version uses training-only
nested selection, training-specific scaling, within-fold Bartlett covariance,
and the actual registered dimension and support. The original results remain
exploratory. They do not establish the performance of that repaired procedure.

For the repaired learner, the high-dimension and larger-support scenarios
covered respectively $499/512$ and $493/512$ requests. Their simultaneous lower
coverage bounds, $0.949140$ and $0.933851$, fell below the frozen $0.95$ threshold.
The nonlinear omitted-nuisance scenario covered $0/512$. The weak-instrument
scenario covered $512/512$, but its median interval width was $3.836470$ in the
synthetic effect units. These were nominal $99\%$ intervals, so comparisons
with the original $95\%$ intervals cannot isolate the effect of repairing the
code. Failure to pass a certification screen is distinct from proof of universal
undercoverage; complete finite availability is also distinct from useful
precision. These results remain the relevant negative baseline.

An independent pilot removes one source of dependence between fitted functions
and evaluation scores. It cannot make a misspecified dictionary correct, turn
a weak instrument into a strong one, or make repeated calendar observations
independent. A successor therefore needs a statement for each of those issues.

\section{The structural target and its observable moment}

The imposed partially linear model is
\begin{equation}
 Y=\theta_0 A+g_0(X)+\epsilon,
 \qquad E[\epsilon\mid X,Z]=0.
 \label{exec13:pilot-pliv}
\end{equation}
The conditional moment excludes a remaining direct effect of the encouragement
and unmeasured causes associated with its residual after conditioning on $X$.
It is a scientific assumption. A prediction fit or source hash cannot verify it.
Here $\theta_0$ is a constant structural coefficient, expressed in outcome
units per unit of action. Interpreting it as an unrestricted heterogeneous
average effect would require a different argument.

Let $m(X)=E[Z\mid X]$, $r(X)=E[A\mid X]$ and
$\ell(X)=E[Y\mid X]$. Define residuals
$v_Z=Z-m(X)$, $v_A=A-r(X)$ and $v_Y=Y-\ell(X)$, and moments
\begin{equation}
 M=E[v_Zv_Y],\qquad Q=E[v_Zv_A].
 \label{exec13:pilot-moments}
\end{equation}
Equation~\eqref{exec13:pilot-pliv} implies $M=\theta_0 Q$. A nonzero $Q$
identifies the scalar coefficient from this relation. If $Q=0$, the relation
can be uninformative even when the observations themselves are measured exactly.

The residualized score
$(Z-m(X))\{Y-\ell(X)-\theta(A-r(X))\}$ is the inherited partially linear IV
score in \citet[Section~4.2, equation~(4.8)]{dml2018}. That source states its
moment, nuisance-product and nonzero-slope conditions. Its independent-sample
theorem does not supply a result for arbitrary serially dependent bank rows.
The following finite construction instead proves its own statement for a
declared observation law.

\section{An observation law that makes separation meaningful}

The pilot contains $m_P$ independent draws from the marginal law of
$W=(X,Z,A,Y)$ and is independent of the entire evaluation sequence. The
evaluation observations $W_1,\ldots,W_n$ are stationary and $d$-dependent:
collections separated by more than $d$ dates generate independent sigma fields.
The integer $d$ is supplied and justified by the design. Uncorrelated residuals
or a small sample autocorrelation are insufficient to establish this property.

Assume known almost-sure ranges $|Z|\le B_Z$, $|A|\le B_A$, and $|Y|\le B_Y$.
Clip predicted conditional means into the respective ranges. Since the true
conditional means lie there, clipping predictions cannot increase their squared
error. Clipping the observed outcome is different: it can change the target
and cannot be introduced silently to make a bound available.

The features $\phi(X)\in\mathbb R^p$ are fixed before the pilot, with
$|\phi_k(X)|\le K$. A feature learned from data needs a separate design sample
and conditional versions of these assumptions. A constant feature can represent
an intercept, but the derivation below penalizes its coefficient too. It does
not silently inherit the previous implementation's unpenalized intercept or
its data-dependent scaling.

These choices exclude the unbounded Gaussian AR experiment in the predecessor.
They can describe a bounded generated benchmark or a justified collection of
finite-dependent observations. They do not describe an arbitrary bank panel.
An extension to geometric mixing requires a proved coupling or concentration
bound, with an explicit additional error allocation. Unknown dependence remains
an information requirement.

\section{The nuisance error enters as two products}

Condition on the independent pilot, so the fitted functions are fixed. Write
$\delta_Z=\widehat m-m$, $\delta_A=\widehat r-r$ and
$\delta_Y=\widehat\ell-\ell$. Expanding the product, then conditioning on $X$,
eliminates the linear error terms because $E[v_j\mid X]=0$. Thus
\begin{align}
 M_{\rm fit}&=E[(Z-\widehat m)(Y-\widehat\ell)\mid\text{pilot}]
             =M+E[\delta_Z\delta_Y\mid\text{pilot}],\\
 Q_{\rm fit}&=E[(Z-\widehat m)(A-\widehat r)\mid\text{pilot}]
             =Q+E[\delta_Z\delta_A\mid\text{pilot}].
 \label{exec13:pilot-bias}
\end{align}
If a simultaneous certificate supplies $\|\delta_j\|_2\le e_j$, Cauchy--Schwarz
gives
\begin{equation}
 |M_{\rm fit}-M|\le e_Ze_Y,\qquad
 |Q_{\rm fit}-Q|\le e_Ze_A.
 \label{exec13:pilot-products}
\end{equation}
Consequently the score bias at a candidate $\theta$ is bounded by
$e_Z(e_Y+|\theta|e_A)$. The encouragement prediction error is essential to
this expression. An outcome--action product alone does not describe the IV
score. Nor does an error norm of exact order $n^{-1/4}$ automatically suffice:
two such errors can leave a root-$n$ scaled remainder of order one.

The bound is exact in its conditional decomposition and conservative in its
norm inequality. It needs neither an estimated effect in the denominator nor
a claim that the remainder is negligible. Those features allow a finite
construction that remains honest when a nuisance certificate is wide.

\section{A sparse learner with a stated population-error certificate}

For each response $T_j\in\{Z,A,Y\}$, suppose its conditional mean has the
representation
\begin{equation}
 f_j(X)=\phi(X)^\top\beta_j+a_j(X),\qquad
 |\operatorname{supp}(\beta_j)|\le s_j,\qquad |a_j(X)|\le A_j.
\end{equation}
Let $\epsilon_j=T_j-f_j(X)$ satisfy
$E[\epsilon_j\mid X]=0$ and $|\epsilon_j|\le E_j$. The approximation bound
$A_j$ is a premise; it is not a training residual. In the exact sparse model
$A_j=0$. Let $\Phi$ be the pilot feature matrix, and fit the exact minimizer
\begin{equation}
 \widehat\beta_j\in\arg\min_b
 \left\{\frac{\|T_j-\Phi b\|_2^2}{2m_P}+\lambda_j\|b\|_1\right\}.
 \label{exec13:pilot-lasso}
\end{equation}

To see where the penalty requirement comes from, each coordinate of
$\phi(X)\epsilon_j$ is centered and bounded in an interval of width $2KE_j$.
Its exponential moment is at most
$\exp\{t^2(2KE_j)^2/8\}$. Independence, the exponential Markov inequality,
optimization in $t$ and a union over $p$ coordinates give, with error at most
$\eta_j$,
\begin{equation}
 \|\Phi^\top\epsilon_j/m_P\|_\infty
 \le KE_j\sqrt{\frac{2\log(2p/\eta_j)}{m_P}}.
\end{equation}
The approximation residual contributes at most $KA_j$. A sufficient penalty is
\begin{equation}
 \lambda_j\ge2K\left\{E_j\sqrt{\frac{2\log(2p/\eta_j)}{m_P}}+A_j\right\}.
 \label{exec13:pilot-penalty}
\end{equation}
A fixed finite family whose every member meets this lower bound shares the
same event. A rate statement also requires that the selected penalty is at most
a fixed multiple of the threshold. An arbitrary validation-selected penalty
does not receive that property merely because its predictive loss is small.

For $h=\widehat\beta_j-\beta_j$ and $S=\operatorname{supp}(\beta_j)$,
optimality in \eqref{exec13:pilot-lasso} and the preceding score event yield
\begin{equation}
 \frac{\|\Phi h\|_2^2}{m_P}+\lambda_j\|h_{S^c}\|_1
 \le3\lambda_j\|h_S\|_1.
 \label{exec13:pilot-basic}
\end{equation}
In particular, $h$ belongs to the cone
$\|h_{S^c}\|_1\le3\|h_S\|_1$. Suppose a certificate establishes
\begin{equation}
 \frac{\|\Phi h\|_2^2}{m_P}\ge\kappa_j^2\|h_S\|_2^2
 \label{exec13:pilot-cone}
\end{equation}
for that cone and every admissible support of size at most $s_j$. Combining
the two inequalities gives
\begin{equation}
 \frac{\|\Phi h\|_2}{\sqrt{m_P}}\le
 \frac{3\sqrt{s_j}\lambda_j}{\kappa_j},\qquad
 \|h\|_1\le\frac{12s_j\lambda_j}{\kappa_j^2}.
\end{equation}
This is an empirical prediction bound. It still needs transfer to the population
in which the evaluation takes place.

Write $\widehat\Sigma=\Phi^\top\Phi/m_P$ and
$\Sigma=E[\phi(X)\phi(X)^\top]$. The same bounded-mean argument, applied to
all $p^2$ feature products, gives with error $\eta_G$
\begin{equation}
 \|\widehat\Sigma-\Sigma\|_{\max}\le
 \tau=K^2\sqrt{\frac{2\log(2p^2/\eta_G)}{m_P}}.
\end{equation}
Since $|h^\top(\Sigma-\widehat\Sigma)h|\le\tau\|h\|_1^2$, a usable
population certificate is
\begin{equation}
 e_j=A_j+
 \sqrt{\frac{9s_j\lambda_j^2}{\kappa_j^2}
       +\frac{144\tau s_j^2\lambda_j^2}{\kappa_j^4}}.
 \label{exec13:pilot-certificate}
\end{equation}
Prediction clipping preserves this bound. The three score events and the Gram
event have total failure probability at most
$\eta_P=\eta_Z+\eta_A+\eta_Y+\eta_G$. They may use the same pilot;
the union bound does not require them to be independent.

Under exact approximation, bounded constants, a positive cone eigenvalue, and
bounded $\tau s_j/\kappa_j^2$, the prediction norm is of order
$\sqrt{s_j\log(p)/m_P}$. The squared error, rather than the norm, has order
$s_j\log(p)/m_P$. For comparable nuisance complexities, negligible root-$n$
bias additionally requires
$\sqrt n\,s\log(p)/m_P\longrightarrow0$. The finite construction below
retains the explicit bias bound even when this asymptotic requirement is not
plausible at the available sample sizes.

\subsection{What must actually be certified}

The cone bound is a substantive requirement. A full Gram condition number is
not a sparse cone certificate when $p$ exceeds the pilot size. A small fixed
dictionary can use a certified minimum eigenvalue. A high-dimensional
construction needs a justified sparse certificate or a generated-design
guarantee. If certification fails, the result must declare the bound unavailable
or use an explicitly wider fallback. The theorem cannot assume that a returned
regression coefficient certifies its own rate.

The minimization also needs a numerical specification. An approximate optimizer
adds a basic-inequality error that must be propagated. A small KKT residual
does not by itself prove equation~\eqref{exec13:pilot-certificate}. The exact
reference uses a 32-row, four-feature orthogonal design, support two and penalty
$0.1$. Soft thresholding gives coefficients $(0.4,0.15,0,0)$; a separate
nonnegative-variable convex optimization agrees. Population squared error is
$0.02$, below the selected bound $0.18$. This checks the algebra and the small
optimization reference; it supplies no certificate for an arbitrary pilot.

\section{Independent calibration as a different information route}

When sparse structure cannot be certified, a frozen clipped learner can be
evaluated on an additional independent calibration sample of $k$ marginal draws.
For response $T_j$, let $L_j$ be average squared predictive loss and let
$v_j^-$ be a justified lower bound on $E[\epsilon_j^2]$. Conditional mean
orthogonality gives
\begin{equation}
 E[(T_j-\widehat f_j(X))^2\mid\text{pilot}]
 =\|\widehat f_j-f_j\|_2^2+E[\epsilon_j^2].
\end{equation}
The observed loss is in $[0,4B_j^2]$. Therefore, with error $\eta_{Cj}$,
\begin{equation}
 \|\widehat f_j-f_j\|_2^2\le
 L_j+4B_j^2\sqrt{\frac{\log(1/\eta_{Cj})}{2k}}-v_j^-.
 \label{exec13:pilot-calibration}
\end{equation}
Use the nonnegative part before taking a square root and cap the norm by the
deterministic $2B_j$ bound. A negative uncapped expression is a diagnostic for
an inconsistent noise bound or a rare confidence event; it is not proof of
perfect learning. Joint error accounting is required if the analyst plans to
select the tighter of multiple certificates after observing them.

The safe choice $v_j^-=0$ needs no noise decomposition. It can leave an
irreducible-noise floor that prevents the certificate from shrinking. Better
noise information can come from a known generated mechanism, independently
justified repeated measurements, or an additional model with its own audit.
This route exchanges structural learning assumptions for calibration data and
noise information. Its full cost includes both samples.

\section{A finite region under a known dependence range}

Set $q=d+1\le n$ and split the evaluation dates by residue modulo $q$. Within
each class the observations are independent, conditional on the independent
pilot. Different classes can remain dependent. The fitted products
$U_{Mt}=(Z_t-\widehat m(X_t))(Y_t-\widehat\ell(X_t))$ and
$U_{Qt}=(Z_t-\widehat m(X_t))(A_t-\widehat r(X_t))$ lie in intervals of
widths $8B_ZB_Y$ and $8B_ZB_A$ respectively.

Let $n_{\min}=\lfloor n/q\rfloor$. A two-sided bounded-mean inequality for
each of the $2q$ class/coordinate combinations and a union bound give
\begin{equation}
 t_j=8B_ZB_j
 \sqrt{\frac{\log(4q/\alpha_E)}{2n_{\min}}},
 \qquad j\in\{Y,A\}.
 \label{exec13:pilot-temporal-band}
\end{equation}
With probability at least $1-\alpha_E$, both overall sample means deviate from
their fitted population moments by at most their respective $t_j$. To verify
the final step, the overall mean is a weighted average of the class means;
bounding every class bounds that weighted average even when class sizes differ.
Neither independence between classes nor independence between numerator and
denominator is assumed.

Let $\widehat M=n^{-1}\sum_tU_{Mt}$ and
$\widehat Q=n^{-1}\sum_tU_{Qt}$. With
$w_M=t_Y+e_Ze_Y$ and $w_Q=t_A+e_Ze_A$, form
\begin{equation}
 C=[\widehat M-w_M,\widehat M+w_M]
   \mathbin\times[\widehat Q-w_Q,\widehat Q+w_Q].
 \label{exec13:pilot-rectangle}
\end{equation}
For the sparse route, $C$ covers $(M,Q)$ with probability at least
$1-\eta_P-\alpha_E$, provided the supplied certificates and model premises
hold. The calibration route replaces $\eta_P$ by the sum of its calibration
errors. The coverage statement concerns the joint rectangle, so later projection
needs no further multiplicity adjustment.

If the nuisance certificate is missing, $e_j=2B_j$ is an unconditional bound
for clipped predictions and bounded conditional means, but it may make $C$
useless. Alternatively the product can withhold a qualified set and report
which information is missing. It must not treat an empirical fit score as the
missing certificate. Likewise, the assertion $W_t=W_1$ for every date describes
a bounded process with arbitrarily many rows but constant mean variance.
Row count alone gives no universal $n^{-1/2}$ precision improvement.

\paragraph{Availability and selection.}
If a pilot fails its cone or numerical certificate, returning the whole line
preserves the all-request coverage statement. Withholding the result instead
is an availability failure and must stay in the denominator. The argument
bounds false exclusions across all requests; it does not establish the same
conditional coverage among only those requests whose certificates pass, or a
minimum fraction of informative results.

\section{Weak-instrument sets and a decision threshold}

Define
\begin{equation}
 S(C)=\{\theta:\exists(M,Q)\in C\text{ with }M=\theta Q\}.
 \label{exec13:pilot-projection}
\end{equation}
On the event that the true moments lie in $C$, their structural relation puts
$\theta_0$ in $S(C)$. This proves coverage without dividing by $\widehat Q$
or treating an estimated denominator as known. It is a set based on this
moment relation and the imposed model; it is not claimed sharp for the entire
observed distribution.

For a proposed value $\theta$, multiply the denominator interval by $\theta$
and test its intersection with the numerator interval, reversing endpoints when
$\theta<0$. This gives a direct feasibility reference independent of a ratio
interval implementation. Exact rational arithmetic checked 18,685 membership
comparisons across 225 rectangles, including boundary points. Examples are
\begin{align*}
 [1,2]\mathbin\times[-1/2,1/2]&\quad\longmapsto\quad
 (-\infty,-2]\cup[2,\infty),\\
 [-1,1]\mathbin\times[-1/2,1/2]&\quad\longmapsto\quad\mathbb R,\\
 [1,2]\mathbin\times\{0\}&\quad\longmapsto\quad\varnothing,\\
 \{1\}\mathbin\times\{2\}&\quad\longmapsto\quad\{1/2\}.
\end{align*}
An empty set can reject the imposed moment relation or reflect a confidence
failure. It does not mean a zero effect. An unbounded set can correctly express
inadequate information and still fail to support a banking action.

For a positive denominator interval and nonnegative numerator interval, the
projection is
\begin{equation}
 \left[\frac{\widehat M-w_M}{\widehat Q+w_Q},
       \frac{\widehat M+w_M}{\widehat Q-w_Q}\right],
 \qquad \widehat Q>w_Q,
\end{equation}
with width
\begin{equation}
 \frac{2(\widehat Qw_M+\widehat Mw_Q)}{\widehat Q^2-w_Q^2}.
 \label{exec13:pilot-width}
\end{equation}
Width diverges as the lower denominator approaches zero. The illustrative
rectangle $[0.91,1.01]\times[0.78,0.82]$ gives
$[91/82,101/78]\simeq[1.109756,1.294872]$. Its radii are hypothetical
inputs, not fitted pilot evidence. A sign-normalized action cost of $1.15$
falls inside this interval, leaving the action unresolved. More independent
training can shrink the nuisance products; more effective evaluation data can
shrink the temporal bands. Neither repairs a zero instrument or establishes
the validity of an exclusion assumption.

\section{An exact explanation for the nonlinear failure}

The repaired predecessor adds $h(X)=0.6(X_1^2-1)$ to the encouragement and
outcome equations. For a standard Gaussian coordinate, $E[h]=0$ and
$E[h^2]=0.72$; the term is orthogonal to the linear Gaussian features.
Even with unlimited pilot data, a linear dictionary therefore leaves $h$
in the encouragement residual and leaves $\theta_0kh+h$ in the outcome
residual, where $k$ is the encouragement coefficient in the action equation.
With unit encouragement-innovation variance, the residualized numerator and
denominator obey
\begin{equation}
 M_{\rm linear}=\theta_0 k(1+0.72)+0.72,\qquad
 Q_{\rm linear}=k(1+0.72).
\end{equation}
For $k=0.8$, the ratio converges to
\begin{equation}
 \theta_0+\frac{0.72}{0.8(1+0.72)}
 =\theta_0+\frac{45}{86}
 \simeq\theta_0+0.523255814.
\end{equation}
This is a population approximation-error explanation, not an exact prediction
of the saved finite-sample lasso bias. It explains why more observations alone
need not cure the failure. Prespecifying the quadratic feature removes this
particular population omission, but finite estimation and dependence still
need their own analysis. Under this Gaussian example the omitted feature is
unbounded, so the earlier bounded approximation theorem does not apply unchanged.

\section{The proposed next experiment and its limits}

A useful bounded prototype would compare a small fixed dictionary, the
certified sparse pilot, and the independent calibration route on the same
declared target. Its full resource record must include feature preparation,
training, tuning, certificate construction, calibration, dependent evaluation,
set projection and retained refusals. A faster optimizer is of little value if
the required pilot or confidence width makes the decision uneconomical.

Before final draws, choose a bounded mechanism with an explicit dependence
range and a separate pilot, freeze the dictionary and approximation bounds,
review the cone and numerical certificates, and profile complete costs. Then
freeze sample sizes, error allocations, adverse cases, alternatives, fresh
draws, stopping rule and useful-width criterion. The old failed outcomes cannot
become the new evaluation data. No final successor study is registered by the
argument in this chapter.

The route is now explicit for this restricted family. General unbounded
dependent learning, unknown approximation error, unverified instruments,
arbitrary learners and useful weak-IV precision remain open. Where the
certificate is too costly or too wide, narrowing the question or changing the
information design is a substantive product recommendation.
\label{exec13:dependent-pilot-end}

\section{Whether the pilot argument warrants a larger experiment}
\label{exec13:dependent-design-review}

A valid conservative construction can be a poor next investment if it
cannot deliver a useful answer at the intended information level. The
independent-pilot argument therefore needs a precision review before a
large simulation campaign. The review preserves the earlier Gaussian
panel failures and evaluates the narrower bounded model on its own
terms. It does not transform known finite dependence into a guarantee
for unbounded Gaussian AR observations~\citep{exec13_ivrd_dependent}.

Use the authored sign-law example with independent fair signs
$X,V,H,E$,
\[
 Z=.3X+V,\qquad A=.8Z+.2X+H,\qquad Y=1.2A+.4X+E.
\]
It has $B_Z=13/10$, $B_A=56/25$, $B_Y=511/125$, $Q=4/5$ and
$M=24/25$. Grant an oracle its exact nuisance means, so the bias
radii are zero, and hold the empirical moments at their population
centers. With evaluation error allocation $.03$, the displayed
bounded-mean construction at $n=640$ contains zero in both moment
coordinates for each planning dependence range $d=0,4,19$.
The projected effect set is the whole line. These are deterministic
planning calculations at a fixed center, not prospective probabilities
or fitted-study outcomes.

For independent evaluation the same centered rectangle first has
a positive denominator lower endpoint at 2,075 rows. A more demanding
decision example stipulates an action threshold of 1.15, only .05
below the true coefficient. A sufficient centered condition for
the whole effect set to exceed that threshold is
\[
 8B_Z(B_Y+1.15B_A)
 \sqrt{\frac{\log(4(d+1)/.03)}{2\lfloor n/(d+1)\rfloor}}
 <M-1.15Q=.04.
\]
For $d=0$, the first integer sample size satisfying this displayed
bound is 7,344,273. This is not a proposed bank sample size. It
shows how the global range bound can obscure a small decision
margin even before fitting error is introduced. A sharper justified
variance-sensitive construction deserves development before a large
final campaign~\citep{exec13_ivrd_dependent}.

The alternative loss calibration can be conservative for another
reason. Even with exact conditional means and infinitely many
calibration observations, a zero lower bound on irreducible noise
leaves squared-loss limits $1$, $41/25$ and $2101/625$ in this law.
The resulting denominator bias radius is $\sqrt{41/25}>.8$ and
the numerator radius also exceeds $.96$. The centered rectangle
therefore remains uninformative as evaluation noise disappears.
These are certificate floors, not actual oracle fitting errors.
Known residual noise in a generated design can supply the missing
subtraction; estimated bank training loss cannot certify it by itself.

Qualification-screen power is separate from these precision calculations.
For the preserved 512 requests and sixteen-comparison family, at
least 500 successes are needed for a one-sided exact lower coverage
bound of .95. Exact binomial calculations give per-cell pass
probabilities about $.001849$, $.234929$, $.770054$ and $.997670$
when actual coverage is $.95$, $.97$, $.98$ and $.99$ respectively.
Thus a coverage guarantee of at least .95 alone does not promise
a high probability of passing the screen. The .99 finite-availability
rule is a raw fraction, so 507/512 suffices; a lower confidence
bound of .99 would be a different rule. The old high-dimension,
larger-support and nonlinear failures retain their original status
\citep{exec13_ivrd_dependent}.

The justified next work is a separately labeled bounded prototype:
fix a finite-dependent generator and independent pilot/calibration
law; implement and certify the actual learner; carry approximation,
numerical and selection errors into the bound; derive a sharper
evaluation region; and compare complete workflows at matched
information and resource levels. Strong, weak and zero relevance,
missing certificates, nonlinear omission and falsely declared
dependence all belong in the design. Only after development profiling
should fresh draws, replication budget, stopping rule, useful-width
scenario and certification-screen power be frozen. Unknown
dependence, arbitrary learners and causal instrument truth still
require new arguments or additional information. They do not
prevent the bounded proposal work, and no final qualification
study is approved by this feasibility calculation.
\label{exec13:dependent-design-review-end}

\section{Structured causal models: restrictions, computation and the target}
\label{exec23:structured-scope}

A universal bank observes accounts within branches, repeated decisions within
customers and exposures connected through markets or payment networks. The
observations are neither an arbitrary collection of independent rows nor
automatically interchangeable. Two recent primary contributions clarify
different parts of this problem. Geometric causal models use specified
symmetries to organize dependence and identification. A hierarchical causal
pipeline translates distributional interventions into symbolic expressions
and fitted numerical factors. Both provide useful ingredients for a proposed
product, but neither permits an agent to infer valid causal meaning merely
from a table schema or a successful program execution.
\citep{exec23_geometric_models,exec23_hierarchical_pipeline}

\subsection{A symmetry is a scientific restriction}
\label{exec23:structured-symmetry}

In Weinstein and Blei's geometric causal model, an endogenous variable
$x^v$ is a structured collection $(x^v_\omega)_{\omega\in\Omega}$,
where $\Omega$ indexes locations, times, nodes or other positions. A
group $G$ acts on these collections. A causal mechanism $f^v$ is equivariant
when applying a transformation before evaluating the mechanism is equivalent
to transforming its output:
\begin{equation}
 f^v(\phi(x^{\mathrm{pa}(v)}),\phi(\epsilon^v))
 =\phi\!\left(f^v(x^{\mathrm{pa}(v)},\epsilon^v)\right),
 \qquad \phi\in G.
 \label{exec23:structured-equivariance}
\end{equation}
Here $\mathrm{pa}(v)$ denotes the parents of variable $v$ in a specified
directed acyclic graph and $\epsilon^v$ is exogenous noise. The model uses
equivariant mechanisms to create dependence among endogenous positions from
the stipulated noise structure. A hard intervention replaces the selected
mechanism with a supplied value. Permutation, spatial-shift and array
symmetries express different models; they are not different software
optimizations of one unrestricted model.
\citep{exec23_geometric_models}

For a banking application, translation of a branch-level model across
locations would assert that the relevant mechanism survives that
transformation after the declared context is represented. A policy change,
regulatory boundary or market break may make that assertion implausible.
The proposal should therefore ask which transformations preserve the
decision mechanism, what variables encode exceptions, and what evidence
could falsify the proposed symmetry. These are proposed elicitation questions.
The paper assumes the causal graph and symmetry group are known and leaves
their discovery to future work. An LLM may help formulate candidate
restrictions and collect supporting documents; this paper supplies no
experiment establishing that an LLM can validate them.
\citep{exec23_geometric_models}

\subsection{Identification and consistency retain their assumptions}
\label{exec23:structured-identification}

The paper separates learning an observational law from one structured
realization, identifying an intervention from that law, and estimating it
from finitely observed coordinates. Its mixing-action condition requires
countably infinite index and transformation sets, with transformations that
eventually move any finite set away from itself. Under the stated model,
ergodicity then makes learning from an expanding observation domain possible.
The do-calculus soundness argument uses the graph's Markov decomposition.
For groups consisting of index transformations, the completeness argument
embeds conventional unrestricted causal models into the geometric class.
Stronger symmetries can add restrictions: the orthogonal-group instrumental
variable example invokes linear-Gaussian structure, a nonconstant relevant
instrument and finite interference. These conclusions have different
premises and should not be compressed into a claim that symmetry identifies
any latent graph.
\citep{exec23_geometric_models}

The finite-data consistency result is likewise conditional. It assumes
finite interference, local information under the transformations, an
amenable group with a tempered F{\o}lner sequence, finite state spaces and
positivity of the required finite observational configurations. Informally,
averages over the permitted transformations estimate finite marginal laws;
the identified intervention functional is then evaluated on those estimates.
The proof uses a finite set of coordinates relevant to the queried outcome
and a continuous-mapping step. The statement is a consistency route under
these conditions. It does not deliver a finite-bank error bound or a
generally valid confidence interval for arbitrary persistent maps, shared
calendar shocks and learned representations. Rate and central-limit
conditions must be established for the actual proposed estimator.
\citep{exec23_geometric_models}

Two apparent slips in the selected paper's extracted proof text also deserve
a bounded response. The example following its amenability assumption prints
an eventually empty intersection for a finite permutation subgroup translated
by one of its own elements. Algebra instead gives $\phi G_n=G_n$, so
$|\phi G_n\cap G_n|=|G_n|$ and the required ratio is one. Enumerating
the six permutations of three objects reproduces that identity. Separately,
the instrumental-variable proof concludes that a covariance denominator is
positive from relevance and nonzero instrument variance. Relevance warrants
nonzero, not positive, covariance. With first-stage coefficient $-2$,
instrument variance $4$ and outcome coefficient $3$, the covariance ratio
is $(-24)/(-8)=3$. Both layout and raw text extraction preserve the printed
passages. These local corrections preserve the intended algebraic routes;
they do not independently refute or fully verify the theorems. Exact
typeset-symbol inspection and the cited proof dependencies remain separate
review obligations.
\citep{exec23_geometric_models,exec23_structured_reference}

The practical evidence has its own limits. The array example explicitly
reports poor absolute uncertainty calibration despite improvement relative
to its comparators, with a mean-field approximation suggested as a cause.
In the genomic semisynthetic table, adding reverse-complement equivariance
changes the R-learner MSE from 1.637 to 2.509 in scenario A, whereas in
scenario B an outcome-model variant has MSE 0.084 compared with 0.104 for
the R-learner without that symmetry. These are author-reported experiments,
with arithmetic differences 0.872 and $-0.020$ respectively. They support
the paper's qualified discussion of interactions among model restrictions,
misspecification and estimation strategy, not a universal ranking or a bank
calibration result.
\citep{exec23_geometric_models,exec23_structured_reference}

\subsection{Hierarchical interventions need an explicit weighting target}
\label{exec23:structured-target}

Aiad and coauthors develop a complementary pipeline for hierarchical
structural causal models. Its unit-level variables represent distributions
or conditional mechanisms of subunits. For example, $Q_i^a$ describes
the treatment distribution within unit $i$. The queried contrast can be
written as a difference between expected outcomes under two interventions
on that distribution, $\mathrm{do}(Q^a=q_1)$ and
$\mathrm{do}(Q^a=q_0)$. The pipeline collapses the hierarchical graph,
augments it where required and marginalizes variables before sending the
transformed graph to pyAgrum for symbolic identification. The identification
engine does not itself inspect the raw nested table.
\citep{exec23_hierarchical_pipeline}

Even a perfectly implemented hierarchy leaves a banking target choice. Let
$n_i$ be the number of customers in branch $i$, let $\tau_i$ be a
stipulated incremental gain per customer under a specified branch policy,
and let $c$ be a uniform per-customer cost. Equal weighting of branch
effects and weighting customers equally give
\begin{equation}
 V_{\mathrm{branch}}=\frac1K\sum_{i=1}^K\tau_i-c,\qquad
 V_{\mathrm{customer}}=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^K n_i\tau_i}{\sum_{i=1}^K n_i}-c.
 \label{exec23:structured-weights}
\end{equation}
For two branches with $n_1=10$, $n_2=90$, effects USD 20 and USD $-4$,
and cost USD 2, the first target is USD 6 and the second is USD $-3.60$.
The branch-weighted quantity is an equally weighted mean of branch-specific
per-customer values; it is not total portfolio profit. Neither target is
wrong merely because the other differs. A product error occurs when one is
reported under the other's name. This is an exact authored example with
stipulated effects, not an empirical result of the hierarchical package.
\citep{exec23_structured_reference}

For an agent translating a business question, the first obligations are thus
to identify the intervention level, whether it changes a distribution or
individual treatment, the units whose outcomes are averaged, and the
sampling/weighting law. A polished diagram or a cluster-robust regression
does not answer those questions by itself. The hierarchical framework is
a candidate representation once these choices are justified; its paper
does not establish an automated business-to-model solution.

\subsection{An auditable expression tree must preserve the evaluated functional}
\label{exec23:structured-ast}

The hierarchical pipeline's abstract syntax tree records products,
marginalizations and fitted density keys. This can expose which conditional
models are required and which computations can be evaluated separately.
That is useful for a library/CLI/MCP interface: the declared estimand,
identified symbolic expression, selected numerical factors and resulting
value can remain separately inspectable. The paper reports parametric,
mixture, categorical and nonparametric fitting options and parallel
evaluation. Those descriptions are primary paper claims. The linked
repository, dependency versions, factor fallbacks and implementation have
not been newly inspected or executed in this review.
\citep{exec23_hierarchical_pipeline}

Crucially, the paper explicitly acknowledges that normalizing unstable
multiplicative factors changes the numerical functional. A constant
representation change that cancels exactly is different from a
nonconstant alteration of relative weights. To see the latter in a
transparent construction, take weights $p=(1/4,3/4)$ and effects
$\tau=(20,-4)$. Their weighted contrast is USD 2. Multiplying the two
weights by $(2,1)$ and renormalizing gives $(2/5,3/5)$, with contrast
USD $28/5=5.60$. The nominal dependency graph did not change, but the
functional did. This constructed modification is not a reconstruction of
the paper's normalization code. It shows why the exact transformation must
be declared and either proved invariant or reported as a different
functional with its own uncertainty argument.
\citep{exec23_hierarchical_pipeline,exec23_structured_reference}

The STAR application makes the distinction concrete without providing a
matched normalization experiment. Its reported mathematics row has
$2402.75-2365.95=36.80$ points. The normalized reading diagnostic has
$1788.10-1766.47=21.63$ points. These rows concern different outcomes;
their difference cannot isolate the effect of factor normalization. The
selected ExactBIC graph is described as plausible, with a substantive
orientation and added latent class context, rather than uniquely recovered.
The paper also distinguishes student-level OLS, an IV class-size coefficient
and the distributional class intervention. A larger number across these
targets is not, by itself, evidence of a more accurate causal method.
\citep{exec23_hierarchical_pipeline,exec23_structured_reference}

The stated analysis uses 322 classes with ten sampled students per class,
and identifies multi-parent factor estimation as a bottleneck. Its
conclusion leaves deeper hierarchies, uncertainty for stabilized
functionals and analysis across plausible graphs open. The reported
3.11-second sequential and 1.9-second four-process evaluations imply a
ratio of about 1.64, but this is a check of the paper's arithmetic, not a
local timing result or a bank service-level claim. These limits should
remain part of the proposed product comparison.
\citep{exec23_hierarchical_pipeline,exec23_structured_reference}

\subsection{A scoped route for the proposal}
\label{exec23:structured-route}

The two contributions suggest an orderly prototype route. First specify
the banking unit, target, information clock and intervention law. Then
justify a particular dependence restriction or hierarchical representation,
retain the assumed graph or plausible graph family, and derive the
identified functional. Preserve every numerical factor and any alteration
introduced for stability. Compare exact finite references before using
public or synthetic data to study finite behavior, uncertainty and cost.
An LLM can propose candidates, explain assumptions and help inspect traces,
but each such role needs its own evaluation and refusal rules.

For software reuse, a typed interface to a symbolic expression and its
numerical factors is worth investigating before porting an entire
implementation. That investigation must inspect the actual code, licenses,
dependencies and supported regimes. For research, the geometric restrictions
provide possible scoped assumptions; they do not replace the unresolved
joint-law and calibration arguments in the broader banking program.
Accordingly these papers strengthen the set of explicit alternatives
while leaving general discovery, arbitrary dependence and automatically
valid stabilized uncertainty as open obligations. Together these comparisons locate the next investment: a better certificate, a justified structural restriction, or genuinely new information. The economic chapters now ask whether such a change can improve a banking decision enough to cover acquisition, computation and review, including the cost of an unresolved answer.

chapters.title: Banking decisions, review effort and the value of assistance

segments.text:
\chapter{Banking decisions, review effort and the value of assistance}
\label{la:economics}

The preceding studies identify what information and computation can establish. This chapter asks what those capabilities are worth under an explicit decision rule. It develops information value, complete workflow cost and evaluation design before examining selective automation, retry mechanisms, ambiguity, staged investment and transport to a bank's requested cases. The numerical accounts are stipulated examples that expose the measurements needed for an actual investment decision.

\section{Value belongs to a decision and an information set}

The value of an agent is the change it makes to a feasible decision after
including its information, review and operating costs. Producing a longer
report, drawing more edges or executing a notebook faster can help that
decision, but none is the economic target itself. The banking application must
specify the action, baseline workflow, affected population, financial horizon
and loss before comparing systems.

Let $a$ range over feasible actions and let $V(a,\theta)$ be their monetary
value under a causal state $\theta$. An information set $\mathcal I$ might
contain observed data, authenticated design records and unresolved alternatives.
If a justified probability law for $\theta$ is available, an expected-value
decision solves
\[
 a^*(\mathcal I)\in\arg\max_a
       \mathbb E\{V(a,\theta)\mid\mathcal I\}.
\]
This expression is a decision rule conditional on a probability model. A
language model's self-reported certainty, the frequency of repeated answers,
or a fraction of retrieved documents is not automatically that probability.
The distinction matters most when a small change in the assumed probability
changes a lending, servicing or funding action.

If the evidence instead supports a set $\Theta(\mathcal I)$ without probabilities,
the bank needs an explicit ambiguity policy. For example, a robust rule can
maximize $\inf_{\theta\in\Theta(\mathcal I)}V(a,\theta)$. Expected value and this
robust criterion answer different decision questions. The software must
preserve the information needed for either and require the policy to be named.
It must not manufacture a distribution by assigning equal weight to whichever
graphs an algorithm happened to enumerate.

\section{An exact example of useful and costly information}

Consider a stipulated one-customer intervention whose incremental gross return
is either CNY~0 or CNY~400, with intervention cost CNY~300. Suppose the two
states have equal prior probability. These are project assumptions for an
arithmetic example, not bank estimates, elicited probabilities or measured
model performance. Acting has expected net return $200-300=-100$, so the
unassisted expected-value decision is to do nothing, with value zero.

Perfect information would permit action only in the CNY~400 state. Its expected
gross value relative to doing nothing is therefore
\[
 \tfrac12\max(0,0-300)+\tfrac12\max(0,400-300)=50.
\]
For this action set and loss, no information service can justify an expected
payment above CNY~50 per decision solely through improved action selection.
The bound would change if the service had other validated benefits or changed
the feasible actions; neither is assumed here.

Now stipulate a binary signal that reports ``positive'' with probability $0.9$
in the high-return state and $0.1$ in the low-return state. Each signal outcome
has marginal probability $0.5$. Bayes' rule gives posterior high-state
probabilities $0.9$ after a positive signal and $0.1$ after a negative signal.
The conditional net returns from acting are respectively
\[
 0.9(400)-300=60,\qquad 0.1(400)-300=-260.
\]
The optimal rule acts only after a positive signal. Its gross expected value
is $0.5(60)=30$. An independent calculation keeps the loss from false positives
visible:
\[
 \underbrace{0.5(0.9)(100)}_{\text{true-positive gain}}
 -\underbrace{0.5(0.1)(300)}_{\text{false-positive loss}}=30.
\]
The information value is below the perfect-information bound, as it should be.

Suppose obtaining and checking the signal costs CNY~2 in computation and CNY~8
in review for every request, including negative ones. The incremental net value
is then CNY~20. Under the additional simplifying assumptions of identical
expected value, linear costs and no discounting, a CNY~50,000 fixed development
cost breaks even at $50{,}000/20=2{,}500$ decisions. These figures are reproduced
with exact rational arithmetic. They are a transparent planning construction,
not a price quotation or an ROI estimate for the implemented prototype.

The threshold for acting is a high-state probability above $300/400=0.75$.
An assistant that says ``90\% confident'' can cross that threshold without
having a calibrated probability. Review must establish the meaning and
reliability of the signal. A syntactically valid report, a correct posterior
formula and an accurate multiplication cannot compensate for an invented
likelihood.

\section{Refusal can preserve value, but it also consumes resources}

If all that is defensible is the set $\Theta=\{0,400\}$, robust net value from
acting is $-300$, while doing nothing guarantees zero incremental value.
The robust rule therefore declines the intervention. This conclusion differs
from a claim that the true effect is zero. It expresses how the bank chooses
under unresolved uncertainty and the stated loss.

A service that exposes the ambiguity can be valuable if the incumbent workflow
would act on a falsely precise estimate. The evaluation must include that
incumbent behavior explicitly. Against an already cautious baseline, the same
refusal may add little decision value while still costing analyst time. A
refusal is neither automatically a failure nor automatically a benefit.

The inspected observational workflow illustrates this problem through critic
declines under poor overlap~\citep{v12_la_2607_22443}. The denominator must include
the declined requests, their review cost and what happened next. Did a reviewer
obtain a better design, narrow the population with explicit authorization,
commission an experiment, or simply lose time? Each path has a different
economic implication. Changing to a selected population must also change the
target rather than make the original request appear successful.

\section{Four banking journeys require different evidence}

For a funding decision, assistance can assemble the rate action, balance units,
margin horizon and policy constraints. It can also flag a mismatch between
calendar covariance and an assumed independent sampling unit. Value arises
only if these corrections improve a decision or avert an error relative to the
baseline. A conservative interval wider than the bank's action threshold may
be scientifically defensible and economically inconclusive.

For sequential servicing, the central object is a policy adapted to information
available at each decision. The total bill includes state measurement,
assignment logging, intervention delivery and customer outcomes, as well as
model calls. An agent can help describe a dynamic regime, but a static ATE
translator cannot evaluate it by substituting a single treatment indicator.
The economic study must compare genuinely feasible policies under common
information and count unsuccessful or unavailable evaluations.

For discovery followed by intervention, a visually simpler graph can conceal
alternative effects. The useful information is whether additional evidence
changes the set of financially acceptable actions. More accurate recovery of
irrelevant edges may have little value for the selected decision. Conversely,
one mistaken orientation near the treatment or outcome can reverse a policy
recommendation. Graph accuracy and decision loss should both be reported, with
neither used as a proxy for the other.

For trustworthy observations, a language system can reconcile field names and
suggest ownership or inclusion questions. The bank must still establish actual
